glossary.definition: A family of theories distinguishing autonomous (Type 1) processing from processing that requires working memory and supports hypothetical thinking (Type 2). Whether there are two distinct types is debated.

Holding a representation of a possibility separate from what you currently believe so that you can reason about it hypothetically; a defining function of Type 2 processing in Evans and Stanovich’s account.
A setting in which observable cues are reliably related to outcomes, so that the regularities can in principle be learned.
Fast, recognition-based judgment that is accurate because it was learned in a high-validity environment with ample practice and timely, clear feedback.
Monitoring and regulating your own thinking: knowing where a judgment came from, how reliable it is likely to be, and when to slow down or seek a check.
A mental shortcut or strategy that ignores part of the available information; efficient and often adequate, but predictably wrong in some environments.
The tendency of numerical estimates to stay close to an initial value, even an arbitrary one, because adjustment from it is insufficient.
How common an outcome or category is in the relevant population before considering the specifics of a case; the starting point for any probability judgment.
Presenting probabilistic information as counts of cases from one reference population (for example, 9 of 98 positives), which makes Bayesian reasoning far easier.
Seeking or interpreting evidence in ways that are partial to existing beliefs, expectations or hypotheses.
Reasoning steered by a directional goal toward a preferred conclusion, constrained by the need to construct a seemingly reasonable justification.
The degree to which a decision strategy is adapted to the structure of the environment in which it is used.
Excessive certainty in the accuracy of one’s beliefs, visible as ranges and forecasts that are too narrow; the most persistent form of overconfidence.
The match between stated confidence and actual frequency: a calibrated forecaster’s 70% predictions come true about 70% of the time.
The mean squared difference between stated probabilities and outcomes (1 or 0); a proper scoring rule in which lower is better and 0.25 is what constant 50% forecasts earn.
Forecasting by first asking how often outcomes of this kind occur in a reference class of similar cases, before adjusting for the specifics of the case.
Unwanted variability in judgments that should be identical; divided into level, pattern and occasion noise.
A study in which several judges evaluate the same cases independently, so that the variability of their judgments can be measured.
Procedures that reduce judgment error without knowing its direction: independent judgments, structured assessments, sequenced information, relative scales, the outside view and aggregation.
Recognizing the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge and that one might be wrong; shown in proportional updating.

exercise.title: Judgment Lab

intro.text: The Judgment Lab measures something most assessments ignore: not only whether you are right, but whether your confidence matches your accuracy. You will answer two kinds of items drawn from science, medicine, law, business, history and sport. For each true-or-false statement, choose an answer and state how confident you are, from 50% (a pure guess) to 100% (certain). For each numeric question, give a range you are 90% sure contains the true value.

Do not look anything up, and do not try to “win” by always saying 50% or by giving enormous ranges: the point is to see your honest pattern. Work at a steady pace, about thirty seconds per item. When you finish, the lab shows your proportion correct, your Brier score, a calibration table comparing stated confidence with actual hit rates, and how many of your 90% ranges contained the truth.

items: Use the whole confidence scale. 100% means you would bet heavily at any odds.
Make the 90% ranges genuinely 90%: you should expect to miss about one in ten.
Before you see results, write down how many of your ranges you expect to contain the truth.

binary.statement: The Wright brothers made their first powered, controlled airplane flights in 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

key.explanation: True. Orville and Wilbur Wright flew at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, on 17 December 1903.

binary.statement: Penicillin was discovered by Louis Pasteur.

key.explanation: False. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. Pasteur, a nineteenth-century chemist and microbiologist, is known for germ theory, pasteurization and vaccines.

binary.statement: The U.S. Supreme Court decided Marbury v. Madison, the case associated with establishing judicial review, in 1803.

key.explanation: True. Marbury v. Madison was decided in 1803; Chief Justice John Marshall’s opinion is the classic statement of judicial review.

binary.statement: Brown v. Board of Education, the U.S. Supreme Court decision holding state-mandated school segregation unconstitutional, was decided in 1964.

key.explanation: False. Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954. The Civil Rights Act was passed in 1964, which is a common source of confusion.

binary.statement: Light from the Sun takes roughly eight minutes to reach Earth.

key.explanation: True. At the average Earth–Sun distance (about 150 million km), light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

binary.statement: An adult human has more bones than a newborn baby.

key.explanation: False. A newborn has roughly 270–300 bones or bony elements, many of which fuse during growth; a typical adult skeleton has 206.

binary.statement: The first modern Olympic Games, in 1896, were held in Paris.

key.explanation: False. The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896. Paris hosted the second, in 1900.

binary.statement: The Panama Canal opened before the Suez Canal.

key.explanation: False. The Suez Canal opened in 1869; the Panama Canal opened in 1914.

binary.statement: The Sarbanes–Oxley Act, which tightened U.S. corporate financial reporting and audit rules after the Enron and WorldCom scandals, was enacted in 2002.

key.explanation: True. The Sarbanes–Oxley Act was signed into law in July 2002.

binary.statement: Antibiotics are effective treatment for viral infections such as the common cold.

key.explanation: False. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses; they do not treat the common cold, and unnecessary use contributes to antibiotic resistance.

binary.statement: The International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006.

key.explanation: True. The IAU adopted its definition of a planet in August 2006, placing Pluto in the new category of dwarf planet.

binary.statement: James Watson and Francis Crick published their double-helix model of DNA in 1953.

key.explanation: True. Their paper appeared in Nature in April 1953, drawing on X-ray diffraction work including Rosalind Franklin’s.

binary.statement: The largest one-day percentage fall in the history of the Dow Jones Industrial Average occurred on “Black Monday” in October 1987.

key.explanation: True. On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell about 22.6%, still its largest one-day percentage decline.

binary.statement: Sound travels through air at sea level faster than 1,000 meters per second.

key.explanation: False. The speed of sound in dry air at about 20 °C is roughly 343 meters per second.

binary.statement: The first FIFA World Cup was held in 1930 in Uruguay, which won the tournament.

key.explanation: True. Uruguay hosted and won the first World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina in the final.

binary.statement: Thomas Bayes’s essay containing the result now called Bayes’ theorem was published after his death.

key.explanation: True. Bayes died in 1761; Richard Price arranged publication of the essay in 1763.

intervals.question: In what year did Charles Darwin publish On the Origin of Species?

key.explanation: Darwin’s book was published in November 1859.

intervals.question: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?

key.explanation: The border crossings opened on 9 November 1989.

intervals.question: What is the height of Mount Everest, in meters?

key.explanation: A joint China–Nepal survey announced in 2020 gave 8,848.86 m; the long-standing earlier figure was 8,848 m. Either value lies inside a well-calibrated range.

intervals.question: In what year was the first human-to-human heart transplant performed?

key.explanation: Christiaan Barnard performed it in Cape Town, South Africa, in December 1967.

intervals.question: In what year did the U.S. Supreme Court decide Miranda v. Arizona, the source of the “Miranda warnings”?

key.explanation: Miranda v. Arizona was decided in 1966.

intervals.question: How many member states does the United Nations have?

key.explanation: There are 193 member states; South Sudan, admitted in 2011, was the most recent.

intervals.question: In what year did Roger Bannister become the first person recorded running a mile in under four minutes?

key.explanation: Bannister ran 3:59.4 at Oxford on 6 May 1954.

intervals.question: In what year was Alexander Graham Bell granted his U.S. patent for the telephone?

key.explanation: Bell’s telephone patent was granted in March 1876.

intervals.question: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, in kilometers per second?

key.explanation: The speed of light is defined as exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, about 299,792 km/s.

intervals.question: How many bones are in a typical adult human skeleton?

key.explanation: A typical adult skeleton has 206 bones; individuals vary slightly (for example, extra small bones).

debrief.text: Look first at your interval hit rate. If fewer than nine of your ten 90% ranges contained the truth, your ranges were too narrow: overprecision, the most persistent form of overconfidence described in Lesson 3. Most people capture far fewer than nine, which is why the useful adjustment is usually to widen ranges deliberately, not to know more facts.

Then read your calibration table. Compare each confidence bin with its hit rate, but remember the counts: with three items at 90%, missing one tells you very little. The Brier score combines calibration and discrimination; always saying 50% would score 0.25, so a score below that shows you added information. Use the score to compare yourself with yourself over time, not with other people on different questions.

What this exercise does **not** show: it measures calibration on general-knowledge items, which may differ from your calibration on professional judgments, where you have expertise and stakes. Its value is to make your pattern visible and to give you a habit — stating probabilities and ranges — that you will apply to real forecasts in your decision journal, where resolved forecasts feed the same Brier score and calibration table.

assumptions: All items are factual statements with well-documented answers; none is a trick question.
Brier score = mean of (p − outcome)², where p is the probability you gave that your chosen answer is correct and outcome is 1 if it was correct, 0 if not.
An interval counts as a hit if the true value lies within or on its endpoints; well-calibrated 90% intervals should capture about 9 in 10 over many items.
With 16 statements and 10 intervals, results are a rough indication, not a stable measurement of your calibration.

case.title: The Pathway and the Patient
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. The risk pathway described is invented for teaching and is not a real clinical instrument; nothing here is medical advice.

body.text: On a Thursday morning in March, Dr. Elena Okafor, chief medical officer of Tamsin Valley Health, a fictional four-hospital system serving a mid-sized metropolitan region, opened two documents on her desk. The first was a twelve-page proposal from her quality department to adopt a structured chest-pain pathway across all four emergency departments. The second was a one-page incident summary about a patient named in the file only as Mr. D., a 46-year-old who had been discharged from the system’s largest emergency department eleven days earlier with a diagnosis of musculoskeletal chest pain and had returned three days later with a heart attack. He survived. The physician who discharged him was one of the most respected clinicians in the system.
The executive committee would decide in two weeks whether to adopt the pathway system-wide. Okafor had to make a recommendation.
The problem the pathway was meant to solve

Chest pain is one of the most common reasons adults come to an emergency department, and one of the most difficult to sort. Most patients with chest pain do not have an acute coronary problem; a small minority do, and missing one can be catastrophic. Physicians decide whether to discharge, observe for further testing, or admit. At Tamsin Valley, those decisions varied far more than anyone had assumed.

Priya Raman, the director of quality, had run what she called a “mirror review”. She took 120 anonymized chest-pain charts from the previous year and asked fourteen emergency physicians across the four hospitals to read each chart independently, as it looked at the moment of decision, and choose discharge, observation or admission. The results (Exhibit 1) startled the committee. On the same charts, the share of patients a physician would have sent home ranged from 31% to 68%. Two physicians agreed with each other on a chart’s disposition only about half the time. When Raman showed six of the physicians a subset of charts they had already reviewed, without telling them, roughly one decision in five changed.
“None of these doctors is careless,” Raman told Okafor. “Each of them has a reason for every decision. The reasons just are not the same reasons.”
The pathway

The proposed Structured Chest Pain Pathway combined three elements: a short risk score built from the patient’s history, ECG, age, risk factors and two blood tests taken a few hours apart; a recommended disposition for each score band; and a requirement that physicians who departed from the recommendation record a reason. Raman’s team had piloted it for six months at Northgate, the system’s smallest hospital. Exhibit 2 shows the results the team reported. The share of chest-pain patients discharged from the emergency department rose, observation stays fell, and the rate of major adverse cardiac events within 30 days among discharged patients stayed low.

The finance team liked the pilot. Observation stays were expensive and frequently unreimbursed. The quality team liked it because it made decisions consistent and auditable. Several younger physicians liked it because it gave them a defensible structure for discharging low-risk patients they would otherwise have kept “just in case”.
The objection

Dr. Marcus Feld, chair of emergency medicine at the largest hospital, did not like it at all. He had practiced for twenty-four years and had trained half of the system’s emergency physicians. He was also, though nobody said so in meetings, the physician who had discharged Mr. D.

Feld’s objection, made in a long email to Okafor, was not defensive. He wrote that Mr. D.’s case had shaken him and that he had reviewed it many times. Mr. D. would have scored as low risk under the proposed pathway too; the pathway would have discharged him just as Feld had. “The lesson of this case,” Feld wrote, “is that some patients do not fit any score. Experienced clinicians catch some of those patients by noticing things a checklist cannot. I missed this one. But I have caught many others that a score would have sent home, and nobody counts those.” He argued that Northgate’s patients were younger and healthier than those at his hospital, that six months was too short to see rare events, and that a pathway would erode exactly the clinical judgment that protects atypical patients.

He added a second point that Okafor found harder to dismiss: “If you make the score the standard, every bad outcome after a physician overrides it becomes indefensible, and every bad outcome after following it becomes ‘the system’s fault’. Physicians will stop thinking.”
The numbers that were not in the room

Okafor asked Raman’s analyst, Tomás Ibarra, for two things the proposal did not contain. First, the base rate: of all chest-pain patients discharged across the system last year, how many had a major adverse cardiac event within 30 days? Second, the denominator for Feld’s claim: how often had experienced physicians admitted a patient the score would have discharged, and how often had that patient turned out to have a cardiac event?

Ibarra could answer the first question roughly (Exhibit 3). The event rate after discharge was low under both current practice and the pilot, which meant that any comparison based on a few hundred discharges would be dominated by chance. At Northgate’s volume, a difference between, say, 0.5% and 1.0% would amount to a handful of patients. He could not answer the second question at all. Physicians’ reasons for admission were not recorded in a structured way, and no one had ever tracked what happened to patients admitted “on instinct”.

He also flagged something the pilot team had not emphasized. Before the pilot, Northgate’s discharge rate had been the lowest in the system; it had risen under the pathway, but the hospital had also added a new rapid-access cardiology clinic during the same months, which may have made physicians more comfortable discharging patients with a follow-up appointment.
The pressure

Mr. D.’s case had reached the system’s board through a complaint from his family, and two board members had asked whether “standardized protocols” would have prevented it. The honest answer was no, but Okafor knew that the case would shape the discussion more than any table. The finance committee wanted a decision before the budget cycle. The physicians’ council had asked for a vote on any change to clinical practice. And Okafor herself had, two years earlier, publicly championed “evidence-based standard work” as a strategic priority. She was aware that this made her an interested party.

She wrote three possible recommendations on a notepad: adopt the pathway system-wide now; extend the pilot to a second, larger hospital with better measurement before deciding; or adopt the pathway as decision support only, with no documentation requirement for departures. Under each she began a list of what she believed, what she assumed, and what would change her mind. The lists were longer than she expected.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — System-wide context (previous year)

Patients admitted against what the proposed score would recommend, later found to have an acute cardiac event

assumptions: The pathway’s risk score is fictional; its accuracy in other settings is unknown to the committee.
Exhibit numbers are synthetic and rounded; the pilot was not randomized.
Physicians’ reasons for admitting patients against expectation were not recorded before the pilot.
No legal or regulatory requirement forces a decision either way in the next two weeks.
questions: Separate the evidence about bias from the evidence about noise in this case. What does the mirror review tell you, and what does it not tell you about which physicians are right?
How much weight should Mr. D.’s case carry in the decision? Explain using availability, base rates and outcome bias.
Evaluate Feld’s claim that experienced clinicians catch patients a score would miss. What evidence would test it, and how would you collect it?
Okafor is an interested party. Which decision-hygiene steps should she take before making her recommendation?
Choose one of the three options and write the forecasts (with probabilities and resolve-by dates) that would tell the committee, a year from now, whether it was the right call.

perspectives.title: Adopt now: noise is the bigger, measurable harm
perspectives.text: The mirror review shows enormous variability in decisions about the same patients; whichever answer is right, many patients are getting a different decision depending on who is on shift. A structured pathway with documented departures reduces that noise immediately, frees observation capacity, and — crucially — creates the record that will finally test Feld’s claim. Mr. D.’s case is a vivid single event that the pathway would not have changed and should not drive the decision. Risk: the Northgate result may reflect a younger population and the new clinic, so monitoring must be tight.

perspectives.title: Extend the pilot with better measurement
perspectives.text: The pilot is uncontrolled, short, confounded by the new clinic and run on a younger population; rare events cannot be compared at this volume. Extending to the largest hospital, with a staggered start and structured recording of departures and their outcomes, would answer the questions that matter within a year. This respects the physicians’ council and Okafor’s own conflict of interest. Risk: a year of continued noise at three hospitals, and the possibility that “more data” becomes a way to avoid a decision.

perspectives.title: Decision support without the documentation requirement
perspectives.text: Offer the score to every physician as information, measure agreement and outcomes, and let practice converge voluntarily. This preserves clinical judgment for atypical patients and avoids a defensive-medicine dynamic in which overrides become indefensible. Risk: without recorded reasons for departures, the system learns little, and the physicians with the most extreme practice patterns are the least likely to change.

case.application: Player-development departments face the same structure. Evaluators looking at the same player reach very different grades (noise); one memorable miss — a released player who succeeded elsewhere, or a highly graded one who failed — dominates the conversation (availability and outcome bias); and the most experienced evaluator argues that a structured model would erode the judgment that catches unusual cases. The case’s moves transfer directly: run a mirror review on past evaluations, state the base rate, record departures from any model with reasons, and agree in advance what evidence would settle the argument.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about the two evaluators is best supported?

stimulus.text: A fictional bank has two senior credit officers. Officer A has approved small-business loans for 15 years; the bank tracks every loan’s repayment and sends each officer a quarterly report showing defaults on the loans they approved. Officer B has spent 15 years approving loans for large, one-off infrastructure projects that take 8–12 years to show whether they will be repaid; the bank has never linked outcomes back to the approving officer. Both are highly confident in their instincts.

options.text: Both have equal claim to skilled intuition, since both have 15 years of experience.

Officer A’s intuition has a stronger claim to trust, because the environment provides many repetitions and clear, timely feedback; Officer B’s confidence carries little information without a track record.
Officer B’s intuition deserves more trust, because larger decisions develop deeper expertise.
Neither intuition deserves any weight; credit decisions should always be made by models.

questions.explanation: Kahneman and Klein’s conditions are a valid environment and an adequate opportunity to learn it through practice with feedback. Officer A has frequent, scored feedback; Officer B has few, slow, untracked outcomes, so experience mostly builds confidence.

optionFeedback.a: Years of experience are not the test; the feedback environment is.
optionFeedback.c: Stakes do not create learning opportunities; feedback does.
optionFeedback.d: Overcorrection: in a valid, high-feedback environment intuition can be skilled and worth combining with models.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in this argument?

stimulus.text: “Our training program teaches managers to switch from System 1 to System 2 when making decisions. Since biases come from System 1 and System 2 is the rational system, managers who complete the program will make unbiased decisions.”

options.text: It assumes deliberate (Type 2) thinking is normatively correct, but deliberation can rationalize a preferred conclusion and is not defined by being right.
It ignores that System 1 is located in a specific brain region.
It wrongly assumes managers can think slowly.
It confuses noise with bias.

questions.explanation: Evans and Stanovich treat accuracy as at most a correlate of Type 2 processing, not its definition, and motivated reasoning shows that deliberation can build sophisticated justifications for wrong conclusions. The two-system picture is itself debated.

optionFeedback.b: The argument’s problem is not anatomical; dual-process theories do not rest on that claim.
optionFeedback.c: Managers can think slowly; the issue is that slow thinking does not guarantee correct thinking.
optionFeedback.d: The argument is about bias; noise is not mentioned or relevant to its main error.

questions.prompt: A pre-employment integrity test is used on applicants. Suppose 5% of applicants would commit serious misconduct. The test flags 80% of those who would and 10% of those who would not. If an applicant is flagged, what is the probability (in %) that they would commit serious misconduct? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.working: Take 1,000 applicants: 50 would commit misconduct, of whom 40 are flagged. 950 would not, of whom 95 are flagged. Flagged total: 135. Probability: 40 / 135 ≈ 29.6%, about 30%.
questions.explanation: Most flagged applicants are false positives because the base rate is low. Counting cases in a fixed population (natural frequencies) makes the calculation straightforward.

questions.prompt: A due-diligence team has concluded that an acquisition target is strong. Which procedures specifically counter confirmation bias? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the team to list the evidence that would show the target is weak, and then look for it.
Ask the team to gather more evidence about the target’s strengths.
Assign a separate reviewer who has not seen the team’s memo to assess the raw data.
Give the team a larger bonus if the deal closes.
Test the conclusion against cases that could disconfirm it, such as comparable targets that failed.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias narrows search to evidence that fits the hypothesis. Seeking disconfirming evidence, testing against cases that could falsify the conclusion and using an independent reviewer all widen the search. More confirming evidence and a stake in closing make the bias worse.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible conclusion from this (fictional) summary?

stimulus.text: Fictional summary: “A multi-site replication project ran the same 12 judgment effects in 30 labs in nine countries, with a pre-registered analysis. Nine effects replicated in nearly every lab, with similar sizes across countries and between online and in-person samples. Three effects were close to zero everywhere. Variation between effects was far larger than variation between labs.”

options.text: Psychology’s findings are unreliable, so none of the twelve effects should inform management practice.
Whether an effect replicates depends mainly on the effect itself rather than on where it is tested; the nine robust effects are reasonable foundations, while the three should not be relied on.
The three null effects probably exist but were masked by differences between countries.
All twelve effects are now proven to work in organizations.

questions.explanation: The pattern mirrors the real Many Labs result: replicability varied by effect, not by setting. Robust laboratory effects are reasonable foundations; their size in organizations is a separate question, and null effects should not be rescued by appeals to hidden moderators the data do not show.

optionFeedback.a: Overcorrection: the study shows most effects were robust.
optionFeedback.c: The summary reports small variation between labs, which argues against masking by setting.
optionFeedback.d: Laboratory replication does not establish organizational effects or their size.

questions.prompt: A project manager forecasts five milestones: 90% (hit), 90% (missed), 80% (hit), 70% (missed), 60% (hit). What is the average Brier score? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Square each gap between the stated probability and the outcome and average. Two confident misses dominate the score, which is worse than the 0.25 earned by always saying 50%.

questions.prompt: Your leadership team gives point estimates for every forecast and is almost always surprised by outcomes. You want to improve calibration within a year without a large program. What is the best next move?

options.text: Send the team to a workshop on cognitive biases.
Require every significant forecast to be stated as a probability or a range with a resolve-by date, recorded, and scored in a quarterly review against outcomes.
Hire an external forecasting firm to replace internal forecasts.
Ask everyone to be more humble in meetings.

questions.explanation: Calibration improves with explicit probabilities, records and feedback; scoring forecasts creates the feedback loop that the environment otherwise lacks. Brief probabilistic training helped in the forecasting tournament, but awareness alone rarely changes behavior.

optionFeedback.a: Awareness of biases does not reliably reduce them; without feedback, nothing tells the team how calibrated it is.
optionFeedback.c: Outsourcing may help some forecasts but does not build the team’s judgment or a record.
optionFeedback.d: Exhortation without measurement does not change calibration.

questions.prompt: A city must forecast how long a new light-rail line will take to build. Rank these approaches from most to least likely to produce a well-calibrated forecast.

options.text: The project engineers’ detailed schedule, presented as a single completion date.
The distribution of actual-versus-planned durations for comparable rail projects, adjusted modestly for verified features of this one, presented as a range.
The mayor’s public commitment date.
The engineers’ detailed schedule presented as a range they consider 80% likely.

questions.explanation: The outside view anchored on a reference class, then adjusted, is best. An inside-view range at least acknowledges uncertainty; a single inside-view date is overprecise; a political commitment adds motivated optimism.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful first step for the firm?

stimulus.text: A fictional consulting firm’s partners rate associates on a 1–5 scale each year. Associates complain that ratings depend on which partner they worked for. The managing partner believes the partners are excellent judges and that complaints reflect sour grapes.

options.text: Replace ratings with a fully automated productivity metric.
Run a noise audit: have several partners independently rate the same set of anonymized associate files, then measure the spread and each partner’s average relative to the group.
Tell associates that ratings are final and cannot be discussed.
Ask each partner whether they think they are fair.

questions.explanation: Whether ratings depend on the rater is an empirical question a noise audit answers without needing to know the right ratings. It separates level noise (harsh versus lenient partners) from pattern noise and gives the firm evidence before it changes anything.

optionFeedback.a: A metric may be gamed and embed its own biases; the firm does not yet know how large the noise is.
optionFeedback.c: This ignores a measurable problem.
optionFeedback.d: Self-assessment of fairness is exactly what motivated reasoning and confidence make unreliable.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures intellectual humility as defined in recent research reviews?

options.text: A low opinion of one’s own abilities.
Deferring to the most senior expert in the room.
A metacognitive recognition that one’s beliefs and knowledge have limits and might be wrong, shown in proportional updating.
Avoiding firm decisions until all uncertainty is resolved.

questions.explanation: Porter and colleagues identify the common core as recognizing the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge. It is about how you hold beliefs, not low self-regard, deference or indecision.

optionFeedback.a: Humility about beliefs is distinct from low self-esteem.
optionFeedback.b: Deference substitutes someone else’s certainty for your own; it is not recognition of limits.
optionFeedback.d: Humble decision-makers still commit; they hold the underlying estimate open to revision.

questions.prompt: Choose one recurring judgment in your professional life (for example rating people, approving budgets or evaluating players). In 150–250 words, (1) say whether it sits in a high- or low-validity environment and how much feedback you receive, (2) identify the bias or noise most likely to affect it, and (3) propose two specific decision-hygiene or calibration practices you could introduce, with one risk of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Example: annual budget requests from department heads. The environment is moderately valid — past spending predicts future needs — but feedback on my approvals is slow and confounded, since I rarely compare what a program delivered with what its budget assumed. The most likely problems are anchoring on last year’s figure and the request itself, and level noise between me and my co-approver, who is consistently more generous. Practice 1: each approver scores each request independently on separate dimensions (strategic fit, evidence of results, cost realism) before we meet, and we discuss only large disagreements. Risk: it adds time and may feel bureaucratic to department heads. Practice 2: every approved request includes two forecasts with probabilities and resolve-by dates (for example, “70% that the program reaches 500 participants by 30 June”), reviewed at the next cycle. Risk: department heads may forecast only safe outcomes, so the approvers must choose the forecasts that matter.

1 — partly addressed
2 — clear and accurate

levels: 0 — none or generic
1 — named but not linked to the judgment

reserve.prompt: Which pair of conditions do Kahneman and Klein require before an intuitive judgment deserves trust?

options.text: Long experience and high confidence.
A high-validity environment and an adequate opportunity to learn it through practice with timely, clear feedback.
A clear explanation of the reasoning and agreement from peers.
High stakes and personal responsibility for the outcome.

reserve.explanation: The two conditions are environmental validity and the opportunity to learn it. Confidence is explicitly not a reliable indicator, and experience without feedback does not create skill.

optionFeedback.a: Confidence is not evidence of accuracy, and experience is insufficient without feedback.
optionFeedback.c: Skilled intuitions are often hard to explain, and peers can share the same errors.
optionFeedback.d: Stakes motivate effort but do not create learnable regularities or feedback.

reserve.prompt: A security screening system flags 99% of genuine threats and 2% of harmless items. One item in 10,000 is a genuine threat. Of flagged items, what percentage are genuine threats? Round to one decimal place.
reserve.working: Use 1,000,000 items: 100 threats, 99 flagged. 999,900 harmless, about 19,998 flagged. Share genuine: 99 / (99 + 19,998) ≈ 0.49%, about 0.5%.
reserve.explanation: With a very low base rate, almost all flags are false alarms even for a highly sensitive system. Natural frequencies make the denominator visible.

reserve.prompt: A forecaster’s 90% intervals contain the true value 55% of the time, with misses evenly above and below. Which description fits best?

options.text: Overestimation
Overplacement
Overprecision
Good calibration with bad luck

reserve.explanation: Intervals that capture the truth far less often than stated are too narrow: overprecision, the most persistent form of overconfidence in Moore and Healy’s taxonomy.

optionFeedback.a: Overestimation would show as a directional error, not symmetric misses.
optionFeedback.b: Overplacement concerns comparison with others.
optionFeedback.d: Over many intervals, 55% versus 90% is far beyond what luck explains.

reserve.prompt: Which practices are decision hygiene for a hiring panel? Select all that apply.

options.text: Each interviewer scores separate competencies independently before the debrief.
Interviewers read the referral note from the CEO before interviewing.
Scores are averaged and the spread is shown before discussion.
The hiring manager states a preferred candidate at the start of the debrief.
Interviews follow a common structure with the same questions for every candidate.

reserve.explanation: Independent, structured, aggregated judgments reduce noise and anchoring. Exposure to a powerful endorsement or a stated preference before judging correlates errors and anchors the panel.

assignment.title: Decision Journal Template

brief.text: This week you build the tool you will use for the rest of the semester: a personal decision journal for important professional decisions. A decision journal is a dated, contemporaneous record of what you decided, what you knew and assumed, what alternatives you considered, and what you predicted — written before the outcome is known, then reviewed after. It is the practical answer to three problems from this week: overconfidence (you cannot see your calibration without a record), outcome bias (you cannot judge process later without knowing what you knew then), and motivated reasoning (a record made in advance is harder to rewrite).

Your template should use the same fields as APERTURE’s Strategic Decision Journal, so that your entries can be kept there and your resolved forecasts can feed its Brier score and calibration table. Adapt the guidance and prompts under each field to your own work; that adaptation is the substance of the assignment.

items: Part 1 — the template: for each field below, write a one- or two-sentence instruction to yourself that makes the field hard to fill in carelessly (for example, under “What would change my mind”, require at least one observable signal and a date).

Part 2 — a first entry: use the template on one real, current decision that is **not confidential** — a personal professional choice, a public decision you are following, or a disguised version with every identifying detail removed. Include at least three forecasts with probabilities and resolve-by dates.
Part 3 — a short note (about 150 words) on how and when you will review entries: the review date rule, and how you will judge process separately from outcome.

brief.text: Privacy and confidentiality: never record confidential employer information, non-public player or personnel information, or anything you would not be comfortable seeing outside your organization. When in doubt, choose a different decision or disguise it completely.

Professional application: many recurring decisions in player development — promotion timing, assignment of development resources, changes to a player’s plan — are ideal for a decision journal because they resolve within months and can be scored. You may design field prompts with such decisions in mind, but your first entry must still meet the confidentiality rule above.

assignment.deliverable: A decision-journal template with field-by-field guidance, one completed non-confidential entry with at least three dated probability forecasts, and a short review plan.

template.heading: Decision and context
template.guidance: State the decision in one sentence as a choice, the date, and the essential context: what prompted it, the deadline, who else is involved, and what you know and do not know.

template.heading: Options considered
template.guidance: List at least three genuine options, including doing nothing or delaying. For each, note the main argument for and against.

template.heading: Choice and rationale
template.guidance: State the option chosen and why, in a few sentences. Note your confidence that it is the best option (as a probability) and the reference class or base rate you used, if any.

template.heading: Key assumptions
template.guidance: List the three to five assumptions that would most change the decision if they were wrong. Mark which are verified and which are guesses.

template.heading: What would change my mind
template.guidance: Name observable signals, with dates, that would lead you to reverse or revise the decision. Avoid signals that can only be interpreted in your favor.

template.heading: Forecasts
template.guidance: Write at least three resolvable forecasts: the outcome, your probability, and a resolve-by date. Make them specific enough that a stranger could score them.

template.heading: Review date and later fields
template.guidance: Set the review date. Leave space for what happened, how each forecast resolved, a process-versus-outcome assessment (sound or poor process; good or bad outcome) and lessons.

template.heading: Review plan
template.guidance: Explain how often you will review entries, how you will compute your calibration, and how you will avoid rewriting entries after the fact.

prompts: Think of a judgment you make with great confidence at work. Does it sit in an environment where you have had many repetitions with clear, timely feedback? If not, what has your confidence been built on?
Recall a time you changed your mind about something important. What evidence did it take, and was the size of your update proportional to it?
Which decision do you most want to judge by its outcome rather than its process? What would a contemporaneous record of it have shown?
After the Judgment Lab: where were you overconfident, and what one habit will you change in how you state ranges and probabilities?

review.front: How do Evans and Stanovich define Type 2 processing?
review.back: By its reliance on working memory and its support for hypothetical thinking (cognitive decoupling) — not by being slow, conscious or correct.

review.front: What is Melnikoff and Bargh’s main objection to dual-process theory?
review.back: The features said to define each type (intentional, controllable, efficient, conscious and their opposites) often do not travel together, so two bins misdescribe mental processes.

review.front: When can an intuition be trusted, according to Kahneman and Klein?
review.back: When the environment has high validity and the person has had an adequate opportunity to learn it through practice with timely, clear feedback.

review.front: Is subjective confidence evidence of accuracy?
review.back: Not reliably. Confidence comes from the coherence of a story and is felt as strongly in low-validity environments.

review.front: Name the three heuristics in Tversky and Kahneman (1974).
review.back: Representativeness, availability, and anchoring and adjustment.

review.front: How do natural frequencies help with base-rate problems?
review.back: Counting cases from one reference population (e.g., of 1,000 people) makes the denominator of positives visible, so Bayesian answers become much easier.

review.front: Confirmation bias vs. motivated reasoning?
review.back: Confirmation bias: searching and interpreting evidence partial to an existing hypothesis, even without a stake. Motivated reasoning: a directional goal steers reasoning toward a preferred conclusion, constrained by the need for a justification.

review.front: What did Many Labs (Klein et al., 2014) find?
review.back: Of 13 effects in 36 samples, ten replicated consistently (including anchoring), one weakly, two priming effects not at all; variation was mostly between effects, not labs.

review.front: What is ecological rationality?
review.back: The degree to which a heuristic fits the structure of its environment; under small samples and high uncertainty, simple rules can beat complex models.

review.front: Three forms of overconfidence (Moore & Healy)?
review.back: Overestimation (of your performance), overplacement (relative to others), overprecision (ranges too narrow). Overprecision is the most persistent.

review.front: How do you compute a Brier score, and what does 0.25 mean?
review.back: Average (p − outcome)² across forecasts. 0.25 is what always saying 50% earns; lower is better.

review.front: Calibration vs. discrimination?
review.back: Calibration: your 70% happens about 70% of the time. Discrimination: higher probabilities for events that happen than for those that do not.

review.front: Order of steps in a disciplined forecast?
review.back: Resolvable question → outside view (base rate) → decompose → adjust modestly for verified differences → record probability and date → score.

review.front: Level, pattern and occasion noise?
review.back: Level: some judges are harsher overall. Pattern: judges react differently to particular cases. Occasion: the same judge varies over time.

review.front: Name four decision-hygiene practices.
review.back: Independent judgments then aggregation; structured, separately scored assessments; sequencing information; relative scales; the outside view.

review.front: What is the common core of intellectual humility?
review.back: A metacognitive recognition of the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge — shown in proportional updating — not low self-regard or indecision.

preview.text: This week’s tools recur throughout the semester. Week 2 moves from individual judgment to the situations, incentives and norms that shape behavior. Week 4 extends base rates and calibration into research literacy and causal inference. Week 7 returns to anchoring in negotiation, Week 10 to the outside view in valuation, and Week 14 to outcome bias, after-action reviews and the decision journal you start now.

weeks.title: Why People Behave the Way They Do
weeks.question: How much of what people do at work is explained by the situations, incentives and social expectations leaders create — and how should that change the way you design them?

overview.text: Week 1 examined how individuals think. This week examines why people act as they do in groups and organizations, and how leaders shape that behavior — often unintentionally. The central claim is uncomfortable for anyone who manages people: behavior that looks like a character flaw is frequently a reasonable response to a situation, an incentive or a norm that someone else designed. The corollary is just as uncomfortable: the famous studies used to make that claim have a mixed replication record, and you need to know which ones to trust.

The four lessons move from the person to the system. Lesson 1 examines situational power — conformity, attribution and the replication audit of classic social psychology. Lesson 2 examines motivation: self-determination theory, when rewards undermine intrinsic interest, and the evidence that intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance. Lesson 3 turns to the economics of incentives: principal–agent problems, the multitask model, metric decay and gaming, with a documented banking example. Lesson 4 examines the social economy of work: reciprocity, norms, fairness, status and psychological safety.

You will practise the ideas three ways. In the Incentive Designer you build an incentive system for a fictional hospital unit and watch effort, gaming, cooperation and motivation trade off. The case puts you inside a fictional payments company whose growth metric has started to decay under pay pressure. The assignment asks you to diagnose incentive misalignments in a fictional professional baseball organization and propose redesigns, with honest predictions about the new problems each redesign will create.

objectives: Diagnose a recurring behavior problem by examining incentives, norms, status and friction before attributing it to individual character.
Classify influential social-psychology findings as robust, context-dependent or failed to replicate, and explain what that implies for using them.
Explain self-determination theory and the conditions under which rewards strengthen or undermine motivation.
Apply the principal–agent and multitask models to predict effort diversion and gaming under a proposed incentive.
Design an incentive system that integrates measure, unit, horizon, payout shape, monitoring and non-financial levers, and state its expected side effects.
Evaluate claims about reciprocity, fairness and psychological safety by distinguishing correlational from causal evidence.

lessons.title: The Power of the Situation — and What Survived Replication
lessons.summary: Behavior is jointly produced by people and the situations they are placed in, and the classic social-psychology evidence for situational power is a mix of robust, fragile and failed findings.
objectives: Explain why observers over-attribute behavior to character and under-attribute it to situations, and what that means for diagnosing performance problems.
Describe what the meta-analytic evidence on conformity does and does not show.
Classify a famous social-psychology finding as robust, context-dependent or failed to replicate, and justify the classification.
lessons.executive: When someone behaves badly at work, the first explanation offered is usually about the person: lazy, political, uncoachable. Social psychology’s most durable lesson is that situations — what is rewarded, who is watching, what the group is doing — explain more behavior than observers expect. But the field’s own evidence is uneven. Conformity to unanimous groups is robust though variable. Ego depletion, once a staple of leadership books, failed a large preregistered test, and a systematic replication project found that published social-psychology effects were often smaller or less reliable than reported. Diagnose the situation first, and ask how well the study you are quoting has held up.

explore.text: Imagine three units in a large hospital system that all post poor hand-hygiene audit results in the same quarter. The chief nursing officer’s first instinct is to identify the careless nurses and retrain them. Before reading on, notice the assumption in that instinct: that the cause lives inside individual people. Now add three facts. In the first unit, the sanitizer dispensers are at the far end of each room. In the second, a respected senior physician routinely skips hand hygiene and nobody comments. In the third, audits are announced in advance everywhere except on night shift. Each fact is a feature of the situation, and each predicts the pattern of failures better than any personality inventory would. This is a hypothetical composite, but the pattern will be familiar to anyone who has investigated a quality problem.

Think of the last time someone in your organization was labelled “not a team player” or “not coachable.” Write down one feature of their situation — what they were measured on, who they reported to, what their peers were doing — that could have produced the same behavior in most people.

This lesson asks two questions that every executive needs to hold together. First, how much of behavior is explained by the situation rather than the person? Second, how much should you trust the famous studies that answer the first question? Social psychology built its public reputation on dramatic demonstrations of situational power. Over the last fifteen years, the field has also become a leader in auditing itself, and the audit produced uncomfortable results. You need both the insight and the audit.

understand.text: Persons, situations and the observer’s bias

Behavior is always produced by a person in a situation. The useful question is rarely “person or situation?” but “which features of the situation are doing the work, and for whom?” Observers, however, are systematically lopsided. Social psychologists use the term *fundamental attribution error* (also called correspondence bias) for the tendency to explain other people’s behavior by their dispositions — character, ability, attitude — while underweighting the pressures acting on them. The term is standard; how universal and how large the tendency is has been debated. Treat it as a reliable default, not a law.

The lopsidedness has a practical structure. When *you* miss a deadline, you see the competing demands, the late data and the unclear brief. When a colleague misses one, you see the colleague. Situational forces are often invisible to outsiders: incentives, informal norms, who is in the room, what happened last time someone raised a concern. The executive implication is direct. A performance problem that recurs across different people in the same role is evidence about the role.

understand.caption: Four situational levers that observers routinely underweight
rows: What would a reasonable person do if paid exactly this way?
What peers actually do and approve of
What happens to the person who behaves differently?
Who is watching; whose opinion carries weight
Who was in the room, and what did dissent cost last time?
How easy the right action is
How many steps does compliance take compared with the shortcut?
understand.note: Original APERTURE diagnostic grid; a teaching device, not an empirical taxonomy.

understand.text: Conformity: robust, but variable

The most studied demonstration of situational power is Solomon Asch’s line-judgment task. A participant sits with a group of confederates who, on some trials, unanimously give an obviously wrong answer about which of several lines matches a reference line. Many participants go along with the group on at least some trials. Bond and Smith’s meta-analysis of studies using Asch’s task found that conformity is a real and repeatable phenomenon, but that its size varies: it rises with the size of the majority, is larger in more collectivist cultures, and declined in U.S. samples over the decades after Asch’s original work.

That combination — real but variable — is what most robust social findings look like. The direction generalizes: people shift toward unanimous groups, especially when they care about belonging to the group. The rate does not generalize: it depends on culture, era, stakes and how ambiguous the judgment is. In organizations, judgments are usually far more ambiguous than the length of a line, which plausibly makes social influence stronger, while dissent can also be rewarded, which makes it weaker. Because the size of the effect depends on the setting, the practical response is structural rather than exhortative: design meetings so that independent views are recorded before discussion.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what “replicate” means

blocks.text: A finding *replicates* when a new study, using the same procedure on new participants, produces a similar result. A *direct* replication repeats the method as closely as possible; a *conceptual* replication tests the same idea with a different method. Direct replications are the stronger test of whether the original result was reliable, because conceptual replications can succeed for different reasons or quietly go unpublished when they fail.

Why would a published result fail to replicate? The most common reasons are small samples (which produce noisy estimates), flexibility in analysis (testing several outcomes or exclusion rules and reporting the one that worked), and publication filters (journals preferring significant results). None requires fraud. Together they produce a literature in which published effects are, on average, larger than the true effects. Week 4 develops this formally; for now, the point is that a famous result is not the same as a reliable one.

understand.text: The replication record

In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration reported the results of repeating 100 studies from three leading psychology journals with high-powered designs and, where possible, the original materials. Most originals had reported statistically significant results; far fewer replications did, and the replication effect sizes averaged roughly half of the original estimates. Social psychology studies replicated less often than cognitive psychology studies. Originals with larger effects and stronger statistical evidence were more likely to hold up.

Ego depletion is the clearest cautionary tale for managers. The idea — that self-control draws on a limited resource that is used up by earlier acts of self-control — spread widely into leadership and productivity advice. A registered replication report in which more than twenty laboratories ran one preregistered protocol found a pooled effect close to zero.

understand.caption: A working classification of social-psychology claims used in management
rows: People conform to unanimous groups on ambiguous or even clear judgments
Use: collect independent judgments before group discussion.
Widely supported default; size varies by culture and prompt
Use: investigate the role before the person.
Self-control is a depletable resource (ego depletion)
Failed a large preregistered multi-lab test
Do not build policy on it.
Published effects in social psychology are reliable at face value
Not supported: replication effects about half the original size on average
Discount single classic studies; look for meta-analyses and preregistered replications.
understand.note: Classification by APERTURE from the cited sources. Status reflects evidence summarized in this lesson, not a final verdict.

challenge.text: The replication debate is not settled in every detail. Critics of the 2015 project argued that some replications differed from the originals in population or procedure, and that a single replication cannot establish that an effect is false. Proponents of ego depletion argued that the multi-lab protocol used too weak a manipulation. These objections deserve a hearing. But they cut both ways: if an effect appears only under narrow conditions that its proponents cannot specify in advance, it is not a reliable basis for designing organizations. The stronger, more general conclusion — published effects are often inflated and some celebrated ones are not real — has held across later many-laboratory projects.

There is also a mirror-image error. Having learned that situations matter, some leaders conclude that individual differences do not. That overcorrects. Ability, conscientiousness and expertise predict performance in many jobs, and selection decisions rest on that fact. Situations also select people: a sales floor with aggressive targets attracts and retains people comfortable with them. The mature position is interactional: people differ, situations differ, and the same incentive or norm produces different behavior in different people. Diagnosing the situation first is a sequencing rule, not a denial of character.

Finally, notice how social influence bears on the replication story itself. Findings became famous partly because they were surprising and partly because many people repeated them — textbooks, consultants and speakers citing each other. Popularity is a social signal, not an evidential one. The same conformity pressures that shape behavior in a meeting shape what a profession “knows.”

challenge.title: Methodological note: why surprising, small-sample findings are fragile

blocks.text: Suppose a true effect is small and a study is small. Only estimates that happen to come out large will clear the significance threshold, so the published estimate is biased upward even when every step was honest. A replication with a larger sample then lands closer to the true, smaller effect and is called a “failure.” This is why the 2015 project’s finding that stronger original evidence predicted replication matters: the size of the original p-value and sample are themselves information. When you read a classic study, ask how many participants it had, whether the analysis was specified in advance, and whether an independent multi-site test exists. Week 4’s Evidence Lab lets you simulate exactly this mechanism.

A second subtlety is the difference between an effect that is *zero* and one that is *unreliable*. A preregistered multi-lab null result for ego depletion is strong evidence that the standard paradigm does not produce a meaningful effect. It is weaker evidence about every possible version of self-control fatigue. Executives rarely need that philosophical precision; they need to know that the confident popular version has no reliable support.

apply.text: Consider a hypothetical government benefits agency where claim-processing errors are concentrated among newer staff. The director proposes a stricter hiring screen. A situational diagnosis asks first what newer staff are measured on (throughput targets that experienced staff have learned to negotiate), who sits near them (whether experienced colleagues are co-located or remote), and what happens when a new hire asks a question (whether supervisors treat it as a sign of weakness). If those features explain the pattern, a hiring screen will change the people and leave the error rate where it is.

In a hypothetical consulting firm, junior analysts rarely contradict partners’ hypotheses in client workshops, and several engagements later turn out to have been built on a wrong premise. The partners read this as a lack of confidence in the analysts. The conformity evidence suggests a structural fix: ask every participant to submit an independent estimate or recommendation in writing before discussion, and have the most senior person speak last. Those changes do not require anyone to become braver.

In player development, the same logic applies to evaluation meetings. If a group of coaches and analysts discusses a prospect after hearing the most senior evaluator’s view, the later views will drift toward it — not because the others lack conviction but because the meeting is structured to produce conformity. Recording independent grades before discussion, and rotating who speaks first, are cheap situational changes. Likewise, when a coach is described as “resistant to data,” ask what the coach is evaluated on, whether using the new information has ever been rewarded, and what happened the last time a coach publicly changed course.

apply.title: Executive twist: when you do not know whether it is the person or the role

blocks.text: You inherit a unit where one manager has had three direct reports quit in a year. You have exit interviews that are polite and vague, and the manager’s numbers are strong. You cannot run an experiment. A defensible approach treats the question as a comparison: how do turnover and engagement in this unit compare with similar units under different managers, and with this manager’s previous team? Is the manager’s span, workload or target different? If the pattern follows the manager across roles, the evidence points toward the person; if it follows the role across managers, toward the situation. You will rarely get a clean answer, so decide what information would change your mind before you look.

retain.text: Behavior is produced by people in situations, and observers systematically underweight the situation. Conformity to groups is a robust finding whose size varies with culture, era and stakes. The replication record of social psychology is mixed: some classics hold, many effects are smaller than published, and some popular claims such as ego depletion failed rigorous tests. Diagnose the role before the person, and check the evidence before quoting the study.
Without looking back: what two features of the conformity evidence make it “robust but variable”?
Name one reason a published effect can be inflated even when no researcher behaved dishonestly.
What sequencing rule does this lesson recommend for diagnosing a recurring performance problem, and what is its limit?

takeaways: A problem that recurs across different people in the same role is evidence about the role.
Conformity is real and repeatable, but its size depends on group size, culture, era and ambiguity.
Replication projects found published psychology effects to be about half their original size on average, with social psychology replicating less often.
Ego depletion failed a large preregistered multi-lab test; do not design policy around it.
Diagnosing the situation first is a sequencing rule, not a denial that people differ.

check.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the meta-analytic evidence on conformity in Asch-type tasks?

options.text: Conformity is a laboratory artifact that disappears in modern samples.
Conformity is robust, but its size varies with factors such as majority size, culture and historical period.
Conformity occurs at the same rate everywhere, which shows it is a fixed human trait.
Conformity only occurs when the correct answer is ambiguous.

check.explanation: The meta-analysis found conformity to be a repeatable phenomenon whose magnitude varies: larger with larger majorities, larger in more collectivist cultures, and lower in later U.S. samples. “Robust but variable” is the right summary.

optionFeedback.a: Conformity declined in U.S. samples over time but did not disappear.
optionFeedback.c: The variation across cultures and decades is precisely what shows it is not fixed.
optionFeedback.d: Asch’s task used unambiguous lines; conformity occurred even there.

check.prompt: What is the most defensible next step?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: a software company’s on-call engineers on three different product teams have all been flagged for slow incident response this quarter. A vice president proposes adding a responsiveness rating to each engineer’s performance review.

options.text: Adopt the rating; slow responders need clearer individual accountability.
Compare the three teams’ alerting tools, paging rules and on-call load before changing individual reviews.
Replace the slowest engineer on each team to signal seriousness.
Run a personality assessment to identify engineers low in conscientiousness.

check.explanation: The same problem recurring across different people and teams is evidence about the role or system. Checking situational causes — tools, rules, load — comes first; individual measures may still be needed if the pattern follows people across conditions.

optionFeedback.a: This assumes a dispositional cause before checking shared situational ones and may add a gameable metric.
optionFeedback.c: Replacing people leaves any situational cause in place.
optionFeedback.d: Personality may matter, but it cannot explain a pattern shared across three teams as well as a shared system can.

check.prompt: A leadership book recommends scheduling hard decisions early in the day because “willpower is a muscle that gets used up.” Based on this lesson, how should you treat that rationale?

options.text: As settled science, because ego depletion was published in many studies.
As unsupported: a large preregistered multi-lab replication found an effect near zero.
As proven false in every form of fatigue.
As valid because many executives report feeling tired in the afternoon.

check.explanation: The multi-lab registered replication found the standard ego-depletion effect close to zero. That does not prove every form of fatigue is irrelevant, but it removes the scientific basis for the popular claim. Scheduling choices may still be sensible for other reasons.

optionFeedback.a: Many published studies can coexist with an unreliable effect when publication bias and flexible analysis inflate results.
optionFeedback.c: A null result for one paradigm is not proof about every form of fatigue.
optionFeedback.d: Self-reported tiredness is not evidence for the specific resource-depletion mechanism.

Systematic replication of 100 psychology studies; average shrinkage of effects and lower social-psychology replication rates.
Preregistered multi-lab test finding an ego-depletion effect near zero.
