questions: Using the multitask model and Kerr’s diagnostic question, explain how the Accelerator’s design made a $1.00 activation an attractive strategy. Which features of the pay structure mattered most?

What should Nadia do in the next six days about the board deck, the 37 accounts and the bonus? Defend a position that a skeptical board member and a skeptical account executive could both accept as fair.
How would you separate the effect of gaming from the effect of the shifting customer mix on 90-day retention? What data would you need, and what would change your recommendation?
Design a replacement incentive. What is measured, over what horizon, with what payout shape and verification? What new form of gaming should Nadia expect, and how will she detect it?
What signals — about trust, fairness and the company’s norms — will 140 account executives read into each option, and how should that shape the way the decision is communicated?

perspectives.title: Suspend now, investigate, claw back
perspectives.text: The integrity of a financial metric and possible unauthorized activity on customer accounts outweigh short-term sales disruption. Suspend the activation bonus immediately, investigate the 37 accounts with risk and legal involvement, disclose to the board that the metric is under review, and introduce clawbacks for unverified activations. The cost is morale and possibly some departures; the benefit is that the company’s numbers, and its account executives, can be trusted again. This view treats the board deck as secondary to getting the facts right.

perspectives.title: Targeted investigation, redesign without public suspension
perspectives.text: Most activations are probably real, and a blanket suspension tells honest employees they are suspects. Investigate the 37 accounts and the individual with 19 of them quietly and promptly; change the definition of activation going forward (for example, a minimum transaction value, multiple transactions or a payroll run, verified as customer-initiated); remove the leaderboard; disclose to the board that the metric is being tightened and why. The risk is that the problem is wider than it looks and the company is later seen to have moved too slowly.

perspectives.title: Replace the measure, not just the rules
perspectives.text: The core mistake was paying on a single early event because it historically correlated with retention. Any single-event activation measure will decay under pay pressure. Replace the activation bonus with a smaller, deferred bonus based on 90- or 180-day revenue from the account, with team-level components to reduce rivalry, and present the board with retention and revenue alongside activation. This sacrifices immediacy and simplicity, and may reduce effort on signing new customers, but aligns the measure with the goal.

case.application: The structure of this case — a measure that predicted the goal until people were paid on it, a top performer whose results look too good, a leaderboard that turned colleagues into rivals, and a leader who must act before the facts are clear — transfers directly to player development and baseball operations. A development staff paid or promoted on how many players reach a level, or a scouting group judged on short-term statistical markers, faces the same decay of a once-informative measure. The same choices also recur: whether to suspend, investigate or redesign; how to protect people who did nothing wrong; and how to present uncertain numbers to ownership without overstating or hiding the problem.

questions.prompt: Across four regional offices of a hypothetical insurer, new hires in the claims role quit at twice the rate of new hires in other roles. Which inference is best supported before any further investigation?

options.text: The claims role attracts people with weaker commitment.
Something about the claims role — workload, measures, supervision or norms — is a likely contributor and should be examined first.
The recruiters hiring for claims are poor judges of character.
Turnover is random and nothing can be inferred.

questions.explanation: A pattern that recurs across many different people and offices in the same role is evidence about the role. Dispositional explanations are possible but should be tested after situational features shared by all those people are examined.

optionFeedback.a: This jumps to a dispositional explanation for a pattern that shared situational features explain more economically.
optionFeedback.c: Possible, but it is still a person-centred explanation that skips the shared role features.
optionFeedback.d: A consistent doubling across four offices is unlikely to be pure noise.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is most defensible?

stimulus.text: Fictional summary: An influential 2009 study (n = 40) reported that employees who first completed a tedious form persisted 40 percent less on a later puzzle. A 2024 preregistered replication across 18 laboratories (total n = 2,300) using the original materials found a difference of 2 percent, with a confidence interval spanning zero.

options.text: The original authors must have fabricated their data.
The original effect was probably inflated or absent; the preregistered multi-lab estimate is far more credible for practical decisions.
The two studies cancel out, so the true effect is about 21 percent.
The replication failed because laboratories differ; the original finding stands.

questions.explanation: A small study with a large reported effect is the profile of an inflated estimate; a large preregistered multi-lab test removes most analytic flexibility and estimates the effect precisely. Inflation does not require fraud, and averaging a tiny study with a huge one is not how evidence should be combined.

optionFeedback.a: Small samples, flexible analysis and publication filters can inflate effects without any misconduct.
optionFeedback.c: Studies should be weighted by precision; the multi-lab estimate dominates.
optionFeedback.d: Lab differences were part of the design and the pooled estimate is still near zero; the objection would need specific, testable conditions.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that is supported by this week’s evidence on motivation.

options.text: Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing an interesting task tend to reduce later free-choice engagement in experiments.
Any payment for work destroys intrinsic motivation.
Intrinsic motivation remained a predictor of performance when incentives were present.
Positive verbal feedback tends to enhance intrinsic motivation.
Self-determination theory treats all extrinsic motivation as equally controlled.
Incentives were associated more with quantity of performance than with quality.

questions.explanation: The undermining effect is conditional on reward type and contingency; verbal feedback tends to help. The forty-year meta-analysis found intrinsic motivation remained predictive alongside incentives, with incentives more related to quantity. Self-determination theory explicitly distinguishes forms of extrinsic motivation, some of which are autonomous.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of the proposal, and the best alternative?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: at a public library system, experienced librarians have for years voluntarily mentored new staff. The director proposes paying $50 per completed mentoring session to “show we value it.”

options.text: No risk; paying for valued behavior always increases it.

Payment may reframe mentoring from professional contribution to a low-paid task and crowd out voluntary effort; recognition, protected time and a mentoring role in promotion criteria are lower-risk ways to show value.
The payment is too large and should be reduced to $10.
Mentoring should be made mandatory instead.

questions.explanation: Small payments for behavior sustained by professional norms risk replacing the norm with a price, as in the day-care example, and can signal that the task is unpleasant. Recognition and resources that support competence and relatedness show value without pricing the behavior.

optionFeedback.a: The crowding-out evidence shows payment does not always increase the paid behavior.
optionFeedback.c: A smaller payment does not avoid reframing and may make the task look less valued.
optionFeedback.d: Mandating it converts autonomous motivation into controlled motivation, the opposite of the goal.

questions.prompt: A salesperson has closed 92 units with ten days left in the quarter. The plan pays a $50 commission per unit plus a one-time $8,000 bonus if the quarter reaches 100 units. If she can pull exactly 8 units forward from next quarter, what is her average payoff per pulled-forward unit from the threshold bonus alone, in dollars? (Ignore the commission, which she earns in either quarter.)
questions.working: The bonus is earned only if she reaches 100. Pulling 8 units forward moves her from 92 to 100 and earns the $8,000 bonus. $8,000 ÷ 8 units = $1,000 per unit — twenty times the $50 commission. This is why thresholds create intense timing incentives near the cliff.
questions.explanation: Near the threshold, each unit moved across the quarter boundary is worth $8,000 divided by the 8 units needed, or $1,000, compared with $50 in commission. Threshold payout shapes concentrate incentive intensity near the target and invite timing games.

questions.prompt: You lead a team of software engineers. A new bonus on story points delivered per sprint has raised throughput by a third, but defect reports from customers are up and senior engineers have stopped reviewing others’ code. With a limited budget and a board that likes the throughput number, what is the best next move?

options.text: Raise the story-point bonus so that engineers can afford to spend time on reviews.
Keep the bonus but add a defect-rate penalty applied to each individual engineer.
Reduce the power of the story-point bonus, move part of it to a team-level measure that includes escaped defects, and protect code review in role expectations.
Abolish all incentives and return to the previous system without explanation.

questions.explanation: The multitask model predicts effort diversion from unmeasured tasks (review, quality) toward the paid one. Weakening the incentive on the narrow measure, broadening it at team level to include quality, and protecting review in the job design addresses the diversion without abandoning accountability.

optionFeedback.a: A stronger incentive on story points increases diversion away from unmeasured work.
optionFeedback.b: Individual defect penalties discourage taking on hard work and helping others, and invite hiding defects.
optionFeedback.d: Abolishing incentives silently forfeits the throughput gain and gives the board and team no rationale.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical regional bank pays branch staff a monthly bonus per new account opened, with self-reported data and a public leaderboard. Rank these redesigns from most to least likely to reduce unauthorized account openings while keeping a sales incentive.

options.text: Pay on accounts still active and funded after 90 days, verified by random audits, with the leaderboard removed.
Keep the per-account bonus but add a code-of-conduct training module.
Keep everything but double the number of accounts required for the bonus.
Pay on new accounts opened, but require a customer signature captured electronically.

questions.explanation: Paying on verified, durable outcomes with audits and no rivalry addresses the measure, the horizon and monitoring together. Requiring a verified customer signature closes the cheapest fabrication route but keeps a volume measure. Training changes nothing structural. Raising the target intensifies pressure on the same gameable measure and likely makes things worse.

questions.prompt: Identify the main flaw in this reasoning.

stimulus.text: Consultant’s slide: “Teams in the top quartile of psychological safety had 30 percent higher performance ratings from their own members. Therefore our psychological-safety workshop will raise your performance by 30 percent.”

options.text: It treats a cross-sectional, self-rated association as the causal effect of an intervention, and assumes the workshop changes safety by a full quartile.
Psychological safety has never been studied.
The comparison should have used the bottom quartile only.
Thirty percent is too small to matter.

questions.explanation: Same-source ratings inflate associations, performance may cause felt safety, and nothing shows the workshop changes safety, let alone by the amount separating quartiles. The meta-analytic evidence supports an association, not a causal effect of this size.

optionFeedback.b: Psychological safety has a sizeable literature, including a meta-analysis.
optionFeedback.c: Changing the comparison group does not fix the causal leap.
optionFeedback.d: The size is not the problem; the inference is.

questions.prompt: Two hospital departments receive the same 3 percent raise. Department A had been told raises would be frozen; Department B learned afterwards that a newly hired group received 8 percent. According to this week’s material, why might B react much worse?

options.text: B’s staff are more materialistic.
Fairness is judged against reference points and inferred intentions; B’s reference point is the new hires’ raise and the undisclosed difference may be read as disrespect.
The raise in B is objectively smaller.
People only care about absolute pay, so the reactions should be identical.

questions.explanation: The same amount is compared with different reference points — a freeze in A, a peer’s larger raise in B — and the way B learned of the difference invites an inference about intentions. Reciprocity responds to perceived kindness or unkindness, not only to amounts.

optionFeedback.a: A dispositional explanation ignores the different situations the two departments are in.
optionFeedback.c: The raises are identical in size.
optionFeedback.d: This contradicts the evidence that fairness judgments are relative and intention-sensitive.

questions.prompt: A team’s willingness to do unglamorous shared work has declined. Select every change that this week’s evidence suggests could help.

options.text: Address visible free riding promptly and consistently.
Introduce a public individual leaderboard on the shared work.
Have senior, high-status members visibly do the shared work.
Recognize contributions to shared work in ways peers can see and endorse.
Announce that anyone not contributing will be monitored by continuous tracking.
Ignore it; norms always recover on their own.

questions.explanation: Conditional cooperators withdraw when free riding goes unaddressed, so addressing it matters. Norms spread through visible behavior by high-status members, and informational, peer-endorsed recognition supports competence and relatedness. Leaderboards add rivalry; blanket surveillance signals distrust; norms that have begun to unravel do not reliably recover unaided.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical public school district plans to pay teachers a bonus based on the share of students passing a standardized test each spring. In 150–250 words, predict two intended and two unintended consequences, using at least two concepts from different lessons this week, and propose one design change that reduces an unintended consequence while keeping some accountability.
questions.modelAnswer: Intended: teachers will spend more effort on tested skills and on students near the passing line, and weak instruction in tested subjects may become visible. Unintended (multitask): effort will move away from untested subjects, deeper projects and students far above or below the passing threshold, because the measure pays only for crossing a line — a threshold payout shape. Unintended (gaming): some schools may narrow who sits the test or teach test formats rather than skills, so the pass rate decays as a measure of learning. A further risk (crowding out and reciprocity) is that teachers who see themselves as professionals may read individual pay on a single test as distrust, weakening voluntary effort such as mentoring colleagues. Design change: base a smaller, school-level bonus on growth across the full score distribution over two years, audited for test participation, combined with peer-reviewed professional goals. This keeps accountability while reducing the threshold incentive and the rivalry and distrust signals of individual pay.

rubric.criterion: Predicts intended and unintended consequences with mechanisms
levels: 0 — consequences listed without mechanisms
1 — some mechanisms named
2 — two intended and two unintended consequences, each tied to a mechanism

rubric.criterion: Uses concepts from at least two lessons correctly
levels: 0 — no course concepts or misused
1 — one lesson’s concept used correctly
2 — concepts from two or more lessons used correctly

rubric.criterion: Proposes a design change that targets a named side effect and keeps accountability
levels: 0 — no change or abolishes accountability
1 — change proposed but not linked to a side effect
2 — targeted change with its own likely trade-off noted

reserve.prompt: You chair a panel deciding which of five vendors to select. Given the conformity evidence, which procedure best protects independent judgment?

options.text: The most senior member states a view first to give the group direction.
Members submit written rankings independently before discussion; the chair speaks last.
Discuss openly and vote by show of hands.
Let the vendor with the most enthusiastic supporter win.

reserve.explanation: Conformity pressure is strongest when people hear a majority or high-status view before forming their own. Independent written judgments before discussion, with the chair last, preserve the information each member holds.

optionFeedback.a: A senior first view invites conformity toward it.
optionFeedback.c: Public voting after discussion adds visible conformity pressure.
optionFeedback.d: Enthusiasm is a social signal, not evidence.

reserve.prompt: Which incentive design fits this task best, given the evidence on incentives and intrinsic motivation?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: a logistics firm needs warehouse staff to scan and shelve a backlog of 40,000 returned items in two weeks. The task is repetitive and staff report little interest in it. Accuracy can be checked automatically by scanner.

options.text: No incentive; intrinsic motivation will carry the work.
A direct per-item incentive with automatic accuracy checks, time-limited to the backlog.
A peer-recognition program only.
A ranking tournament where the bottom quartile loses shifts.

reserve.explanation: For low-interest, volume tasks with cheap quality checks, direct incentives raise quantity with little intrinsic motivation at stake. Automatic accuracy checks limit gaming, and time-limiting avoids converting an ongoing role into piece work.

optionFeedback.a: There is little intrinsic interest to rely on for this task.
optionFeedback.c: Recognition is valuable but weak for a short, repetitive volume push.
optionFeedback.d: Penalizing the bottom quartile adds rivalry and fear without a quality benefit.

reserve.prompt: Why do principals use incentive pay at all, according to agency theory?

options.text: Because agents are dishonest.
Because the principal cannot directly observe the agent’s effort and pays on outcomes correlated with it.
Because incentive pay is always cheaper than salary.
Because incentives eliminate the need for monitoring.

reserve.explanation: Incentive pay is a response to hidden action: when effort is unobservable, paying on correlated outcomes motivates effort. The cost is that pay then depends on noise and on what the measure misses.

optionFeedback.a: The model needs only divergent interests and hidden effort, not dishonesty.
optionFeedback.c: Incentive pay shifts risk to agents, who typically require compensation for bearing it.
optionFeedback.d: Incentives on imperfect measures increase the need to monitor for gaming.

reserve.prompt: Near-miss reports in your clinical laboratory have dropped to almost zero since a technician was disciplined after reporting a sample mix-up. What is the best next move?

options.text: Pay a bonus for each near-miss report.
Separate reporting from performance evaluation, make the response to honest error visibly non-punitive, and have senior staff report their own near-misses first.
Require every technician to file at least two reports per month.
Wait; reporting will recover once people forget the incident.

reserve.explanation: The drop is a predictable response to a punished messenger. Changing the consequences of reporting and having high-status members model the norm addresses the cause. Paying per report or setting quotas invites trivial or fabricated reports.

optionFeedback.a: Paying per report risks pricing a professional norm and inviting low-value reports.
optionFeedback.c: Quotas turn reporting into a gameable count.
optionFeedback.d: Norms reinforced by a visible punishment rarely recover on their own.

assignment.title: Incentive Misalignment Audit: The Mesa Verde Condors

brief.text: The Mesa Verde Condors are a fictional professional baseball organization with a major-league club, several minor-league affiliates, an amateur scouting department, an international program, a player-development staff and a research and analytics group. Use only generic, hypothetical situations; do not draw on confidential information or the practices of any real organization. Invent the specific measures and pay arrangements you analyze, stating them as assumptions.

Your task is to audit the organization’s incentive structure and identify at least three plausible misalignments between groups — for example between amateur scouting and player development, between player development and the major-league coaching staff, or between front-office metrics and what any of these groups are asked to do. For each, explain the mechanism using this week’s concepts, propose a redesign, and predict the side effects of your redesign honestly. A redesign that creates no new problem has not been examined carefully enough.

items: Possible measures to consider (invent and state your own): signing-class outcomes credited to scouts; the number of players promoted or reaching the majors credited to development staff; short-term statistical improvement credited to coaches; win–loss and individual statistics at affiliates; report volume or model adoption credited to analysts; budget adherence credited to department heads.
Possible levers: what is measured, whose performance counts, horizon and deferral, payout shape, monitoring and discretion, status and recognition, decision rights.
Remember the social economy: reciprocity between departments, norms about sharing information, fairness of credit, and whether staff can safely report that something is not working.

brief.text: Write as an internal memo to a fictional general manager. Data, if any, must be labelled synthetic.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,400-word memo identifying three incentive misalignments in a fictional baseball organization, with mechanisms, redesigns and predicted side effects.

template.heading: Summary and recommendation
template.guidance: In three to five sentences, state the three misalignments and the single redesign you would prioritize first, and why.

template.heading: Assumed incentive structure
template.guidance: Describe the measures, rewards, horizons and decision rights you are assuming for each group. Make clear these are hypothetical.

template.heading: Misalignment 1–3: mechanism
template.guidance: For each misalignment, describe what is rewarded, what is hoped for, and the mechanism (multitask diversion, gaming, crowding out, free riding, fairness, status). Cite course concepts.

template.heading: Redesigns
template.guidance: For each misalignment, propose a specific change in measure, unit, horizon, payout shape, monitoring or non-financial levers. Explain why it should help.

template.heading: Predicted side effects and how you would detect them
template.guidance: For each redesign, name the most likely new problem (new gaming route, cost, weaker effort, fairness concerns) and the early-warning signal you would watch.

template.heading: Evidence and uncertainty
template.guidance: Distinguish which parts of your reasoning rest on robust evidence, which on theory, and which on your own judgment. Say what information would change your recommendation.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Three distinct, plausible misalignments across different groups, each with a clear rewarded-versus-hoped-for contrast and a precise mechanism.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Three plausible misalignments with mechanisms; one is less precise or overlaps another.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Misalignments are generic or mechanisms are asserted rather than explained.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Fewer than three misalignments, or problems described as individual character flaws.

rubric.criterion: Use of course concepts and evidence

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Uses concepts from at least three lessons accurately, with evidence strength stated correctly (meta-analysis vs. theory vs. heuristic).

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Uses concepts from two or three lessons accurately; evidence strength mostly stated.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Concepts used loosely or evidence strength overstated.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Concepts absent or misapplied; popular claims presented as settled science.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Redesigns are specific, target the named mechanism, integrate several levers and remain feasible.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Redesigns are specific and targeted; integration across levers is partial.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Redesigns are vague or would not address the mechanism.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No redesigns, or redesigns simply remove all accountability.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Each redesign has a credible predicted side effect and a concrete early-warning signal.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Most redesigns have credible side effects and signals.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Side effects are generic or signals missing.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Side effects not considered.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Recommendation leads; concise and well structured; hypothetical status and synthetic data clearly labelled; no confidential or real-organization material.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear and labelled, with minor structure or length issues.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recommendation buried or labelling inconsistent.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Disorganized, or relies on real organizations or confidential detail.

prompts: Recall a time you attributed a colleague’s behavior to their character. What situational feature — measure, norm, status, friction — might have produced the same behavior in most people? What would you do differently now?
Which parts of your own work do you do for intrinsic reasons, and which for external ones? Has any reward, metric or evaluation ever changed how you felt about work you used to enjoy?
Identify one measure in your professional world that you think has started to decay under pressure. Who benefits from it continuing to be used, and what would it cost to replace it?
When did you last see someone in a meeting hold back a dissenting view? What about the situation made dissent costly, and what could the person chairing have changed?

review.front: What does it suggest when the same performance problem recurs across different people in the same role?
review.back: That features of the role or situation — measures, norms, status, friction — are likely contributors and should be examined before individual character.

review.front: Summarize the meta-analytic evidence on conformity in Asch-type tasks.
review.back: Robust but variable: larger with larger majorities and in more collectivist cultures, and declining in U.S. samples over the decades after Asch.

review.front: What did the 2015 Open Science Collaboration find about replication effect sizes?
review.back: Replication effects averaged roughly half the original estimates; far fewer replications than originals were significant, and social psychology replicated less often than cognitive psychology.

review.front: What happened when ego depletion was tested in a preregistered multi-lab replication?
review.back: The pooled effect was close to zero; the popular “willpower runs out” claim lacks reliable support.

review.front: Name the three basic needs proposed by self-determination theory.
review.back: Autonomy, competence and relatedness.

review.front: Which rewards most reliably undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation in experiments?
review.back: Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing, completing or performing the task. Verbal positive feedback tended to enhance it; unexpected rewards had little effect.

review.front: What happened after a fine for late pickup was introduced at Israeli day-care centers?
review.back: Late pickups rose and stayed high after the fine was removed — the price replaced a moral obligation.

review.front: According to the forty-year meta-analysis, how do intrinsic motivation and incentives relate to performance?
review.back: They jointly predict it; intrinsic motivation remained predictive with incentives present, relates more to quality, and matters less when incentives are directly tied to performance. Incentives relate more to quantity.

review.front: Why do principals use incentive pay, and what does it cost?
review.back: Effort is unobservable, so they pay on correlated outcomes. The cost: pay depends on luck and on whatever the measure misses.

review.front: State the multitask problem in one sentence.
review.back: Strong incentives on easily measured tasks pull effort from hard-to-measure ones, so weaker incentives or job redesign can be optimal.

review.front: Why does a measure decay once pay depends on it?
review.back: People find cheaper ways to move the measure than to move the goal, so the measure’s correlation with the goal weakens (Goodhart’s and Campbell’s laws).

review.front: What behavior does a threshold (cliff) bonus invite?
review.back: Shifting results across periods near the threshold and easing off when the target is far above or out of reach.

review.front: What happens to cooperation in repeated public-goods games with and without sanctions?
review.back: Without sanctions it typically declines as conditional cooperators withdraw; with the option to punish free riders it can be sustained.

review.front: Why can identical raises feel fair in one unit and unfair in another?
review.back: Fairness is judged against reference points (prior pay, peers, expectations) and inferred intentions, not only amounts.

review.front: What is the main limitation of the evidence that psychological safety improves performance?
review.back: Most studies are cross-sectional and same-source, so causal direction and common-method bias are unresolved.

preview.text: This week’s ideas recur throughout the semester. Motivation reappears in Week 3 as a condition for learning and skill acquisition. The replication record is examined statistically in Week 4. Trust, feedback and psychological safety become leadership practices in Week 5, and status and informal power become organizational politics in Week 6. Principal–agent problems return in Week 7’s negotiation and contracting, and incentive alignment, Goodhart’s law and performance management are the core of Week 8’s organizational design. Week 13 asks who is accountable when systems produce misconduct.

weeks.title: How Humans Learn and Develop Expertise
weeks.theme: Learning Science, Skill Acquisition & Deliberate Practice
weeks.question: What actually makes people get better at difficult skills — and how would you know whether a development system is producing learning or only good-looking practice?

overview.text: Every organization that develops people — a surgical residency, a flight school, a consulting firm, a conservatory, a professional sports club — runs on a theory of how humans learn, whether or not anyone has written it down. That theory decides how practice is scheduled, how much coaches talk, what feedback looks like, what gets measured and who is judged to be improving. This week asks you to make that theory explicit and to test it against the evidence.

The week moves from memory to mastery. Lesson 1 establishes the distinction that organizes everything else: performance during practice is not the same as learning, and conditions that make practice look worse — retrieval, spacing, interleaving — often make learning last. Lesson 2 examines deliberate practice: a valuable description of high-quality practice, attached to a popular myth about hours, and the subject of a live dispute about how much practice explains. Lesson 3 turns to motor learning, where laboratory findings on practice schedules, feedback and attention are striking, but several shrink in applied settings or under bias correction, and two theoretical camps disagree about what is being learned. Lesson 4 covers cognitive load, the limits of transfer, the learning-styles myth and the measurement of learning.

Throughout, you will grade claims rather than collect them. Some principles are well supported; some are contested; some are plausible hypotheses; some are myths with excellent marketing. Your exercise asks you to design practice plans and see the learning–performance trade-off in action; your case puts you inside a residency program choosing between an expensive evidence-informed system and an established process its faculty trust; and your assignment asks you to build a development framework that is honest about which of its elements are research-supported and which are coaching hypotheses.

objectives: Distinguish learning from performance and design evaluations that measure retention and transfer rather than practice success.
Evaluate deliberate-practice theory and its critiques, interpreting variance-explained estimates and range restriction correctly.
Grade motor-learning principles — contextual interference, feedback frequency, attentional focus, constraints-led design — by laboratory, applied and bias-corrected evidence.
Explain cognitive load, the limits of transfer and the learning-styles myth, and individualize instruction by expertise rather than by labels.
Build an evidence-informed development framework that separates research-supported elements from coaching hypotheses.

concepts.name: Feedback frequency and the guidance hypothesis
Ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach

lessons.title: Learning Is Not Performance: Memory, Retrieval and Desirable Difficulties
lessons.summary: What you see during practice is performance; learning is what survives a delay and a change of context — and the two can move in opposite directions.
objectives: Distinguish learning from performance and explain why only delayed or changed-context tests can reveal learning.
Explain retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving, and rank them by the strength of their evidence.
Diagnose a training program whose success metrics reward performance at the expense of learning.
lessons.executive: Most organizations judge training by how it looks while it happens: smooth sessions, high completion scores, confident trainees. Research on learning shows that these signals are unreliable and sometimes inverted. Conditions that make practice harder — retrieving instead of rereading, spacing sessions apart, mixing problem types — tend to depress in-session performance and improve what is retained weeks later. Learners and instructors routinely prefer the easier, less effective condition because it feels like progress. For an executive, the implication is managerial, not academic: if your dashboards measure only practice performance, you are rewarding the wrong thing. Ask for delayed and transfer measures before you judge any development program.

explore.text: Two hospitals train new nurses on the same rapid-response protocol. Hospital A runs a polished two-day course: instructors walk through the algorithm, trainees reread a laminated card, and on Friday afternoon everyone passes the checklist with near-perfect scores. Hospital B spreads the same content over three weeks. Each short session begins with trainees trying to reconstruct the algorithm from memory before they see it, and scenarios are mixed so that no one knows which emergency comes next. Hospital B’s trainees make more mistakes in their sessions and rate the course as harder and less satisfying. The scenario is hypothetical, but the pattern it describes is one of the best-documented findings in the science of learning.

Before reading on, predict: on the Friday of training, which hospital’s nurses score higher? Six weeks later, when a real alarm sounds on a night shift, which group is more likely to recall the algorithm correctly? How confident are you in each prediction?

A classic experiment makes the pattern concrete. Students read prose passages and then either restudied them or took a recall test with no feedback. On a test five minutes later, restudying won. On tests two days and one week later, the students who had been tested remembered more. The students who restudied also felt more confident about how much they would remember — confidence pointed the wrong way ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](R-roediger-2006-test-enhanced)).

If you predicted that Hospital A wins on Friday and Hospital B wins on the night shift, you already hold the central idea of this week. The difficulty is not knowing it; it is acting on it when every signal available during training — scores, smiles, trainee ratings, the instructor’s sense that the session went well — points the other way.

understand.title: Prerequisite: memory in three verbs

blocks.text: Memory researchers describe three processes. **Encoding** turns an experience into a memory trace. **Storage** keeps it over time. **Retrieval** brings it back when it is needed. Working memory is the small, temporary workspace in which you hold and manipulate information right now; long-term memory is the large store of what you know. Training is useful only if what is encoded today can be retrieved later, in a different place, under different pressure. A training session therefore has to be judged by what it does to future retrieval, which you cannot observe during the session itself.

understand.text: Two quantities that look like one

**Performance** is what a learner does during or immediately after practice. **Learning** is a relatively permanent change in capability that supports retention (doing it later) and transfer (doing it in new conditions). Soderstrom and Bjork’s integrative review shows that the distinction runs through decades of research in animal learning, motor learning and verbal learning: learning can occur without visible gains in performance, performance gains can fail to produce learning, and some manipulations push the two in opposite directions ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)).

A useful way to picture this, developed in Bjork’s research program and discussed in the review, separates how well something is stored from how easily it can be retrieved at this moment. Practice that makes retrieval easy right now — repeating the same thing, rereading, being told the answer — produces high current performance but adds relatively little to durable storage. Practice that makes retrieval effortful, but still successful, does more to strengthen what remains available later ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)).

understand.caption: Practice conditions sorted by what they do to in-session performance and to long-term learning
cells: Undesirable difficulty: tasks beyond the learner’s current capability, overload, confusion without success
The illusion zone: massed repetition, rereading, constant guidance — practice looks excellent and fades
Desirable difficulty: retrieval, spacing, interleaving, varied practice — practice looks worse and lasts
The rare ideal: practice that is both fluent and durable, usually because the skill is already well learned
understand.note: APERTURE teaching device. Placement of particular techniques reflects the evidence summarized in this lesson; the boundaries between quadrants depend on the learner and the task.

understand.text: Desirable difficulties and the evidence behind each

“Desirable difficulties” is the label for conditions that slow down or complicate acquisition yet improve retention and transfer. The best-supported are retrieval practice and spacing. In a long review of ten study techniques, Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice as having high utility; interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation as moderate; and summarization, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic, imagery for text and rereading as low ([Dunlosky et al., 2013](R-dunlosky-2013-improving)).

understand.caption: Evidence ratings for common learning techniques
rows: Recalls information or solves a problem without looking, then checks
Effortful retrieval strengthens later access and exposes gaps
Spreads practice across sessions instead of cramming
Partial forgetting between sessions makes each retrieval more effortful and more useful
Mixes different problem types or categories within a session
Forces the learner to choose the right approach, not just execute it
Explains why a step or fact is true
Links new material to what the learner already knows
Reviews or marks the material again
Creates familiarity, which feels like knowing but is not recall
understand.note: Ratings from the cited review, which concerns academic learning (facts, concepts, problem solving). The right-hand column is a simplified summary.

understand.text: The ratings come with an important boundary. The review concerns academic material — facts, concepts and problem solving — and its strongest conclusions apply to knowledge that must be retrieved later ([Dunlosky et al., 2013](R-dunlosky-2013-improving)). Motor skills have their own literature, which shows the same learning–performance pattern in laboratory studies ([Shea and Morgan, 1979](R-shea-1979-contextual)) but, as you will see in [the motor-learning lesson](#w03-l3), with more uncertainty about how far the effects carry into real practice.
How each difficulty works in practice

**Retrieval practice** means pulling information out of memory rather than putting it back in. Low-stakes quizzes, explaining a procedure from memory before checking it, sketching a play diagram from scratch, or answering “what would you do next?” before the answer is shown all qualify. The retrieval must be genuinely effortful: looking at the answer and nodding along is rereading in disguise.

**Spacing** means distributing the same amount of practice over more sessions with gaps between them. The gaps allow some forgetting, which makes the next retrieval harder and more productive. Spacing has an awkward property for organizations: it takes longer on the calendar, even when total practice time is identical, and so it collides with schedules built around intensive courses and boot camps.

**Interleaving** means mixing different kinds of problems or tasks within a session instead of practicing one kind at a time. Its value lies in forcing a choice. When every problem in a block is the same type, the learner never practices deciding which approach applies; in a mixed set, choosing is part of the task. Interleaving is especially relevant when the real challenge is recognizing which situation you are in — a diagnosis, a market condition, an opponent’s tendency.

Why do people resist these methods? Because the feeling of learning comes from fluency — how easily material comes to mind during practice — and fluency is highest under exactly the conditions that produce the least durable learning. Learners in the testing-effect experiments were more confident after restudying, not after testing ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](R-roediger-2006-test-enhanced)), and the review of learning versus performance documents the same misreading among learners and instructors across many paradigms ([Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](R-soderstrom-2015-learning)).

understand.caption: Why easy practice misleads everyone in the room

steps.label: Easy condition
steps.text: Massed, repetitive, guided practice keeps the answer close at hand.

steps.label: High fluency
steps.text: Performance rises quickly; errors are rare; the session feels productive.

steps.label: Misread signal
steps.text: Learner and instructor treat fluency as learning and rate the session highly.

steps.label: Delay or new context
steps.text: Days later, or under different conditions, retrieval fails.

steps.label: Wrong lesson drawn
steps.text: The failure is blamed on the learner, the pressure or the context — not on the practice design.

challenge.text: Three limits keep this idea honest. First, a difficulty is desirable only if the learner can eventually succeed. Retrieval that fails completely, with no feedback, may teach nothing; random mixing of tasks a beginner cannot yet perform may produce only confusion. Difficulty is a dose, not a virtue, and the right dose depends on what the learner already knows.

Second, the evidence is uneven across techniques. Retrieval practice and spacing rest on broad bodies of work; interleaving was rated only moderate because its evidence base was narrower ([Dunlosky et al., 2013](R-dunlosky-2013-improving)). A principle that is strong for learning vocabulary or medical facts is not automatically strong for learning a swing, a surgical knot or a negotiation.

Third, organizations do not only want learning. Sometimes they need performance now: a team preparing for tomorrow’s inspection, a player who must compete tonight, a pilot about to take a check ride. In those moments, warm-up repetition that boosts immediate performance may be exactly right. The learning–performance distinction does not tell you to always choose difficulty; it tells you to know which outcome you are buying.

challenge.title: Methodological note: the retention interval is the whole story

blocks.text: Many training evaluations measure outcomes at the end of the session. The testing-effect experiments show why that can mislead: the ranking of conditions reversed between the five-minute test and the delayed tests ([Roediger and Karpicke, 2006](R-roediger-2006-test-enhanced)). When two conditions cross over like this, an immediate test will not merely underestimate the better method; it will pick the wrong winner.

Three design rules follow. Measure after a delay long enough for forgetting to occur, ideally matched to how long the skill must last. Measure in a context that differs from practice (a transfer test), because practice conditions supply cues that real conditions will not. And keep learners’ self-ratings separate from performance measures: confidence is data about the learner’s beliefs, not about their memory. Each rule raises the cost of evaluation, which is one reason most organizations skip them.

apply.text: Consider how the distinction plays out in settings that look nothing alike. A bank’s annual compliance course ends with a quiz taken minutes after the content, and nearly everyone passes; a better design would quiz employees again, briefly, months later, and teach by asking questions first. A law firm onboarding new associates on court deadlines could replace a reading packet with short weekly retrieval exercises spaced across the first quarter. An army unit drilling a procedure could mix scenarios unpredictably instead of rehearsing them in a fixed order. These are hypothetical designs, but each applies a principle with strong evidence for knowledge that must be recalled under pressure.

apply.title: Executive twist: your dashboard rewards the wrong thing

blocks.text: Imagine you run a development department whose quarterly report shows practice-session success rates rising, trainee satisfaction at record highs and every module completed on time. A new staff member proposes redesigning sessions so that success rates will fall and satisfaction will probably drop for a while. You have no long-term data, your budget review is in six weeks, and the people who report to you are proud of the current numbers.

The question is not whether the new design is better — you do not yet know. It is what evidence you would need, and how to buy that evidence cheaply. A defensible move is to run both designs for one cohort, add a delayed retention test and a transfer test that neither group practiced, and tell your own leadership in advance that the new design is expected to look worse during sessions. Pre-registering the expectation protects the experiment from being killed by the very signal it predicts.

apply.text: In player development, the same trap appears in the metrics staff watch daily. Practice data — strike rates in a bullpen session, contact quality in the cage, success on a receiving drill — are performance measures taken in conditions the practice itself controls. Durable learning shows up later and elsewhere: in the first session after a few days off, in a different drill, in a game. A development program that wants to know whether its practice designs work needs scheduled “cold” checks and transfer checks, not only better tracking of what happens inside each session.
Name one training program you have led or attended. What did it measure, and when? What single change to its measurement would have told you whether anyone learned?

retain.text: Performance is what you observe during practice; learning is what remains after a delay and transfers to new conditions. Retrieval practice and spacing have the strongest evidence for durable learning of knowledge; interleaving is promising with a narrower base. Desirable difficulties lower in-session performance and feel worse, so learners, instructors and dashboards systematically prefer the less effective condition. The defense is measurement: delayed tests, transfer tests, and confidence measured separately from competence.
Without looking back: what reversed between the five-minute test and the one-week test in the testing-effect experiments, and what happened to students’ confidence?
Which two techniques received the highest utility rating in the review of ten learning techniques, and which two popular techniques received low ratings?
Explain to a skeptical colleague, in two sentences, why a session with more errors might be the better session.

takeaways: Learning must be inferred from delayed and changed-context tests; in-session performance can mislead in either direction.
Retrieval practice and spacing have the strongest evidence; interleaving is promising but less certain.
Desirable difficulties are desirable only when the learner can eventually succeed.
Learner confidence and instructor impressions tend to favor the less effective practice condition.
Decide whether you need performance now or learning later, and measure accordingly.

check.prompt: A sales team completes a product-knowledge course and scores 94% on a quiz taken at the end of the final session. Which additional result would give you the strongest evidence that the team learned the material?

options.text: Trainees rate the course 4.8 out of 5 for usefulness.
A different set of questions, given unannounced five weeks later, still produces high scores.
The same quiz, retaken an hour later, produces 97%.
Instructors report that trainees were engaged and made few errors in role-plays.

check.explanation: Learning is a durable change that supports retention and transfer, so it must be measured after a delay and ideally with items that were not practiced. An unannounced test five weeks later with new questions tests both. The other options measure satisfaction, immediate performance or in-session impressions, all of which can be high when little is retained.

optionFeedback.a: Satisfaction ratings measure how the course felt. Easier, more fluent courses often feel better while producing less durable learning.
optionFeedback.c: Retaking the same quiz an hour later measures short-term performance on familiar items, not retention or transfer.
optionFeedback.d: Engagement and low error rates during practice are performance signals; desirable difficulties often increase errors during practice.

check.prompt: According to the review of ten learning techniques discussed in this lesson, which techniques received a HIGH utility rating? Select all that apply.

options.text: Practice testing (retrieval practice)
Rereading
Distributed practice (spacing)
Highlighting
Interleaved practice

check.explanation: Dunlosky and colleagues rated practice testing and distributed practice as high utility. Interleaved practice was rated moderate because its evidence base was narrower, and rereading and highlighting were rated low despite being popular.

lessons.title: Deliberate Practice and Its Critics: What Explains Expertise?
lessons.summary: Deliberate practice describes what high-quality practice looks like, but the claim that accumulated practice explains most differences between people has not held up well.
objectives: Define deliberate practice and distinguish it from play, work, competition and mere repetition.
Interpret “variance explained” correctly and explain why a modest figure does not mean practice is unimportant.
Evaluate both sides of the deliberate-practice debate, including the replication of its founding study.
lessons.executive: Deliberate-practice theory gave organizations a valuable description of high-quality practice: specific goals, effortful work on weaknesses, immediate feedback, expert design. It also produced a popular myth — that roughly ten thousand hours of practice make anyone an expert. The evidence separates the two. Meta-analyses find that accumulated practice explains a real but modest share of performance differences — about 18% in sport, and about 1% among elite athletes — and the founding study replicated with a smaller effect. Its defenders reply that the critics measured the wrong kind of practice. For leaders, the practical conclusion is to invest in practice quality while not treating hours, or a single theory, as a talent strategy.

explore.text: A hypothetical software company launches an internal “mastery academy.” Its pitch deck states that expertise takes ten thousand hours of deliberate practice, so every engineer will log practice hours in a dashboard, and promotion committees will see the totals. A technology consultancy, a regional orchestra and a youth sports federation have adopted similar language. The idea is attractive because it is egalitarian, measurable and actionable: anyone can become excellent, and the path is time.

Before reading on, write down your estimate: across studies of sport, what share of the differences in performance between athletes do you think is explained by differences in how much they have practiced? Then estimate the same share among elite athletes only.

Hold your estimates. This lesson asks two questions that are often blurred together. First, what makes a practice hour valuable? Second, how much of the difference between people — between the good and the great, the starter and the reserve — does accumulated practice explain? Deliberate-practice theory has a strong answer to the first question and a contested answer to the second.

understand.text: The original theory

Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Römer proposed that expert performance results from a long period of **deliberate practice**: effortful activity designed specifically to improve current performance, typically with a teacher who identifies weaknesses and designs tasks to address them, and with immediate feedback and repetition with refinement. They argued that many characteristics once attributed to innate talent are the result of intense practice extended for a minimum of ten years. Their supporting evidence came from music students grouped by skill level, whose retrospective estimates of accumulated practice were higher in the more skilled groups ([Ericsson et al., 1993](R-ericsson-1993-role)).

understand.caption: Not all time spent on a skill is deliberate practice
rows: Performing what you can already do; feedback is noisy and delayed
A surgeon operating on a routine list; a team playing a league match
Planned sessions, often in groups, not individualized
Individualized, effortful, designed by a teacher or expert, immediate feedback, repetition with refinement
A violinist working one bar at a time on a passage her teacher flagged
understand.note: APERTURE synthesis of the definitions used in the cited debate. The boundary between structured and deliberate practice is exactly what the two sides dispute.

understand.text: The definition is demanding. Deliberate practice is not simply “time on task.” It is targeted, usually not inherently enjoyable, and depends on someone who knows what the next improvement should be ([Ericsson et al., 1993](R-ericsson-1993-role)). That is why the theory became so influential among coaches, surgeons and music teachers: it describes good teaching.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what “variance explained” means

blocks.text: When researchers say practice “explains 18% of the variance in performance,” they mean the following. Take a group of people who differ in performance. Some of those differences line up with differences in how much they practiced. The share of the spread in performance that can be predicted from the spread in practice is the variance explained, written R² — for a single predictor, the square of the correlation r. A correlation of about .42 corresponds to roughly 18% of variance explained (.42 × .42 ≈ .18).

Three cautions follow. Variance explained describes differences between people in a particular sample, not how much any individual would improve by practicing more. It depends on how much the sample varies: if everyone practices about the same amount, practice cannot explain differences among them even if it is essential for everyone. And a small R² can still matter a great deal in competitive settings where small differences decide outcomes.

understand.text: What the meta-analyses found

understand.caption: Share of performance differences explained by accumulated deliberate practice, by domain
understand.note: Source: Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014). Professions are plotted at 1 as an upper bound; the paper reports less than 1%.

understand.text: A meta-analysis across domains found that deliberate practice explained about 26% of performance variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions. The authors concluded that deliberate practice is important but not as important as had been argued ([Macnamara et al., 2014](R-macnamara-2014-deliberate)). A sport-specific meta-analysis reached a similar overall figure — about 18% — and found that among elite athletes, accumulated practice explained only about 1% of performance differences ([Macnamara et al., 2016](R-macnamara-2016-relationship)).

The founding study was also revisited. A replication of the violin study did not reproduce the original core finding that accumulated deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level; the relationship was substantial but considerably smaller than first reported. Participants also rated teacher-designed practice as less relevant to improvement than practice alone, which complicates the original definition ([Macnamara and Maitra, 2019](R-macnamara-2019-role)).

Return to the estimates you wrote at the start of this lesson. The popular account of expertise implies that practice explains most of the differences between athletes and matters most at the top. The meta-analytic answers — under a fifth overall and close to nothing among elite athletes — contradict both implications. If your estimates were well above these figures, the gap is useful: it marks a belief held more strongly than the evidence warrants.
From hours to quality

Both sides of the debate converge on one recommendation: stop measuring practice only by its duration. Ericsson and Harwell urge researchers to record the quality of practice — whether the performer is concentrating, analyzing errors and solving problems — rather than hours alone ([Ericsson and Harwell, 2019](R-ericsson-2019-deliberate)). For an organization, that recommendation is more actionable than any variance estimate.

items: **Target:** Is there a specific, current weakness the session addresses, stated before the session starts?
**Difficulty:** Is the work near the edge of current capability — hard enough to produce errors, not so hard that success is impossible?
**Feedback:** Does the performer find out quickly and accurately how each attempt compares with the target?
**Design:** Has someone with relevant expertise designed or approved the task, rather than defaulting to habit?
**Attention:** Is the performer mentally engaged, or completing repetitions on autopilot?
**Follow-up:** Is progress on the target checked later, after a delay, rather than only within the session?

understand.caption: How a modest correlation became a popular rule

steps.label: Original claim
steps.text: Groups at higher skill levels reported more accumulated deliberate practice, over at least ten years.

steps.label: Simplification
steps.text: A group average is retold as a threshold number of hours.

steps.label: Generalization
steps.text: The number is applied to every domain and every person.

steps.label: Causal leap
steps.text: Practice is assumed to cause the skill difference, rather than skill, enjoyment or support causing more practice.

steps.label: Policy
steps.text: Organizations count hours and treat them as a measure of development.

challenge.text: The two sides of the debate are worth stating at full strength. Ericsson and Harwell argue that the meta-analyses averaged across activities that do not meet the original definition — they call it structured practice — and that when only studies matching the definition are analyzed, practice explains considerably more variance: 29%, and 61% after correcting for measurement error. They urge researchers to measure the quality of practice, such as concentration, analysis and problem solving, not just its duration ([Ericsson and Harwell, 2019](R-ericsson-2019-deliberate)). On the other side stand estimates drawn from all available studies that relate practice to performance, and a direct replication of the founding study that found a smaller effect ([Macnamara et al., 2014](R-macnamara-2014-deliberate); [Macnamara and Maitra, 2019](R-macnamara-2019-role)). APERTURE’s reading: a reanalysis restricted to a small, selected subset of studies, with corrections that depend on uncertain reliability estimates, is a weaker basis for the strong claim than its headline figures suggest — but the critics’ broad definitions may indeed dilute the effect of high-quality practice. The honest summary is that the size of the effect is unresolved.

You do not need to settle this debate to act well. Notice where the two sides agree: the quality of practice matters more than its quantity, and hours alone are a poor measure. They disagree about how much of the difference between people practice can explain, which matters for talent identification and selection more than for practice design.

Two further problems sit under both sides. First, almost all of this evidence is correlational and retrospective: people estimate, years later, how much they practiced. Second, causation can run backward. People who are initially better at something often enjoy it more, receive more coaching and opportunity, and therefore practice more. A correlation between practice and skill is consistent with practice causing skill, skill causing practice, or a third factor causing both.

The sport meta-analysis authors suggest that other factors deserve study — for example, the age at which people start an activity and certain cognitive abilities — while emphasizing that practice still matters ([Macnamara et al., 2016](R-macnamara-2016-relationship)). This is a multifactorial view of expertise: practice is necessary and helpful, but differences in outcome reflect many interacting causes.

challenge.title: Methodological note: range restriction and the elite paradox

blocks.text: Why would practice explain about 18% of differences across all athletes but only about 1% among elite athletes? Part of the answer is statistical. Elite samples are selected: everyone in them has practiced a great deal. When a variable barely varies within a sample, it cannot predict much of the variation in an outcome, even if it was essential for getting into the sample in the first place. The same logic explains why height predicts little about scoring among professional basketball players, although almost all of them are tall.

The implication is subtle. The elite-level result does not show that practice stops mattering at the top. It shows that, among people who have all practiced a lot, differences in accumulated hours are not what separates them. For a decision-maker comparing elite candidates, practice history is weak evidence; for a decision-maker designing a development pathway, practice quality is still central.

apply.text: Translate this into three hypothetical decisions. A hospital deciding whether a surgeon is ready for independent practice should look at observed performance on representative cases, not only at logged case numbers. A consulting firm that promotes on “years of experience” is using a variable that may explain little of the difference between strong and weak consultants. A music conservatory selecting students cannot infer ability from reported practice hours, but it can teach every student to practice more deliberately. In each case the theory helps with design and the critique helps with selection.

apply.title: Executive twist: the practice-hours budget

blocks.text: Suppose your department proposes a 20% increase in scheduled practice time across all developing performers, funded by cutting individualized coaching. The proposal cites deliberate-practice research. You have no internal data on how practice time relates to development outcomes, and the coaches who would lose individualized time are the most experienced.

A disciplined response distinguishes the two claims. The research cited supports the value of individualized, feedback-rich, effortful practice — which is precisely what the proposal cuts. It does not support the idea that more hours of generic practice reliably produce better outcomes. Before approving, you might ask for a small trial that varies the quality of practice rather than its quantity, with retention and transfer measures, and for a plan to track whether added hours raise injury or burnout risk.

apply.text: In player development, deliberate-practice ideas are most useful as a checklist for session quality: Does each player have a specific, current target? Is the work effortful and near the edge of capability? Is feedback immediate and informative? Has someone with expertise designed the task? They are least useful as a talent theory. A club that treats practice volume as the main driver of development risks overloading players, rewarding attendance over improvement, and misreading individual differences in response to the same program. Logging hours is easy; logging the quality of practice — target, difficulty, feedback, outcome — is harder and far more informative.

Think of a performer you know who practiced more than almost anyone and plateaued, and one who practiced less and improved fast. What, other than hours, differed between them? Which of those differences could an organization influence?

retain.text: Deliberate practice is effortful, individualized practice designed to improve specific weaknesses with immediate feedback. Its description of practice quality remains useful. Its stronger claim — that accumulated deliberate practice explains most differences in expertise — is not well supported: meta-analyses find modest shares of variance explained, about 18% in sport and about 1% among elite athletes, and the founding study replicated with a smaller effect. Defenders argue the critics measured the wrong kind of practice. Both sides agree that quality beats quantity.
Without looking: what share of performance variance did deliberate practice explain in sport overall, and among elite athletes, in the sport meta-analysis?
State the strongest argument Ericsson and Harwell make against the meta-analyses, and the strongest response to it.
Explain range restriction in one sentence using an example from outside sport.

takeaways: Deliberate practice is defined by quality — targeted, effortful, expert-designed, feedback-rich — not by hours.
Accumulated practice explains a real but modest share of performance differences, and very little among elite performers.
Variance explained describes differences between people in a sample, not how much one person can improve.
The founding study replicated with a smaller effect; the debate over definitions is unresolved.
Use the theory to design practice; do not use practice hours as a talent measure.

check.prompt: A meta-analysis finds that among elite athletes, accumulated practice explains about 1% of the variance in performance. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Practice does not matter for elite athletes, so elite programs can safely reduce training.
Among athletes who have all practiced a great deal, differences in accumulated hours do little to distinguish better from worse performers.
Elite performance is determined by genetics.
The meta-analysis must be flawed, because practice obviously matters.

check.explanation: Variance explained describes differences between people in a sample. Elite samples are selected for high practice, so practice varies little among them and cannot predict much of their variation in performance. This says nothing about whether practice was necessary to reach that level, and nothing about the specific causes of the remaining variance.

optionFeedback.a: The result does not show that practice stops mattering; it shows that differences in accumulated practice do not separate elite performers. Reducing training is a different, untested intervention.
optionFeedback.c: The result says practice explains little of the variance; it does not identify what explains the rest. Jumping to genetics is an unsupported inference.
optionFeedback.d: A small variance explained is expected when the predictor is restricted in range. It is not by itself a sign of a flawed study.

check.prompt: Which activity best fits the ORIGINAL definition of deliberate practice?

options.text: A tennis player plays three competitive sets against a regular partner.
An analyst works through a training module at her own pace with no assessment.
A pianist’s teacher identifies a weak transition, and the pianist works on it slowly with immediate correction until it is reliable.
A team runs its standard weekly practice plan.

check.explanation: The original definition requires an activity designed, often by a teacher, to improve a specific aspect of performance, with effortful work and immediate feedback. The pianist case has all of these elements. Competition, self-paced study without feedback and generic team practice lack individualized targeting or feedback.

optionFeedback.a: Competition is performing what you can already do; it lacks a targeted weakness and immediate, specific feedback.
optionFeedback.b: Self-paced study without assessment lacks feedback and expert design of the task.
optionFeedback.d: A standard group plan is structured practice, not individualized practice targeting a specific weakness.
