assumptions: The residency has forty residents, eight per year; only interns are in scope for this decision.
The department budget for education is flat for the next two years.
The accreditation site visit in ten months will ask how technical competence is assessed, but does not require any particular training model.
Simulation equipment could be leased for about 40% of the purchase price per year instead of bought (an assumption for discussion).
No patient-outcome data are available that could distinguish the two training models within the decision timeline.
questions: What does the pilot actually show, and what can it not show? List at least three explanations for the week-twelve difference other than “the Pathway works better.”

Which outcome should carry the most weight in this decision — instructor ratings during training, blinded retention and transfer tests, attending operating-room ratings, or patient outcomes — and what would it cost to measure each well?
How should Abara involve Pruitt and the less enthusiastic attendings, given that they would have to deliver whatever is chosen?
Draft the recommendation Abara could defend in a fifteen-minute meeting with Okafor, including the result that would make you reverse it in twelve months.

perspectives.title: Adopt in phases, with a fair comparison
perspectives.text: Run the Pathway for half of next year’s interns, assigned at random, with equal total practice hours in both arms, leased equipment and blinded retention, transfer and operating-room assessments. Decide on full adoption after one year. This answers the confounds Pruitt raised, limits irreversible spending and gives the accreditation visit a credible assessment story. Its costs: a year’s delay, administrative effort, and the risk that a half-hearted control arm or a half-hearted Pathway arm biases the comparison.

perspectives.title: Keep the model; add the cheap, well-supported parts
perspectives.text: Retain the boot camp and operating-room apprenticeship, but add low-cost elements with the strongest evidence: brief spaced refresher sessions before rotations that use specific devices, short retrieval-based checks, and a blinded video assessment at twelve weeks for everyone. This respects faculty capacity and internal support, costs a fraction of the Pathway, and builds the measurement system the program lacks. Its weakness: it may preserve a massed design that the evidence suggests is weak for retention, and it postpones the larger question.

perspectives.title: Adopt the Pathway now
perspectives.text: The near miss, the accreditation question and the retention data all point the same way, and every year of delay sends another cohort into the operating room with skills learned nine months earlier. The evidence on spacing and retention is strong enough to act on, and perfect evidence will never come. The risks are real: a mandated program delivered by unwilling faculty, an irreversible equipment purchase, coverage strain, and a decision that will be read as defeating Pruitt.

perspectives.title: Fix measurement first
perspectives.text: The program cannot evaluate any training model because it cannot measure technical competence: operating-room ratings do not discriminate. Spend the next year building a blinded assessment system, applied to the current model, and decide afterward. This is the most defensible epistemically and the least confrontational, but it may look like avoidance, and it leaves the identified retention gap untouched for another cohort.

case.application: Player development departments face this choice constantly: a new practice system, technology or curriculum with an evidence-informed rationale and a higher cost, against an established process that staff trust and that seems to produce good players. The same traps apply. Practice-session data favor massed, blocked, guided designs; small pilots are confounded by volunteers and unequal practice volume; game outcomes are too noisy and delayed to judge a training change quickly; and the coaches who would deliver the new system are the people whose expertise it implicitly questions. The transferable moves are the ones this case invites: separate what the evidence supports from what is hypothesis, design a fair comparison with equal practice volume, measure retention and transfer rather than only practice performance, keep commitments reversible, and give the defenders of the current system a real role in testing its replacement.

questions.prompt: A fictional bank compared two compliance-training formats. Which interpretation of the results is best supported?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. 120 new employees were randomly assigned to Format A (one four-hour session; read the policy manual twice and highlight key rules) or Format B (four one-hour weekly sessions, each beginning with a short quiz on earlier material before review).

stimulus.caption: Results (synthetic)
stimulus.note: Synthetic data for a fictional study.

options.text: Format A is better because it produced higher immediate scores and higher satisfaction.
Format B produced more durable learning; judging by the immediate test would have picked the wrong format.
Format B is better, and the study shows that spacing alone caused the difference.
No conclusion is possible because satisfaction differed between the formats.

questions.explanation: The delayed test is the measure of learning, and it favors Format B by a wide margin, while the immediate test and satisfaction favor Format A — the crossover pattern described in the learning–performance literature. Because Format B combined spacing and retrieval quizzes, the study cannot say which component produced the benefit.

optionFeedback.a: Immediate scores and satisfaction are performance and experience measures; they often favor the less effective format.
optionFeedback.c: Format B differed from A in both spacing and retrieval practice (and in reading/highlighting), so the study cannot attribute the effect to spacing alone.
optionFeedback.d: Satisfaction is an outcome, not a confound; randomization makes the delayed-test comparison interpretable.

questions.prompt: An analyst is learning a new valuation method over three weeks. Which practices would add DESIRABLE difficulty? Select all that apply.

options.text: Begin each session by reconstructing last week’s steps from memory before checking the guide.
Reread the step-by-step guide three times before starting each problem.
Spread the six hours of training across three weeks instead of one day.
Mix problems that require different methods so the analyst must decide which applies.
Assign problems far beyond the analyst’s current ability, with no feedback.
Highlight the key passages of the manual.

questions.explanation: Retrieval before checking, spacing and interleaving all make practice harder in ways that support durable learning. Rereading and highlighting are low-utility techniques that create familiarity, and impossible tasks without feedback are undesirable difficulty: the learner cannot succeed, so the effort teaches little.

questions.prompt: You lead a training function. End-of-course scores for a new client-service program are very high, and your finance partner proposes cutting the planned 30-day follow-up test to save money. The program will be rolled out to 2,000 employees next quarter. What is the best next move?

options.text: Agree; the end-of-course scores already show the program works.
Keep a short, unannounced delayed test for a random sample of participants, and state in advance what result would change the rollout.
Replace the follow-up test with a satisfaction survey, which is cheaper and covers more people.
Add more questions to the end-of-course test to make it more rigorous.

questions.explanation: End-of-course scores measure performance, which can be high when little is retained. A delayed test on a random sample is cheap relative to a 2,000-person rollout and is the only option that measures learning; stating the decision rule in advance prevents the result from being explained away.

optionFeedback.a: Immediate scores can rank programs in the wrong order; they do not show retention.
optionFeedback.c: Satisfaction measures experience, which tends to favor easier, less effective training.
optionFeedback.d: A longer immediate test is still an immediate test; rigor does not substitute for delay.

questions.prompt: Identify the most serious flaw in this argument.

stimulus.text: “Our analysis of 300 engineers shows that top performers logged twice as many hours on our internal learning platform as everyone else. Research shows that expertise comes from ten thousand hours of deliberate practice. Therefore, requiring every engineer to log more platform hours will turn more of them into top performers.” — fictional internal memo

options.text: It treats a correlation as causal (stronger engineers may log more hours, or a third factor may drive both) and equates logged hours with deliberate practice.
Three hundred engineers is too small a sample to detect any relationship.
It cites research, and research is never relevant to individual companies.
It ignores that the top performers might simply have been lucky in their assignments.

questions.explanation: The memo moves from a correlation to a causal policy without ruling out reverse causation or confounding, and it equates platform hours with deliberate practice, which is defined by targeted, effortful, feedback-rich work. It also leans on the popular ten-thousand-hour rule, which misreads the original research.

optionFeedback.b: Three hundred is a reasonable sample for detecting a correlation; the problem is the inference drawn from it.
optionFeedback.c: Research can be relevant; the problem is that this research is misread and misapplied.
optionFeedback.d: Luck is one possible confound, but the central flaw is the causal leap and the misdefinition of practice.

questions.prompt: A study reports a correlation of r = .45 between accumulated practice and performance. What percentage of the variance in performance does practice explain? Give a percentage to two decimal places.
questions.working: For a single predictor, variance explained equals the square of the correlation: R² = r × r = 0.45 × 0.45 = 0.2025, or 20.25%. The remaining 79.75% of the differences in performance are associated with other factors or measurement error.
questions.explanation: Squaring the correlation converts it into the share of variance explained. A correlation that sounds substantial (.45) corresponds to about a fifth of the variance — similar to the figure reported for practice in sport overall.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of this finding?

stimulus.text: A fictional professional soccer academy analyzes its 40 top-tier players, all of whom train full time. Accumulated training hours do not predict which players later sign professional contracts. The academy director proposes cutting training time by 25% across the academy, arguing that “the data show practice does not matter.”

options.text: The director is right; practice is irrelevant once players reach the top tier.

The finding reflects range restriction among players who all train heavily; it does not show that practice is unimportant, and any change should be tested on practice quality rather than imposed on volume.
The academy should increase training hours, because more practice always helps.
The analysis must be wrong, because practice obviously matters.

questions.explanation: When everyone in a sample trains heavily, differences in hours barely vary and cannot predict much — the same pattern as the elite-level result in the sport meta-analysis. The finding says hours do not distinguish these players; it does not say what would happen if training were cut. The defensible response is to test changes, especially in practice quality.

optionFeedback.a: A weak predictor within a restricted sample says nothing about the effect of reducing the predictor for everyone.
optionFeedback.c: The evidence does not show that more hours help these players either; it suggests hours are not what distinguishes them.
optionFeedback.d: A null correlation within a restricted range is expected and is not evidence of a flawed analysis.

questions.prompt: Rank these claims from STRONGEST to WEAKEST current evidential support, based on this week’s sources.

options.text: Random practice improves transfer of motor skills in applied sport settings.
Retrieval practice improves delayed retention of studied knowledge.
Random practice improves retention and transfer of laboratory motor tasks.
Matching instruction to learners’ preferred sensory style improves learning.

questions.explanation: Retrieval practice is rated high utility across a broad body of work. The laboratory contextual-interference effect is consistent, with a medium-to-large transfer effect in laboratory studies. In applied settings the transfer effect was small and not statistically significant, and one meta-analysis calls the benefit a myth. The learning-styles matching hypothesis lacks the crossover evidence it requires.

questions.prompt: A coach returning from a workshop wants to run every session for a group of novices with fully random practice and minimal feedback, “because the research says so.” The novices cannot yet perform the basic movement consistently. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Implement the workshop design for everyone immediately; research findings apply to all learners.
Begin with more blocked practice and more frequent feedback until the basic pattern is stable, then progressively mix tasks and fade feedback, and add a weekly cold check to see whether it works.
Reject the idea entirely, because contextual interference has been called a myth.
Let each novice choose their own schedule and feedback.

questions.explanation: Difficulty is desirable only when the learner can eventually succeed, and the evidence suggests the benefits of high interference depend on learner stage and are weaker in applied settings. A progressive design calibrates difficulty and guidance to skill, and a cold check turns the change into a testable hypothesis.

optionFeedback.a: Applied benefits are smaller and uncertain, and for learners without a stable pattern random practice is more likely to overload than to help.
optionFeedback.c: The applied evidence is contested, not settled against the principle; abandoning it entirely overcorrects.
optionFeedback.d: Learner choice may support engagement, but it does not address the calibration problem, and its learning benefits are uncertain.

questions.prompt: Two published meta-analyses of the same literature on attentional focus report the results summarized below. What should a coaching director conclude?

stimulus.caption: Summary of two meta-analyses of external versus internal focus
rows: Not the focus of the conclusion
Moderate to strong evidence in every analysis; Bayes factors favor no effect
stimulus.note: Figures as reported by Chua et al. (2021) and McKay et al. (2024).

options.text: Trust the 2021 analysis, because it is the original and was conducted by experts in the field.
The average benefit of external cues is uncertain; they are cheap and low-risk to use, but should not be taught as an established principle or used to justify bigger decisions.
External cues are harmful and should be banned from coaching.
The disagreement shows that meta-analysis is useless, so coaches should rely on their own experience.

questions.explanation: When a bias-corrected reanalysis of the same studies shrinks the effect toward zero, the honest conclusion is uncertainty. Bias corrections have assumptions of their own, so the result does not prove external cues never help; it means the principle cannot be presented as established. Because external cues cost little, using them as a default while not overselling them is reasonable.

optionFeedback.a: Being first or authored by proponents does not protect a literature from publication bias; the reanalysis used the same studies.
optionFeedback.c: Neither analysis found harm; the dispute is whether there is a reliable benefit.
optionFeedback.d: The disagreement is informative: it shows how publication bias can inflate effects. Personal experience is subject to the same fluency illusions this week describes.

questions.prompt: A vendor’s brochure for a fictional athlete-development platform makes the claims below. Select EVERY claim that should be challenged before purchase.

options.text: The platform profiles each athlete’s learning style and matches drills to it.
Its puzzle games improve on-field decision speed.
Playbook content is reviewed through spaced retrieval quizzes.
Success is shown as rising accuracy on the platform’s in-app drills.
High-repetition drills “build motor engrams” that guarantee consistency.
Delayed retention tests are built in, and results can be exported.

questions.explanation: Learning-style matching lacks supporting evidence; improvement from puzzle games to on-field decisions is a far-transfer claim that should be tested directly; rising in-app accuracy is a performance measure under practice conditions; and “building engrams” is an unfalsifiable neuroscience gloss. Spaced retrieval for knowledge content and exportable delayed retention tests are well-supported features.

questions.prompt: A hospital is considering a commercial brain-training app to improve residents’ clinical reasoning. Which judgment is best supported by evidence on transfer?

options.text: Adopt it; general cognitive training reliably improves performance in specialized professional tasks.
Be skeptical: far transfer from general training to distant tasks is rare, so invest first in practice on clinical reasoning cases themselves and test any app directly against that.
Adopt it only for residents who are visual learners.
Reject all training technology, since transfer never occurs.

questions.explanation: Reviews of chess, music and working-memory training find that far transfer to general abilities is rare and shrinks in better-controlled studies. Near transfer — practicing reasoning on cases like the real ones — is far more likely to help. Any claim of far transfer should be tested against that alternative.

optionFeedback.a: This asserts far transfer, which the evidence suggests is rare.
optionFeedback.c: Learning-style matching lacks supporting evidence and does not address the transfer problem.
optionFeedback.d: Near transfer is common; technology that practices the target task can help. The problem is distance, not technology.

questions.prompt: Choose one skill that matters in your work (technical, physical or professional). In 150–250 words, design a measurement plan that would let you tell, within three months, whether a new practice design is producing learning rather than only better practice performance. Name the measures, when they are taken, what you will deliberately NOT treat as evidence of learning, and the result that would make you abandon the new design.
questions.modelAnswer: Skill: a second-year analyst’s ability to build a defensible valuation model. Current practice: worked examples followed by similar problems. New design: spaced sessions that open with retrieval and mix problem types. Measures: (1) a short, unannounced cold problem at the start of each fortnight, before any review, scored by a reviewer who does not know which design the analyst received; (2) a transfer problem every six weeks using an industry not covered in training; (3) error rates on real deliverables, tracked but treated as noisy. Not evidence of learning: accuracy on in-session practice problems, the analyst’s confidence, and the trainer’s impression of the sessions, because all three are inflated by easier designs. Comparison: if possible, half of the cohort, assigned at random, continues the old design, with equal total practice time. Decision rule, stated in advance: if after three months the cold-check and transfer scores are not at least as good for the new design, revert, since it costs more trainer time; if they are clearly better, extend it and keep the checks running.

rubric.criterion: Separates learning measures (delayed, changed-context) from performance measures
levels: 0 — relies on in-session or immediate measures
1 — includes a delayed or transfer measure but also treats practice performance as evidence
2 — clear delayed and transfer measures
3 — clear delayed and transfer measures, and explicitly excludes practice performance and confidence
0 — no comparison
1 — before/after only
2 — a comparison group or schedule, ideally with equal practice time
0 — none
1 — vague criterion
2 — specific result that would trigger reverting or continuing

rubric.criterion: Feasibility and fit to the chosen skill
levels: 0 — impractical or generic
1 — realistic for the skill and setting

reserve.prompt: In the testing-effect experiments, students who restudied a passage rather than taking recall tests were MORE confident about remembering it. Why does this finding matter for training design?

options.text: It shows that confident learners always remember more.
It shows that learners’ sense of progress can favor the less effective method, so their preferences and confidence are poor guides to how to practice.
It shows that testing reduces motivation and should be avoided.
It shows that restudying and testing are equally effective.

reserve.explanation: Restudying produced more confidence and worse delayed retention. Fluency during study feels like learning, so learner confidence and satisfaction can systematically favor weaker methods. Training designers need delayed measures, not only learner judgments.

optionFeedback.a: The opposite occurred: the more confident group remembered less after a delay.
optionFeedback.c: The study measured confidence, not motivation, and testing improved long-term retention.
optionFeedback.d: Restudying won on an immediate test, but testing won on delayed tests.

reserve.prompt: What is the strongest version of the argument this coach is making, and its main weakness?

stimulus.text: A fictional conservatory teacher argues: “Those meta-analyses averaged everything from casual rehearsal to group lessons and called it deliberate practice. When you look only at individualized practice designed by a teacher, practice explains far more of the difference between students.”

options.text: It mirrors Ericsson and Harwell’s definitional argument; its weakness is that the supporting reanalysis rests on a small, selected set of studies and corrections that can inflate estimates.
It shows that the meta-analyses were fraudulent; it has no weakness.
It is an argument that talent is innate; its weakness is that practice obviously matters.
It is irrelevant to the debate because it concerns music rather than sport.

reserve.explanation: This is the definitional rebuttal: the meta-analyses counted structured practice, and studies matching the original definition show larger effects. The reanalysis, however, uses a small subset of studies and attenuation corrections that depend on uncertain reliability estimates, so its larger figures should be held loosely.

optionFeedback.b: Disagreement about definitions is not evidence of fraud, and the argument has real limitations.
optionFeedback.c: The teacher argues that practice matters more than the meta-analyses suggest, not that talent is innate.
optionFeedback.d: The deliberate-practice debate spans music, games, sport, education and professions; the definitional point applies across them.

reserve.prompt: Which statements accurately describe the 2024 meta-analysis of contextual interference and transfer discussed this week? Select all that apply.

options.text: Overall, random practice was favored with a medium effect on transfer.
In applied settings, the effect was small and not statistically significant.
The effect was larger in laboratory studies than in applied settings.
In young participants, the effect was especially large.
It proved that contextual interference is a myth.

reserve.explanation: The meta-analysis found a medium overall effect (SMD = 0.55), a larger and significant laboratory effect (0.75), a small non-significant applied effect (0.34) and a negligible effect in young participants (0.12). It is a different research group that argues the applied benefit is a myth.

reserve.prompt: A training lead reconciles two pieces of advice: “reduce cognitive load” and “add desirable difficulties.” Which reconciliation is best?

options.text: They contradict each other; choose one philosophy and apply it consistently.
Cut load created by poor presentation (too many cues, redundant information) and add productive difficulty (retrieval, spacing, mixing once basics are stable), calibrated to the learner’s expertise.
Reduce load for experts and add difficulty for novices.
Add as much difficulty as possible, because harder practice always produces more learning.

reserve.explanation: Extraneous load comes from how information is presented and should be cut; productive difficulty comes from what the learner must retrieve, space or choose and can be added in doses the learner can handle. Because methods that help novices can become redundant for experts, the calibration depends on expertise.

optionFeedback.a: The two ideas address different sources of difficulty and are compatible.
optionFeedback.c: This reverses the expertise logic: novices generally need more guidance and less added difficulty than experts.
optionFeedback.d: Difficulty is desirable only when the learner can eventually succeed; too much becomes undesirable.

assignment.title: An Evidence-Informed Development Framework

brief.text: Write a framework that a player development department could adopt to guide how skills are practiced, coached and measured. The framework should be general enough to apply across positions and levels, and specific enough that a new coach could use it to design a week of practice. It must contain no confidential or club-specific material; describe a fictional or generic organization.

The defining requirement is honesty about evidence. Every principle in your framework must carry a label: **Supported** (consistent evidence, including outside the laboratory where relevant), **Contested** (credible evidence on both sides, or effects that shrink under scrutiny), **Coaching hypothesis** (plausible, drawn from experience or theory, not yet tested) or **Not supported** (claims the framework explicitly rejects). A framework that labels everything “Supported” will score poorly, however persuasive it is.

items: Cite this week’s sources where you rely on research, and state the strength of the evidence in your own words.
Include at least one element you would test in your own organization, with the measure and decision rule.
Address learner stage: how the framework changes for a beginner, a developing player and an established professional.
Write for two readers at once: the head of the department, who needs the logic and the risks, and a coach, who needs to know what to do on Monday.

brief.text: Before drafting, list the five practice habits most common in the environments you know best. You will need to place each in your evidence ledger.

assignment.deliverable: A 1,400–2,000-word development framework with an evidence ledger that labels each principle Supported, Contested, Coaching hypothesis or Not supported.

template.heading: Purpose, scope and learners
template.guidance: Which skills and levels the framework covers, and what “development” means here — learning that is retained and transfers to competition, not practice success.

template.heading: Core principles
template.guidance: Five to eight principles, each with its evidence label and a one-sentence rationale citing this week’s sources where relevant.

template.heading: Practice design by learner stage
template.guidance: Scheduling (blocked, serial, random, progressive), spacing, variability and representative design for beginners, developing players and established professionals.

template.heading: Feedback and coaching language
template.guidance: Feedback frequency and type, how it fades, cue policy (one cue at a time; how external and analogy cues are used without overselling them) and how coaches avoid overloading working memory.

template.heading: Measuring learning
template.guidance: A measurement calendar with retention (cold) checks and transfer checks; which data you will not treat as evidence of learning; how competition data are used despite their noise.

template.heading: Evidence ledger
template.guidance: A table of every element: label, source or basis, and what evidence would change its label. Include at least two items you reject as Not supported.

template.heading: Implementation, coach development and review
template.guidance: How coaches learn the framework, one pilot you would run (with comparison, equal practice volume, measures and decision rule), and when the framework is reviewed.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Every research claim is accurate and appropriately cited; labels match the evidence, including laboratory–applied gaps and bias-corrected results.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Claims are accurate with minor overstatement; most labels are well matched.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Some claims are overstated or mislabelled (for example, contested principles presented as settled).

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Frequent inaccuracies or unsupported claims presented as research.

rubric.criterion: Quality of practice and feedback design

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Design is specific, coherent and calibrated by learner stage; difficulty, variability and feedback move together with skill.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Design is sound and specific, with some stage differentiation.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Design is generic or applies one prescription to all learners.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Little actionable design; principles are not translated into practice.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Clear retention and transfer measures on a realistic calendar; explicitly excludes practice performance and confidence as evidence of learning; includes a pilot with a comparison and decision rule.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Includes delayed and transfer measures and a plausible pilot, with minor gaps.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Relies mainly on practice or game data; delayed measures are vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No meaningful plan to distinguish learning from performance.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: The ledger is complete and candid; hypotheses are named as such, with tests that could change them; at least two popular claims are rejected with reasons.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Most elements are labelled honestly; tests are proposed for some hypotheses.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Labels are present but uneven; hypotheses are often presented as findings.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No meaningful distinction between evidence and belief.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A department head and a coach could both act on it; costs, staff capacity and risks are addressed concisely.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear and usable, with some gaps on cost or capacity.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Usable by one audience but not the other; feasibility is assumed.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Hard to follow or impractical.

prompts: Think of the skill you have taught or coached most often. Describe the practice design you default to — schedule, feedback, cues, measurement. Which parts did you choose because of evidence, and which because that is how you were taught?
Recall a time you judged someone’s progress from what you saw in practice and later found you were wrong. What signal misled you, and what would you measure differently now?
Which belief about talent, practice or feedback did this week challenge most for you? Write down the evidence that would make you abandon it completely — and the evidence that would make you keep it.

Apply the week to yourself: schedule three short retrieval sessions on this week’s material over the next three weeks, without rereading first. What do you predict you will remember, and how confident are you?

review.front: What is the difference between learning and performance?
review.back: Performance is what a learner does during or right after practice. Learning is a relatively permanent change that supports retention and transfer, so it must be inferred from delayed or changed-context tests.

review.front: In the testing-effect experiments, which condition won on the five-minute test, and which after one week?
review.back: Restudying won at five minutes; testing won after two days and one week. Restudiers were also more confident despite remembering less.

review.front: Which two techniques received high utility ratings in the review of ten learning techniques? Which two popular ones were rated low?
review.back: High: practice testing and distributed practice. Low (among others): rereading and highlighting.

review.front: When is a difficulty “desirable”?
review.back: When it slows acquisition but improves retention or transfer and the learner can eventually succeed. Difficulty that prevents success, or comes from poor presentation, is undesirable.

review.front: Why does interleaving help when the real task involves recognizing the situation?
review.back: Mixing problem types forces the learner to choose the right approach on each item, which blocked practice never requires.

review.front: Define deliberate practice in its original sense.
review.back: Effortful, individualized practice designed (often by a teacher) to improve a specific weakness, with immediate feedback and repetition with refinement — not simply time on task.

review.front: About how much of the variance in performance did deliberate practice explain in sport overall, and among elite athletes?
review.back: About 18% overall and about 1% among elite athletes (Macnamara, Moreau and Hambrick, 2016).

review.front: Why can a variable matter a great deal yet explain little variance among elite performers?
review.back: Range restriction: if everyone in the sample has a lot of it, it barely varies and cannot predict differences among them.

review.front: What is Ericsson and Harwell’s central objection to the deliberate-practice meta-analyses?
review.back: They counted structured practice in general rather than deliberate practice as originally defined; studies matching the definition show larger effects. The reanalysis rests on a small, selected set of studies.

review.front: What did Shea and Morgan (1979) find for blocked versus random practice?
review.back: Blocked practice was better during acquisition; random practice was better for retention (especially under random testing) and transfer.

review.front: What happens to the contextual interference effect in applied settings, according to the 2024 transfer meta-analysis?
review.back: It was small and not statistically significant (SMD 0.34), versus 0.75 in the laboratory; negligible in young participants. Another meta-analysis calls the applied benefit a myth.

review.front: What does the guidance hypothesis predict about feedback after every attempt?
review.back: Better practice performance but weaker retention, because the learner comes to depend on augmented feedback rather than their own error detection.

review.front: What is the status of the external-focus advantage?
review.back: Contested: a 2021 meta-analysis reported medium learning effects; a 2024 bias-corrected reanalysis found effects near zero with Bayes factors favoring no effect.

review.front: How does a constraints-led coach change a practice?
review.back: By manipulating task, environment and individual constraints (space, rules, equipment, opponents) so solutions emerge, rather than prescribing and correcting one technique.

review.front: What is the expertise reversal effect?
review.back: Methods that help novices, such as detailed guidance and worked examples, can become redundant or harmful for more expert learners.

review.front: What evidence would be needed to support the learning-styles matching hypothesis?
review.back: Learners classified by style, randomly assigned to matched or mismatched instruction, the same test for all, and a crossover interaction. Such evidence has not been found.

preview.text: This week gave you a working rule: judge development by what lasts and transfers, and grade every claim before you build on it. Week 4 supplies the research-literacy tools behind that rule — statistical power, publication bias, effect sizes and causal inference — so you can read a meta-analysis such as the attentional-focus dispute on your own. Week 5 treats coaching and development as a social system in which credibility and relationships decide whether good ideas are adopted, and the later weeks on organizations and execution return to the problem in this week’s case: changing an established process that people trust.

links.why: Publication bias, power and causal inference — the methods behind this week’s contested findings.
Coaching, feedback and leadership as a social system, not only a technique.
Designing the department that delivers development, including roles and incentives for coaches.
Implementing a change like the Skills Pathway against established practice.

weeks.title: How to Know What Is True
weeks.question: When a study, a dashboard or a trusted colleague says something works, how do you decide how much to believe it and what to do about it?

overview.text: Executives are paid to act on evidence they did not produce: analyses from their staff, studies from consultants and vendors, research from universities, and the apparent lessons of their own experience. Most of that evidence is neither worthless nor conclusive. This week builds the skills to tell the difference and to act sensibly in between.

The week moves in five steps. Lesson 1 separates signal from noise: regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and power, and the Bayesian logic that connects them to Week 1’s base rates. Lesson 2 examines the replication crisis as a system — flexible analysis, low power and selective publication — that operates inside organizations as well as in journals. Lesson 3 is a compact course in causal inference for executives: counterfactuals, confounding and selection, randomized trials, and the quasi-experimental designs that have transformed economics and policy evaluation. Lesson 4 adds the questions that remain after a design is credible: effect size, measurement, Goodhart’s law, external validity and survivorship. Lesson 5 asks how to combine imperfect evidence, using evidence hierarchies and meta-analysis without being ruled by them.

The Evidence Lab lets you generate thousands of simulated studies and watch exaggerated effects, false positives and missed effects emerge from design choices. The case, set in a health system, puts two respected executives on opposite sides of the same data. The assignment asks you to critique a real published study with a structured rubric. The aim is not cynicism. It is calibrated belief: knowing how much a piece of evidence should move you, and how to design your organization’s decisions so that it learns.

objectives: Distinguish signal from noise using regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and statistical power.
Explain how researcher degrees of freedom, low power and publication bias produce exaggerated and false findings, and evaluate remedies.
Identify confounding, selection and collider bias and match randomized and quasi-experimental designs to causal questions.
Critique a study’s effect size, measurement, external validity and susceptibility to metric gaming.
Combine several imperfect lines of evidence into a stated degree of belief and a proportionate decision.

concepts.name: p-values: what they are and are not
Type M and type S errors

lessons.title: Signal, Noise and the Meaning of p
lessons.summary: Every measurement mixes signal with noise; regression to the mean, confidence intervals, p-values and power are tools for keeping the two apart.
objectives: Explain regression to the mean and identify it in a performance story that offers a causal explanation instead.
Interpret a confidence interval and a p-value correctly and state what each does not tell you.
Use statistical power and prior plausibility to judge how much a significant result should change your belief.
lessons.executive: Most numbers that reach your desk are a true level plus luck. When you select people, units or quarters because they were extreme, the luck you selected on will not repeat, so they drift back toward average whatever you do: regression to the mean. A p-value tells you how surprising the data would be if nothing were going on; it does not tell you the probability the claim is true, how big the effect is, or whether it matters. Ask for the estimate with its confidence interval, the sample size, and how plausible the claim was before the data. Treat a small study’s significant result as a hypothesis, not a finding.

explore.text: A regional hospital system ranks its twenty emergency departments every quarter on door-to-provider time. The three worst departments are placed on an improvement plan: a consultant visits, managers attend a workshop, and dashboards are posted in the break rooms. Next quarter, all three improve markedly. The three best departments, which received a congratulatory letter, all get worse. The chief operating officer concludes that improvement plans work and that praise breeds complacency. This scenario is hypothetical, but the pattern is everywhere.

Before reading on: what would you expect to happen to the three worst departments next quarter if the improvement plan had done nothing at all? Write down a number of departments (0–3) you would expect to improve, and why.

Tversky and Kahneman described the same pattern in flight training. Instructors noticed that cadets who were praised after an unusually smooth landing usually did worse on the next attempt, while cadets criticized after a rough landing usually improved. The instructors concluded that criticism works and praise backfires. The authors’ point was that the instructors had discovered regression to the mean and mistaken it for a causal effect of their feedback ([Tversky & Kahneman, 1974](R-tversky-1974-judgment)).

This lesson is about the difference between signal and noise. It covers four tools that every executive who reads evidence must handle comfortably: regression to the mean, the confidence interval, the p-value and statistical power. None of them requires advanced mathematics. All of them are misunderstood by many of the people who will present evidence to you.

understand.text: Observed performance is a true level plus luck

Think of any measured result — a department’s quarterly wait time, a fund’s annual return, a salesperson’s monthly bookings, a hitter’s batting average over three weeks — as the sum of two parts: a stable underlying level and a transient component that does not repeat. The transient part includes genuine randomness, measurement error, and temporary circumstances such as a flu outbreak or an easy schedule. The proportion of variation that is stable is called the *reliability* of the measure. When reliability is high, last period predicts next period well. When it is low, last period is mostly noise.

Now select units because they were extreme. The worst three departments are, on average, departments with a somewhat worse true level *and* a bad draw of luck in that quarter. Next quarter the true level persists but the luck is redrawn, so on average they move back toward the middle. The same is true in reverse for the best performers. Regression to the mean is not a force and it does not require any intervention. It is a consequence of selecting on a noisy measure. The lower the reliability and the more extreme the selection, the larger the expected regression.

understand.caption: Why selected extremes drift back

steps.label: Measure
steps.text: Observed result = true level + transient noise

steps.label: Select
steps.text: Pick the extreme cases on the observed result

steps.label: Hidden bias
steps.text: Selected cases carry unusually large noise in the selected direction

steps.label: Re-measure
steps.text: Noise is redrawn; the true level remains

steps.label: Drift
steps.text: The group moves toward the average with or without any intervention

understand.text: A simple prediction rule follows. Your best forecast of next period is not last period’s observed value but a weighted average of it and the group mean, with the weight on the observed value equal to the measure’s reliability. If a quarterly metric has a reliability of 0.4, a department that was 10 minutes worse than average should be expected to be about 4 minutes worse next quarter. If the improvement plan produces a 6-minute gain, most of it was expected anyway. The only clean way to know whether the plan did anything is to compare treated departments with similarly extreme departments that were not treated, ideally chosen at random.

understand.title: Prerequisite: samples, sampling variability and the standard error

blocks.text: A *sample* is the subset of cases you actually observe; the *population* is the larger set you want to learn about. If you surveyed a different random sample, you would get a different average. That variation from sample to sample is *sampling variability*. Its typical size is the *standard error*: roughly the standard deviation of individual cases divided by the square root of the sample size. Quadrupling a sample halves the standard error. This square-root law is why small samples bounce around so much and why doubling a pilot’s size buys less precision than intuition suggests.

Two numbers therefore always travel together: the estimate (for example, a 3-point improvement) and its uncertainty (for example, a standard error of 2 points). An estimate without its uncertainty is half a fact.

understand.text: Confidence intervals

A 95% confidence interval is a range constructed by a procedure that, across many repeated samples, would capture the true value 95% of the time. In practice, read it as the range of effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data under the analysis assumptions. Two features matter more than whether it excludes zero. Its *location* tells you the most plausible magnitudes. Its *width* tells you how much the study actually taught you. An interval from −1 to +9 minutes and an interval from +3.8 to +4.2 minutes can both have the same center; only the second one supports a confident operational decision.
What a p-value is, and is not

A p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as what was observed, *if* a specified statistical model — usually one in which the true effect is zero — were correct, and if all its assumptions held. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued its first formal statement on a matter of statistical practice to correct widespread misuse. Among its principles: p-values can indicate how incompatible data are with a specified model; they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or that the data arose by chance alone; decisions should not rest only on whether a p-value crosses a threshold; proper inference requires full reporting; and a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect ([Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016](R-wasserstein-2016-asa)).

understand.caption: Statements about “p = .03”: which are correct?
rows: If there were truly no effect and the model were right, data this extreme would arise about 3% of the time.
There is a 3% chance the result is a fluke.
That is a statement about the hypothesis given the data; the p-value is about the data given the hypothesis.
There is a 97% chance the effect is real.
That probability depends on prior plausibility and power, which the p-value ignores.
The effect is large or important.
A tiny effect in a huge sample can produce a tiny p-value.
A replication would be significant 97% of the time.
The probability of replication depends on the true effect and the replication’s power.
p = .06 means there is no effect.
Absence of significance is not evidence of absence, especially in small samples.
understand.note: Original teaching table based on the principles in the ASA statement.

understand.text: Power: the probability of detecting what is really there

*Statistical power* is the probability that a study will produce a significant result when a true effect of a given size exists. It depends on the size of the effect, the noise in the measure, the sample size and the significance threshold. A study of 20 people per group looking for a modest effect (about a third of a standard deviation) has power of roughly 15%: it will miss the true effect about 85% of the time. Low power has a less obvious cost, taken up in [Lesson 2](#w04-l2): when a low-powered study does reach significance, its estimate is usually far too large.

understand.caption: Approximate power to detect a true effect of d = 0.3 (two-sided, p < .05)
understand.note: Synthetic illustration computed from the standard two-sample formula and simulation; values rounded.

understand.title: Methodological note: why the p-value is not the probability you want

blocks.text: The question an executive cares about is: given this result, how likely is it that the effect is real? That is a *posterior* probability. Bayes’ rule says it depends on three things: the prior probability that the tested idea is true, the power of the study, and the significance threshold. Suppose your analytics team tests 100 product ideas, of which perhaps 10 genuinely work. With power of 50% and a 5% threshold, about 5 of the 10 real effects come back significant, and about 4.5 of the 90 null ideas come back significant by chance. Roughly half of the “wins” are false. Raise power to 80% and only 8 of about 12.5 wins are real; lower the prior to 1 in 100 and false wins dominate.

This is the logic of Ioannidis’s argument that, under realistic priors, power and bias, many claimed findings in some fields are likely to be false ([Ioannidis, 2005](R-ioannidis-2005-most)). It also explains why the same p-value should move you more for a plausible, mechanistically grounded claim than for a surprising one. Week 1’s base-rate reasoning is the same arithmetic applied to research.

challenge.text: Three objections deserve a serious answer. First, some argue that p-values are fine and the problem is misinterpretation, so better training rather than new methods is the remedy. That is partly right: a p-value correctly understood is a legitimate measure of surprise under a model. But a tool that is routinely misread by trained researchers is a poor tool for executive communication. Estimates with intervals carry the same information and more.

Second, Bayesian analysts argue that executives should ask for posterior probabilities directly. That is attractive, but priors can be chosen to flatter a conclusion, and a Bayesian analysis with a hidden prior is no more transparent than a frequentist one with a hidden analysis plan. The disciplined position is to ask for the prior to be stated and for the result to be shown under a skeptical prior as well.

Third, not everything that drifts toward the mean is regression. Interventions can work, and true levels can change. The ASA statement’s emphasis on context and on full reporting is a reminder that statistical tools never substitute for design: the question is always what the comparison group was ([Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016](R-wasserstein-2016-asa)).

challenge.title: Executive twist: the board wants a yes or no

blocks.text: You chair a review of a pilot in a financial-services contact center. The pilot reduced complaint rates by an estimated 11%, with a 95% interval from −2% to +23%. The p-value is 0.09. The vendor calls it “directionally positive”; your finance lead calls it “not significant, so it failed”. Both are reasoning from the threshold. The interval says the program could plausibly do nothing or could do a great deal. The decision turns on costs: if extending the pilot is cheap and reversible, buying more information is worth it; if full rollout is expensive and hard to undo, it is not yet justified. Your job is to reframe the decision around the range of plausible effects and the cost of being wrong in each direction, not around p.

apply.text: Player development is an ideal environment for regression to the mean, because nearly every early-season statistic has low reliability and nearly every intervention is triggered by an extreme. A hitter who opens the season badly is given a mechanical adjustment and a new routine; three weeks later he has improved and the adjustment gets the credit. A pitcher with an exceptional first month is promoted and then “struggles to adjust to the level”. Some of each story may be true. The disciplined question is how much improvement or decline you would have predicted with no intervention, given the reliability of the measure over that sample.

items: Before an intervention, record the forecast for the player without it (the observed value shrunk toward his own longer-run baseline or the group mean).
Judge the intervention by performance relative to that forecast, not relative to the slump.
Where possible, compare with similarly extreme players who did not receive the intervention, or randomize which players receive it first.
Prefer process measures with higher reliability over short-sample outcomes when you need to judge quickly.

apply.text: The same discipline applies in other domains. A government agency that audits the schools with the worst test scores will see improvement next year; a private-equity firm that replaces the managers of its worst-performing portfolio companies will see recoveries; an asset manager that hires last year’s top fund will often be disappointed. In each case the honest benchmark is the regression-adjusted forecast, not last year’s extreme.

Worked problem: a quarterly employee-engagement score has a reliability of 0.5 across teams. A team scores 20 points below the company average and receives coaching. Next quarter it is 6 points below average. How much of the 14-point improvement would you have expected without coaching? (Answer: about 10 points, because the expected position is 0.5 × −20 = −10. The coaching is credited with at most about 4 points, and even that needs a comparison group.)

retain.text: Observed results combine a stable level with transient noise. Selecting on extremes guarantees drift back toward the mean, which looks like an effect of whatever you did in between. A p-value measures surprise under a null model, not the truth of a claim or the size of an effect; confidence intervals and power tell you how much a study can teach you. How much a significant result should move you depends on prior plausibility and power.
Explain to a colleague, in two sentences, why the worst performers on a noisy metric usually improve.
List three things a p-value does not tell you.
Why does the same p-value deserve less belief when power is low and the hypothesis is surprising?

takeaways: Selecting on extremes of a noisy measure produces regression to the mean with or without any intervention.
Judge an intervention against a regression-adjusted forecast or a comparison group, never against the slump that triggered it.
A p-value is the probability of data this extreme under a null model — not the probability the claim is true, and not a measure of importance.
Ask for estimates with confidence intervals, sample sizes and power; the interval’s width shows how much was learned.
The credibility of a significant result depends on prior plausibility and power, as Bayes’ rule makes explicit.

check.prompt: A sales organization gives its bottom-decile reps an intensive coaching program. Their bookings rise substantially the next quarter. What is the most important missing piece of information?

options.text: The satisfaction scores the reps gave the coaching program.
How much similarly ranked reps who were not coached improved over the same period.
Whether the improvement was statistically significant.
Whether top-decile reps declined over the same period.

check.explanation: Bottom-decile reps were selected partly for bad luck, so they would be expected to improve without coaching. Only a comparison with similarly extreme reps who were not coached separates the coaching effect from regression to the mean. Significance of the before-after change would not help, because the regression itself is a real, systematic change.

optionFeedback.a: Satisfaction with a program is not evidence of its effect on bookings.
optionFeedback.c: A before-after change can be highly significant and still be entirely regression to the mean.
optionFeedback.d: Decline at the top is what regression predicts too; it does not isolate the coaching effect.

check.prompt: A study reports a difference with p = .02. Select every statement that is correct.

options.text: If there were no true difference and the model were correct, results at least this extreme would occur about 2% of the time.
There is a 98% probability that the difference is real.
The result says nothing by itself about whether the difference is large enough to matter.
If the study had low power, the estimated difference is more likely than usual to be exaggerated.
A replication with the same design would be significant about 98% of the time.

check.explanation: Option a is the definition of a p-value. Option c follows from the ASA principle that p-values do not measure effect size or importance. Option d anticipates type-M error: in low-powered studies only overestimates clear the threshold. Options b and e confuse the p-value with the probability of the hypothesis or of replication.

The flight-instructor example of regression mistaken for a feedback effect.
Prior plausibility, power and the probability that a significant finding is true.

lessons.title: The Replication Crisis and the Garden of Forking Paths
lessons.summary: Low power, flexible analysis and selective publication combine to fill literatures with exaggerated and false findings; preregistration and registered reports are partial remedies.
objectives: Explain how researcher degrees of freedom and publication bias inflate false positives and effect sizes.
Interpret type-S and type-M errors and estimate when a significant result is likely to be exaggerated.
Evaluate preregistration and registered reports as remedies, including their limits.
lessons.executive: A large share of published behavioral science has not replicated, and the published effects that do replicate are usually smaller than first reported. The cause is not mainly fraud. It is a system: small studies, many defensible analytic choices made after seeing data, and journals and managers who reward significant, surprising results. The same system operates inside organizations whenever analysts can choose metrics, segments and stopping points after the fact. Ask whether the analysis was specified before the data arrived, how many outcomes were examined, and how large the sample was. Expect real effects to be smaller than the first study suggested.

explore.text: Imagine a technology company’s growth team that reports a string of successful experiments: a new checkout button lifted conversion 9%, a revised onboarding email lifted retention 12%, a loyalty badge lifted engagement 15%. Finance notices that the company’s overall conversion, retention and engagement have barely moved in two years. Every experiment was “significant”. Where did the gains go? This scenario is hypothetical, but its arithmetic is exactly the arithmetic of the replication crisis.
Before reading on: list three ways an honest analyst on that team could produce a significant result even if none of the changes worked.

In 2015 a collaboration of researchers repeated 100 studies published in three leading psychology journals. About 97% of the originals had reported significant results; about 36% of the replications did, and the average replication effect was roughly half the original ([Open Science Collaboration, 2015](R-osc-2015-estimating)). Large-scale replication projects in other fields have produced similar warnings. The question for an executive is not whether psychology is broken but which mechanisms produce this pattern — because the same mechanisms operate in your own organization’s analytics.

understand.text: Mechanism 1: researcher degrees of freedom

Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn showed that common analytic decisions, each defensible on its own, can push the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%. Their list included choosing among several dependent variables, deciding whether to collect more data after checking significance, adding or dropping covariates, and dropping experimental conditions. Combined in a simulation, such flexibility produced false-positive rates above 60%. In a deliberately absurd demonstration, they “showed” that listening to a particular song made participants younger ([Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn, 2011](R-simmons-2011-false-positive)).

The deeper point, often called the *garden of forking paths*, is that the analyst need not try many analyses consciously. If the choice of analysis depends on the data — which outcome looks cleanest, which outliers seem odd, which subgroup is interesting — the effective number of comparisons is large even when only one is run. A p-value is valid only for an analysis that would have been run regardless of the data.
Mechanism 2: low power and the significance filter

Gelman and Carlin argued that the main danger of underpowered studies is not missed effects but misleading discoveries. When power is low, only estimates that happen to be much larger than the truth can clear the significance threshold. Conditional on being significant, such estimates are systematically exaggerated — a *type M* (magnitude) error — and with very low power a non-trivial share have the wrong sign — a *type S* (sign) error ([Gelman & Carlin, 2014](R-gelman-2014-beyond)).

understand.caption: Average estimated effect among significant results when the true effect is d = 0.3
understand.note: Synthetic: results of a simple simulation of two-group studies; values rounded. The Evidence Lab reproduces this.

understand.text: Mechanism 3: publication bias

If significant results are published, promoted or presented and non-significant ones are filed away, the visible literature is a filtered sample. Even if every study were analyzed honestly, the filter alone exaggerates average effects and can manufacture an apparent effect from nothing. Inside organizations the file drawer is the pilot that “didn’t pan out” and was never written up.

A useful benchmark comes from Registered Reports, a format in which a journal reviews and accepts the study design before the results exist. Scheel, Schijen and Lakens compared standard psychology papers with Registered Reports: about 96% of standard papers supported their first hypothesis, against about 44% of Registered Reports ([Scheel, Schijen & Lakens, 2021](R-scheel-2021-excess)). The comparison is not randomized — Registered Reports may test riskier ideas — but a gap of that size is hard to explain without selective reporting.

understand.caption: How a noisy idea becomes an accepted finding

steps.text: Low power; true effect modest or zero

steps.label: Forking paths
steps.text: Outcome, sample and model chosen after seeing data

steps.label: Significance filter
steps.text: Only large, significant estimates are written up

steps.label: Publication and press
steps.text: Surprising results attract attention and citations

steps.label: Policy and practice
steps.text: Organizations adopt an exaggerated effect

steps.label: Replication
steps.text: A larger, preregistered test finds a much smaller effect, or none

understand.title: Prerequisite: false positives, false negatives and the 5% convention

blocks.text: A *false positive* (type I error) is concluding there is an effect when there is none. A *false negative* (type II error) is missing an effect that exists. The conventional significance threshold of 5% caps the false-positive rate *for one pre-specified test when the null is true*. It says nothing about what happens when you run twenty tests and report the best, when you stop collecting data the moment p dips below .05, or when only significant results are shown to you. Each of those practices quietly raises the real false-positive rate. If you test ten independent outcomes on a program with no effect at all and report any that is significant, you will “find” something about 40% of the time.

understand.title: Methodological note: why significant-and-small-sample is a warning sign, not a strength

blocks.text: People often reason that a result significant in a small sample must reflect a large effect, since it overcame so much noise. Gelman and Carlin’s analysis shows the opposite inference is safer. In a small sample, the standard error is large, so the threshold for significance is a large estimate. If prior knowledge suggests the true effect is modest, then significance in a small sample implies the estimate is mostly noise in a favorable direction. The *exaggeration ratio* — expected significant estimate divided by true effect — can exceed two or three when power is below 20%. The remedy is a *design analysis*: before believing an estimate, ask what effect size is plausible from external evidence, compute the power the study had for that effect, and from that infer the likely exaggeration.

Gelman and Carlin recommend that the plausible effect come from outside the study, such as prior literature or domain knowledge, rather than from the study’s own estimate, which is precisely the number in doubt ([Gelman & Carlin, 2014](R-gelman-2014-beyond)).

challenge.text: The size of the problem is debated. Gilbert, King, Pettigrew and Wilson argued that the Open Science Collaboration’s design could not support its pessimistic conclusion: single replications have limited power, some replications differed from the original populations or procedures, and with these factors accounted for the results looked less alarming ([Gilbert et al., 2016](R-gilbert-2016-comment)). The original authors replied that the critique misread their design, and most methodologists accept that replication rates in that literature were low even if the exact number is uncertain ([Open Science Collaboration, 2015](R-osc-2015-estimating)). Two lessons survive the debate: a single failed replication is itself weak evidence, and interpreting replications requires the same attention to power and fidelity as interpreting originals.

Another objection is that the logic is too pessimistic. Ioannidis’s model shows that the share of true findings depends heavily on assumed priors, power and bias; in fields with strong theory, large samples and pre-specified analyses, most findings can be true ([Ioannidis, 2005](R-ioannidis-2005-most)). The replication crisis is not evidence that research is useless. It is evidence that the reliability of a literature can be predicted from its design features.

Remedies have limits too. Preregistration constrains forking paths only if the plan is specific and deviations are reported; vague plans and undisclosed deviations are common. Registered Reports address publication bias but not poor measurement or weak theory. Large replications can estimate an average effect precisely while missing that it varies across contexts. And some exploratory flexibility is valuable: the aim is not to forbid exploration but to label it honestly and confirm it on fresh data.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the analyst who is always right

blocks.text: A gifted analyst on your staff has produced eleven “wins” in a row from internal pilots. Colleagues admire the record; you are uneasy. You cannot see the analysis decisions, the pilots that were dropped, or what was planned in advance. Accusing the analyst would be unfair and damaging. Changing the system is not: require short pre-analysis plans for decisions above a threshold, keep a register of every pilot started, and ask for a hold-out confirmation before scaling. Frame it as protection for the analyst’s credibility, which it is.

apply.text: For an executive, the replication crisis translates into a short set of questions you can ask of any result, internal or external. They do not require you to re-run the analysis.

apply.caption: Replication-risk questions and what a reassuring answer looks like
rows: Was the analysis specified before the data were seen?
A dated plan naming the outcome, sample and model
“We looked at several metrics and this one moved”
How many outcomes, segments and time windows were examined?
Only the significant ones are shown
What was the sample size and power for a plausible effect?
Power of 80% or more for a modest effect
How big is the effect relative to prior evidence?
Similar to or smaller than comparable studies
Several times larger than anything seen before
Has it been confirmed on fresh data?
What happened to the pilots that did not work?

apply.text: In professional baseball, the forking-paths problem is acute because the data are rich. An analyst evaluating a new hitting drill can choose among exit velocity, launch angle, hard-hit rate, whiff rate and a dozen derived metrics; among different windows; among levels and handedness splits. With enough choices, something will move. A department that wants to learn rather than to celebrate can pre-commit to a primary outcome and window, report every metric examined, and treat secondary findings as hypotheses for the next cohort. Staggered rollouts across affiliates, with the order chosen at random, turn routine program launches into replications.

The same structure appears elsewhere. Pharmaceutical regulators require trial registration and pre-specified primary endpoints for exactly these reasons. Financial firms back-testing trading strategies face the same problem as “data snooping” and reserve untouched out-of-sample periods. Product teams that run many A/B tests and stop when significance appears inflate false positives in the same way as a lab that peeks at its data. The remedy in every field is the same family: pre-commitment, full reporting, adequate samples and confirmation.

Worked problem: your team ran 20 independent A/B tests of minor interface changes, none of which (unknown to you) had any effect. How many “significant” results at p < .05 should you expect? (About one. If the team presents one win and does not mention the other nineteen tests, the win is almost certainly noise.)

retain.text: Exaggerated and false findings arise systematically from three interacting mechanisms: flexible analysis decided after seeing the data, low power combined with a significance filter, and selective publication. Significant results from small studies are usually overestimates. Pre-commitment and full reporting reduce the problem; they do not replace good measurement or theory.
Name the three mechanisms that produce the replication pattern, and give an organizational example of each.
What is a type-M error, and why does low power make it worse?
What does a Registered Report change about the publication process?

takeaways: Most failed findings come from a system of incentives and flexibility, not from fraud.
Undisclosed analytic flexibility can raise the real false-positive rate far above 5%.
In low-powered studies, significant estimates are exaggerated (type M) and sometimes have the wrong sign (type S).
Publication filters manufacture inflated literatures; Registered Reports show far fewer positive results.
Ask for pre-specified outcomes, all analyses examined, power, and confirmation on fresh data.

check.prompt: Which interpretation of this report is most defensible?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract: A consulting firm trained 24 managers in a new feedback method and compared them with 24 untrained managers. Of 9 engagement measures collected, “team voice” improved significantly (d = 0.85, p = .01). The authors conclude the method produces large improvements in team voice.

options.text: The large effect is especially convincing because it was detected in a small sample.
The finding is a reasonable hypothesis, but the estimate is probably inflated and may be a false positive given nine outcomes and a small sample.
The result should be dismissed because p-values are invalid.
The result is confirmed because d = 0.85 is a large effect by conventional standards.

check.explanation: Nine outcomes with one significant result is close to what chance alone produces, and a small sample means only large estimates can reach significance, so the effect size is likely exaggerated. The right status is an unconfirmed hypothesis to test with a pre-specified outcome in a larger sample.

optionFeedback.a: This is the reverse of the correct inference: small samples make significant estimates more likely to be exaggerated.
optionFeedback.c: p-values are valid for what they measure; the problem here is multiple outcomes and low power.
optionFeedback.d: The conventional label says nothing about whether the estimate is reliable.

check.prompt: What is the main problem that a Registered Report addresses that ordinary preregistration alone does not?

options.text: Measurement error in the outcome.
Publication decisions that depend on whether the results were significant.
Lack of random assignment.
Low external validity.

check.explanation: In a Registered Report the journal commits to publish based on the question and design before results exist, so the result cannot determine publication. Preregistration alone constrains analytic flexibility but does not stop a null study from staying in the file drawer.

optionFeedback.a: Neither format fixes a poor measure.
optionFeedback.c: Registered Reports can be observational; they do not impose randomization.
optionFeedback.d: Generalizability depends on the sample and setting, not on the publication format.
