assumptions: The city cannot compel the county to provide treatment slots.
Sharing identifiable patient data across departments requires a formal agreement; whether consent is needed in each case is unresolved and would require legal advice.
The mayor will support whatever design Solís recommends if it can be announced in three weeks, but will not spend political capital forcing department heads to comply.
The informal program’s treatment-entry estimate has not been verified and may be optimistic.
questions: Map the power in this case using dependence: what does each actor control that the office needs, how much discretion do they have, and what alternatives exist? Who are the hidden power holders?
Which design best balances effectiveness, legitimacy and the coalition needed to sustain it? What would you have to concede to make it work, and to whom?
Brandt’s support may require giving Fire visible ownership. Using Selznick’s analysis of co-optation, what would that buy, what could it cost, and where would you draw the line?
Joel Haddad is the only reliable bridge between Fire and Public Health. What are the risks of that structure, and what would you do about them in the first month?
Should Solís name a director before the press event? Whom, and how would each choice change the coalition?

perspectives.title: Build around the dependency: Fire-led with conditions
perspectives.text: Fire controls the two things the office cannot do without — access to survivors and their trust — and Brandt has a working program. A Design B variant, with a peer specialist from the community group, Public Health running evaluation under a written data agreement, and settlement funds released by the council against agreed measures, turns the strongest potential blocker into the owner. The risk is Selznick’s: Fire may narrow the mission to what paramedics are comfortable doing. The line is that evaluation and the outcome measures sit outside Fire and are reported publicly.

perspectives.title: Own the money and the measures: a small central office
perspectives.text: Design C is weak on authority but strong on legitimacy with the council and the advocates, and it avoids giving any single department a veto over a cross-cutting problem. Its success depends on the director’s ability to build exchange relationships — funding Fire’s visits, paying for the county coordinator, giving Public Health the evaluation role — so that each department gains something it values. Naming the Fire captain as director, with a Public Health deputy for evaluation, bridges the two networks. The risk is that a coordinating office without authority becomes ceremonial; the safeguard is a budget it actually controls and quarterly public results.

perspectives.title: Slow down: secure the county and the data first
perspectives.text: Every design fails if there are no treatment slots and no timely data. Announcing an office before those exist risks a visible program that cannot deliver, eroding legitimacy for years. On this view, Solís should recommend that the mayor announce a commitment and a working group, fund the county coordinator immediately, negotiate the data agreement with Fire as a partner, and name the director only when the design has the two dependencies in hand. The cost is political: the mayor wanted a launch, and delay may be read as weakness.

case.application: The same structure appears whenever a leader in a sports organization must introduce a process that crosses departments — for example a player-health and performance program that needs data from the medical staff, buy-in from coaches, budget from senior executives and cooperation from an international operation the department does not control. Map what each group controls, recognize who is already doing the work informally and deserves credit, decide which dependency must be secured before launch, and be explicit about what you will not trade for support. Do not let the pressure for a visible announcement substitute for the coalition that makes the process work.

questions.prompt: A newly appointed head of analytics at a hospital system has a vice-presidential title, but unit managers routinely route data questions to a long-tenured database administrator instead. In French and Raven’s terms, the head of analytics holds mainly which base of power over unit managers, and the administrator which?

options.text: Head: expert; administrator: legitimate.
Head: legitimate; administrator: expert.
Head: referent; administrator: coercive.
Head: reward; administrator: referent.

questions.explanation: The title confers legitimate power — an accepted right to direct. Unit managers go to the administrator because they believe she knows more about the data, which is expert power. The gap between the two is the gap between formal authority and practical power this week examines.

optionFeedback.a: This reverses the bases: the title is the legitimate base; being consulted for knowledge is expert.
optionFeedback.c: Nothing suggests identification with the head or that the administrator can punish anyone.
optionFeedback.d: Reward power would require control over things managers value; referent power would require identification. Neither is described.

questions.prompt: Using the ratings in the table, what share of the power held by people who have taken a side (stance not 0) belongs to supporters? Give a percentage to one decimal place.

stimulus.caption: Stakeholder ratings for a proposed change (synthetic)

questions.working: Supporters (stance above 0): A (5) and C (3), total 8. Opponents (stance below 0): B (4) and D (2), total 6. Committed power = 8 + 6 = 14. Supporters’ share = 8 / 14 = 0.571 = 57.1%. E (power 4, neutral) is excluded — and is the largest swing factor: if E opposed, the share would fall to 8 / 18 = 44.4%.
questions.explanation: Supporters hold 8 of the 14 points of committed power, or 57.1%. The more important observation is that a single high-power neutral, E, could reverse the balance, which is why stakeholder maps flag powerful neutrals for early engagement.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the weak-ties research are supported by the evidence discussed this week? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bridges between dense clusters tend to be weak ties, so weak ties tend to carry information that is new to a group.
A randomized test on a professional networking platform found that the weaker a tie, the more it helped job mobility, without limit.
The randomized test found an inverted-U pattern in which moderately weak ties were most helpful for job mobility.
Granovetter’s original job-search evidence was descriptive rather than causal.
The randomized test showed that strong ties are useless in every industry.

questions.explanation: Granovetter’s structural argument explains why bridges are weak ties and why they carry novel information; his own evidence was descriptive. The LinkedIn experiments provided causal evidence but found an inverted U, and weak ties mattered more in more digital industries — not that strong ties are useless.

optionFeedback.b: The study found diminishing and then reversing returns: the weakest ties were less helpful than moderately weak ones.
optionFeedback.e: Strong ties were relatively more valuable in less digital industries.

questions.prompt: Which is the most important structural risk, and the best first response?

stimulus.text: A global consulting firm’s Latin American and U.S. healthcare practices share clients but rarely work together. One bilingual principal, Andrés, has worked in both and is the person each practice calls when it needs the other. Joint proposals have doubled since he took on this role. He has just been approached by a competitor. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Andrés is a broker whose role creates a single bridge between groups — a bottleneck and a memory risk. Build additional ties between the practices and capture what he knows, while recognizing and rewarding his role.
Andrés is too central in the trust network; reduce his involvement so that the practices learn to work alone.
The practices are too densely connected; separate them further to protect their distinct cultures.
The risk is purely financial; counter the competitor’s offer and change nothing else.

questions.explanation: Andrés spans a structural hole; the doubling of joint proposals is consistent with the value of brokerage. But a single bridge is fragile: if he leaves, so do the paths along which cross-practice knowledge travels. Retaining him may be wise, but the structural fix is redundancy plus recognition.

optionFeedback.b: Reducing his role removes the value he creates without building an alternative bridge.
optionFeedback.c: The problem is too few ties between the practices, not too many.
optionFeedback.d: A counteroffer may be sensible, but it leaves the organization exposed to the same single-point failure next time.

questions.prompt: Identify the central weakness in this argument.

stimulus.text: “Eight of the ten largest health systems in our region have created a Chief Experience Officer in the past three years. We are falling behind. The board should approve the role this quarter so that we are seen as a modern organization by patients and regulators.”

options.text: It provides no evidence that the role improves outcomes in the systems that adopted it; adopting it because peers have it is mimetic isomorphism, which risks a ceremonial role.
It relies on coercive pressure from regulators, which is illegitimate.
It ignores that the role is too expensive for any health system.
It assumes that patients care about organizational structure, which they never do.

questions.explanation: The argument treats peer adoption as sufficient reason. That is the signature of mimetic isomorphism under uncertainty. Legitimacy has real value, but the question the board should ask is what the role would change and how that would be checked, so that the organization adopts the function rather than only the form.

optionFeedback.b: No regulatory mandate is cited; “seen as modern” is about legitimacy, not coercion. Coercive pressure is not inherently illegitimate either.
optionFeedback.c: Cost is not discussed in the argument and may be justified; the flaw is the missing evidence of effect.
optionFeedback.d: An absolute claim of this kind is unsupported; the flaw lies in the reasoning from peer adoption.

questions.prompt: A county is merging its housing-inspection and code-enforcement units. The code-enforcement manager, respected by council members, opposes the merger because inspectors will report to a housing director. Rank these responses from best to worst, considering support gained, mission protection and trust.

options.text: Invite the manager to lead the design of the merged unit’s field procedures and cross-training, while the reporting line and service standards remain fixed and published.
Give the manager an honorary title on the transition steering committee, which has no decision rights.
Proceed without engaging the manager and ask council members to stay neutral.
Let the manager decide the reporting line in exchange for public support.

questions.explanation: Bounded informal co-optation (a) gives real influence over matters that can be conceded while protecting the core purpose. Symbolic participation (b) buys little but costs little. Ignoring a respected opponent (c) invites quiet obstruction through council allies. Handing over the reporting line (d) buys support with the mission itself — the outcome Selznick warned about.

questions.prompt: From the coalition perspective, what is the most useful interpretation of the planners’ resistance, and the best next step?

stimulus.text: A regional airline introduces a new crew-scheduling optimization system. Senior schedulers, who have long had informal discretion to swap shifts for crews they know well, raise repeated technical objections and delay training. The project lead calls them “resistant to change”. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: The schedulers fear technology; schedule more training until they are comfortable.

The system removes a side payment — discretion that gives schedulers status and goodwill with crews — and their objections may also contain real information about constraints the system ignores. Find out what the discretion did, and redesign or compensate for what is legitimate.
The objections are purely self-interested; escalate to senior management and mandate use.
Resistance shows the system is flawed; cancel the project.

questions.explanation: In the coalition view, resistance often defends a threatened bargain. Here the bargain is informal discretion, which also served crews and may encode constraints the optimizer misses. Treating resistance as information separates the principled part (constraints) from the self-interested part (lost status), and lets you address each.

optionFeedback.a: Training addresses skill, not lost discretion; this misdiagnoses the cause.
optionFeedback.c: Mandating may win compliance but forfeits the information in the objections and damages trust with people the system still depends on.
optionFeedback.d: Resistance is information, not a verdict; it does not by itself show the system is flawed.

questions.prompt: You want your organization’s chief executive to prioritize a data-privacy weakness you have identified. She is focused this quarter on a large customer renewal. Using Dutton and Ashford’s framework, what is the best first move?

options.text: Raise it at the next all-leaders meeting so that the issue is on the record.
Frame the weakness in terms of the renewal — for example the customer’s security review — and raise it first in a private conversation, with a peer whose function is affected ready to co-sponsor.
Wait until the renewal is complete so as not to distract her.
Send a detailed technical memo to the whole executive team.

questions.explanation: Packaging links the issue to a goal the executive owns; process chooses a private first channel (reducing her surprise and your image risk) and involves an ally. Timing matters too: tying the issue to the renewal turns a distraction into a contribution.

optionFeedback.a: A public first raising risks surprising the executive in front of others and raises your image risk.
optionFeedback.c: Waiting may be wise for some issues, but here the issue can be framed as relevant to the current priority; delay forgoes the window.
optionFeedback.d: A technical memo to everyone ignores framing and channel and is likely to be read as alarmism or ignored.

questions.prompt: In Yukl and Tracey’s field study, which tactics were most associated with target commitment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rational persuasion
Pressure
Inspirational appeals
Legitimating tactics
Consultation
Coalition tactics

questions.explanation: Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation were most associated with commitment. Pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics were least effective. Remember that the study was correlational: tactic choice partly reflects expected resistance.

optionFeedback.b: Pressure was among the least effective tactics.
optionFeedback.d: Appeals to rules or authority were among the least effective.
optionFeedback.f: Using others to pressure the target was among the least effective — different from building a coalition behind a proposal.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest alternative explanation for this finding?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. In a survey of 310 project managers, those who reported using pressure tactics with peers were rated by those peers as less effective, and their projects were more often late. The authors conclude that pressure tactics cause project delays and recommend training managers to avoid them.

options.text: Managers may resort to pressure on projects that are already in trouble or facing resistance, so delays and pressure could share a cause or delays could cause pressure.
The sample is too small for any conclusion.
Peers cannot rate managers’ effectiveness accurately.
Pressure tactics are effective, so the finding must be wrong.

questions.explanation: Tactic choice is endogenous: managers choose pressure when they already expect resistance or are behind schedule. The correlation fits the hypothesis that pressure causes delay but equally fits reverse causation and confounding. The training recommendation may still be reasonable on other grounds, but this design cannot establish it.

optionFeedback.b: Three hundred respondents is a reasonable sample; size is not the main problem.
optionFeedback.c: Peer ratings carry bias but are informative; this is a weaker objection than reverse causation.
optionFeedback.d: This asserts the opposite conclusion without evidence.

questions.prompt: In 150–250 words: a regional hospital’s new chief operating officer wants to centralize operating-room scheduling, which surgical department chiefs have controlled for years. The surgeons’ informal leader is a senior surgeon with no administrative title, central in the surgeons’ trust network. Outline an engagement strategy that uses at least three ideas from this week (dependence, networks, coalitions/co-optation, influence tactics, ethics), states what the COO should be willing to concede and what not, and names one ethical line.
questions.modelAnswer: The COO should begin by mapping dependence: the hospital depends on surgeons for revenue and on the department chiefs for schedule adherence, while chiefs depend on the COO’s office for staffing and equipment. Centralization removes a side payment — chiefs’ discretion over OR time, a source of status and leverage — so resistance is predictable and partly rational. The senior surgeon is a hidden power holder: no title, but control over the credibility of the change among surgeons. The COO should consult him early, privately, with data on idle OR time and delays, framed around patient access and surgeons’ own frustrations. A bounded co-optation is appropriate: invite him and two chiefs to design the allocation rules and the appeals process, while keeping centralized scheduling, published utilization data and the final authority fixed. The COO can concede block-time protections for high-volume surgeons and a phased start; not the principle of centralized, transparent allocation. Tactics should favor rational persuasion and consultation over legitimating appeals (“the board decided”). Ethical line: no selective sharing of data to make particular chiefs look bad, and no private promises of OR time in exchange for public support.

rubric.criterion: Diagnosis of power and dependence (including the hidden power holder)
levels: 0 — Absent or limited to titles
1 — Mentions power loosely
2 — Identifies dependence or the informal leader
3 — Specific dependence analysis and the informal leader’s source of power

rubric.criterion: Coalition strategy with explicit concessions and limits
levels: 0 — Absent
1 — Vague “involve stakeholders”
2 — Concessions named but no limit
3 — Bounded co-optation: what is conceded and what is not
0 — None or pressure-led
1 — Tactics named without rationale
2 — Favors commitment-producing tactics, with a reason
0 — Absent
1 — Generic (“be ethical”)
2 — Specific, testable line tied to the situation

reserve.prompt: According to resource dependence theory, which change would most reduce a product team’s dependence on a single cloud vendor?

options.text: Praising the vendor’s account manager publicly.
Developing the capability to run critical workloads on a second provider.
Increasing the product team’s budget.
Appointing a senior executive to manage the vendor relationship.

reserve.explanation: Dependence rises with importance, the other party’s discretion and the scarcity of alternatives. Creating an alternative source is the most direct way to reduce it. The other options may improve the relationship but leave the dependence intact.

optionFeedback.a: Goodwill may help the relationship but does not change the structure of dependence.
optionFeedback.c: More budget does not create alternatives on its own.
optionFeedback.d: Seniority may help negotiation but leaves importance, discretion and alternatives unchanged.

reserve.prompt: What does Krackhardt and Hanson’s framework suggest the director should do first?

stimulus.text: A research hospital’s new laboratory director wants to introduce a new specimen-tracking procedure. She asks for a list of “key influencers” and is given the five most senior technologists. Two months later the procedure is followed inconsistently. Informal conversations reveal that technologists on every shift ask a mid-career technologist, Mei, how to handle unusual cases, and that night staff confide problems in a phlebotomy supervisor, Tomás. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Re-train the five senior technologists more intensively.
Recognize that seniority approximated neither the advice nor the trust network; engage Mei (advice) and Tomás (trust) in revising and championing the procedure.
Issue a written directive requiring compliance.
Conduct a large network survey before taking any action.

reserve.explanation: The informal advice network runs through Mei and the trust network through Tomás. Seniority is a formal attribute that may not coincide with either. Engaging those who are actually consulted and trusted is the most direct way to make the procedure credible.

optionFeedback.a: The problem is not the seniors’ skill; they are not where advice and trust flow.
optionFeedback.c: A directive relies on legitimate power and may yield compliance without commitment.
optionFeedback.d: A survey can help but is slow; the conversations already reveal the key figures.

reserve.prompt: In Cyert and March’s behavioral theory of the firm, what role does organizational slack play?

options.text: It is waste that efficient organizations eliminate entirely.
It provides surplus resources that allow the organization to satisfy several coalition members’ demands at once, easing conflict.
It is the time managers spend on informal networking.
It is the gap between legitimate and expert power.

reserve.explanation: Slack is surplus beyond what is strictly needed. In the coalition view, it lets the organization make side payments to several members simultaneously, which keeps the coalition together. When slack shrinks, conflicts become harder to manage, which is one reason change during budget cuts is so politically difficult.

optionFeedback.a: Slack may look like waste, but Cyert and March showed it serves a political function.
optionFeedback.c: This is not the meaning of slack.
optionFeedback.d: This confuses concepts from different lessons.

reserve.prompt: A colleague suggests opening a budget discussion with a deliberately inflated request you expect to be refused, so that your real request seems reasonable by comparison, and not telling the finance director this is the plan. Which response best reflects this week’s treatment of influence?

options.text: Use it: the door-in-the-face technique replicated, so it will work.

Decline: it fails the disclosure test in a repeated relationship, and if the finance director recognizes the tactic, the trust cost may exceed the gain. Make the real request with reasons and offer options.
Use it, but only with peers, because influence tactics work better laterally.
Decline because door-in-the-face has been shown not to replicate.

reserve.explanation: A staged concession only works if hidden, so it fails the disclosure test. In repeated relationships, recognition damages trust. The replication evidence concerns whether the technique works with strangers, not whether it is wise or ethical with a colleague.

optionFeedback.a: Replication with strangers does not settle effect size or consequences in a repeated relationship, nor the ethical question.
optionFeedback.c: The finance director is not clearly a peer, and direction does not resolve the ethical problem.
optionFeedback.d: This misstates the evidence: the door-in-the-face technique replicated well in a direct replication.

assignment.title: Stakeholder Engagement Plan

brief.text: Write a stakeholder engagement plan for introducing a change initiative of your choosing. The default is the owner’s brief for this week: **a new analytical or operational process in a professional sports organization**, with particular attention to implementing the improvement without undermining existing relationships. You may instead choose a change in another kind of organization. The initiative must be non-confidential: describe a hypothetical or generalized situation, use roles rather than names, and include no proprietary data or details that would identify a real organization or person.

Your plan should read like a working document a senior leader could actually use: specific about people (by role), dependencies and sequence; honest about uncertainty; and explicit about what you will and will not do to win support. Use the week’s tools — dependence, networks, coalitions and legitimacy, influence tactics — and label any practitioner heuristic (such as a power/interest grid) as a heuristic.

items: Treat existing relationships as assets the change must protect: name which ones and how your plan protects them.
Distinguish what you know about each stakeholder from what you are assuming, and say how you will test the assumptions.
Prefer tactics associated with commitment; justify any use of pressure or appeals to authority.
State your ethical lines concretely enough that someone could tell whether you crossed them.

assignment.deliverable: A 1,200–1,800-word stakeholder engagement plan with the eight sections below, including a stakeholder map (table or grid) of 6–12 roles.

template.heading: Objective and the change
template.guidance: In 100–150 words: what will change, for whom, by when, and what success looks like in behavior, not only in approval. State why the change is worth its political cost.

template.heading: Stakeholder map
template.guidance: A table of 6–12 roles with power over this change (and its source: what do they control, with what discretion and alternatives?), interest, current stance, and what each gains or loses. Mark hidden power holders and known ties. Label the power/interest grid as a practitioner heuristic.

template.heading: Relationships to protect
template.guidance: Which existing relationships — between people, departments or with outside partners — carry trust or institutional memory the change depends on? How could the change damage them, and how will your plan avoid that?

template.heading: Coalition strategy
template.guidance: Who must be part of the winning coalition, who can be kept satisfied, and who will remain opposed? Which brokers or trusted figures will you work through? If you co-opt anyone, what influence do they get and over what?

template.heading: Sequencing of conversations
template.guidance: The order of your first 6–10 conversations, with the purpose of each, the tactic you will lead with, and what you need to learn. Explain why the order matters (who must not be surprised; whose early support changes others’ calculations).

template.heading: Concessions and their limits
template.guidance: What you are prepared to give — timing, design input, credit, resources, pilots — and what is non-negotiable because it is the purpose of the change. Tie each concession to a stakeholder interest.

template.heading: Risks and early warning signs
template.guidance: Three to five specific risks (for example ceremonial adoption, a broker’s departure, a sponsor’s exit, passive resistance) with an observable early signal and a response for each.

template.heading: Ethical lines
template.guidance: Two to four concrete commitments about how you will and will not influence people (for example the disclosure test, no selective use of data, no private promises), and how you would handle a conflict between winning support and keeping them.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Power is analyzed through specific dependencies (importance, discretion, alternatives) and bases; hidden power holders are identified and justified; known facts are separated from assumptions.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Sources of power are identified for most stakeholders beyond titles; at least one informal power holder is recognized.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Power is mostly read from titles; dependencies are mentioned in general terms.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Stakeholders are listed without analysis of where their power comes from.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Uses advice and trust networks, brokers and single bridges; the coalition strategy is explicit about side payments and any co-optation, with its limits.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Identifies key relationships and a credible coalition; co-optation, if used, is bounded.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Coalition is described as “get buy-in” without specifying who, why or at what price.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No coalition logic; the plan relies on authority or announcement.

rubric.criterion: Sequencing and influence tactics grounded in evidence

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A reasoned order of conversations with purposes and tactics; favors commitment-producing tactics, adapts to direction (up, lateral, down) and culture, and justifies any exceptions.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear sequence and appropriate tactics for most conversations.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Sequence present but unexplained, or tactics generic.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No sequence; tactics absent or pressure-led.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Concessions are tied to specific interests, with a clear non-negotiable core; the plan names the relationships at stake and protects them concretely.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Concessions and limits are stated; relationships are considered.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Concessions vague or unlimited; relationships mentioned only in passing.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No concessions or no attention to existing relationships.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Specific risks with observable signals and responses; concrete, testable ethical lines; practitioner heuristics labelled as such; uncertainty acknowledged.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Risks and ethical lines are specific; most claims are appropriately qualified.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Risks generic; ethical lines stated as general values.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Risks or ethics missing; heuristics presented as science.

prompts: Think of a change you championed that was adopted on paper but not in practice. Using this week’s tools, who held the practical power over adoption, and did you engage them?
Where in your own network are you a broker — across departments, languages, countries or professions? What does that position give you, and what does it oblige you to do for the people on each side?
Which influence tactic do you reach for first under time pressure, and what does the evidence suggest it costs you?
Write down one influence approach you have used or seen used that you would not want disclosed to its target. What would you do differently now?

review.front: What are French and Raven’s five original bases of power, and from whose perspective is each defined?
review.back: Reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert — each defined by the target’s beliefs about the agent. Raven later added informational power.

review.front: State the power-dependence principle and the three conditions that increase dependence.
review.back: A’s power over B equals B’s dependence on A. Dependence rises with the importance of the resource, A’s discretion over it, and the scarcity of alternatives.

review.front: Name three ways organizations manage external dependence, according to resource dependence theory.
review.back: Co-opting outsiders (e.g. onto boards), alliances and joint ventures, mergers, and diversifying sources of the resource.

review.front: What is a “hidden power holder”?
review.back: Someone with little formal authority who controls a critical dependency for a specific decision — for example credibility with front-line staff — and can therefore make or break a change.

review.front: Why are bridges between groups almost always weak ties?
review.back: Strong ties pull people’s contacts together, so two strongly tied clusters would merge; the ties that remain between separate clusters are weak, and they carry non-redundant information.

review.front: What did the randomized LinkedIn study find about weak ties and job mobility?
review.back: A causal effect with an inverted-U shape: moderately weak ties helped most; the weakest ties helped less. Weak ties mattered more in more digital industries.

review.front: What is a structural hole, and what did Burt find about brokers who span them?
review.back: A gap between unconnected groups. In one electronics firm, brokers’ ideas were more often judged valuable, and brokerage was associated with pay, evaluations and promotion — an observational finding.

review.front: Distinguish the advice network from the trust network.
review.back: Advice: whom people ask for technical help. Trust: with whom they share sensitive information and whom they back in a crisis. A change needs the trusted as well as the expert.

review.front: In Cyert and March’s view, how is an organization held together despite conflicting goals?
review.back: By bargaining among coalition members, side payments, organizational slack and sequential attention to different goals; conflict is managed, not resolved.

review.front: Name and define the three mechanisms of institutional isomorphism.
review.back: Coercive (pressure from those depended on and the state), mimetic (copying peers under uncertainty), normative (professional training and associations).

review.front: What is the hidden cost of co-optation in Selznick’s TVA study?
review.back: Interests brought into the decision structure gain leverage over the organization’s real commitments, so support can be bought at the price of drift from the mission.

review.front: What is ceremonial adoption, and when is it most likely?
review.back: Adopting the visible form of a practice without changing the underlying work; most likely when adoption is driven by legitimacy (mimetic or coercive pressure) rather than evidence of results.

review.front: Which influence tactics were most and least associated with commitment in Yukl and Tracey’s study?
review.back: Most: rational persuasion, inspirational appeals, consultation. Least: pressure, legitimating, coalition. Ingratiation and exchange worked with peers and subordinates, not bosses.

review.front: What are the two levers of an issue-selling attempt in Dutton and Ashford’s framework?
review.back: Packaging (framing, bundling with leaders’ concerns) and process (timing, channel, involving others) — with image risk shaping whether people try at all.

review.front: Summarize the replication picture for compliance principles in one sentence.
review.back: The principles name real mechanisms and some classic effects (e.g. door-in-the-face) replicate well, but many specific effect sizes are smaller or less certain than early studies suggested, especially for repeated relationships.

review.front: State the disclosure test for influence.
review.back: Would the approach still work, and would you still be comfortable, if the target knew exactly what you were doing and why? If not, it is probably manipulation.

preview.text: This week’s map of power becomes next week’s bargaining table. In Week 7, leverage in negotiation turns out to be dependence again — your alternatives set your power — and the ethics of influence return as negotiation ethics. Week 8 moves from the informal architecture to the formal one: designing structures, decision rights and incentives that create or dissolve the coalitions you studied here. Week 12 puts both together in implementing change, where the stakeholder engagement plan you write this week becomes the first section of a 90-day roadmap.

links.why: Bargaining power, alternatives and negotiation ethics build directly on dependence and influence tactics.
Formal organizational design allocates the authority and creates the coalitions analyzed this week.
Change implementation uses stakeholder mapping, sequencing and coalition-building at scale.
Governance and ethics revisit legitimacy, co-optation and the ethics of influence.

weeks.title: Negotiation & Bargaining
weeks.question: When two parties need each other but want different things, what determines whether they reach an agreement, how much value it creates, and who captures that value?

overview.text: Executives negotiate far more often than their calendars show. Budgets, hires, vendor contracts, partnerships, the division of scarce staff between departments, the terms on which a colleague will support your proposal: each is a negotiation, whether or not anyone calls it one. This week treats negotiation as a discipline with an analytic core, a body of behavioral evidence and an ethical boundary, rather than as a talent some people are born with.

The five lessons build in sequence. Lesson 1 sets out the architecture every negotiation shares: alternatives, reservation values, aspirations and the zone of possible agreement. Lesson 2 shows how value is created from differences between the parties, through logrolling and contingent contracts, and why the moves that create value expose you to the moves that claim it. Lesson 3 brings in the psychology: anchoring and first offers, the fixed-pie perception, fairness, emotion and the evidence on gender, read carefully. Lesson 4 moves negotiation inside organizations and across borders: agents and principals, internal mandates, coalitions and culture. Lesson 5 draws the line between hard bargaining and deception and distinguishes statements from commitments.

The evidence this week is mixed in kind, and you should keep track of which kind you are reading. Some of the most influential ideas, including BATNA and principled negotiation, are practitioner prescriptions. Others rest on laboratory experiments with simulated negotiations, meta-analyses of many such studies, or surveys of stated judgments. Each lesson says which is which and where the evidence runs out.

You will practice in the Negotiation Chamber, a four-issue licensing negotiation against a rule-based counterpart; analyze an international financial-services case in which the hardest negotiations happen inside each organization; and write a negotiation strategy memo for a hypothetical negotiation you could plausibly lead. The week also prepares you for the cumulative midterm that follows it, which asks for a negotiation plan alongside behavioral and evidentiary analysis.

objectives: Prepare a negotiation by estimating both sides’ BATNAs, reservation values and aspirations and the resulting zone of possible agreement.
Identify distributive, integrative and compatible issues and construct trades and contingent terms that move an agreement toward the Pareto frontier.
Apply the evidence on anchoring, fixed-pie perception, fairness and situational moderators to decisions about first offers and defenses, stating that evidence’s limits.
Design mandates, incentives and processes for negotiations conducted through agents, with internal constituencies, among several parties or across cultures.
Distinguish legitimate competitive tactics from deception, including paltering, and distinguish estimates from commitments.
Write a negotiation strategy memo that a decision-maker could approve and a negotiator could execute.

concepts.name: Best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA)
The negotiator’s dilemma (creating versus claiming value)
Fairness norms and the ultimatum game
Context-dependent gender differences in negotiation outcomes

lessons.title: The Architecture of a Negotiation: Alternatives, Reservation Values and the Zone of Agreement
lessons.summary: Before anyone speaks at the table, each side’s alternative, reservation value, aspiration and opening determine whether a deal is possible and roughly where it can land.
objectives: Define BATNA, reservation value, aspiration and ZOPA, and derive a reservation value from an uncertain alternative.
Determine whether a zone of possible agreement exists from both sides’ reservation values, and explain what should happen when it does not.
Explain how alternatives, deadlines, commitments and information asymmetry shape bargaining power.
lessons.executive: Most negotiations are decided before the meeting. Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) is what you will do if talks fail; your reservation value converts it into the worst terms you should accept; your aspiration sets how much of the available surplus you try to claim. The other side carries the same numbers, hidden from you. A deal is possible only when reservation values overlap (the ZOPA), and where it lands inside that zone depends on information, anchors and perceived power. The executive discipline: estimate both sides’ numbers explicitly, improve your alternative before you negotiate, and never let the table talk you below what walking away is worth.

explore.text: Consider two senior data engineers interviewing for the same role at a payments company. They are equally skilled and equally articulate. One holds a written offer from another firm that expires on Friday; the other has only a current job she is eager to leave. The company makes both the same initial offer. Almost everyone can say instantly which candidate is in the stronger position. Far fewer can say precisely what that strength consists of, how large it is, or what the second candidate should do about it. This lesson supplies that precision. (Hypothetical example.)

Now change industries. A mid-sized city is renegotiating its waste-collection contract, and the incumbent hauler asks for a 22 percent increase. The city’s position depends far less on its negotiator’s charm than on a question its public-works director should have answered months earlier: could the city run collection itself, or bid the work to a second hauler, and at what cost? If the answer is known and credible, the hauler’s demand meets a ceiling. If nobody has done the work, the city is negotiating with nothing behind it, and the hauler can usually tell. (Hypothetical example.)

Before reading on: for a negotiation you expect to face in the next six months, write down what you will do if no agreement is reached. Then write down what the other side will do if no agreement is reached. Which answer are you less sure of, and what would it cost to find out?

understand.text: Four numbers on each side

Roger Fisher and William Ury’s *Getting to Yes* introduced the term [BATNA](#gl:g-batna), the best alternative to a negotiated agreement, and argued that it, rather than an arbitrary “bottom line”, is the standard against which any proposed agreement should be measured. A BATNA is a course of action, not a number: accept the other firm’s offer, bring waste collection in-house, license to the second customer, keep the old system. Developing it starts with listing what you could actually do if no agreement is reached, then improving the most promising options and choosing the best of them.

The analytic tradition associated with Howard Raiffa’s *The Art and Science of Negotiation* converts that course of action into a number. Your [reservation value](#gl:g-reservation-value) is the point at which you are indifferent between agreeing and taking your BATNA. Your counterpart has one too. When the most a buyer would pay exceeds the least a seller would accept, every price between the two leaves both better off than walking away. That overlap is the [zone of possible agreement](#gl:g-zopa) (ZOPA). When reservation values do not overlap, no agreement is better for both than their alternatives, and the correct outcome is a polite impasse.

Two further numbers complete the structure. Your [aspiration](#gl:g-aspiration), or target, is the outcome you are realistically trying to achieve; it sits well above your reservation value and governs how much of the zone you try to claim. Your opening offer is the first number you put on the table; it sits at or beyond your aspiration so that you have room to concede. The reservation value protects you from bad deals. The aspiration protects you from mediocre ones. Negotiators who prepare only a reservation value tend to settle near it, because it is the only number they have thought hard about.

understand.caption: The four numbers in a software license (synthetic example)
headers: Does the other side see it?
rows: License to a smaller customer that has offered $1.5M a year
Keep the incumbent system: $1.8M a year all-in, including an amortized upgrade
$1.6M a year (the smaller deal plus the sales effort it would still require)
$2.1M a year (the incumbent’s $1.8M plus about $0.3M of value from better defect detection)
understand.note: Synthetic. The ZOPA runs from $1.6M to $2.1M a year, a surplus of $0.5M a year that the parties will divide. Both aspirations sit inside the zone; both openings sit outside it.

understand.caption: Preparation runs backward from alternatives to the opening offer

steps.label: Interests
steps.text: Why do you want a deal at all? List what matters and how much.

steps.label: Alternatives
steps.text: What could you do without this counterpart? List them; improve the best ones.

steps.label: BATNA
steps.text: Choose the best alternative, honestly valued.

steps.label: Reservation value
steps.text: Convert the BATNA into the worst terms you would accept here.

steps.label: Aspiration
steps.text: Set an ambitious but defensible target inside your estimate of the ZOPA.

steps.label: Opening
steps.text: Choose a first offer you can justify with criteria, at or beyond the aspiration.

understand.text: Information asymmetry and bargaining power

Each side knows its own reservation value and must estimate the other’s. That [information asymmetry](#gl:g-information-asymmetry) drives distributive bargaining: each party tries to learn the other’s reservation value while concealing its own, and tries to persuade the other that its own is less flexible than it really is. Most tactics you will meet are attempts to move those estimates: “this is the board’s limit”, “we have another bidder”, the long silence after an offer, the deadline that appears late in the process.

Bargaining power, in this frame, is not a personality trait. It is primarily the relative cost of no deal. The side whose alternative is closer to the value of the agreement needs the agreement less and can credibly claim more of the zone. Deadlines matter because they change alternatives over time: the engineer’s outside offer expires Friday; a licensee’s regulatory audit approaches. Commitments matter because a credible statement that you cannot accept less, such as a board resolution or a published price schedule, moves the other side’s estimate of your reservation value. Reputation matters because in repeated relationships, how you claim value today changes which alternatives you will have tomorrow.

understand.title: Prerequisite: turning an uncertain alternative into a number

blocks.text: Alternatives are often uncertain. If the competing offer might be withdrawn, you can approximate its value with a probability-weighted average, called an expected value. Suppose the outside offer is worth $180,000 a year if it holds, which you judge 70 percent likely, and you fall back on your current salary of $150,000 if it does not. The expected value is 0.7 × 180,000 + 0.3 × 150,000 = 126,000 + 45,000 = $171,000. (Hypothetical numbers.)

Expected value is a starting point for judgment, not a replacement for it. A person who dislikes risk might set a reservation value somewhat below $171,000; a person who badly wants to leave the current job might set it above, because staying has costs the salary figure omits. What matters is that the adjustment is deliberate and written down before the conversation, not improvised under pressure.

understand.title: Methodological note: prescriptive analysis and descriptive research

blocks.text: Raiffa’s book is often described as a bridge between popular negotiation advice and formal game theory. It moves from two parties bargaining over one issue, to two parties with many issues, to negotiations among many parties, and uses cases such as the Panama Canal and Camp David negotiations to illustrate the analysis.

This course uses that analysis prescriptively: it tells one negotiator how to reason, given realistic assumptions about how the other side behaves. That differs from classical game theory, which assumes every party reasons flawlessly, and from behavioral research, which documents how real negotiators depart from the analysis. The two views complement each other. The prescriptive frame tells you what to calculate; the behavioral evidence in [Lesson 3](#w07-l3) tells you where your calculations, and your counterpart’s, are likely to be distorted.

challenge.text: The BATNA–reservation value–ZOPA structure is the most useful single preparation tool in negotiation. It is also a simplification, in at least four ways that matter for executives.

items: **Alternatives are rarely one number.** A competing job offer differs in location, title, team and risk; a second vendor differs in quality and switching cost. Collapsing an alternative into a figure requires judgments about what you value, and those judgments are where self-deception enters. Negotiators who want a deal tend to undervalue their alternatives.

**Reservation values should move, but for reasons.** New information during the negotiation, such as what the other system really does or how long implementation will take, should change your reservation value. Fatigue, sunk effort and a pleasant counterpart should not.

**Power is not only alternatives.** Deadlines, commitments, coalitions, legal rules, public scrutiny and the future of the relationship all affect outcomes. A city with a strong alternative may still settle generously because a service gap would be politically intolerable.
**The model is single-issue at heart.** Real deals have several issues. Treating a five-issue negotiation as one price hides the trades that create value, the subject of [Lesson 2](#w07-l2).

challenge.text: *Getting to Yes* deserves the same scrutiny you would give any influential framework. It is practitioner prescription drawn from its authors’ experience, not a report of controlled studies. Its principles (separate the people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain, insist on objective criteria) have proven durable in teaching, and later laboratory work on joint gains is broadly consistent with them. But the book says less about the distributive moment when someone must give up money, and a negotiator who treats it as a complete theory can be outmaneuvered by one who claims hard. Read it as a vocabulary and a set of heuristics.

Your knowledge of the structure also has a psychological payoff. In Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments, the advantage of making the first offer disappeared when the recipient concentrated on the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target. Knowing the architecture is therefore not only an analytic aid; it is a defense against being pulled by the other side’s numbers.

challenge.title: Executive twist: you have not priced your alternative, and the offer expires at noon

blocks.text: You lead a department that has negotiated for three months with an analytics vendor. At 7 p.m. the vendor’s chief revenue officer calls: sign by noon tomorrow at a price 15 percent above your budget, or the price rises and the implementation slot goes to another client. You have never formally priced your alternative. A reasonable twelve-hour plan:

items: Separate the deadline from the decision. Ask what makes the deadline real and whose interest it serves; exploding offers are a common claiming tactic.
Build a rough BATNA in hours rather than weeks: call the second-ranked vendor, and estimate what a six-month delay would cost in staff time and lost capability.
Write a provisional reservation value before the call, with the reasoning behind it.
If you still cannot estimate a reservation value, treat that ignorance as information. Accepting an exploding offer is sensible only when the cost of delay clearly exceeds the premium being demanded.

apply.text: Worked example from healthcare. A regional hospital system is negotiating a two-year contract with a nurse staffing agency for intensive-care coverage. The hospital’s BATNA is to accelerate permanent hiring and pay overtime in the meantime; its finance team estimates an all-in equivalent of $112 an hour once vacancy risk is included, so the hospital’s reservation value is $112. The agency’s BATNA is to place the same nurses with another health system; after its own costs, it would accept as little as $98 an hour from this hospital. The ZOPA is $98 to $112, a $14 surplus per hour. The agency opens at $125. (Synthetic numbers.)

Three lessons follow. First, the agency’s opening sits outside the zone, which is normal; it tells you about the agency’s strategy, not about its reservation value. Second, the hospital’s strongest response is not a counter-number pulled from the air but a counter-offer near its aspiration (say $103) justified by objective criteria such as published regional rates, together with a credible signal of its alternative: “We have approved twenty permanent positions and start interviews next month.” Third, the hospital should know in advance what would change its reservation value. Learning that the agency guarantees continuity of the same nurses for the full term, which reduces training costs, is a legitimate reason to pay more. Learning that the agency is impatient is not a reason to pay less than fair value if the relationship will be renewed.

The same structure governs negotiations in player development, most of which are not about player contracts. When you negotiate a license for a biomechanics or tracking system, a lease for a training facility abroad, a data-sharing arrangement with a university laboratory, or your department’s budget with your own leadership, the questions are identical: what will you do if this does not happen, what is that worth, and what is the other side’s equivalent? An internal budget request has a BATNA too: reallocating from another line, phasing the project, or running a smaller pilot. You are stronger in the meeting when you have priced that alternative beforehand, and more credible when you can say what you will do if the answer is no.

items: Write your BATNA as an action, then as a number, with the assumptions behind the number.
Estimate the other side’s BATNA with a range and a confidence level, and list what you would need to learn to narrow it.
Set your reservation value and aspiration in writing before the first conversation.
Identify one way to improve your BATNA before you negotiate, and one way the other side might be improving theirs.
Decide which commitments, deadlines or criteria you will use to make your claims credible.

retain.text: A negotiation’s outcome is bounded by each side’s alternatives before anyone speaks. The ZOPA tells you whether a deal is possible; information, credibility and aspiration decide where in the zone it lands. Bargaining power is mostly the relative cost of no deal, which you can often change before the meeting.
Without looking back: define BATNA, reservation value, aspiration and ZOPA in one sentence each, and explain how the first two are related.
In the staffing example, name one piece of information that should legitimately raise the hospital’s reservation value and one that should not.
Think of a negotiation you lost or regretted. Was the problem the size of the zone, your estimate of the other side’s numbers, or how you claimed inside the zone?

takeaways: Your BATNA is a course of action; your reservation value is that action translated into the worst acceptable terms here.
A deal is possible only when reservation values overlap; when they do not, impasse is the correct outcome.
Aspirations, not reservation values, determine how much of the zone you claim; prepare both in writing.
Bargaining power is mainly the relative cost of no deal, shaped by alternatives, deadlines, commitments and reputation.
Knowing the structure is also a psychological defense against the other side’s anchors.

check.prompt: A seller will accept no less than $3.4M for a business unit (its reservation value). A buyer will pay at most $4.1M (its reservation value). The seller opens at $4.6M and the buyer at $3.0M. How wide is the zone of possible agreement, in millions of dollars?
check.working: The ZOPA runs from the seller’s reservation value ($3.4M) to the buyer’s reservation value ($4.1M): 4.1 − 3.4 = $0.7M. Opening offers do not define the zone; they are claims about it.
check.explanation: The zone is bounded by reservation values, not by opening offers: $4.1M − $3.4M = $0.7M. The openings ($4.6M and $3.0M) sit outside the zone, which is normal, and the gap between them ($1.6M) overstates the real bargaining range.

check.prompt: Which statement best describes bargaining power in the BATNA framework?

options.text: It is mainly a matter of personal assertiveness and presence at the table.
It is mainly the relative cost of no deal to each side, which alternatives, deadlines and credible commitments can change.
It belongs to whichever side makes the first offer.
It is fixed by the size of each organization.

check.explanation: In the BATNA framework, the side that needs the agreement less, because its alternative is closer to the deal’s value, can credibly claim more of the zone. Alternatives can be improved, deadlines shift them over time, and commitments change the other side’s estimate of your reservation value.

optionFeedback.a: Assertiveness without a credible alternative is bluster; experienced counterparts discount it.
optionFeedback.c: First offers can anchor outcomes (Lesson 3), but they do not change what happens if talks fail.
optionFeedback.d: Large organizations can have weak alternatives in a particular deal; size matters only through alternatives and constraints.

sources.use: Origin and definition of BATNA; principled negotiation as practitioner prescription.
Analytic structure of reservation values and zones of agreement; prescriptive negotiation analysis.
Focusing on the other side’s alternatives and reservation price neutralizes first-offer anchors.

Shows how anchors and perception distort the numbers you prepared here.

lessons.title: Creating and Claiming Value: Integrative Bargaining, Logrolling and Contingent Contracts
lessons.summary: Valuable deals are built from differences in priorities, forecasts, risk tolerance and timing, but the moves that create value also expose you to the moves that claim it.
objectives: Distinguish distributive, integrative and compatible issues and identify the sources of joint value in a multi-issue deal.
Construct a logrolling trade and a contingent contract, and judge an agreement against the Pareto frontier.
Explain the negotiator’s dilemma and choose information-sharing moves that create value without giving it away.
lessons.executive: Negotiators who split the difference on every issue routinely leave a large share of the available value unclaimed by anyone. Value comes from differences: one side cares more about price, the other about speed; one expects strong results, the other doubts them; one can bear a risk more cheaply. Trading across issues (logrolling) and making terms depend on future facts (contingent contracts) turn those differences into gains for both. The obstacles are perceptual, because negotiators assume the pie is fixed, and strategic, because revealing your priorities helps create value and helps the other side claim it. Executives need both skills: enlarge the pie deliberately, then divide it firmly.

explore.text: A cloud-services provider and a mid-sized bank spend six weeks negotiating a three-year hosting agreement. They are $400,000 a year apart on the fee, and each negotiator has told colleagues that the other side is difficult. In the seventh week a junior lawyer for the bank asks why the provider keeps resisting the bank’s request to store all data in-country. The answer surprises everyone: the provider already runs an in-country data center with spare capacity and had assumed the bank wanted a costly bespoke arrangement. The bank, for its part, cares far more about data residency, which its supervisors scrutinize, than about the fee. Within a day the parties agree on in-country hosting, a slightly higher fee and the longer term the provider wanted for its own financing. Both report a better deal than they expected. Nothing about either side’s interests changed in week seven. What changed was what each knew about the other’s priorities. (Hypothetical example.)

Before reading on: when two negotiators split the difference on each of four issues, what share of the available joint value do you guess they leave unclaimed? Write a number. You will test the guess in this week’s Negotiation Chamber.

understand.text: Two activities in one conversation

David Lax and James Sebenius describe every negotiation as two intertwined activities. Creating value enlarges what is available to divide, through sharing information about priorities, inventing options and solving problems jointly. Claiming value determines who gets what, through withholding sensitive information, anchoring and committing to favorable terms. Their central claim is that the two are inextricably linked. Earlier advice tended to address one or the other; managers face both in the same conversation.

An issue is [distributive](#gl:g-distributive-bargaining) when one side’s gain is the other’s loss, point for point: the fee in a license, the price of a building. Bargaining is [integrative](#gl:g-integrative-bargaining) when the parties can find agreements that leave both better off than other agreements they could reach, usually because they value the issues differently. Most real negotiations are mixed. Some issues are distributive, some integrative, and a few are compatible: both sides want the same outcome, such as confidentiality or an early start, without realizing it.
Where joint value comes from

understand.caption: Sources of joint value and the instruments that capture them
rows: Priorities: each cares more about different issues
Logrolling: concede what matters less to you for what matters more
A hospital accepts a longer contract in exchange for faster implementation
Forecasts: each expects a different future
Contingent contract: terms depend on an observable outcome
An acquirer pays an earnout if revenue reaches the seller’s forecast
Shift a risk to the party that bears it more cheaply
A large vendor guarantees a fixed price; a small client pays a modest premium
A start-up accepts less cash now and a renewal option later
Assign each task to the lower-cost party
The supplier with spare in-country capacity hosts the data

understand.text: Raiffa’s analysis treats two-party, multi-issue bargaining as a different problem from single-issue haggling. With one issue, every gain for one side is a loss for the other. With several issues that the parties value differently, they can trade across issues and improve both positions.

Keep trading until no package can make one side better off without making the other worse off, and you have reached the [Pareto frontier](#gl:g-pareto-frontier). An agreement below the frontier is inefficient: some other package would be better for at least one party and worse for neither. Inefficiency is not a moral failing. It is money, time or capability that neither side receives.

understand.caption: Logrolling versus splitting the difference (synthetic point schedules)
rows: Split the difference on every issue
Logroll: hospital gets speed, licensor gets length
understand.note: Synthetic. Speed is worth 0/15/30 to the hospital and 10/5/0 to the licensor; length (1/2/3 years) is worth 0/15/30 to the licensor and 10/5/0 to the hospital; price (high/middle/low) is worth 20/10/0 to the licensor and 0/10/20 to the hospital.

understand.caption: Joint points by package in the logrolling example
understand.note: Synthetic data from the table above. The logroll is on the Pareto frontier; the split is not.

understand.text: Notice two things. The logroll leaves both parties better off than the split (40 against 30 each), so it is not a compromise but an improvement. And “winning” every issue produces no more joint value than splitting: the hospital captured everything, but the pie did not grow. Price, the only purely distributive issue, was held at the middle in both of the first two packages; the gains came entirely from speed and length.

understand.caption: Issue-priority matrix: where to trade and where to claim
cells: Low stakes for both: settle quickly; use as goodwill
Give it, but get credit: cheap for you, valuable to them
Ask for it and trade for it: valuable to you, cheap for them
Genuinely distributive: prepare criteria and claim carefully
understand.note: Practitioner heuristic for planning trades. It assumes you have estimated the other side’s priorities, which you must test at the table.

understand.text: Why do capable negotiators miss trades like these? Leigh Thompson and Reid Hastie reported that most negotiators enter a negotiation expecting the other side’s interests to be completely opposed to their own, and argued that misperceiving the other side’s interests is a primary cause of inefficient agreements. This [fixed-pie perception](#gl:g-fixed-pie) leads negotiators to treat every issue as distributive and to split differences issue by issue.

A related mistake is assuming that on every issue the other side wants the opposite of what you want. On compatible issues, both want the same thing; a negotiator who “concedes” such an issue, or demands payment for it, wastes value or credibility.
Contingent contracts: betting on disagreement

When parties disagree about the future, the disagreement itself can create value. A founder convinced that her company will reach $40 million in revenue next year and a buyer who doubts it can argue about price indefinitely. Or they can agree on a base price plus an earnout that pays more if revenue reaches the target. Each side is then paid according to its own forecast, and both may prefer the contingent deal to any fixed price. Performance bonuses, success fees, price-adjustment clauses and options to extend are all [contingent contracts](#gl:g-contingent-contract). They work only under conditions:

items: The trigger is observable to both sides and measurable without dispute.
The party that controls the outcome cannot easily manipulate the measure.
The contingency does not distort behavior in ways that destroy value elsewhere, such as a revenue target that rewards discounting.
The terms are enforceable and specify who measures, when, and how disputes are resolved.

understand.title: Prerequisite: Pareto efficiency in plain language

blocks.text: An outcome is Pareto efficient when no change could make someone better off without making someone else worse off. Imagine plotting every possible agreement on a chart, your points on one axis and the other side’s on the other. The outer edge of that cloud is the frontier. Points inside it are wasteful, because moving outward helps someone and hurts no one. Efficiency says nothing about fairness: an agreement that gives one side almost everything can sit on the frontier. Negotiators therefore face two separate questions: are we on the frontier, and where on it are we?

understand.title: Methodological note: how researchers measure joint gains

blocks.text: Laboratory studies of integrative bargaining usually give each negotiator a confidential point schedule, as this week’s Negotiation Chamber does, and measure the sum of both sides’ points against the maximum available. The design makes efficiency measurable and comparable across pairs. Its cost is realism: the experimenter, not the negotiators, assigns values; issues are separable; and there is no future relationship.

Studies with managers rather than students, and with coded transcripts rather than outcomes alone, strengthen the inference. Wendi Adair, Tetsushi Okumura and Jeanne Brett coded what U.S. and Japanese managers actually said in an integrative simulation and linked patterns of information exchange to the joint gains pairs achieved, a design you will meet again in [Lesson 4](#w07-l4).

challenge.text: “Win–win” is one of the most abused phrases in management. Three cautions keep the idea honest.

items: **Integrative potential is an empirical question.** Some negotiations are genuinely distributive: one issue, one-shot, no relationship. Pretending otherwise invites concessions labelled “creative” that are simply concessions.

**Creating value says nothing about who gets it.** In the logrolling example, a sharper licensor could have taken most of the gain by also holding the price high. A deal can be efficient and lopsided at once.

**Joint gains can come at third parties’ expense.** Two department heads who trade support for each other’s budgets may both “win” while the organization loses; two firms that logroll may be colluding against customers. Efficiency between the parties at the table is not efficiency for everyone affected.

challenge.text: The [negotiator’s dilemma](#gl:g-negotiators-dilemma) is the sharpest form of the problem. If you reveal that implementation speed matters enormously to you, a cooperative counterpart will trade for it efficiently, while an opportunistic one will concede speed slowly and charge heavily for it. If you conceal your priorities, you protect yourself but make the efficient trade harder to find. Because creating and claiming are linked, neither pure openness nor pure secrecy is safe.

Experienced negotiators manage the dilemma with moves that are practitioner heuristics rather than tested rules. Share relative priorities (“speed matters more to us than term”) before anything resembling a reservation value. Reciprocate disclosure in small steps and notice whether the other side does the same. Put two or three complete packages of equal value to you on the table at once, often called multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, and learn from which one the other side prefers. Ask diagnostic questions (“What would a longer term let you do?”) rather than leading with positions.

The fixed-pie finding should itself be read with care. The error is assuming opposition without checking, not believing in opposition. In a genuinely distributive negotiation the negotiator with a fixed-pie view is simply correct, and later work in this literature makes exactly that point. The skill is diagnosis: test for differences before you conclude there are none.

apply.text: Worked example from finance and law. A private-equity buyer and the founder of a pharmacy-software company are $12 million apart: the founder values the company at $90 million on her growth forecast; the buyer will pay $78 million on its own. A contingent structure might offer $78 million at closing plus up to $12 million if audited recurring revenue in the second year exceeds an agreed target. The founder is paid on her forecast if it proves right; the buyer pays more only when the business is worth more. The drafting questions decide whether the earnout creates value or a lawsuit: who controls pricing and sales hiring after closing, how revenue is defined, whether acquisitions count, and how disputes are resolved. [Week 11](#w11) returns to these clauses. (Synthetic numbers.)

Player development is full of integrative structure. In a technology agreement, a club typically cares more about data access, integration with its own systems and support during the busiest weeks of the season than about a modest difference in fee; the vendor cares about a multi-year commitment, a reference customer and permission to describe the partnership. When two departments share scarce staff, such as a biomechanist or a video coordinator, they usually differ in when they need the person, which is an ideal setting for a trade across time rather than a contest over headcount.

items: List every issue, including the ones nobody has raised yet (term, timing, data, support, publicity, exclusivity, termination).
Score your own priorities with points that sum to 100, then estimate the other side’s, and mark each estimate as a guess.
Place each issue in the priority matrix; plan trades from the off-diagonal cells.
Identify at least one forecast disagreement that a contingent term could resolve, and write its trigger.
Decide in advance what you will disclose about relative priorities, and what you will not disclose about your reservation value.

retain.text: Value is created from differences and claimed through information and commitment, and the two cannot be separated. Splitting the difference issue by issue is a symptom of the fixed-pie perception. Logrolls and contingent terms move agreements toward the frontier; firm, criteria-based claiming determines where on it you land.
Explain, using the hospital–licensor example, why the logroll is not a compromise.
State the negotiator’s dilemma in two sentences, then name one move that reduces it.
Name the four conditions a contingent contract needs to create value rather than disputes.

takeaways: Most negotiations mix distributive, integrative and compatible issues; diagnose which is which.
Logrolling trades issues the parties value differently and can leave both better off than any split.
Contingent contracts turn disagreement about the future into value, if the trigger is measurable and hard to manipulate.
The negotiator’s dilemma means openness creates value and exposes you; disclose relative priorities incrementally.
Efficiency and fairness are separate questions: first reach the frontier, then claim your share of it.

check.prompt: Which instrument best addresses the core obstacle in this negotiation?

stimulus.text: A city health department wants to buy a predictive-staffing tool for its clinics. The vendor insists the tool will cut overtime by 20 percent and prices it accordingly; the department’s analysts expect perhaps 5 percent and will not pay the vendor’s price. Both sides have shared their forecasts and neither will move. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Split the difference on price.
A contingent fee: a base price plus a payment tied to audited overtime reductions.
A logroll that trades contract length for price.
A longer silence to pressure the vendor into conceding.

check.explanation: The parties disagree about a measurable future outcome. A contingent fee lets each be paid according to its own forecast: the vendor earns more if it is right, and the department pays more only if the savings materialize. It needs a clear, audited measure that neither side can easily manipulate.

optionFeedback.a: Splitting leaves the forecast disagreement unresolved; each side still thinks the price is wrong.
optionFeedback.c: A logroll exploits different priorities, but here the obstacle is a different forecast, not different priorities.
optionFeedback.d: Pressure may move the price but does not address the underlying disagreement and risks impasse.

check.prompt: What does the negotiator’s dilemma (Lax and Sebenius) claim?

options.text: Negotiators must choose between being liked and being effective.
Moves that create value, such as revealing priorities, also expose a negotiator to the other side’s value-claiming moves, so the two activities cannot be separated.
Integrative bargaining always produces better outcomes than distributive bargaining.
A negotiator should never reveal any information before the other side does.

check.explanation: Creating value requires information about priorities; claiming value exploits information. Because the same disclosure serves both, negotiators cannot simply choose cooperation or competition; they must manage both, usually by disclosing relative priorities incrementally and reciprocally.

optionFeedback.a: Likability is a separate question; the dilemma concerns information and its strategic use.
optionFeedback.c: Some negotiations are genuinely distributive; integrative moves cannot create value that is not there.
optionFeedback.d: Total secrecy protects you but makes efficient trades hard to find; it is one horn of the dilemma, not its solution.

sources.use: Creating versus claiming value; the negotiator’s dilemma.
Multi-issue bargaining as distinct from single-issue haggling.
Fixed-pie perception as a cause of inefficient agreements.
Behavioral coding of information exchange linked to joint gains.

Information-exchange routines differ across cultures and affect joint gains.
