questions: Map this as at least three linked negotiations: inside Brisamar, inside the federation, and across the table. Which should Tomás work on first, and what must come out of it?
Estimate each side’s BATNA and identify the issues on which their priorities differ. Which trades or contingent terms could create value, and which issue is mainly distributive?
How should Tomás treat the $2.40 figure? Draft one question he could put to Ernesto that tests it without accusing anyone of bluffing.
Identify the principal–agent problems on both sides. What, if anything, should Nadia change before Tuesday?
What did Brisamar misread in March, and how should Tomás structure Tuesday’s meeting differently without relying on national stereotypes?

perspectives.title: Build the coalition the federation can ratify
perspectives.text: Altagracia has told Tomás how to win eight votes: do not force the urban cooperatives to choose, and give the rural ones something visible. A non-exclusive master agreement with a fee between Brisamar’s offer and the federation’s ask, Brisamar-funded training for the rural branches (paid once, as an investment, rather than shared), and voluntary exclusivity for rural cooperatives in exchange for a volume bonus can be ratified on both sides. The currency spread stays with Brisamar, which protects the margin story. The risk is overpaying if the $2.40 rumor is false; Tomás should test it before conceding on fee.

perspectives.title: Do not let the funding round set the timeline
perspectives.text: Renée and the bank, not the federation, control when the first payout can happen. A signed agreement that cannot launch for three months does little for investors, and an implied launch date that compliance then refuses would damage Brisamar with the federation and the bank at once. Tomás should tell Nadia that the deadline is self-imposed, negotiate a nonbinding letter of intent now with clear statements of what is and is not committed, and sign the definitive agreement after compliance review. The cost is time and perhaps Tomás’s bonus; the benefit is a deal that does not unravel in the first audit.

perspectives.title: Use contingent terms to resolve the forecast disagreement
perspectives.text: Much of the conflict is a disagreement about the future: Brisamar fears that a deposit invitation will cost it customers; the federation believes it will build loyalty; Brisamar projects 38,000 transfers a month and the federation may doubt it. A volume-tiered payout fee, a rural bonus pool triggered by audited corridor volume, and a measured pilot of the deposit invitation let each side be paid on its own forecast. The objection is Ernesto’s: formulas the board cannot explain will not pass. The contingent terms must be few and simple, with a one-page explanation in Spanish.

perspectives.title: Fix the agent before the negotiation
perspectives.text: Tomás’s bonus rewards volume signed by June 30, which pushes him toward speed and concessions whatever his intentions. Nadia should restructure it, for example to reward twelve-month corridor contribution and clean compliance results, and should approve a written mandate (fee range, no spread share, conditions on launch dates) before Tuesday. On the federation’s side, Ernesto’s position and Altagracia’s signals may reflect different constituencies; Tomás should learn who on the board needs what rather than treating the federation as one negotiator.

case.application: The structure transfers directly to international operations in professional baseball. An agreement for a training facility or academy abroad typically has the same three tables: inside your organization (finance, legal and compliance, baseball leadership), inside the partner (owners, local institutions, community stakeholders) and across the table, often through intermediaries whose incentives differ from those of the people they represent. The same disciplines apply: build the internal mandate first, let compliance and legal set what can be promised, distinguish cultural signals from individual ones, test claims about competing offers with questions rather than accusations, and do not let an internal deadline become the other side’s leverage.

questions.prompt: A hospital is deciding how far it can go in renegotiating a contract with its outside laboratory. Its alternative is to build an in-house laboratory, which would cost $2.4M a year if the build finishes on schedule (60 percent likely). If the build is delayed, the hospital must buy a year of spot testing at $3.1M. What is the expected annual cost of the hospital’s alternative, in millions of dollars? (Synthetic numbers; ignore risk attitudes.)
questions.working: Expected cost = 0.6 × 2.4 + 0.4 × 3.1 = 1.44 + 1.24 = $2.68M. A risk-neutral hospital should not agree to pay the laboratory more than about $2.68M a year; a risk-averse one might accept somewhat more to avoid the chance of a $3.1M year.
questions.explanation: The BATNA is uncertain, so its value is a probability-weighted average: 0.6 × $2.4M + 0.4 × $3.1M = $2.68M. That figure is the starting point for the hospital’s reservation value; risk attitudes and non-financial factors then adjust it deliberately.

questions.prompt: What is the soundest conclusion for both parties?

stimulus.text: After months of talks over the sale of a software business, the seller’s board has documented that it will not sell below $5.2M, because a strategic buyer has offered $5.2M in a binding bid. The buyer’s investment committee has documented that it cannot justify more than $4.9M on its own valuation. A mediator proposes $5.05M “to meet in the middle.” Price is the only open issue, and both sides’ figures are well grounded. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Both should accept $5.05M, since splitting the difference is fair.

There is no zone of possible agreement on price alone; unless the parties can create value on another dimension (for example a contingent payment), impasse is the correct outcome and the seller should take the strategic bid.
The buyer should accept $5.05M because it has invested months in the deal.
The seller should accept $5.05M because a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

questions.explanation: The seller’s reservation value ($5.2M) exceeds the buyer’s ($4.9M), so no price leaves both better off than their alternatives. A midpoint is worse for each side than walking away. Only new value, such as an earnout that bridges different forecasts, could create a zone; otherwise impasse is the right result.

optionFeedback.a: Splitting the difference is not fair or sensible when it leaves both parties below their alternatives.
optionFeedback.c: Months of effort are sunk costs; they do not change what the business is worth to the buyer.
optionFeedback.d: The seller has a binding $5.2M bid in hand; $5.05M is a worse bird.

questions.prompt: Rank the four packages from highest to lowest joint value (sum of both parties’ points).

stimulus.caption: Point schedules for a facilities-management contract (synthetic)

options.text: Medium price, 4-hour response, 3-year term
Medium price, 24-hour response, 1-year term
Low price, 4-hour response, 1-year term
High price, 24-hour response, 3-year term

questions.explanation: Joint values: (a) client 10 + 30 + 0 = 40, contractor 10 + 0 + 20 = 30, joint 70; (c) client 20 + 30 + 5 = 55, contractor 0, joint 55; (d) client 0, contractor 20 + 10 + 20 = 50, joint 50; (b) client 10 + 0 + 5 = 15, contractor 10 + 10 + 0 = 20, joint 35. The logroll in (a) gives the client fast response (worth 30 to it, costing the contractor 10) and the contractor a long term (worth 20 to it, costing the client 5). Price is purely distributive: every price option adds 20 joint points, so it cannot change the ranking.

questions.prompt: A buyer and a founder agree to bridge a valuation gap with an earnout. Which trigger is most likely to create value rather than a dispute?

options.text: Post-closing EBITDA as reported by the buyer, which will control costs and allocations after closing.
Gross revenue, with no constraints on discounting.
Audited recurring revenue under defined accounting rules, with pricing floors, a defined treatment of acquisitions and a named dispute-resolution process.
The founder’s own assessment of whether the targets were met.

questions.explanation: A contingent term works when the trigger is observable to both sides, measured without dispute, and hard for the party controlling the outcome to manipulate. Audited recurring revenue with defined rules, pricing floors and a dispute process meets those conditions far better than measures one side controls.

optionFeedback.a: The buyer controls costs and allocations after closing, so it could depress EBITDA and the founder would rightly fear manipulation.
optionFeedback.b: Unconstrained revenue rewards discounting that may destroy value elsewhere.
optionFeedback.d: A measure controlled by the party being paid invites the opposite manipulation.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation is best supported by this (fictional) study?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. “We analyzed 312 municipal contract renegotiations. When the city made the first offer, final prices averaged 6 percent lower than when the contractor made the first offer. Among renegotiations in which the city had no recent market price data, however, city first offers were associated with higher final prices than contractor first offers. Cities chose for themselves whether to open first.”

options.text: Opening first causes cities to obtain lower prices in all circumstances.

The data are consistent with first offers helping when the opener is informed and hurting when it is not, but because cities chose whether to open, the study cannot establish that opening first caused the differences.
The study shows anchoring does not occur in real negotiations.
Because the sample is 312, the effect is certainly causal.

questions.explanation: The pattern matches the laboratory logic: informed first offers anchor favorably, uninformed ones can give away surplus. But the study is observational and cities self-selected into opening first; better-prepared cities may both open first and negotiate better. It suggests a hypothesis consistent with Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments without proving causation in the field.

optionFeedback.a: The study itself reports the opposite pattern when cities lacked market data, and it cannot establish causation.
optionFeedback.c: A 6 percent difference associated with who opened is consistent with anchoring, not evidence against it.
optionFeedback.d: Sample size reduces noise; it does not remove selection bias.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in the vice president’s reasoning?

stimulus.text: A vice president preparing a final offer to a small supplier says: “Their alternative is worth about $400,000 a year to them. Our offer is $410,000, so they will accept. Whether they think it’s fair after last year’s price cuts is irrelevant; they’re rational.” (Hypothetical.)

options.text: The vice president has overestimated the supplier’s alternative.

It assumes a counterpart accepts anything that beats its alternative; evidence from ultimatum-game research shows people reject offers they see as unfair even at a cost to themselves, so fairness is a second constraint.
Offers should always be made in round numbers.
The reasoning is sound; fairness matters only in laboratory games.

questions.explanation: Meta-analytic ultimatum-game evidence shows that responders reject offers they regard as unfair even though rejecting costs them money. A supplier that feels squeezed after last year’s cuts may refuse a deal that beats its alternative by a small margin, or accept and look for the exit. Objective criteria and attention to precedent reduce that risk.

optionFeedback.a: The estimate may be wrong, but the flaw in the reasoning holds even if the estimate is right.
optionFeedback.c: Irrelevant to the logic of the argument.
optionFeedback.d: The laboratory games simplify, but the fairness constraint they reveal is one of the more robust lessons for real deals.

questions.prompt: A company uses an outside broker, paid 3 percent of the purchase price on closing, to negotiate the purchase of a warehouse. Which measures reduce the principal–agent problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pay the broker a fee that increases as the purchase price falls below an agreed benchmark.
Give the broker a written mandate with a maximum price and the terms that require the company’s approval.
Let the broker decide the maximum price, since the broker knows the market better.
Require the broker to provide comparable transactions and the seller’s likely alternatives in writing before the final offer.
Keep the 3 percent fee and add a bonus for closing within two weeks.
Arrange a direct principal-to-principal conversation before the final terms are agreed.

questions.explanation: A percentage-of-price fee paid on closing rewards a higher price and any closing. Aligning pay with the buyer’s outcome, setting a written mandate, requiring the agent’s evidence and keeping direct principal contact at key moments all reduce the problem. Delegating the reservation value to the agent or rewarding speed makes it worse.

optionFeedback.c: Delegating the reservation value to the agent hands the decision to the party with the misaligned incentive.
optionFeedback.e: A speed bonus adds a second incentive to close regardless of price.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: In a negotiation with a family-owned distributor abroad, you have asked direct questions about priorities in two meetings and received polite, general answers. Your counterpart has, however, made offers that consistently hold firm on payment terms and move readily on delivery schedules. A colleague says, “They’re evasive. That’s how people from that country negotiate.” (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Push harder with direct questions until you get a straight answer.
Accept your colleague’s cultural explanation and lower your expectations for joint gains.
Treat the pattern of offers as information about priorities (payment terms appear to matter more), propose packages that trade on it, and say explicitly how you would like to exchange information.
Switch to a single-issue price negotiation to avoid confusion.

questions.explanation: Research on U.S. and Japanese managers found that negotiators differ in how they exchange information, directly through questions or indirectly through offers, and that mismatched routines lower joint gains. Reading the offers, testing the inference with packages, and making the process explicit adapts to the counterpart you observe, without a stereotype.

optionFeedback.a: Repeating a routine that is not working is unlikely to surface priorities and may read as disrespect.
optionFeedback.b: A country label predicts an individual’s behavior poorly (the ecological fallacy), and the offers already carry usable information.
optionFeedback.d: Collapsing to one issue destroys the trades the offers are revealing.

questions.prompt: Read the negotiation notes. Select every genuine ethical or legal-commercial issue they raise.

stimulus.text: Notes from a services negotiation (fictional). (1) Our lead declined to disclose our budget when asked. (2) She told the vendor we had a “signed competing quote at $310,000”; no such quote exists. (3) The vendor said its platform “passed its last security audit”; we later learned a newer audit found open findings. (4) We opened at a price well below our target. (5) We both signed a “letter of intent” that includes an exclusivity clause for 90 days but says the letter is “non-binding”. (6) The outside adviser who introduced the vendor receives a referral fee from the vendor that we were not told about.

options.text: Item 1: declining to disclose the budget
Item 2: the invented competing quote
Item 3: the vendor’s statement about its security audit
Item 4: the low opening offer
Item 5: the letter of intent’s exclusivity clause
Item 6: the adviser’s undisclosed referral fee

questions.explanation: The invented quote is a false statement of fact and may carry legal exposure in many jurisdictions. The audit statement is a palter on a material fact. A “non-binding” letter that contains an exclusivity clause needs review, because some clauses in such letters can bind depending on wording and governing law. The adviser’s undisclosed fee is a conflict of interest, a principal–agent problem. Declining to disclose and an ambitious opening are widely accepted competitive tactics. (Educational material, not legal advice.)

optionFeedback.a: Declining to disclose is open and widely accepted; it is not deception.
optionFeedback.d: An ambitious opening is traditional competitive bargaining, widely judged acceptable.

questions.prompt: In general terms, which statement made by a seller in a negotiation is most likely to create legal exposure if it is false?

options.text: “This is the best platform on the market.”
“We won’t go below $900,000.”
“Our system is certified under the security standard your regulator requires.”
“I think you’ll find our team easy to work with.”

questions.explanation: A specific, verifiable claim about a material fact the buyer is likely to rely on is the kind of statement that can support claims such as misrepresentation. Opinions, sales talk and statements about one’s own limits are generally treated differently in many common-law systems, though rules vary by jurisdiction. (Educational material about general legal concepts, not legal advice.)

optionFeedback.a: Broad superlatives are usually treated as opinion or sales talk rather than verifiable fact.
optionFeedback.b: Statements about your own willingness to pay or accept are generally treated as negotiating positions, though they can still be ethically questionable when false.
optionFeedback.d: An expression of opinion about the future relationship is not a statement of material fact.

questions.prompt: You are negotiating a two-year contract for a video-analysis platform. Near the end of the second meeting, the vendor asks: “What’s your budget for this?” Write the response you would give (60–120 words). Then explain in two or three sentences how your response handles the negotiator’s dilemma and the ethics of disclosure.
questions.modelAnswer: Response: “I’m not going to share a budget figure; it would only anchor both of us. What I can tell you is what matters most to us: integration with our existing systems and on-site support in the first three months matter more than the license fee, and a two-year term works for us. If you can show us a package that is strong on integration and support, we can talk about how the fee fits, using what comparable organizations pay.” Explanation: The answer declines openly rather than inventing a number or paltering, so nothing in it is false or misleading. It protects the reservation value while disclosing relative priorities, which creates room for trades, and it moves the price discussion toward objective criteria.

rubric.criterion: Honesty: no false statement and no misleading true statement about budget or alternatives
levels: 0 — states or implies a false budget or alternative
1 — no false statement, but the wording invites a misleading inference
2 — declines openly; everything said is true and not misleading

rubric.criterion: Protects the reservation value while creating value
levels: 0 — reveals the budget or reservation value
1 — protects the number but offers nothing that would help find trades
2 — protects the number and discloses relative priorities or invites package proposals

rubric.criterion: Moves the discussion toward criteria or interests
levels: 0 — no redirection
1 — redirects to interests, comparables or objective criteria

rubric.criterion: Explanation links the response to the negotiator’s dilemma and disclosure ethics
levels: 0 — missing or generic
1 — explains which information is shared, which is withheld, and why

questions.prompt: You will negotiate a three-year analytics partnership with a university laboratory. Your finance chief wants the lowest cost, your coaching staff want rapid access to findings, and your legal team insists on data-protection terms the laboratory has resisted before. The first external meeting is in two weeks. What should you do first?

options.text: Open talks with the laboratory immediately to learn its position, then report back to the three internal groups.
Convene the three internal groups to agree a written mandate: priorities, reservation value, non-negotiable terms and the trades you may make, then negotiate externally.
Ask the legal team to negotiate, since data protection is the hardest issue.
Let each internal group contact the laboratory directly so that each can represent its own interests.

questions.explanation: Every external deal is also an internal negotiation. Agreeing the mandate first prevents the deal from collapsing at ratification, gives you credible constraints (the data-protection terms are real) and lets you plan trades across issues the internal groups value differently.

optionFeedback.a: Learning early has value, but negotiating without a mandate risks commitments your constituencies will not ratify.
optionFeedback.c: Delegating to one function hands the whole negotiation to the group with one priority.
optionFeedback.d: Multiple uncoordinated channels let the counterpart play your constituencies against each other.

reserve.prompt: A negotiator prepares only a reservation value and no aspiration. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: She will reach impasse more often.
She will tend to settle close to her reservation value, because it is the only number she has thought hard about.
She will anchor the other side more effectively.
Nothing; the reservation value contains all the information she needs.

reserve.explanation: The reservation value protects against bad deals but does not tell you how much of the zone to claim. Without a prepared aspiration, negotiators tend to treat the reservation value as the goal and settle near it.

optionFeedback.a: A reservation value alone does not make impasse more likely; it makes mediocre deals more likely.
optionFeedback.c: Anchoring requires an ambitious opening tied to an aspiration; the reservation value should not be revealed.
optionFeedback.d: The reservation value marks the floor, not the target.

reserve.prompt: Using the hospital–licensor point schedules from Lesson 2 (speed worth 0/15/30 to the hospital and 10/5/0 to the licensor; length of 1/2/3 years worth 0/15/30 to the licensor and 10/5/0 to the hospital; price high/middle/low worth 20/10/0 to the licensor and 0/10/20 to the hospital), how many joint points does splitting the difference on every issue leave below the maximum joint value?
reserve.working: Split (medium, 2 years, middle): hospital 15 + 5 + 10 = 30; licensor 5 + 15 + 10 = 30; joint 60. Maximum: fast speed (30 + 0 = 30 joint), 3 years (0 + 30 = 30 joint), any price (20 joint) = 80. Gap = 80 − 60 = 20.
reserve.explanation: Price always contributes 20 joint points, so the gains come from speed and length. Choosing fast rollout and a 3-year term yields 80 joint points; splitting yields 60. The 20-point gap is value neither side receives.

reserve.prompt: What is the best approach for the founder?

stimulus.text: A founder is selling a niche software product to a larger firm. She has no comparable sales data and no idea what the buyer’s internal valuation is. The buyer’s corporate-development head asks her to “name a number.” (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Name a high number immediately, since first offers always win.
Avoid naming a number until she has more information: ask questions about the buyer’s plans and alternatives, seek comparables, and, if the buyer opens, re-anchor with her own justified figure.
Ask the buyer to split the difference between two numbers she has not yet chosen.
Name a low number to build goodwill.

reserve.explanation: The first-offer advantage depends on information. Uninformed, she risks anchoring below what the buyer would pay. Gathering information first, and re-anchoring with her own analysis if the buyer opens, applies the evidence and its limits.

optionFeedback.a: The laboratory advantage assumed an informed offer; an uninformed number can give away surplus or look absurd.
optionFeedback.c: This has no content and cedes the anchor.
optionFeedback.d: Goodwill bought with a low anchor is expensive and rarely reciprocated in price.

reserve.prompt: Asked whether her company has other bidders, a seller who has none says, “We’ve had a lot of interest since the announcement,” which is true only of inquiries that went nowhere. How would the targets in Rogers and colleagues’ experiments most likely judge this statement if they discovered the facts?

options.text: As acceptable, because the statement is literally true.
As about as unethical as a false statement.
As more ethical than declining to answer.
As irrelevant, because buyers expect sellers to exaggerate.

reserve.explanation: The statement is a palter: true words chosen to create a false belief. Targets in the experiments judged paltering about as unethical as making false statements, while palterers and observers judged it more favorably, a perception gap that matters for reputation.

optionFeedback.a: That is how palterers tend to see it; targets do not.
optionFeedback.c: Declining to answer is open; paltering actively misleads.
optionFeedback.d: Expectations of exaggeration attach to opinions and openings, not to misleading statements about facts such as other bidders.

assignment.title: Negotiation Strategy Memo

brief.text: Choose a negotiation you could plausibly lead in the next year and prepare it as a senior executive would: in writing, before the first conversation, for a reader who must approve your mandate. Suitable examples include licensing a technology platform for your department, a data-sharing or research partnership with a university laboratory, an agreement for a training facility abroad, a resource or budget negotiation with your own leadership, or an offer to a candidate you are hiring.

Keep it hypothetical and non-confidential. Use fictional organization names and synthetic numbers, and mark every assumption. Do not include information about real players, colleagues, contracts or club business. The aim is to practice the analysis, not to document a real negotiation.

items: Estimate both sides’ BATNAs and reservation values with ranges and confidence, not single numbers presented as facts.
List at least four issues and score your priorities; estimate the other side’s, labelled as estimates.
Identify at least one trade and, where a forecast disagreement exists, one contingent term.
Write walk-away rules you would actually follow, and a disclosure policy you would be comfortable having quoted.

brief.text: Before writing: in one sentence, what decision does your reader need to make after reading the memo?

assignment.deliverable: A 1,000–1,500-word negotiation strategy memo, organized under the template headings, for a hypothetical negotiation you could plausibly lead.

template.heading: Situation and recommendation
template.guidance: Two or three sentences: the negotiation, what you recommend as the mandate, and the decision you need from your reader.

template.heading: Interests
template.guidance: Your interests and, separately, your best understanding of the other side’s. Distinguish interests (why) from positions (what is demanded). Name internal constituencies on both sides.

template.heading: BATNA — both sides
template.guidance: Your BATNA as a course of action and its estimated value; the other side’s likely BATNA with a range and your confidence. Note how either could be improved before the negotiation.

template.heading: ZOPA estimate
template.guidance: Both reservation values (yours firm, theirs estimated), the resulting zone, your aspiration, and what would change your reservation value for good reasons.

template.heading: Issues and trades
template.guidance: At least four issues with your priority points (summing to 100) and estimated priorities for the other side. Mark each issue distributive, integrative or compatible; propose the trades and any contingent terms.

template.heading: Opening strategy
template.guidance: Whether you will open, with what package, and the criteria that justify it; how you will respond if they open first.

template.heading: Concessions plan
template.guidance: The sequence and size of concessions, what you will ask for in return for each, and which issues you will not concede.

template.heading: Information to seek
template.guidance: The questions that would most change your plan, how you will ask them, and what you will disclose about relative priorities.

template.heading: Walk-away rules
template.guidance: Explicit conditions under which you will stop, pause or escalate, including deadlines and who must approve exceptions.

template.heading: Relationship and ethics
template.guidance: Your disclosure policy for this negotiation, how you will handle being asked about your budget or alternatives, ratification steps, and what the relationship should look like after signing.

rubric.criterion: Analytic preparation: interests, both BATNAs, reservation values and the ZOPA

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Both sides’ interests, BATNAs and reservation values are estimated with ranges, explicit assumptions and confidence; the ZOPA follows logically; good reasons to revise are named.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All elements present and reasonable; some estimates lack ranges or stated assumptions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Own side analyzed; the other side’s BATNA or reservation value is asserted without reasoning.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Positions are listed in place of interests; BATNA or ZOPA is missing or confused with an opening offer.

rubric.criterion: Value creation: issues, priorities, trades and contingent terms

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Four or more issues with scored priorities; distributive, integrative and compatible issues identified; trades and a contingent term are specific and plausible.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Multiple issues and at least one credible trade; contingent options thin or generic.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Issues listed but treated mostly as separate price-like contests.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Single-issue framing; no trades.

rubric.criterion: Claiming strategy: opening, concessions and walk-away rules

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Opening decision justified by information and criteria; concession plan is sequenced and conditional; walk-away rules are explicit and credible.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Sound opening and concessions; walk-away rules present but partly vague.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Opening chosen without rationale; concessions unplanned or unconditional.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No opening, concession or walk-away plan.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Identifies the few unknowns that matter most, how to learn them, what to disclose and what to protect; assumptions are labelled throughout.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Useful questions and a disclosure stance; some assumptions unlabelled.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Generic questions; no disclosure plan.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Treats estimates as facts; no information plan.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A specific disclosure policy with no deceptive or paltering tactics; internal mandate and ratification steps planned; post-agreement relationship considered.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Ethical stance and ratification addressed, with limited specificity.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Ethics mentioned generically; ratification ignored.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Plan relies on misleading statements or ignores who must approve.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Recommendation and decision needed in the first paragraph; concise, organized under the headings, within the word range.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear and organized; recommendation slightly buried or some redundancy.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Hard to find the recommendation; uneven sections.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No clear recommendation; disorganized.

scenario.text: Draft your negotiation strategy memo for a reader who must approve your mandate before you negotiate. Lead with the recommendation and the decision needed, then work through the template headings.

audience.who: The executive who must approve your mandate
audience.cares: What you will agree to, what it costs, what you will not concede, and what could go wrong.
Economic limits, binding commitments, data and regulatory terms, and who signs.

checklist: Recommendation and decision needed appear in the first two sentences
Both BATNAs are stated as actions with estimated values and ranges
At least one trade across issues and, where relevant, one contingent term
Walk-away rules are explicit
No statement in the plan would mislead the other side if quoted
All names and numbers are fictional or synthetic, and assumptions are labelled

prompts: Recall a negotiation from the past two years whose outcome you later regretted. Which number did you not prepare well: your BATNA, your reservation value, your aspiration, or your estimate of the other side’s? What would preparing it have changed?
Where is your default on the negotiator’s dilemma: do you tend to disclose too much or too little? Give one concrete example as evidence, and one situation in which your default served you badly.
Write the disclosure policy you actually followed in your last difficult negotiation, not the one you would like to have followed. Where do the two differ, and why?
Think of a negotiation conducted across languages or organizational cultures. What did you assume about how the other side exchanged information, and how, if at all, did you check that assumption?

review.front: What is a BATNA, and how does it differ from a reservation value?
review.back: A BATNA is the course of action you will take if talks fail; the reservation value converts it into the worst terms you would accept in this deal.

review.front: When does a ZOPA exist?
review.back: Only when the most one side would give exceeds the least the other would accept — when reservation values overlap. Otherwise impasse is the correct outcome.

review.front: Why prepare an aspiration as well as a reservation value?
review.back: Negotiators who prepare only a floor tend to settle near it; the aspiration governs how much of the zone you try to claim.

review.front: In the BATNA framework, what is bargaining power mainly?
review.back: The relative cost of no deal, shaped by alternatives, deadlines, credible commitments and reputation.

review.front: What is the difference between a distributive and an integrative issue?
review.back: Distributive: one side’s gain is the other’s loss. Integrative: the parties value it differently, so a trade can leave both better off.

review.front: Why can a logroll beat splitting the difference for both sides?
review.back: Each side gives ground on what it values less and gains on what it values more, moving the agreement toward the Pareto frontier.

review.front: What conditions does a contingent contract need?
review.back: An observable, measurable trigger that the controlling party cannot easily manipulate, no value-destroying distortions, and enforceable terms with a dispute process.

review.front: State the negotiator’s dilemma.
review.back: Moves that create value (sharing priorities) expose you to moves that claim it; creating and claiming cannot be separated (Lax and Sebenius).

review.front: What eliminated the first-offer advantage in Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments?
review.back: The recipient focusing on the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target.

review.front: What is the fixed-pie perception, and when is it not an error?
review.back: Assuming the other side’s interests are completely opposed to yours. It is correct in genuinely distributive negotiations; the error is assuming it without checking.

review.front: What does ultimatum-game evidence imply for negotiators?
review.back: People reject offers they see as unfair even at a cost, so fairness is a second floor beneath the other side’s reservation value.

review.front: What did the Mazei et al. meta-analysis find about gender and negotiation outcomes?
review.back: A difference favoring men that depended on context and shrank or reversed with advocacy for others, information about the range, and experience.

review.front: Name three controls for a principal–agent problem in negotiation.
review.back: A written mandate with authority limits, incentives aligned with the principal’s outcome, and required evidence plus principal contact at key moments.

review.front: Why did intercultural pairs reach lower joint gains in Adair, Okumura and Brett’s study?
review.back: Partly because their information-exchange routines differed (direct questions versus indirect inference from offers).

review.front: What is paltering, and how do targets judge it?
review.back: Using true statements to mislead. Targets judged it about as unethical as lying; palterers judged it more favorably.

weeks.title: Building Effective Organizations
weeks.question: How should an organization divide work, assign decisions and measure performance so that capable people accomplish more together than they could alone?

overview.text: Organizations exist because some work is too large, too specialized or too continuous for individuals acting alone. That advantage has a price. Once work is divided, someone must decide who does what, who decides what, how information moves, and how anyone knows whether it is working. This week treats organization design as a set of choices with predictable trade-offs, not a matter of taste, fashion or the latest reorganization.

You will move from the field’s founding ideas—differentiation and integration, the information-processing view, Mintzberg’s configurations and the arithmetic of spans and layers—to decision rights and the economics of delegation, then to the strongest modern evidence that management practices matter, including a randomized experiment and its long-run follow-up. The week ends below the chart, with routines, culture and team design: the parts of an organization that carry its knowledge and resist change.

Keep two disciplines from earlier weeks in view. From [Week 4](#w04): ask what kind of evidence supports each claim—theory, comparative study, survey correlation or experiment. From [Week 6](#w06): remember that formal design competes with informal power. The Organization Builder lets you feel the trade-offs under a budget that does not stretch far enough; the hospital case asks you to apply them where money and people’s working lives are both at stake; and the assignment asks you to design and defend a department of your own.

objectives: Explain how differentiation, integration and information-processing load determine which structure fits a task and its environment.
Allocate decision rights by locating specific knowledge and weighing agency costs, and record them with a labelled practitioner tool.
Evaluate the evidence that management practices cause performance, distinguishing correlational, experimental and long-run findings.
Diagnose metric gaming with Goodhart’s law and the multitask incentive problem, and design countermeasures within an operating rhythm.
Design a department—roles, spans, decision rights, coordination mechanisms, operating rhythm and metrics—and defend the trade-offs it accepts.

lessons.title: Why Structure Exists: Differentiation, Integration and Information Load
lessons.summary: Structure is a bet about where information and coordination problems will arise; good designs match differentiation, integration, spans and layers to the uncertainty of the work.
objectives: Explain differentiation and integration and why effective organizations need both in the degree their environment demands.
Use the information-processing view to choose among slack resources, self-contained units, vertical information systems and lateral relations.
Match coordinating mechanisms to types of work, and calculate how span of control changes layers and management cost.
lessons.executive: An organization chart is not a picture of status; it is a theory about which conversations matter most. Every structure divides work so specialists can go deep (differentiation) and then pays to reconnect them (integration). Contingency theory and the information-processing view give a practical test: the more uncertain the work, the more exceptions it throws up, and the sooner a hierarchy alone will choke. You can respond by reducing the information load—slack, self-contained units—or by raising capacity—better information systems, lateral roles. Spans and layers are the cost side of that choice. Before any reorganization, ask what information problem the new chart solves and which working routines it will break.

explore.text: Picture two regional banks that decide, in the same year, to merge their fraud-detection team and their credit-underwriting team into one “risk analytics” unit. The logic sounds unanswerable: both teams build models on customer data, both report to the chief risk officer, and both complain that the other hoards data. One bank’s merged unit thrives. The other loses its best fraud analysts within a year, and fraud losses climb. The banks are hypothetical, but the pattern is familiar to anyone who has lived through a reorganization: identical boxes on a chart, opposite results.

The difference usually lies in something the chart does not show. Fraud work runs on minutes: an attack begins on a Saturday night and someone must change a rule before Sunday morning. Credit work runs on quarters: a cutoff change is tested, documented, reviewed and defended to regulators. The two teams do not merely sit in different rooms; they live on different clocks, answer to different definitions of a good outcome and need different kinds of supervision. Merging them can let them share data and talent, or it can force one rhythm onto work that needs another.

Before reading on: when two units are merged to improve coordination, list two things the merged organization gains and two it can lose. Which of the losses would show up on a dashboard, and which would not?

This lesson gives you the vocabulary to answer that question with more than intuition. It starts from the oldest problem in organization design—how to divide work and then put it back together—and ends with the arithmetic of spans and layers, which turns abstract design choices into headcount and cost.

understand.text: Two opposing forces

Paul Lawrence and Jay Lorsch framed organization design as a tension between two forces. *Differentiation* is the degree to which subunits develop different goals, time horizons, interpersonal styles and degrees of formal structure as each adapts to its own part of the environment. *Integration* is the quality of collaboration among those subunits that the organization needs to achieve unity of effort. Comparing organizations that operated in the same industrial environment, they reached a conclusion that still surprises managers: the more effective organizations were not the least differentiated. They achieved both the differentiation their environment demanded and the integration needed to hold it together. And because differentiated units see the world differently, the more differentiation an organization needs, the harder and more deliberate its integration must be.

This is the core of *contingency theory*: there is no single best structure, only structures that fit or misfit their task and environment. Fit is not a matter of taste. A structure fits when it supplies the coordination the work actually requires at a cost the organization can bear.
Structure as an information-processing system

Jay Galbraith sharpened the idea by treating organizations as information-processing systems. His starting proposition is that the greater the uncertainty of a task, the more information must be processed among decision-makers while the task is being done. Routine work can be coordinated by rules and programs, by referring exceptions up the hierarchy, and by setting targets that leave the method to the people doing the work. As uncertainty rises, exceptions multiply and the hierarchy overloads: managers become the bottleneck through which every unusual case must pass.

Galbraith described two families of response. An organization can *reduce the need* for information processing, by creating slack resources (longer lead times, spare capacity, buffers, less demanding targets) or by creating self-contained units that hold every skill a product, customer or region needs. Or it can *increase its capacity* to process information, by investing in vertical information systems that move better data up and down faster, or by creating lateral relations—direct contact, liaison roles, task forces, teams, integrating roles and, at the extreme, matrix structures—that let decisions be made across units without climbing the hierarchy. Each strategy has a cost; choosing none of them means accepting lower performance by default.

understand.caption: Galbraith’s four design strategies, with hypothetical illustrations
rows: Lowers the information load by loosening targets, schedules or capacity
A hospital keeps a few staffed beds open for surges instead of re-planning every shift
Idle capacity; slack that quietly becomes permanent
Gives each unit every skill it needs, so fewer cross-unit decisions arise
A software company gives each product team its own engineers, designer and data analyst
Duplicated specialists; thinner depth in each specialty
Moves better information to decision-makers faster
A bank builds a real-time fraud dashboard so the risk officer sees attacks within minutes
Systems cost; more data can still overload the person at the top
Lets units coordinate directly without escalating
A law firm names a partner to integrate tax, litigation and corporate work for one large client

understand.note: APERTURE’s summary of Galbraith (1974); the examples are hypothetical.

understand.text: Five ways to coordinate

Henry Mintzberg synthesized the research on structure into five coordinating mechanisms: direct supervision (one person instructs others), standardization of work processes (the method is specified), standardization of outputs (the result is specified), standardization of skills (the training is specified, so trained people can coordinate almost automatically) and mutual adjustment (people coordinate through informal communication). He argued that organizations cluster into five configurations, each dominated by one mechanism and pulled by one part of the organization.

understand.caption: Mintzberg’s five configurations at a glance
rows: A founder-led startup or a small clinic
A multi-hospital system or diversified company
Consulting engagements, research labs, film production
understand.note: Configurations as summarized from Mintzberg (1980); settings are illustrative.

understand.text: The configurations are ideal types, not boxes that real organizations fit neatly. Their value lies in the diagnostic question they force: which coordinating mechanism is actually doing the work here, and is it the right one for this task? A professional bureaucracy that tries to coordinate surgeons through detailed process scripts will meet resistance, because the professionals already coordinate through shared training. An adhocracy that drifts into standard procedures will lose the improvisation it exists to produce.
Spans, layers and the cost of control

*Span of control* is the number of people who report directly to one manager. It is where design meets arithmetic. Wider spans mean fewer managers and fewer layers, so information passes through fewer filters and decisions are made closer to the work. Narrower spans mean more coaching time per person and closer supervision, at the price of more managers and more layers. There is no research-backed universal number. The right span depends on how similar and standardized the work is, how expert the reports are, how much of the manager’s own time goes to non-supervisory work, how dispersed the team is and how much development each person needs.

understand.caption: How span of control changes layers and managers for 1,000 frontline staff
understand.note: Synthetic arithmetic: divide each level by the span and round up until one executive remains.

understand.text: The table is deliberately simple, but the pattern is real arithmetic: moving the average span from five to twelve removes two layers and almost two thirds of the management positions. That is why delayering appeals to finance teams. It is also why it is risky: every manager removed was absorbing exceptions, coaching people and translating between levels. If rules, information systems and lateral links do not absorb that load, the remaining managers become Galbraith’s bottleneck.

understand.title: Prerequisite: reading an organization chart

blocks.text: A solid line on a chart usually means formal authority: the manager can assign work, evaluate performance and influence pay. A dotted line usually means a second, advisory relationship—someone whose input matters but who does not control the person’s job. Three basic structures recur. A *functional* structure groups people by expertise (all engineers together, all nurses together); it builds depth but makes cross-functional work slow. A *divisional* structure groups people by product, customer or region; it speeds work within each division but duplicates specialists. A *matrix* gives people two bosses, one functional and one divisional, to capture both benefits; it works only when the organization can handle the conflict it deliberately builds in.
When you read any chart, ask three questions: who can say yes, who can say no, and whose phone rings when something unusual happens.

understand.title: Methodological note: what contingency research can and cannot show

blocks.text: Contingency theory makes a causal claim—fit between structure and environment improves performance—from evidence that is mostly comparative and cross-sectional. Lawrence and Lorsch compared a small number of organizations at one point in time. Studies of this kind are excellent for generating hypotheses and weak at ruling out alternatives: a better-managed firm may achieve both differentiation and integration because it is better managed, not because fit causes success.

A second problem is circularity. If fit is defined after the fact as whatever the successful organizations did, the theory cannot fail. A testable version must define the required differentiation and integration in advance—for example, from measurable uncertainty in the task—and then predict which organizations will struggle. When anyone tells you a structure “fits” your strategy, ask what observation would have shown that it did not.

challenge.text: Three objections deserve a hearing. First, the information-processing view treats people as channels and decisions as data transfers. Real organizations are also political systems. A structure that routes information efficiently may still fail if it strips a powerful group of status or control; [Week 6](#w06-l1) examined how informal authority reshapes formal design. Second, ideal types tempt leaders to copy a configuration rather than diagnose their own work. Most organizations are hybrids: a hospital is a professional bureaucracy in the operating room, a machine bureaucracy in billing and an adhocracy in its innovation unit.

Third, structure may matter less than executives believe. Reorganizations are visible, quick to announce and easy to attribute to a new leader, which makes them attractive whether or not they solve the underlying problem. APERTURE’s working hypothesis—not an established finding—is that many reorganizations change the chart while leaving the real coordination problem untouched (unclear decision rights, missing information, weak routines), and impose a transition cost by breaking the informal routines people had built ([Lesson 4](#w08-l4)). Treat claims that delayering or reorganizing improves performance as hypotheses to test in your setting, not as general laws.

There is also a competing account of why structure matters: incentives rather than information. A self-contained unit can be measured on its own results, which sharpens accountability but encourages it to optimize locally at the expense of the whole. A matrix blurs accountability precisely because it shares it. The next two lessons take up that thread—who holds decision rights, and how measures and rewards change behavior.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the reorganization you inherit

blocks.text: You join an organization six months after a reorganization. Morale is low, two respected people have left, and the chief operating officer asks whether to reverse it. No one measured performance before the change, so you cannot compare. Reversing it would be a second disruption; keeping it may lock in a mistake. A defensible first move is diagnostic rather than structural: identify the three or four recurring decisions and hand-offs that matter most, trace how each worked before and how it works now, and ask which coordinating mechanism was lost. Often the answer is a specific routine or integrating role that can be restored without undoing the whole design.

apply.text: Consider a hypothetical 400-bed hospital whose emergency department and elective surgery service fight constantly over beds. The emergency department lives on a minute-to-minute clock and values speed; surgery plans weeks ahead and values predictability. Differentiation is appropriate—each unit should be good at its own work—but integration is failing. Galbraith’s menu clarifies the options. Slack: hold a small number of beds in reserve, accepting idle cost. Self-contained units: give surgery its own dedicated recovery ward, accepting duplication. Vertical information: a real-time bed board visible to both, accepting systems cost. Lateral relations: a bed-management coordinator with authority to arbitrate in real time, accepting a new role and some conflict. A thoughtful leader usually combines two of these and is explicit about the cost of each.

The same diagnosis travels. A hypothetical consulting firm whose industry practices and functional practices compete for the same partners faces differentiation between client knowledge and technical depth; it often responds with a matrix and staffing coordinators. A government agency that must align field offices with a central policy unit faces differentiation in time horizon and formality; liaison roles and standardized reporting are its usual answers. A professional soccer club’s first-team staff and academy differ in horizon and in what counts as success; a technical director often serves as the integrating role.

In player development, differentiation is built in. Field coaches work on a daily clock and value relationships and feel; analysts work on longer horizons and value measurement; performance science and medical staff answer to health standards that are not negotiable; international operations work across languages, distances and legal systems. The design question is not how to erase those differences but how much integration the work requires and which mechanism supplies it: a coordinator role that spans field and analytics, standardized individual plans that carry information between levels, a short daily huddle, or a shared information system. Each choice costs people, time or autonomy. Naming the information problem first keeps you from buying the wrong mechanism.

retain.text: Structure divides work so specialists can go deep, and then spends money and attention to reconnect them. The uncertainty of the work sets how much reconnecting is needed; Galbraith’s four strategies, Mintzberg’s five mechanisms and the arithmetic of spans tell you how to supply it and what it will cost. Fit is a hypothesis to test, not a label to award after the fact.
Name the two units in your own organization that are most differentiated. What integrating mechanism connects them today, and what does it cost?
Using Galbraith’s menu, which strategy would you try first for a team drowning in escalations, and why?
Without looking back, explain why moving from a span of five to a span of twelve can be both a saving and a risk.

takeaways: Every structure trades the depth that differentiation buys against the cost of integration; effective organizations achieve both in the degree their work requires.
Task uncertainty drives information load: when exceptions overwhelm the hierarchy, reduce the load (slack, self-contained units) or raise capacity (information systems, lateral relations).
Mintzberg’s configurations are diagnostic ideal types—identify which coordinating mechanism actually does the work.
Span of control is arithmetic with consequences: wider spans remove layers and cost, and also remove exception-handling and coaching capacity.

check.prompt: A software company’s product teams escalate dozens of cross-team dependencies to the chief technology officer every week, and releases stall. In Galbraith’s terms, which response *increases information-processing capacity* rather than reducing the need for it?

options.text: Lengthen release cycles so dependencies have more time to resolve
Give each product team its own platform engineers so most dependencies disappear
Create a cross-team integration role with authority to resolve dependency conflicts directly
Lower release targets so fewer features compete for shared engineers

check.explanation: An integrating role is a lateral relation: it adds capacity to make cross-unit decisions without sending every exception up the hierarchy. Longer cycles and lower targets are slack, and dedicated engineers create self-contained units; both of those reduce the need for information processing instead of increasing capacity. All four are legitimate strategies—the question asks you to classify, not to rank them.

optionFeedback.a: Longer cycles are slack resources: they reduce the information load by loosening time pressure rather than adding capacity.
optionFeedback.b: Dedicated engineers make each team more self-contained, which reduces the need for coordination rather than increasing capacity to handle it.
optionFeedback.d: Lower targets are another form of slack; they shrink the coordination problem instead of adding capacity to solve it.

check.prompt: A service organization has 480 frontline staff. If every manager has a span of control of 8, rounding up at each level until a single executive remains, how many managers does it need in total, including the executive?
check.working: 480 ÷ 8 = 60 first-line managers. 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5, rounded up to 8 second-level managers. 8 ÷ 8 = 1 executive. Total = 60 + 8 + 1 = 69 managers in three layers.
check.explanation: Divide each level by the span and round up: 60 first-line managers, 8 second-level managers and 1 executive, for 69 in total. The calculation shows why span decisions are expensive: at a span of 4 the same organization would need well over 150 managers, each absorbing exceptions and coaching—capacity that disappears when spans widen.

lessons.title: Who Decides? Decision Rights, Knowledge and Coordination
lessons.summary: Decision rights should sit where the relevant knowledge is cheapest to find, but every move toward the knowledge raises agency costs, so rights, measures and rewards must be designed as one system.
objectives: Distinguish specific from general knowledge and use the distinction to locate decision rights.
Weigh the costs of centralizing and decentralizing particular decisions, and pair any delegation with measurement and accountability.
Use RACI or RAPID as labelled practitioner tools, and evaluate Conway’s law as an observation with mixed evidence.
lessons.executive: Many coordination failures that leaders call “communication problems” are decision-rights problems: nobody knows who decides, or three people think they do. Jensen and Meckling’s rule of thumb is to put a decision where the knowledge it needs is cheapest to find—often close to the work—while recognizing that the person holding that knowledge may not share the organization’s goals. Delegation therefore comes bundled with measurement and rewards; one without the others fails. Practitioner tools such as RACI and RAPID help you write the answer down, but they do not supply the answer. And remember Conway’s observation: what you build will tend to mirror how your teams communicate, unless shared standards and tools break the mirror.

explore.text: A hypothetical national retail bank lets branch managers approve small-business loans up to a set limit. Branch managers know things no model captures: that the bakery owner has run three businesses successfully, that the new shopping strip is half empty, that a borrower’s partner just left the business. Losses on branch-approved loans are low. Then a new chief credit officer centralizes approval in a head-office team using a scoring model, citing inconsistency and two fraud cases. Approval times triple, branch managers stop sending their best prospects, and the small-business portfolio shrinks. Two years later, a different executive decentralizes again—and loses money on a wave of loans approved by branch managers who are paid on volume.

Neither executive was foolish. Each saw half of a real trade-off. The first saw that branch managers held knowledge the center could not cheaply obtain. The second saw that people paid on volume will not always use that knowledge in the bank’s interest. The design problem is to get both halves right at once, and it is the same problem whether the decision is a loan, a hospital discharge, a software release or a player’s promotion.
Before reading on: for one recurring decision in your work, write down who actually makes it, who believes they make it, and who holds the information that matters most. Are they the same person?

understand.text: Specific and general knowledge

Michael Jensen and William Meckling built a theory of organizational structure on a distinction between two kinds of knowledge. *General knowledge* is cheap to transmit: prices, volumes, a model score, a regulation. *Specific knowledge* is costly to transmit: it is tacit, perishable or local, like a nurse’s sense that a patient is deteriorating before the vital signs show it, or a branch manager’s read of a borrower. Because specific knowledge is expensive to move to the decision-maker, organizations face a choice: move the knowledge up to where the decision rights are, or move the decision rights down to where the knowledge is.

Moving rights down reduces the cost of decisions made with poor information. But it raises a second cost: the people now holding the rights have their own interests, and the organization must spend on monitoring, measurement and incentives to keep their decisions aligned—agency costs. Jensen and Meckling’s picture is a trade-off: as decision rights move lower, information costs fall and agency costs rise, and the best level is the one that minimizes their sum. That is why they treated structure as interlocking systems that must be designed together: the assignment of decision rights, the system for measuring performance, and the system for rewarding and punishing.

understand.caption: Where should the decision sit? Knowledge type against interest alignment
x: Knowledge needed is general (cheap to move)
Knowledge needed is specific (costly to move)
cells: Either level works; choose for speed and consistency
Decentralize: put the right with the knowledge
Centralize: move the information up and keep the right at the center
Decentralize with a strong control system—measures, audits, rewards—or redesign roles so interests align
understand.note: APERTURE teaching device built on Jensen and Meckling’s trade-off.

understand.text: Centralization versus decentralization

With that frame, the familiar debate becomes a list of specific trade-offs rather than a matter of philosophy. Centralization buys consistency, economies of scale, concentrated expertise, coordination across units and protection against local self-interest. Decentralization buys speed, local adaptation, use of specific knowledge and the motivation that comes from owning a decision. Every organization centralizes some decisions and decentralizes others; the skill lies in sorting decisions, not in choosing a side. Galbraith’s self-contained units from [Lesson 1](#w08-l1) are one form of decentralization: they move decisions to where the work is by giving each unit everything it needs.

rows: Knowledge is general or already at the center
Knowledge is specific, local or perishable
High: fairness, legal exposure, brand, safety
Low: local variation is harmless or useful
The decision can wait for review
The decision loses value in minutes or hours
One unit’s choice affects many others

understand.text: Writing decision rights down: practitioner tools

Two practitioner tools help organizations record who does what in a decision. They are heuristics from management practice, not research findings, and their value depends on the conversation they force rather than the grid they produce. *RACI* assigns, for each task or decision, who is Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome and signs off—ideally exactly one person), Consulted (gives input beforehand) and Informed (told afterward). *RAPID*, a framework that originated in management consulting, focuses on decisions rather than tasks: who Recommends, who must Agree (a formal veto, to be used sparingly), who Performs the decision once made, who gives Input, and the one person who Decides.

understand.caption: RACI and RAPID compared (practitioner heuristics)
rows: Everyone becomes Consulted; Accountable and Responsible blur
Too many Agree roles recreate gridlock
Recurring high-stakes decisions that cross units
understand.note: Practitioner heuristics, not empirically validated instruments.

understand.text: Conway’s observation

In 1968 a programmer, Melvin Conway, observed that organizations which design systems tend to produce designs that mirror their own communication structures. Researchers later restated the idea as the *mirroring hypothesis*: the ties among people and units in a project or firm will correspond to the technical dependencies in the work. Lyra Colfer and Carliss Baldwin reviewed 142 empirical studies and found mirroring common but not universal across industries and firms. The main exceptions came from open collaborative projects, mostly in software, where distributed contributors coordinated through shared code, documentation and tools rather than organizational ties.

Treat Conway’s law as an observation and a design heuristic, not a law of nature. Its practical use is diagnostic: if a hospital’s patient record is fragmented along department lines, or a company’s product feels like three products stitched together, look at how the teams that built it communicate. Its practitioner corollary—sometimes called the “inverse Conway maneuver”—is to organize teams around the architecture you want. The review’s exceptions are the warning: when coordination can travel through shared standards and transparent tools, the mirror can be broken.

understand.title: Prerequisite: the principal–agent problem in one paragraph

blocks.text: A *principal* (an owner, a board, a manager) delegates a decision or task to an *agent* (an executive, an employee, a contractor) whose interests are not identical and whose effort or information the principal cannot fully observe. The agent may shirk, take too much or too little risk, or pursue private goals. *Agency costs* are the sum of what the principal spends on monitoring and incentives, what the agent spends to reassure the principal, and the value lost when decisions still diverge. [Week 7](#w07-l4) met the idea in negotiation; here it explains why delegation is never free.

understand.title: Methodological note: why the decision-rights trade-off is hard to test

blocks.text: Jensen and Meckling’s argument is theory, built from first principles rather than from data. Testing it is difficult because organizations choose how much to decentralize, and they choose in response to the same unobserved conditions—competition, trust, the quality of their managers—that affect performance. A raw correlation between decentralization and performance therefore says little about what would happen if a given firm decentralized. Credible evidence comes from settings where the allocation of decision rights changes for reasons unrelated to performance, or from careful within-organization comparisons over time. When someone tells you that “empowered” organizations outperform, ask how the empowered organizations came to be empowered.

challenge.text: Four limits matter. First, decision-rights theory assumes that formal rights are the rights that matter. In practice, informal power often overrides the chart: the person who controls a key relationship or a scarce resource may hold an effective veto that appears in no grid. Writing rights down helps only if powerful people accept them; [Week 6](#w06-l1) explained why they may not.

Second, decentralization has costs that do not appear in the information–agency trade-off. Local discretion produces unequal treatment, which can become a fairness or legal problem in hiring, lending or clinical care. It can also fragment learning: ten units each solving the same problem in different ways learn more slowly than one that pools its experience. Third, crises pull decisions toward the center—sometimes appropriately, for speed and coordination, and sometimes because anxious leaders want control. An organization that has never practiced decentralized decisions will not perform them well on the day the center is overwhelmed.

Fourth, tools like RACI and RAPID can become theater. A grid that lists eleven Consulted parties for a routine decision documents a coordination problem without solving it. A useful test: for each recurring decision, could a new employee identify the one person who decides within a minute? If not, the grid is decoration. And the Conway evidence cuts in both directions: mirroring is common enough to take seriously and broken often enough that reorganizing teams is neither necessary nor sufficient to change what they build.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the decision nobody owns

blocks.text: Your product team wants to launch a feature that lets customers move money instantly. The fraud team says it will raise losses; the growth team says delay will cost the quarter. The decision sits between two vice presidents, each believing the other must sign off. You have 48 hours, partial loss estimates and no agreed decision owner. You cannot redesign the organization before Thursday. What you can do is name, for this decision only, one person who Decides, who Recommends, whose Input is required and whether anyone holds a veto—and write down what evidence after launch would trigger a reversal. A temporary, explicit allocation beats a permanent, implicit one, and it gives you a case to argue for a standing rule afterward.

apply.text: Consider a hypothetical consulting firm deciding how to staff engagements. Partners hold specific knowledge about clients; a central staffing team holds general knowledge about everyone’s availability and development needs. Fully decentralized staffing lets partners hoard stars and starve junior development; fully centralized staffing ignores client fit. A workable allocation: the staffing team Recommends, the engagement partner gives Input on client fit, the practice leader Decides contested cases, and the consultant is Informed early enough to raise concerns. The control system follows: partners are evaluated partly on the development of the people they staff, which reduces the incentive to hoard.

Apply the same logic to a player development department and the decision to move a player between levels. Field staff hold specific knowledge about readiness and how the player handles adversity; analysts hold knowledge from performance data; medical and performance staff hold knowledge about health and workload; the department head holds organizational context such as roster needs and other players’ timelines. One defensible allocation: the coordinator for that position group Recommends after a structured meeting; analysts, performance staff and current coaches give Input; medical staff hold an Agree right limited to health clearance, not performance judgment; the department head Decides; and the receiving coaches are Informed, with the player’s plan, before he arrives. The choices worth debating are where the veto stops and who decides when the head is unavailable.

apply.caption: Decision-rights sketch for a hypothetical development department (RAPID-style, a practitioner heuristic)
rows: Clear a return to play after injury
apply.note: Hypothetical and fictional; one defensible allocation among several.

apply.text: Notice what the table does and does not settle. It removes ambiguity about who owns each decision, and it puts the veto exactly where the non-negotiable constraint (health) sits. It does not say whether the people in each role will share information honestly, or whether the head’s decisions will be good. Those depend on the measurement and reward systems—the other two legs of Jensen and Meckling’s structure—and on the routines examined in [Lesson 4](#w08-l4).

retain.text: Decision rights belong where the knowledge is cheapest to find, but delegation creates agency costs, so rights, measures and rewards are one system. Centralize or decentralize decision by decision, using knowledge, consistency, speed, interdependence and alignment as signals. Record the answer with a labelled practitioner tool, and expect your products to mirror how your teams communicate—while remembering that the mirror can be broken.
Pick one decision in your organization that is made slowly. Is the bottleneck the location of knowledge, the fear of agency costs or the absence of a single decision owner?
Explain, without notes, why Jensen and Meckling insist that decision rights cannot be designed separately from measurement and rewards.
Where could a shared standard or tool in your work replace a reporting line as the main coordinating mechanism?

takeaways: Specific knowledge is costly to move and general knowledge is cheap; place decision rights near specific knowledge unless the added agency costs outweigh the information gain.
Decision rights, performance measures and rewards are one system—change one and the others must change too.
Sort decisions one by one: knowledge location, cost of inconsistency, speed, interdependence and alignment decide which to centralize.
RACI and RAPID are practitioner heuristics for recording decisions; Conway’s law is an observation that holds often, not always.

check.prompt: A hospital system is deciding where discharge-timing decisions should sit. Bedside nurses and attending physicians notice subtle signs of readiness that never reach the electronic record; central bed managers see system-wide capacity. In Jensen and Meckling’s framework, what is the strongest argument for keeping the core discharge decision with the clinical team?

options.text: The knowledge about readiness is specific—costly to transmit—so moving the decision to the center would degrade it
Clinicians’ interests are perfectly aligned with the hospital’s, so agency costs are zero
Centralized decisions are always slower and therefore always worse
General knowledge such as bed counts should never influence clinical decisions

check.explanation: The framework places decision rights near specific knowledge when moving that knowledge is costly, as with tacit clinical judgment about readiness. It does not assume perfect alignment; agency costs still exist and are managed through measurement and review. General capacity information remains relevant and can be moved to the clinical team cheaply, which is the point of the distinction.

optionFeedback.b: Jensen and Meckling never assume zero agency costs; decentralization is justified when the information gain outweighs them, not because they vanish.
optionFeedback.c: Centralization is sometimes the better choice—when knowledge is general, consistency matters or interests diverge. “Always” misreads a trade-off as a rule.
optionFeedback.d: Bed counts are general knowledge that can be sent cheaply to the clinical team; the framework uses them, it does not exclude them.

check.prompt: A company documents its quarterly pricing decision using RAPID and lists five executives in the Agree role. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: Gridlock or delay, because any of five vetoes can block the decision
Faster decisions, because more people have approved in advance
No effect, because Agree roles are informational only
The Decide role becomes unnecessary, because the Agree holders jointly decide

check.explanation: In RAPID, Agree is a formal veto. Five vetoes multiply the ways a decision can stall and blur ownership, recreating the gridlock the tool was meant to prevent. The practitioner advice is to reserve Agree for genuine non-negotiable constraints, such as legal or safety sign-off.

optionFeedback.b: Each Agree holder can block or delay; adding vetoes slows decisions rather than speeding them.
optionFeedback.c: Agree is not informational—that is the Informed role. Agree carries the power to block.
optionFeedback.d: RAPID keeps a single Decide role precisely to avoid collective ownership; multiple vetoes undermine it rather than replace it.

sources.use: Specific versus general knowledge, the information–agency trade-off and the linked systems of decision rights, measurement and rewards.
The mirroring hypothesis (Conway’s law) and the review of 142 studies showing it is common but not universal.
Links decentralization to self-contained units as a way of reducing information-processing needs.
