lessons.title: Presenting and Defending Decisions to Senior Leaders and Boards
lessons.summary: A decision presentation is an argument made under questioning: structure it around the decision, stress-test it with a premortem and a steelmanned alternative, and answer hard questions directly.
objectives: Structure a decision presentation so that the decision requested, the recommendation, the main reason and the main risk appear first, with the warrant made explicit.
Use a premortem and a steelmanned alternative to anticipate the strongest objections before the meeting.
Answer hard questions directly, recognizing how evasive answers can pass undetected and why that is a governance risk rather than a technique.
Distinguish composure under questioning from projected certainty.
lessons.executive: Senior audiences do not need all of your analysis; they need your judgment and evidence that it was reached carefully. Lead with the decision you need and your recommendation, then the one reason that carries most weight, the main risk and the signal that would tell you early that you were wrong. Before the meeting, run a premortem — imagine the decision has failed and explain why — and write the strongest case for the option you rejected. In the room, answer the question asked. Experiments show that listeners often miss a fluent answer to a slightly different question; that is a reason to hold yourself to a higher standard, not a technique to borrow. Presence is composure under questioning, not certainty.

explore.text: Picture a hospital system’s board meeting (a composite, not a real one). The chief strategy officer has fifteen minutes and forty slides. In minute four, the board chair interrupts: “Before you go on — what are you asking us to approve, and what happens if you’re wrong?” The officer says the answer is on slide thirty-one. The meeting never recovers. The analysis was excellent. The presentation was organized like a research paper — background, method, results, conclusion — for an audience that needed it organized like a decision.
Think of the last time you presented a recommendation upward. How many minutes passed before your audience knew what you wanted them to decide — and what did they ask first?

Boards, owners and presidents are not hostile by default, but their role is skeptical. They carry responsibility for decisions they did not analyze, and their main instrument is the question. A decision presentation is therefore an argument that will be tested in real time by people who know less about the subject than you do and more about the consequences of being wrong. This lesson covers how to build that argument, how to stress-test it before the room does, and how to answer the questions that come. It revisits the communication work of [Week 5](#w05-l4) under pressure.

understand.text: Organize for a decision

You met answer-first communication in Week 5: the conclusion comes before the reasoning, as in the military convention BLUF (“bottom line up front”) and the consulting pyramid principle. Both are practitioner heuristics rather than research findings, but their logic is strongest exactly here. If the meeting is cut short, the most important content has been delivered; and every later piece of evidence can be judged against a claim the audience already knows. For a decision presentation, answer-first means something more specific than “conclusion first”. It means the audience knows within the first minute what they are deciding, what you recommend, why, what could go wrong, and what you want from them today.

understand.caption: The structure of a three-minute decision opening

steps.label: The ask
steps.text: What decision you need, from whom, and by when.

steps.label: The recommendation
steps.text: What you recommend, in one sentence.

steps.label: The reason
steps.text: The one or two reasons that carry the most weight, with the strength of their evidence.

steps.label: The alternative
steps.text: What else you considered, and why the strongest alternative loses here.

steps.label: The risk
steps.text: The main way this could fail, and the early signal you will watch.

steps.label: The request
steps.text: Exactly what you want approved today, and what you will bring back.

understand.text: The warrant is where questions land

Underneath the format sits an argument. A useful scheme from the philosopher Stephen Toulmin separates a claim (what you recommend), the grounds (the evidence), the warrant (why that evidence supports that claim), a qualifier (how confident you are) and a rebuttal (the conditions under which the claim would not hold). Most weak presentations state a claim and grounds and leave the warrant implicit — and the warrant is precisely where skeptical questions land. “The pilot reduced costs by 18%” is grounds. “And the pilot sites resemble the rest of the network in the ways that affect cost” is the warrant. If the warrant is false, the grounds are irrelevant, and a board member who spots that will stop listening to the rest. Say the warrant out loud, and say how you checked it.
Stress-testing before the room: the premortem

The research psychologist Gary Klein proposed the [premortem](R-klein-2007-performing) as a structured way to surface risks before a project begins. The team is told to imagine that it is some time in the future and the plan has failed — not that it might fail, but that it has — and each member writes down, independently, the reasons it failed. The leader collects the reasons, and the plan is revised. Klein grounds the method in earlier laboratory research on “prospective hindsight”, which found that imagining an event as having already happened makes it easier to generate explanations for it. He also argues that the premortem gives permission to dissent: in a normal review, raising a risk can feel like disloyalty; in a premortem, it is the assignment. This is a practitioner method, and its benefits in organizations have not been measured in controlled trials.
Steelmanning the alternative

A straw man is a weak version of an opposing view, built to be knocked down. A steelman is the strongest version — the one its most thoughtful advocate would recognize and endorse. Writing the steelman of the option you rejected does three things. It tests whether you rejected it for a good reason. It prepares you for the board member who favors it. And it shows the audience that your recommendation survived contact with a serious alternative, which is a large part of what they are trying to judge. Steelmanning is a practitioner discipline rather than a tested intervention, but it applies to your own recommendation the remedy for confirmation bias from [Week 1](#w01): search deliberately for the best case against your view before someone else supplies it.

understand.caption: Hard questions and how to answer them
rows: Whether you have thought about failure
Name the main failure mode, the early signal and the exit or adjustment
State its strongest case, then the specific reason it loses here
Attack a weak version of it
The evidence and, above all, the warrant
Name the evidence, its design and its main weakness
Total cost including people’s time, and what you will not do because of it
Name them, their interest and your plan to engage them
“Is this legal? Could it embarrass us?”
What counsel has reviewed, what remains open, what you would do if challenged publicly
Treat it as someone else’s problem
Ask what they see; concede what is true; hold what is not
understand.note: APERTURE teaching device.

understand.text: The dodge

Answering a hard question honestly is harder than it sounds, partly because evasion often works. In four studies, Todd Rogers and Michael Norton (2011) showed participants debate answers in which a speaker responded to the question asked, to a similar question, or to a clearly different one. When the answer addressed a similar question, many listeners did not notice the switch and rated the speaker as trustworthy and likable as one who had answered directly. Listeners were harsher on a clearly different answer — and on a speaker who answered the right question but stumbled; a smooth dodger could be preferred to a halting answerer. Dodges became far easier to detect when the original question was displayed while the speaker answered: in the American Psychological Association’s summary of the study, detection rose from 39% to 88% of listeners.

challenge.text: The dodging research is uncomfortable for anyone who teaches presentation, because it implies that fluency can substitute for honesty in the short run. There are three reasons to refuse that bargain. First, boards and owners are repeated players: they see you again, compare what you said with what happened, and accumulate a record of evasions even when individual dodges pass unnoticed. Second, the governance role you studied in [Week 13](#w13) depends on accurate information reaching the people who carry final responsibility; an answer engineered to avoid the question corrupts the channel the institution relies on. Third, the experiments themselves show the remedy: when the question stays visible, dodges are caught. Skilled board members keep the question visible by asking it again, and you should assume that yours will.

Executive presence returns here. In [Week 5](#w05-l4) you treated presence as other people’s inference about your judgment and trustworthiness rather than as a measured trait, and you saw that the research on presence itself is thin. The dodging studies add a warning: the cues observers use to infer confidence — fluency, smoothness, not stumbling — are separable from the substance of an answer, and audiences reward them. A better working definition for this course is composure under questioning: staying calm, listening to the actual question, answering it directly, conceding what is true, and saying “I don’t know yet; here is how and when I will find out” when that is the honest answer.

The premortem has limits too. It surfaces risks the team can imagine, not those outside its experience; a homogeneous team produces a homogeneous list. It can generate so many risks that none is prioritized. And because its support comes from practice and from adjacent laboratory work rather than from controlled tests in organizations, the size of its benefit is unknown. Use it as a cheap, structured prompt for dissent, rank the failure stories by likelihood and severity, and invite at least one person from outside the team to write one.

Finally, structure can be overdone. Some audiences — a founder-owner who wants to think aloud with you, or a board in the middle of a crisis — will not follow your six steps. The structure is for your preparation, not a script to defend. If the chair’s first question is about the risk, start with the risk; you have done the work to answer in any order.

challenge.title: Prerequisite: what a board or an owner actually decides

blocks.text: A board of directors or trustees holds ultimate responsibility for an organization’s direction and oversight. It typically approves strategy, major investments and senior appointments, and monitors management rather than running operations. The owner of a privately held organization may combine those roles with day-to-day authority. A president or chief executive decides within limits the board sets. Knowing which of these you face tells you what you are asking for — approval, funding, endorsement or simply awareness — and what they will be held accountable for if it fails. Their questions follow from that accountability, which is why “what happens if you’re wrong?” comes so early.

challenge.title: Methodological note: what the dodging experiments can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: The Rogers and Norton studies used debate answers evaluated by participants who had no stake in the outcome and no history with the speaker. That design isolates the content of an answer from relationships and consequences, which is both its strength and its limitation. A board member who has read the pre-read, knows your track record and will be accountable for the decision is a different listener. The findings establish that similar-question dodges can pass unnoticed and that fluency is rewarded; they do not tell you how often dodges succeed in boardrooms or what they cost later, when the evasion is discovered. Apply them as evidence about a mechanism, not as an estimate of its size in your setting.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the question you cannot answer in the room

blocks.text: The owner asks: “If we do this and the league changes the rule next year, what is our exposure?” You do not know. You can speculate, deflect to something you do know, or say: “I don’t know yet. The exposure depends on two things — how the rule would be written, and whether our agreements let us exit. Counsel can answer the second by Friday; I will come back with a range and a recommendation on whether to build an exit clause into the agreement.” The third answer concedes ignorance, shows you know what the answer depends on, commits to a date and turns a weakness into a next step. It is almost always the strongest answer available — and it is the one the dodging research suggests you will be most tempted to avoid.

apply.text: A worked example from finance (hypothetical). The head of a mid-sized asset manager’s newly created risk function must recommend to the investment committee that the firm stop offering a popular but illiquid fund to new retail investors. A premortem with her team produces nine failure stories. Three recur: the sales team routes clients to a similar affiliate product, so risk moves rather than falls; competitors capture the clients, and the firm loses revenue without reducing risk in the market; the decision leaks before clients are told. The steelman of the alternative — keep the fund open, add liquidity limits and stronger disclosure — is genuinely strong: it preserves revenue and addresses the main harm. But counsel has advised that the redemption limits it depends on may not be available under the fund’s existing documents without investor consent. That is the binding constraint, and she says so in the first minute.

items: **Ask:** Approval to close the fund to new retail investors from next quarter, and to bring a wind-down options paper to the next meeting.
**Recommendation and reason:** Close to new investors now; the alternative depends on fund terms counsel says we may not be able to change without investor consent.
**Alternative:** Liquidity limits plus disclosure — its strongest case, and why the legal uncertainty makes it unreliable for now.
**Risk and signal:** Sales migration to the affiliate product; affiliate flows will be reported to the committee monthly.
**Request:** A decision tonight on new investors; the options paper returns in six weeks.

apply.text: Her hardest question will be the committee chair’s: “If the alternative is so strong, why not try it first?” A strong answer starts with a direct answer (“Because we may not be allowed to impose the limits it relies on”), concedes what is true (“If counsel confirms we can, I would prefer it”), names the evidence and its weakness (“The liquidity analysis is based on the last two years, which did not include a severe outflow”), and ends with what would change the recommendation (“If the documents permit the limits, I will bring the alternative back as the recommendation”). Notice that the answer is stronger because the steelman was written in advance.

In baseball operations, the same structure serves a recommendation to a president or owner — to restructure a department, to change how a key decision is made, or to invest in a new capability. The audience will ask what it costs, what happens if it fails and why not the cheaper alternative; it will also be judging whether you understand the people who must carry the plan out. The board-question rehearsal at the end of this week prepares those answers before the capstone defense asks for them.

retain.text: A decision presentation is an argument under questioning. Lead with the ask and the recommendation; make the warrant explicit; stress-test with a premortem; write the steelman of the rejected option; answer the question asked. Fluency can hide evasion, which is exactly why you should not use it that way.
What are the six elements of a three-minute decision opening?
Why does a premortem ask people to imagine the plan has failed rather than that it might fail?
What did Rogers and Norton find about answers to a similar question, and what made dodges easier to detect?

takeaways: Organize for a decision, not a research paper: the ask and the recommendation come first.
The warrant — why your evidence supports your claim — is where skeptical questions land; make it explicit.
A premortem and a written steelman are cheap ways to meet your strongest objections before the room does.
Fluent dodges often pass unnoticed; that makes direct answers a matter of integrity and governance, not style.
Presence is composure under questioning, including the words “I don’t know yet — here is when I will.”

check.prompt: A presenter says: “We recommend rolling out the scheduling protocol system-wide. The pilot cut overtime costs by 18%.” In Toulmin’s terms, which statement is the warrant the board is most likely to question?

options.text: The pilot units resemble the rest of the system in the ways that drive overtime costs.
The pilot cut overtime costs by 18%.
We recommend a system-wide rollout.
Unless the vendor raises its prices next year.

check.explanation: The warrant connects the grounds (the pilot result) to the claim (system-wide rollout). It is usually left implicit, and it is where skeptical questions land: if the pilot units are unrepresentative, the 18% says little about the rest of the system.

optionFeedback.b: This is the grounds — the evidence offered — not the reasoning that links it to the claim.
optionFeedback.c: This is the claim itself.
optionFeedback.d: This is closer to a rebuttal or qualifier: a condition under which the claim might not hold.

check.prompt: In Rogers and Norton’s (2011) experiments, which kind of response was rated about as favorably as a direct answer, with many listeners failing to notice that it was evasive?

options.text: A fluent answer to a clearly different question.
A halting, stumbling answer to the question actually asked.
Any answer at all, as long as the original question was displayed while the speaker answered.
A fluent answer to a similar but different question.

check.explanation: Similar-question dodges often went unnoticed and were rated as favorably as direct answers. Clearly different answers were penalized, stumbling answers were judged harshly, and displaying the question made dodges much easier to detect.

optionFeedback.a: Listeners noticed clearly different answers more often and judged them more harshly.
optionFeedback.b: This answer was not evasive, but it was rated poorly — the study found a smooth dodger could be preferred to a halting answerer.
optionFeedback.c: Displaying the question had the opposite effect: it made dodges far easier to detect.

Experimental evidence that similar-question dodges pass undetected and fluency is rewarded.

lessons.title: The Leader’s Learning Agenda: Outcomes, Process and After-Action Reviews
lessons.summary: Executives make too few big decisions to learn from outcomes alone, so they learn by judging process separately from results, running honest after-action reviews and keeping a personal evidence practice.
objectives: Distinguish decision quality from outcome quality and explain outcome bias and its organizational consequences.
Design an after-action review using the structure of U.S. Army practice and the evidence on debriefs.
Build a personal evidence practice — decision journal, forecasts, scheduled reviews and a learning agenda — sized to the small number of major decisions you make.
lessons.executive: The decisions that matter most in a career are few and their outcomes are noisy, so you cannot learn from results alone. People rate the same decision as better when it happens to turn out well — outcome bias — which leads organizations to reward luck and punish sound bets that failed. Separate two questions: was the decision good given what was knowable, and how did it turn out? After-action reviews make that separation routine. The U.S. Army built its practice around comparing what was supposed to happen with what did, and why; a meta-analysis of debriefs found sizable average gains. Make the practice personal: write decisions down, attach probabilities, and review on schedule.

explore.text: A pharmaceutical company’s leadership approves a large late-stage trial on a careful reading of earlier data. The trial fails. The board asks who approved it, and the head of research leaves within the year. Three years earlier, a competitor approved a trial on thinner evidence, partly to beat a rival to market; it succeeded, and the executive who pushed it was promoted. (Hypothetical composite.) Ask which organization learned the right lesson — and what each will do the next time the evidence is mixed.
Before reading on: when your organization reviews a decision, does the review start from the outcome or from the decision as it looked at the time? How would you know?

Most organizations learn from outcomes because outcomes are visible and decisions are not. The record of what was known, what was assumed, which alternatives were considered and what probability was assigned usually does not exist. So the review reconstructs the decision from the outcome — and that reconstruction is exactly where hindsight and outcome bias do their work. This lesson closes the semester with the question that will matter after it ends: how will you keep learning from your own decisions when no course is grading them?

understand.text: Outcome bias

In five studies, Jonathan Baron and John Hershey (1988) gave participants descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty — medical choices and monetary gambles — and told them how things turned out. Participants rated the same decision as better reasoned, and the decision-maker as more competent, when the outcome was good than when it was bad, although the information available at the time of the decision was identical. Participants who said that outcomes should not affect such evaluations were influenced by them anyway. The studies used students and written scenarios, so they establish the direction of the bias rather than its size in organizations; but there is little reason to think executives reviewing real decisions are immune.

understand.caption: Decision quality versus outcome quality
cells: Deserved failure: the process predicted it — fix the process
Dumb luck: the most dangerous cell, because it teaches the wrong lesson
Bad luck: keep the process; check whether the risk was priced and disclosed
Deserved success: reinforce it, but ask how much was luck
understand.note: A teaching device; versions of this matrix are common in decision analysis.

understand.text: The matrix makes two organizational errors visible. The poor-process, good-outcome cell is where organizations learn the wrong lesson: they promote the people who took unpriced risks that happened to pay off. The sound-process, bad-outcome cell is where they punish the right behavior, teaching people to avoid any decision that could fail visibly. An organization that judges decisions by outcomes therefore selects for luck and for timidity at the same time — a combination you saw in Week 2’s discussion of incentives that reward the measurable result rather than the behavior you want.

Judging process separately is difficult because process is rarely recorded. That is the purpose of the decision journal you designed in [Week 1](#w01): a dated record of the decision, the alternatives, the key assumptions, your probability estimates and what would change your mind, written before the outcome is known. Without it, every review of a decision is a review of its outcome wearing the costume of a review of the decision.
After-action reviews

The U.S. Army’s after-action review (AAR) is one of the best-documented institutional learning routines. The Army’s 1993 training circular, A Leader’s Guide to After-Action Reviews (TC 25-20), presents the AAR as a professional discussion of an event, focused on performance standards, that lets participants discover for themselves what happened, why it happened, and how to sustain strengths and improve on weaknesses. It distinguishes formal reviews, with facilitators and supporting data, from informal reviews held on the spot after training. The practice has since been adapted in firefighting, healthcare and business. Its emphasis on discovery rather than critique is the point: a review that tells people what they did wrong produces compliance; a review that helps them see it produces learning.

understand.caption: The core questions of an after-action review
rows: Re-establish the plan, objectives and standards as they were understood at the time
Rewriting the plan in light of the outcome
Build a shared factual account from several vantage points
Letting the most senior person’s account become the record
Find causes in conditions, decisions and execution
Stopping at the first person to blame
What will we sustain, and what will we change?
Convert findings into specific, owned actions with dates
Lists of “lessons learned” that nobody owns or revisits
understand.note: Question structure as commonly taught in Army AAR practice; failure modes are APERTURE’s synthesis.

understand.text: Does debriefing actually improve performance? The strongest summary is a meta-analysis by Scott Tannenbaum and Christopher Cerasoli (2013), which pooled 46 samples with 2,136 participants across team and individual debriefs drawn from published and unpublished research. On average, debriefs improved performance relative to control conditions by approximately 25%, a standardized effect of about d = 0.67. Effects were stronger when debriefs were aligned with specific objectives, and the analysis pointed to facilitation and structure as likely contributors. To be included, an intervention had to meet the authors’ definition of a debrief, built on a set of essential elements, so a loosely run “lessons learned” meeting is not what the estimate describes.
A personal evidence practice

Organizations need after-action reviews; individual leaders need a personal version. A personal evidence practice has four parts, each borrowed from earlier weeks. Its purpose is not self-improvement in the motivational sense. It is the same thing Week 4 asked of any claim: what is the evidence, and how strong is it — applied to your own judgment.

items: **A decision journal** for consequential decisions, written before the outcome, as in Week 1. Keep the bar for an entry high enough that you sustain the habit: a few serious entries a month beats a daily habit abandoned by spring.
**Forecasts with probabilities** attached to each entry, with a resolve-by date, so that your calibration can be scored with the Brier score and calibration table from Week 1.
**Scheduled reviews**: a personal after-action review on the review date, judging process and outcome separately with the matrix above, and reviewing some successes as well as failures.

**A learning agenda**: three to five questions you are trying to answer better this year — for example, “How accurately do I forecast how long implementations take?” — each paired with the evidence that would show improvement.

challenge.text: The learning agenda has a statistical problem. Executives make few large decisions; outcomes depend on many factors outside their control; and feedback often arrives months or years later. With so few observations, a leader’s record of big results says little about the quality of their judgment, and even a careful calibration record takes a long time to become informative. The depth note below works through the arithmetic. The implication is not to stop keeping score. It is to score many smaller, faster-resolving forecasts — about timelines, adoption, costs, other people’s reactions — so that your record accumulates faster than your career-defining decisions do.

After-action reviews also fail in predictable ways. When reviews are used to assign blame, people stop telling the truth in them, and the shared factual account — the core of the method — becomes a negotiated story. That is the psychological-safety problem from [Week 2](#w02-l4) and Week 5 operating inside a learning routine: in Amy Edmondson’s field study of work teams, a shared belief that the team was safe for interpersonal risk was associated with learning behaviors such as discussing errors. Leaders also over-review failures and under-review successes, which leaves the poor-process, good-outcome cell unexamined. The remedy is to review a sample of successes on the same schedule as failures, using the same questions.

There is a legal dimension leaders often discover late. Written reviews are records. Depending on the jurisdiction and the context, internal reviews of an incident can become evidence in a later dispute or investigation, and some fields — hospital peer review is a common example — have specific statutory protections whose scope varies from place to place. This is educational information about a general concept, not legal advice. If your reviews concern events with potential legal exposure, ask counsel how they should be conducted and documented before you hold them, not after. The answer may change the format of the review; it should not stop you from learning.

Finally, the meta-analytic average is not a promise. The studies Tannenbaum and Cerasoli pooled vary in setting, task and design, and an average gain of about 25% does not tell any particular organization what its reviews will produce. What the moderators suggest is more useful than the headline: align the review with specific objectives, give it structure, and consider a facilitator who is not the most senior person in the room.

challenge.title: Prerequisite: process versus outcome

blocks.text: A decision’s process is everything under the decision-maker’s control at the time: the information gathered, the alternatives considered, the reasoning and the probabilities assigned. Its outcome is what happened afterward, which also depends on chance and on events no one could have known. A good process can produce a bad outcome — a well-priced bet that lost — and a bad process can produce a good outcome — a reckless bet that won. Judging a decision fairly means asking what a careful person could reasonably have known and done at the time, and only then looking at the result.

challenge.title: Methodological note: how many decisions do you need to judge your judgment?

blocks.text: Suppose you make 20 forecasts at 70% confidence. If you are perfectly calibrated, you expect 14 of them to come true. Chance alone produces variation around that number: the standard error of a proportion is the square root of p(1 − p)/n, here √(0.7 × 0.3 / 20) ≈ 0.10. A rough 95% range for your observed hit rate is therefore about 50% to 90% — between 10 and 18 hits — even if your judgment is perfect. Twenty forecasts cannot reliably distinguish a well-calibrated forecaster from a substantially overconfident one.

With 100 forecasts at the same level, the standard error falls to about 0.046 and the range narrows to roughly 61% to 79%. With 200, it narrows further. The lesson is not that personal scorekeeping is useless. It is that scorekeeping on a handful of big decisions is nearly uninformative, while scorekeeping on many small, quickly resolved forecasts can become informative within a year or two.

blocks.caption: Width of a rough 95% range for a perfectly calibrated forecaster’s hit rate at 70% confidence, by number of forecasts
blocks.note: Synthetic calculation: width of ±1.96 standard errors around a true 70% hit rate, normal approximation, rounded; illustrative only.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the board wants a review that ends with a name

blocks.text: A major initiative has failed publicly, and the board wants “a full review” by Friday. The pressure is to produce an account that ends with a person. A principled alternative is to agree on the review’s questions in advance (the four AAR questions), separate a factual timeline from interpretations, reconstruct what was known at each decision point from the records that existed then, and evaluate process and outcome separately. If someone made a poor decision given what was knowable, say so plainly; if the decision was sound and unlucky, say that too, and explain why. Boards accept this more readily than leaders expect when the review is rigorous and the leader states clearly what they themselves would do differently.

apply.text: A worked example from technology (hypothetical). After a major outage, a cloud-software company’s reliability team adopts blameless post-incident reviews built on the AAR logic: a timeline assembled from logs and chat records; the decisions people made, with what they knew at the time; contributing conditions, such as alerts that fired so often they were ignored and an undocumented dependency; and specific actions with owners and dates. Six months later the head of reliability runs a second-order review. Of the 22 actions assigned across all reviews, how many were completed? Did the same contributing conditions reappear? That second review is what turns a ritual into a learning system, because it tests whether the first reviews changed anything.
Now build your own learning agenda for the year after this semester. A starter set might look like this — adapt the questions to the decisions you actually make:

items: **Judgment:** “Am I overconfident about timelines?” Evidence: at least 30 dated timeline forecasts, scored each quarter.
**Influence:** “Are my recommendations adopted, and why or why not?” Evidence: a log of recommendations, the decision taken and the stated reason.
**Leading others:** “Do people bring me bad news early?” Evidence: in each review, the time between a problem’s onset and when you learned of it.
**A developing lens:** “When does finance or law change my answer?” Evidence: decisions in which that lens altered the recommendation, noted in the journal.

apply.text: In player development, outcome bias is everywhere because outcomes are public and noisy. A prospect promoted aggressively who then thrives makes the decision look wise; one who struggles makes the same reasoning look reckless. A development group that records its promotion reasoning and probabilities at the time, and reviews a sample of successes and failures on a fixed schedule, can begin to separate the quality of its judgment from the variance of player outcomes. The same practice serves an individual leader. The capstone’s final deliverable asks you to reflect on your demonstrated strengths and areas for development; a decision journal kept through the capstone gives that reflection evidence rather than impressions.

retain.text: Judge process and outcome separately, because outcomes reward luck and punish sound bets. After-action reviews make the separation routine, and a meta-analysis found substantial average gains from debriefs, especially when they were aligned with objectives and structured. For an individual leader, the unit of learning is the forecast, not the career-defining decision — there are too few of those to learn from.
Describe the four cells of the process–outcome matrix and the error each invites.
What are the four core questions of an after-action review, and which one most often goes wrong?
Why do 20 forecasts tell you little about your calibration? What would you change?

takeaways: Outcome bias leads organizations to promote luck and punish sound bets; record decisions before outcomes are known.
An AAR asks what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to sustain or change — and it fails when used to assign blame.
A meta-analysis of 46 samples found debriefs improved performance by about 25% on average; alignment and structure matter.
Score many small forecasts, not a few big decisions; that is how a personal record becomes informative.

check.prompt: Which situation is the clearest example of outcome bias?

options.text: An investor becomes more cautious after losing money on a trade.
A hospital committee praises a surgeon’s decision to operate after a good result, although it criticized an identical decision by a colleague last month that ended badly.
A manager prefers whichever of two proposals she read first.
After an election, a commentator says he “knew all along” who would win.

check.explanation: Outcome bias is judging the quality of a decision by its result when the information at the time was the same. The committee evaluated identical decisions differently because of how they turned out — the pattern Baron and Hershey documented.

optionFeedback.a: Changing behavior after a loss may reflect loss aversion or learning; it is not an evaluation of decision quality by outcome.
optionFeedback.c: Preferring the first proposal is an order or anchoring effect, not outcome bias.
optionFeedback.d: This is hindsight bias — overestimating how predictable an outcome was. It is related to outcome bias but concerns perceived predictability, not the rated quality of a decision.

check.prompt: You record 50 forecasts at 60% confidence. If you are perfectly calibrated, what is the standard error of your hit rate, expressed as a proportion? Round to three decimals.
check.explanation: The standard error shows how much your hit rate would vary by chance alone if your judgment were perfect. With 50 forecasts the plausible range is still wide — roughly 46% to 74% — so a single season of forecasts is weak evidence about calibration.

glossary.definition: Roger Martin’s practitioner term for holding two opposing models in mind and constructing a new option that keeps the core of each and is better than either, instead of choosing one or splitting the difference.
APERTURE’s written procedure for testing a decision through behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law and ethics, with each lens answered independently before discussion.
A limit that actually restricts the choice you would otherwise make; relaxing it would improve the outcome, whereas relaxing a non-binding constraint changes nothing.
Procedures that reduce judgment error without needing to diagnose which bias is operating, such as independent estimates before discussion, structured criteria and an outside view.
Stinchcombe’s argument that new organizations fail at higher rates than old ones because roles must be learned, routines built, trust formed among strangers and ties established with those served.
A pattern in which failure risk is low at first, rises as an organization’s initial endowment of resources and goodwill runs out, and then declines.
The probability that something fails in a short period, given that it has survived until the start of that period; its shape over time shows when risk peaks.
The generalized belief among relevant people that a unit’s actions are appropriate and worth relying on; it can rest on authority, conformity to standards, results or relationships.
A modest, finished result that people outside a new unit value for its own sake — distinct from a publicity win, whose value lies mainly in its announcement.
Michael Watkins’s practitioner typology of leadership situations: start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment and sustaining success.
In Stephen Toulmin’s scheme of argument, the reasoning that connects the evidence (grounds) to a claim; the step skeptical questions most often target.
Gary Klein’s practitioner method in which a team imagines that a plan has already failed and each member independently writes the reasons before the plan is finalized.
The strongest version of an opposing position — one its most thoughtful advocate would endorse; the opposite of a straw man.
An answer to a different question from the one asked; Rogers and Norton (2011) found that fluent answers to similar questions often go unnoticed by listeners.
Rating the quality of a decision by how it turned out rather than by what was known and reasonable at the time it was made.

A structured discussion after an event that compares what was supposed to happen with what happened, explains the difference and assigns actions to sustain or change; formalized in U.S. Army practice.
A short list of questions a leader is trying to answer better over a defined period, each paired with the evidence that would show improvement.

exercise.title: Decision Presentation Studio

intro.text: You will draft the opening of a decision presentation three ways for the same fictional decision: a three-minute spoken opening statement (about 450 words at 150 words per minute), a one-slide summary (about 120 words), and your answer to the hardest question the board will ask (about 150 words). The scenario is deliberately outside baseball so that you practice the structure rather than lean on domain knowledge. It is integrative by design: the decision has behavioral, evidentiary, strategic, financial, legal and ethical dimensions, and one of them binds.

What to notice as you draft: whether the decision you need appears in the first two sentences of every format; whether each evidence claim carries its strength (measured, forecast, assumption); whether the main risk and its early signal survive compression to 120 words; and whether your hardest-question answer begins by answering. The studio shows word count, speaking time, sentence length, hedge words and a passive-voice heuristic. It does not grade content — use the checklist and the debrief for that, and read your three-minute opening aloud at least once with a timer.
Before drafting, write one sentence: what exactly do you want the board to decide on the night of the meeting?

scenario.text: **The Pell Harbor Sports and Recreation Authority** (fictional) is a public authority created by a mid-sized coastal city to run its parks, two golf courses, three pools and a network of youth fields. Imagine you are its executive director, eleven months into the job. The authority’s nine-member board — appointed by the mayor and the city council — meets in three weeks to decide the future of Alder Point, a municipal 18-hole golf course on about 140 acres.

Your staff recommends converting Alder Point into a 9-hole course plus a youth multi-sport complex: eight fields, two of them lit synthetic turf, and a small community building. The plan would be financed by a $14 million revenue bond repaid from field-rental and program fees, supported by a 15-year naming-rights agreement with Harrowgate Savings, a regional bank, worth $450,000 a year. Rounds at Alder Point have declined for six straight years; youth leagues turn away teams every spring for lack of fields.

scenario.text: Complications. The 1938 deed that conveyed the land to the city restricts its use to “public park and recreation purposes.” The authority’s counsel believes youth athletics qualify but has flagged two open questions: whether the bank’s naming rights and on-site advertising are consistent with the deed, and whether the bond requires a public referendum under the authority’s charter. The Alder Point Golfers’ Association — about 600 members, many of them older residents who have played there for decades — has collected 4,000 signatures against the plan. A youth sports coalition supports it, as do two council members; a third council member, facing re-election, has called it “selling the park to a bank.”

The arithmetic matters. At forecast participation, the complex’s income plus the naming-rights payment covers debt service comfortably. At 70% of forecast, the complex covers its bond payments only with the naming-rights income — and the bank may exit after year five if usage is low. The board chair, a retired accountant, has told you privately that she will ask one question before any other: “If the bank walks away in year six and participation is at seventy percent, who pays the bond?” Your answer must be honest.

items: **Your task:** draft (1) a three-minute opening statement, (2) a one-slide summary and (3) your answer to the chair’s question.
**You may change the plan** — phase it, resize the bond, restructure the naming-rights terms, set conditions — if you can say why. You may also recommend against it.
**Treat the legal questions as questions for counsel.** Say what has been asked and what remains open; do not state legal conclusions.

audience.cares: Debt coverage, downside scenarios, whether the forecast deserves the weight the plan puts on it.
Public reaction in an election year; fairness to long-time park users; whether the city is exposed.
Losing a valued place and routine; whether a 9-hole course is a real course; being consulted rather than informed.
Field access, affordability for low-income families, and how soon fields open.
Deed restrictions, charter requirements for borrowing, procurement rules and the naming-rights terms.

formats.label: Answer to the hardest question
sections: What is true in the concern

checklist: The decision you need from the board appears in the first two sentences of every format.
The recommendation names the strongest alternative (including “do nothing” or a smaller plan) and the specific reason it loses.
Every number is labelled as measured, forecast or assumption, and the forecast’s single comparison site is acknowledged.
The main risk and an early warning signal survive in the one-slide summary.
The binding constraint — financial, legal or political — is named, not implied.
Legal points are framed as questions put to counsel, with what remains open, not as conclusions.
The hardest-question answer starts with a direct answer, concedes what is true, and ends with what would change your recommendation.
The golfers’ loss is acknowledged in plain words rather than minimized.
No sentence stacks more than one hedge (“may possibly”, “could potentially”).

debrief.text: Compare your three drafts side by side. In most first attempts, the one-slide version loses the risk, and the hardest-question answer begins with context rather than an answer. If yours did, rewrite the first sentence of each before moving on. Then check the speaking time of your opening: if it runs over three minutes at 150 words per minute, cut the “what we weighed” section first — the board can read the detail in the pre-read.

A strong answer to the chair’s question probably begins with the honest arithmetic: in that scenario the complex does not cover its debt service from its own income, and the shortfall falls on the authority’s reserve unless the plan changes. It then says what the plan does about that risk — for example, phasing the build so that borrowing grows with demonstrated demand, sizing the bond to cover debt service without the naming-rights income, setting aside reserve funds before borrowing, or negotiating an exit clause that requires notice and a payment — and what evidence would trigger each step. Conceding the vulnerability and showing the mitigation is stronger than defending the forecast; it is also the answer the chair can repeat to the council.

Notice how the six lenses appeared. Finance and law were candidates for the binding constraint (debt coverage; the deed and the charter). Evidence was weak in a specific way (one comparison site, an outside-view forecast). Behavior and ethics were present in the golfers’ loss, the equity of access and the council’s politics. Strategy was the question of what the authority is for. A recommendation that addresses all six in three minutes is possible only if it is selective — which is the skill.

What the exercise shows: the structural discipline of decision-first communication and what survives compression. What it does not show: whether your recommendation is right, or how a real board would react. The studio’s metrics measure form only. The legal issues in the scenario are fictional and general; in real life they are questions for qualified counsel.

assumptions: All organizations, people, places and figures in the scenario are fictional; the numbers are synthetic.
Speaking time is estimated at 150 words per minute; real pace varies with the speaker and with pauses.
The studio’s metrics (length, speaking time, sentence length, hedge words, a passive-voice heuristic) are transparent text measures, not a grade of quality or persuasiveness.
Legal issues in the scenario are general illustrations for practice, not legal advice about any real deed, charter or agreement.

case.title: The Hollis Creek Decision
case.fiction: All people, organizations, places and data in this case are fictional. Legal, regulatory and contractual details are simplified and invented for teaching; they do not describe any real jurisdiction or agreement.

body.text: A request after the finance committee

Daniel Iturbe had been chief strategy officer of the Merriton County Health System for five months when the board chair asked him to stay behind after the finance committee meeting. “We need a recommendation on Hollis Creek obstetrics by the December board meeting,” Graham Whitlow said. He was a retired banker who chaired the board with the patience of someone who had seen several turnarounds and believed in few of them. “Not options. A recommendation. And I want it defended, because the room will be full.”

Merriton is a county-owned safety-net system: a 410-bed main hospital, Merriton General, in the county seat, and two smaller community hospitals — Hollis Creek, 46 miles to the northwest in a farming region, and Easton Ridge, 22 miles to the south. The system had lost money in each of the last three years. Daniel’s Office of Strategy and Transformation had been created in June by the chief executive, Elena Marsh, at the same time as his appointment. It consisted of Daniel, two analysts and a project manager on loan from finance. Its charter read: “to lead the system’s return to financial sustainability while protecting access to care.” Several department heads still referred to it, not always kindly, as “Elena’s office.”
The numbers

Priya Venkataraman, the chief financial officer, put the numbers simply. The system’s bond agreements required it to keep at least 75 days of cash on hand. It had 96 today and, on current trends, would reach about 78 within eighteen months. Falling below the covenant would allow bondholders to require remedies — at a minimum an outside consultant and closer oversight, and potentially higher borrowing costs for years. “We are not in crisis,” she told Daniel. “We are in the period when we can still choose. That period is shorter than people think.”

Hollis Creek’s labor and delivery unit had delivered 172 babies the previous year, down from 241 five years earlier (Exhibit 1). It lost $2.9 million. Of its 19 budgeted nursing positions, 11 were filled by employees; the rest were covered by travel nurses at roughly twice the cost. One of its two obstetricians, Dr. Ruth Harlan, had said she would retire the following summer. Two attempts to recruit an obstetrician to Hollis Creek had failed.
By late October, Daniel’s team had narrowed the field to three options (Exhibit 2):

items: **Close** labor and delivery at Hollis Creek within six months; keep prenatal and postpartum clinics there; fund a transport and patient-navigation program; and expand capacity at Merriton General.

**Partner:** keep the unit open through a staffing partnership with a university health system in the next county, adding tele-obstetrics consultation and a shared on-call rotation — contingent on recruiting one obstetrician.

**Stage:** keep the unit open for eighteen months while building the transport program and clinic capacity, and decide at month fifteen between closure and continuation, against criteria the board would set now.

body.text: The people

Marjorie Toll, the chief nursing officer, worried most about the staff. “The Hollis Creek nurses have heard the rumors since spring,” she said. “Every month we don’t decide, another one takes a job in the city. If we’re going to keep the unit, we need to say so and mean it. If we’re going to close it, the worst thing we can do is close it slowly.” Tom Wexler, president of the nurses’ union local, had already asked for a meeting. The collective agreement required 90 days’ notice before layoffs and a meeting to discuss their effects on staff, and Tom had made clear that the union would contest any closure in public.

Dr. Samuel Adeyemi, the chief medical officer, favored closure on quality grounds. He brought a folder of studies suggesting that very low-volume units find it harder to maintain the skills and staffing needed for rare obstetric emergencies. County Commissioner Rosa Delgado-Pike, whose district included Hollis Creek, brought her own folder: studies associating longer travel times to obstetric care with worse outcomes for some groups of patients. Daniel’s analyst, Kwame Asante, read both. “They’re mostly observational,” he said. “Different countries, different decades, different definitions of ‘low volume’ and ‘rural’. Each folder is honest. Neither one tells us what happens in Hollis Creek if we close, or if we stay.”
The law and the calendar

Laura Kessling, the general counsel, laid out the legal map in a memo marked privileged. Under the state’s rules, as she summarized them, a hospital that discontinues an inpatient service must give the health department 120 days’ notice and hold a public hearing. The emergency department at Hollis Creek would stay open under every option, and it would still see women in active labor; it had legal obligations to screen and stabilize them, and Laura wanted a written plan — staffing, training, transfer agreements — before any announcement. The university partnership would require a contract covering liability, credentialing and data sharing that her office estimated would take four months to negotiate. “None of this decides the question,” she said. “But it decides the calendar.”
The vendor

Then there was the vendor. Quillfeather Analytics, a staffing-software company, had been pitching the system for months. Its predictive scheduling tool, the sales team said, had cut travel-nurse spending by 31% in a pilot at another health system — enough, on Priya’s spreadsheet, to reduce the Hollis Creek loss by about $400,000 a year under the Partner or Stage options. Kwame asked how the pilot unit had been chosen. It had been the client’s unit with the highest travel-nurse spending in the previous year. There had been no comparison unit.
The politics

The politics were not subtle. Commissioner Delgado-Pike sat on the committee that approved the county’s annual contribution to the system — $6 million the previous year. She had told Elena that a closure “would be remembered.” The local newspaper had run a front-page story under the headline “Will Hollis Creek Babies Be Born on the Highway?” At the same time, Easton Ridge’s emergency department needed a $3.5 million renovation that had been deferred twice, and the system’s foundation had a donor willing to fund half of it if the system committed the other half this year. Priya’s view was that the system could afford one of the two — the renovation or a sustained investment at Hollis Creek — but not both without endangering the covenant.
The office

Daniel’s own position was part of the problem. A recommendation to close would make the Office of Strategy and Transformation the public face of the system’s most unpopular decision in a decade, five months after its creation. A recommendation to keep the unit open, if the partnership failed, would cost money the system might not have and leave him defending the choice at the next budget review. Elena had told him she would support whatever he recommended, “as long as I can explain it to the commissioners.” Whitlow had told him he wanted it defended. Neither had said what would happen if the board split.

There were things Daniel did not know and could not learn by December: whether an obstetrician would accept the Hollis Creek position, how many expectant mothers would choose a hospital in the next county rather than Merriton General, what the county would do with its contribution, and how many Hollis Creek nurses would stay through an eighteen-month wait. He did know what the board would ask first. He had heard Whitlow ask it at every meeting he had attended: “What happens if you’re wrong?”

On the first of November, Daniel blocked two hours on his calendar, opened a blank document and typed a single line at the top: “What is the binding constraint?” He looked at it for a while. Then he typed a second line beneath it: “What would I need to believe for each option to be right?”

Which option would you recommend to the board? State what you would need to believe for it to be right, and what evidence would change your mind.
How should Daniel present the vendor’s pilot and the two folders of studies? Write the sentence he should say about each.

Daniel’s office is five months old. How should the liability of newness shape the way he makes this recommendation — and should his office be its public face at all?

perspectives.title: Close, decisively and well
perspectives.text: This position treats the staffing trend and the covenant as the binding constraints: the unit is losing staff, volume and money every year, recruitment has failed twice, and a slow decline is the worst outcome for patients and nurses alike. Close within the legal timetable, but spend real money on the transport and navigation program, the emergency department’s stabilization plan and a generous transition for nurses, and announce it with clarity. Its strengths are honesty about the trends and certainty for staff. Its risks are access harms that will be hard to measure, the county contribution, and a new office spending legitimacy it has not yet earned — which argues for the chief executive, not the strategy office, being its public face.

perspectives.title: Partner and test
perspectives.text: This position treats the ethical and political lenses as binding: a county-owned safety-net system exists partly to provide access that the market will not, and the commissioner’s committee funds $6 million a year. The partnership is an integrative option — it keeps local access while sharing the staffing burden. Its weakness is that it depends on recruiting an obstetrician where two searches have failed, and on a four-month contract negotiation; if either fails, the system will have spent a year and money it may need for Easton Ridge. A defensible version sets a hard recruitment deadline before signing.

perspectives.title: Stage, with criteria committed now
perspectives.text: This position treats the uncertainty itself as the problem and asks the board to adopt a decision rule rather than a decision: specific thresholds (births, employed-nurse ratio, recruitment, a signed partnership, days of cash) and a date, with the transport program built either way. It preserves options and turns a political fight into a test. Its risks are the ones Marjorie Toll named — nurses leaving during the wait — and the risk that, when the date arrives, the board moves its own goalposts. Without a credible commitment to the criteria, staging becomes a disguised deferral.

case.application: The structure transfers directly to player development and baseball operations. Consolidating a development facility, ending a program in a particular country or region, or changing an affiliate arrangement can involve the same lenses: staff and families affected, noisy evidence about developmental outcomes, financial pressure, contractual and regulatory obligations, community relationships, and ethical questions about who bears the cost. The new-office dimension also transfers. A recently created department that becomes the public face of an unpopular consolidation may spend legitimacy it has not yet earned, which is a reason to think carefully about who presents a decision as well as what is decided. The questions the board will ask Daniel are close to those a president or owner would ask about any consolidation — and the capstone defense will ask versions of them about your own fictional department.

quiz.title: Week 14 cumulative quiz — integrating the semester

questions.prompt: A city transit authority’s board is asked to extend a driver-coaching program system-wide. Read the summary. What is the most important reason to doubt that the program caused the improvement?

stimulus.text: Fictional summary. Last year the authority chose the four bus depots with the highest accident rates for a new driver-coaching program. This year, accidents at those four depots fell 22%. Accidents at the other eleven depots fell 5%. The program’s sponsor concludes that coaching cut accidents by about 17 percentage points relative to the rest of the system and asks the board to fund a system-wide rollout.

options.text: Four depots are too few to compute a percentage change.
The comparison depots also improved, which shows the program spilled over to them, so the true effect is larger than 17 points.
Depots chosen for extreme accident rates would be expected to move back toward the average the next year even without coaching, so part of the 22% fall is likely regression to the mean.
The improvement must be a placebo effect, because drivers knew they were being coached.

questions.explanation: The pilot depots were selected because they had the worst year, and extreme values tend to be followed by values closer to the average (Week 4). A fair estimate needs comparable high-accident depots that were not coached — ideally assigned at random. In the six-lens review, this is the evidence lens catching a problem before the finance lens prices a system-wide rollout.

optionFeedback.a: Small numbers make estimates noisy, but a percentage can be computed; the larger problem is how the depots were selected.
optionFeedback.b: Improvement at the other depots more plausibly reflects a system-wide trend. It does not demonstrate spillover, and it does not enlarge the estimate.
optionFeedback.d: Being observed can change behavior, but nothing here points to it as strongly as selection on extreme values; “must be” overstates any single explanation.

questions.prompt: Identify the central flaw in the reasoning below.

stimulus.text: Fictional memo from an investment firm’s committee chair: “Last year Elena’s team put 12% of the fund into a single biotech position against the risk team’s advice. The company’s drug was approved and the position tripled. The result speaks for itself: her process was sound, our risk limits are too conservative, and we should raise single-position limits across the firm and make her approach our standard.”

options.text: It fails to calculate the position’s net present value.
It ignores the possibility that Elena traded on inside information, which would make the trade illegal.
It relies on the risk team, whose incentives are to be conservative.
It infers that the decision process was sound from a single good outcome, ignoring what was knowable and the risk taken at the time.

questions.explanation: One success says little about the process: a concentrated bet can be reckless and still pay off — the “dumb luck” cell of the process–outcome matrix. Baron and Hershey showed that people rate identical decisions more favorably when outcomes are good. Before changing firm-wide limits, the committee should review what Elena knew, what probability she assigned and how the position was sized — and it should look at concentrated bets that lost as well as this one.

optionFeedback.a: Net present value is not the issue; the memo’s error is inferring the quality of a process from one outcome.
optionFeedback.b: Insider trading would be a serious legal issue, but nothing in the memo suggests it. The reasoning flaw stands even if the trade was entirely lawful.
optionFeedback.c: The memo actually dismisses the risk team rather than relying on it; its central move is generalizing from a single favorable outcome.

questions.prompt: You lead strategy at a regional grocery chain with capital for one major initiative this year. What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: Fictional. Option 1: build a same-day delivery service in-house; it is expensive, and competitors already offer the same service through third-party apps. Option 2: buy a small regional meal-kit company whose two founders created its popular recipes and built a loyal subscriber base; their employment agreements expire in four months, and the state where it operates generally does not enforce non-compete clauses. Option 3: renovate twenty stores. The board favors Option 2 because the brand is distinctive.

options.text: Pursue Option 2, but treat founder retention and ownership of the recipes and brand as the binding constraint: tie a substantial part of the price to the founders staying, and have counsel confirm what the company actually owns before signing.
Pursue Option 2 immediately at the asking price, before a competitor bids; the brand is the asset.
Choose Option 1, because building in-house always creates more durable advantage than buying.
Split the capital three ways so that each option gets some funding and the board can see which works.

questions.explanation: Option 2’s value rests on resources that can walk out of the door — the founders and their know-how — and on intellectual property whose ownership must be confirmed (Weeks 9 and 11). With non-competes unlikely to protect the buyer, the legal and behavioral lenses bind the strategy, so the deal structure must tie value to retention and secure ownership. That is an integrative answer rather than a choice between buying and not buying.

optionFeedback.b: Speed does not address the risk that the valuable resources leave; paying the full price up front transfers that risk to the buyer.
optionFeedback.c: Build-versus-buy depends on the resource in question; “always” is not a strategy, and Option 1 replicates what competitors already offer.
optionFeedback.d: Spreading capital across three initiatives may leave none adequately funded. It is a compromise, not an integration.

questions.prompt: A university hospital is considering a new patient-flow office. It costs $600,000 to set up today and is expected to save $200,000 at the end of each of the next four years, after which the savings end. At an 8% discount rate, what is the project’s net present value? Answer in dollars, rounded to the nearest hundred.
questions.working: Present value of four end-of-year savings at 8%: 200,000 × [1 − 1.08^(−4)] / 0.08 = 200,000 × 3.3121 ≈ 662,400. NPV = 662,400 − 600,000 ≈ $62,400. Sensitivity: if savings are 10% lower ($180,000 a year), PV ≈ 596,200 and NPV ≈ −$3,800.
questions.explanation: Discounting converts future savings into today’s dollars (Week 10). The NPV is positive but small relative to the investment, and a 10% shortfall in savings makes it slightly negative — so the recommendation depends on the savings estimate, which is exactly what a skeptical board will probe. Present the sensitivity before you are asked.

questions.prompt: Educational exercise on general legal concepts — not legal advice. A newly created analytics unit at a regional hospital system is planning its first six months. Select every item that raises a genuine legal or contractual issue to put to counsel before acting.

options.text: Hiring a senior analyst from a competitor who offers to bring “templates and data from my last job”.
Selling a benchmarking product to other hospitals, built on patient data the system licensed from a vendor for “internal quality improvement only”.
Engaging three data scientists as independent contractors who will work full time on site, under the unit’s direction, with no end date.
Choosing between two programming languages for the unit’s code.
Sharing de-identified results with a university research partner without any written data-use agreement.
Deciding whether the unit’s weekly meeting is on Monday or Tuesday.

questions.explanation: (a) risks misuse of a former employer’s confidential information or trade secrets; (b) exceeds the license’s permitted use; (c) may misclassify employees as contractors, with tax and employment-law consequences that turn on how much control the organization exercises; (e) health data sharing, even de-identified, normally calls for written terms on permitted use, re-identification and security. Programming languages and meeting days are management choices. New units are especially exposed because they set precedents quickly and have no institutional memory of past disputes (Lesson 2, Week 11).

questions.prompt: You present a request for $1.2 million to fund a newly created function. The chief financial officer replies: “I can find $700,000. Take it or leave it.” Your analysis shows that the function cannot deliver its core service below about $900,000, and you have learned that the CFO’s main worry is committing recurring costs before the function proves itself. What is the best next move?

options.text: Accept $700,000 to preserve the relationship and do as much as possible.
Split the difference at $950,000 to show flexibility.

Propose a phased structure: $900,000 for year one, with recurring funding beyond that tied to two pre-agreed results reviewed at mid-year, and an offer to return $150,000 if the first result is missed.
Escalate to the chief executive immediately, since the offer is below your reservation point.

questions.explanation: Your reservation point is about $900,000; below it, accepting is worse than rescoping or walking away (Week 7). The CFO’s interest is limiting recurring risk, not the headline number, so a contingent, phased structure trades on the issue the two sides value differently — certainty for the CFO, viability for you. It also builds results-based legitimacy (Lesson 2) instead of relying on a sponsor to override the CFO.

optionFeedback.a: Accepting below your reservation point guarantees a function that cannot do its core job — an outcome you would later have to defend.
optionFeedback.b: Splitting the difference anchors on the CFO’s number and ignores the interest behind it; it may still leave the CFO’s worry about recurring costs unaddressed.
optionFeedback.d: Escalation may eventually be necessary, but doing it before addressing the CFO’s stated interest spends relationship capital and signals that you negotiate through hierarchy.

questions.prompt: You have just been appointed to lead a new, four-person operational-excellence unit in a large logistics company. Rank these opening moves from best to worst as the sequence for your first three months.

options.text: Agree in writing with your sponsor and two key operating heads what the unit will decide, recommend or only advise on.
Solve one problem that a skeptical operating head has named, and deliver a modest, finished result.
Publish a company-wide dashboard of operational metrics for all regions.
Move the analysts currently embedded in the operating regions into your unit in the first month.

questions.explanation: Decision rights come first (Week 8): without them every request becomes a negotiation and every result can be ignored. A finished answer to a problem a skeptic named builds results- and relationship-based legitimacy; some leaders would put it first, and both are defensible early moves. A broad dashboard is not harmful but has little value before the unit has users who trust it. Pulling embedded analysts out of the regions in month one takes resources from the very people whose trust the unit needs — the quickest way to turn the liability of newness into open resistance.

questions.prompt: What should you do?

stimulus.text: Fictional. You are rehearsing a board presentation recommending a new dispatch protocol for a city’s emergency medical service. A pilot in two districts showed faster response times. A team member points out that a third district also ran the protocol for one month and saw slower times — possibly because of a major road closure. She suggests leaving the third district out: “It will confuse the board, and the road closure explains it anyway.”

options.text: Leave it out; the board needs clarity, and the road closure is a sufficient explanation.
Mention it only if a board member asks about other districts.
Postpone the presentation until the third district has six more months of data.
Include the third district’s result, say what you think explains it and how confident you are, and state what data would show whether the protocol or the road closure drove it.

questions.explanation: Boards carry responsibility for decisions made on the information management gives them (Week 13). Omitting disconfirming evidence because it is inconvenient corrupts that channel, and if it surfaces later it damages your credibility on everything else. Presenting it with your interpretation and its uncertainty is both the honest choice and the persuasive one: it shows the recommendation survived contact with the worst fact.

optionFeedback.a: The road closure may well explain the result, but that is an interpretation the board is entitled to weigh. Selective omission is the problem.
optionFeedback.b: Holding back material evidence unless asked is a quieter form of the same omission — and Rogers and Norton’s work shows how easily a question can be steered around.
optionFeedback.c: Delay might be justified if the decision is not urgent, but the issue here is disclosure, not timing; you can present now with the uncertainty stated.

questions.prompt: Which opening sentence best fits a decision-first presentation to a hospital board?

options.text: Over the past six months our team has conducted an extensive review of patient-flow data across all three campuses, and I would like to walk you through what we found.

Tonight I am asking you to approve $2.1 million to open a discharge lounge at the main hospital by March, because it is the fastest way to free about twenty beds a day; the main risk is staffing, and by May we will know whether it is working.
Patient flow is one of the most complex challenges facing any health system, and there are many perspectives on how to address it.
I want to begin by thanking the many people who contributed to this analysis, especially our nursing leadership.

questions.explanation: Option b states the ask, the amount, the deadline, the main reason, the main risk and the early signal in one breath; the board knows immediately what it is deciding and how it will judge success. The other openings place the decision behind method, generalities or thanks.

optionFeedback.a: This is a research-paper order — method before conclusion; the board waits to learn what it is deciding.
optionFeedback.c: A general statement about complexity spends the most valuable seconds without telling the board anything it can act on.
optionFeedback.d: Acknowledgment has a place, but not as the opening of a decision presentation; it can come at the end or in the pre-read.

questions.prompt: A hospital network wants to introduce after-action reviews following major operational events. Which design features are supported by U.S. Army AAR practice, by the debrief meta-analysis discussed this week, or by this week’s reasoning about outcome bias? Select all that apply.

options.text: Begin by re-establishing what was supposed to happen, using the plan as it was understood at the time.
Align each review with specific objectives or standards for the event.
Use a consistent structure and, where possible, a trained facilitator.
Hold reviews only after failures, to save time.
End each review by naming the individual responsible and recording a corrective action against that person.
Review a sample of successes as well as failures.

questions.explanation: An AAR begins by comparing what was supposed to happen with what did (a). Tannenbaum and Cerasoli found larger effects when debriefs were aligned with objectives and pointed to facilitation and structure (b, c). Reviewing successes (f) guards against the poor-process, good-outcome blind spot. Reviewing only failures (d) teaches people that reviews are punishments, and ending with a name (e) turns a learning routine into a blame process, which degrades the honesty the method depends on.

questions.prompt: A national youth-soccer federation must decide whether to require all member clubs to use a new player-tracking app for injury monitoring. Evidence: a vendor study shows fewer injuries at clubs that adopted the app voluntarily. Finance: the federation would subsidize half the cost for three years. Law: the players are minors, and the app collects location and health data. Behavior: many volunteer coaches resist new technology. Ethics: families have not been consulted. In 150–200 words, identify the binding constraint, explain why it binds, and give an integrative recommendation that addresses at least four of the six lenses. (Self-assessed.)
questions.modelAnswer: The binding constraint is law and ethics together: the app collects health and location data about minors, and the federation cannot responsibly mandate it until counsel has established what consent, parental notice and data-protection obligations apply, and until families have been asked. Those questions rule out a mandate this season regardless of cost or evidence. The evidence lens also argues against a mandate: clubs that adopted voluntarily probably differ from those that did not, so the injury difference may reflect selection rather than the app. My recommendation is a voluntary, consent-based pilot in a sample of clubs — randomized among volunteers if possible — with counsel-approved data terms, a parent information session and minimal data collection. The federation subsidizes the pilot clubs, offers coaches simple onboarding, and commits to a decision in twelve months based on pre-specified injury and usage measures. This keeps the strategic aim of better injury monitoring while respecting the constraints, and it produces evidence a later mandate could rest on.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a defensible binding constraint and shows which options it eliminates
levels: 0 — no binding constraint named, or named without explanation
1 — names one but does not show why it binds
2 — names it and shows which options it removes

rubric.criterion: Integrates at least four lenses into a single recommendation rather than listing them
levels: 0 — fewer than three lenses, or a list without a decision
1 — four lenses mentioned but weakly connected
2 — four or more lenses shape one coherent recommendation

rubric.criterion: Treats the vendor evidence critically (self-selection, lack of comparison)
levels: 0 — accepts the vendor study at face value
1 — identifies self-selection or the absence of a fair comparison

rubric.criterion: Recommendation is specific and decision-ready (who, what, when, how it will be judged)
levels: 0 — vague or conditional on unnamed future work
1 — specific actions, timing and decision criteria

questions.prompt: Over two years you recorded 25 forecasts in your decision journal at 80% confidence; 17 came true (68%). If you were perfectly calibrated, your expected hit rate would be 80%, with a standard error of √(0.8 × 0.2 / 25). How many standard errors below 80% is your observed hit rate? Round to one decimal place.
