synthesis.text: Read together, the fifteen programs agree on more than their marketing suggests. The five doctoral programs share a two- or three-discipline foundation: psychology for individual judgment, motivation and group behavior; sociology for networks, institutions and culture; and, at Wharton and Booth, economics for incentives and decisions. Every one of them front-loads research-methods training — Stanford’s micro track repeats an experimental-design course for three years, Booth requires both experimental and non-experimental methods, Wharton requires a research-design seminar and Kellogg examines two core methods courses after year one. The message is that behavioral knowledge is only as good as the evidence behind it.

The five MBA programs converge on a recognizable core: financial accounting and corporate finance, microeconomics, statistics or data analysis, strategy, operations, marketing, and leadership and organizational behavior. Several cores also reach beyond the classic functions. HBS now requires Data Science and AI for Leaders, Leadership and Corporate Accountability, and Purpose of the Firm; Stanford requires Ethics and practices leadership through simulations in Leadership Labs; Wharton puts legal studies and business ethics and a communication course in its core; MIT Sloan teaches organizations through strategic-design, political and cultural lenses; Booth’s single required course, LEAD, joins negotiation with interpersonal communication. Leadership, in other words, is taught as a skill that requires practice and feedback, and accountability and ethics are treated as core, not elective.

The JD/MBA programs add a layer of institutional literacy. Their law cores (contracts, torts, property, legislation and regulation, civil procedure, constitutional law) and professional-responsibility requirements teach how rules allocate risk and constrain organizations. Their distinctive features are integrative: Harvard’s joint seminar, Penn’s transaction capstone following one company from formation to restructuring, and the compressed three-year designs at Penn, Northwestern and Chicago, which force business foundations to be learned quickly and used at once.

APERTURE’s fourteen weeks reflect this shared structure. Weeks 1–4 correspond to the doctoral foundations: judgment and decision science (the Booth and Stanford micro model), motivation and social behavior, learning, and a research-literacy week built on the methods emphasis common to all five PhD programs. Weeks 5–8 correspond to the MBA leadership and organization cores, with negotiation placed in Week 7 as Booth, Stanford’s micro OB topics and the MIT negotiation course suggest. Weeks 9–10 correspond to the strategy and finance cores, Week 11 to the first-year law curriculum read for legal literacy, Weeks 12–13 to operations, governance and accountability, and Week 14 to the capstones and integrative experiences that HBS, Stanford, Penn and Harvard’s joint program use.

APERTURE also departs from these programs on purpose. It is a self-directed program for a single learner and grants no credit, degree or credential. It does not train researchers: it teaches the learner to judge evidence, not to produce publishable studies, so methods are compressed into one week and then applied throughout. It does not train lawyers: Week 11 aims at issue spotting and knowing when to call counsel, and it is labelled as general education, not legal advice. It replaces proprietary cases and course packs with original cases built on fictional organizations and synthetic data, and it links open resources rather than reproducing copyrighted materials. Finally, it grades the evidence behind every major claim and names replication failures, which program pages — written to describe programs, not to evaluate findings — do not do. The reference programs set the breadth; APERTURE’s own standards set the depth and the honesty of the evidence.

mapping.how: Booth’s decision-research focus and Stanford’s micro-OB topic of cognition and decision-making set the content (heuristics, calibration, base rates); the psychology-based micro track at Harvard reinforced starting with individual judgment; MIT’s Data, Models and Decisions informed the probability and decision-analysis framing; Booth’s behavioral-science faculty group informed the managerial angle.

The psychological foundations shared by the PhD programs (motivation, social influence, group behavior) and the economic foundations at Wharton (incentives) shaped a week that joins social psychology with incentive design; Stanford’s Organizational Behavior and Managing Groups and Teams courses informed the managerial application.

No reference program teaches learning science or motor learning directly; the week draws on the practice-and-feedback design of Stanford’s Leadership Labs and HBS’s LEAD and FIELD, and on the cognitive-psychology basis of Booth’s program, with Open Yale PSYC 110 as the open foundation. Most content rests on the research literature rather than program pages.

Every PhD program’s methods core (experimental and non-experimental design, research-design seminars, statistics sequences, Harvard’s research apprenticeship and field-research requirement) set the scope; MIT’s Data, Models and Decisions, HBS’s Data Science and AI for Leaders, Stanford’s data-analysis core and the Wharton and Booth statistics requirements set the executive level of the treatment.

Leadership cores (HBS LEAD, Stanford Leadership Foundations and Leadership Labs, Wharton Foundations of Teamwork and Leadership, Booth LEAD) and communication requirements (Wharton management communication, MIT Communication for Leaders) shaped the coaching, feedback and three-format writing work; Stanford’s micro-OB leadership topic informed the evidence review of leadership theories.

MIT’s political and cultural lenses and Booth’s Power and Influence course set the frame; the macro-OB and sociology tracks at Stanford, Harvard and Kellogg (networks, diffusion, institutions, culture) informed the network and legitimacy material.

Booth’s LEAD (negotiation with interpersonal communication) and Stanford’s micro-OB topic of negotiation and bargaining set the scope; Booth’s decision research informed anchoring and judgment in bargaining; the JD/MBA programs informed contractual commitments and principal-agent material; MIT OCW 15.667 is the open companion.

MIT’s strategic-design lens, HBS LEAD’s progression to organizational design, Wharton’s organization-theory and strategy-and-organization-design seminars and Kellogg’s complex-systems perspective informed structure, decision rights, coordination and systems thinking.

The MBA strategy cores (HBS Strategy, Stanford general management, strategy and non-market strategy, Booth’s strategy function) and Wharton’s doctoral strategy seminars (corporate, innovation, non-market) set the content; the economics-first foundations at Booth informed opportunity cost and trade-offs.

All five MBA cores require financial accounting and corporate finance (HBS Finance 1–2 and Financial Reporting and Control; Stanford finance and accounting; Wharton flexible core; MIT Financial Accounting and Managerial Finance option; Booth accounting foundation); the JD/MBA programs’ waivable finance and accounting cores informed the foundation-level entry point.

The first-year law cores (contracts, torts, legislation and regulation) set the legal-literacy scope; Penn’s transaction capstone informed reading provisions for business risk; Wharton’s legal-studies core supported teaching law to managers rather than lawyers.

Operations cores (HBS Technology and Operations Management, Stanford operations, Wharton operations options, Booth’s operations function) and Wharton’s technology-and-innovation strategy seminar informed implementation and technology adoption; Kellogg’s systems perspective informed feedback loops.

HBS’s Leadership and Corporate Accountability, Purpose of the Firm and Data Science and AI for Leaders, Stanford’s Ethics course, Wharton’s legal-studies and business-ethics requirement and the JD/MBA professional-responsibility requirements informed governance, accountability and data ethics; Stanford’s moral-judgment topic and Booth’s decision research informed ethical decision-making under uncertainty.

HBS’s FIELD Global Capstone, Stanford’s Executive Challenge, Penn’s JD/MBA Capstone, Harvard’s integrative joint seminar and MIT’s core team project informed an incremental, integrative capstone with a defended recommendation.

gaps.text: **Syllabi.** Public program pages describe structures, course titles and milestones, not syllabi, reading lists or weekly topics. No claim is made about what any course teaches week by week, and no course’s readings were used.

**Pages not opened.** Every statement rests on search-result excerpts from 2026-11-01. Several programs showed conflicting figures across handbook years (Wharton PhD unit counts, HLS/HBS pro bono hours, Northwestern law credits, Booth’s three-year eligibility, Stanford PhD field-exam timing); these are reported, not resolved.

**Incomplete course lists.** MIT Sloan’s full six-course core, Stanford GSB’s current numbered course list, Kellogg’s micro-track courses, Booth PhD proseminar topics and the course titles behind several Booth MBA category numbers could not be confirmed. Negotiation could not be confirmed as part of Wharton’s current MBA core.

**Thin coverage of learning science.** None of the reference programs teaches learning science, skill acquisition or motor learning as a core subject; Week 3 relies on the research literature rather than on program curricula.

**Open resources not yet confirmed.** The search budget ran out before OpenStax Business Law I Essentials, OpenStax Business Ethics, Open Yale ECON 159 Game Theory (only its title and address were seen), and MIT OpenCourseWare courses in behavioral economics and statistics could be verified. They are omitted rather than cited from memory and should be checked in a later session. The MIT OpenCourseWare collection of Sloan first-semester core materials was seen in search results but its publication details were not.

**Faculty publications.** The owner asked for faculty research to be considered; the audit did not attempt to characterize faculty publications at the program level, because doing so from search excerpts would risk misattribution. Faculty research enters APERTURE through the verified resource records of each week.

labs.name: Behavioral Decision Lab
labs.summary: Probability estimates, calibration, hypothetical outcomes and decisions under competing obligations.
labs.description: Practice the judgments that sit underneath every executive decision: how confident to be, how to weigh base rates against vivid stories, and how to act when obligations collide. Scores here are about calibration and reasoning, not about being right by luck.

labs.name: Negotiation Simulator
labs.summary: Multi-round, multi-issue bargaining against a rule-based counterpart with explicit assumptions.
labs.description: Negotiate packages across several issues against a counterpart whose behavior follows published rules. The debrief shows the value you created and claimed, the trades that mattered, and the deals you left on the table.

labs.name: Organizational Design Studio
labs.summary: Design incentives, practice systems, structures, stakeholder strategies and change sequences.
labs.description: Adjust responsibilities, reporting lines, staffing, incentives and budgets, and see which design risks each choice creates. Every effect is an ordinal teaching heuristic with its rationale and sources shown.

labs.name: Research Critique Lab
labs.summary: Simulate how sample size, selection, measurement and multiple testing distort what studies report.
labs.description: Run thousands of simulated studies to see sampling error, publication filters and undisclosed multiple testing at work, then apply the same skepticism to real research with the critique rubric.

labs.name: Financial Decision Studio
labs.summary: Budgets, discounted cash flows, capital rationing and strategic resource allocation.
labs.description: Compare investments by NPV, IRR, payback and profitability index under scenarios, find the opportunity cost of a portfolio, and test whether a resource allocation actually expresses a strategy.

labs.name: Executive Communication Studio
labs.summary: Difficult conversations, recommendations in three lengths, and decision presentations.
labs.description: Rehearse conversations where trust and clarity pull against each other, and draft recommendations against transparent text measures (length, speaking time, sentence load, hedging) and a self-check list. Content is never machine-graded.

labs.name: Contract Issue-Spotting Lab
labs.summary: Read fictional agreements clause by clause and flag commercial and legal risk.
labs.description: Practice legal-commercial reasoning on fictional documents: flag clauses, classify the risk, and compare your reading with an annotated key. Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice.

labs.name: Strategic Decision Journal
labs.summary: Structured records of consequential decisions, forecasts and later reviews.
labs.description: Record decisions before you know how they turn out: options, assumptions, what would change your mind and probability forecasts with resolve-by dates. Resolving forecasts later builds your personal calibration record.

library.title: First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus
library.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 657–669
library.license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 11642352); faculty listings at london.edu and kellogg.northwestern.edu agree. Findings below are taken from the PubMed abstract.

library.summary: Three experiments on buyer–seller price negotiations found that whichever side made the first offer, buyer or seller, obtained the better outcome, and that first offers strongly predicted final prices. The first-offer advantage disappeared when the recipient focused on information inconsistent with the offer: the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target. The effects appeared in face-to-face and e-mail negotiations.
arguments: A first offer works as an anchor: it pulls the final settlement toward itself.
Making the first offer advantaged the offerer regardless of role (buyer or seller).
Recipients can neutralize an anchor by deliberately focusing on the other side’s alternatives or reservation price, or on their own target.
library.design: Three laboratory experiments with simulated price negotiations, face-to-face and by e-mail.
library.strengths: Experimental control; tests both the effect and practical countermeasures; consistent with the broader, well-replicated anchoring literature.
library.limitations: Simulated single-issue price negotiations with student participants; modest stakes; does not test what happens when an anchor is so extreme that it ends the conversation, or when the offerer lacks information.
library.contested: The basic anchoring effect is among the more robust findings in judgment research, but the size of first-offer advantages in high-stakes field negotiations is less well established than the lab evidence; treat the countermeasure findings as promising rather than settled.
library.generalizability: Moderate to high for price-like issues where the value is uncertain (fees, salaries, budgets); lower when both sides have reliable market data.
library.relevance: Required reading. It turns the “should I go first?” question into a reasoned choice and gives you a tested defense when the other side anchors.

library.title: Value-based Business Strategy
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 5, issue 1, pages 5–24 and DOI matched on EconPapers (RePEc) and Scilit; the abstract’s main points (definition of value, added value, asymmetries, four value-based strategies, cooperative game theory) appeared in the same records.

library.summary: Brandenburger and Stuart define the value created in a vertical chain as buyers’ willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost, and a firm’s added value as the value lost if the firm were removed. Using cooperative game theory, they argue that added value limits how much value a firm can capture, and that positive added value requires asymmetries between a firm and its rivals. The analysis gives supplier and buyer relationships equal weight.
arguments: Value created equals willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost.
A firm’s added value caps the value it can capture.
Positive added value requires an asymmetry between the firm and its competitors.
Strategies can work on the supplier side as well as the buyer side.
library.design: Formal conceptual analysis based on cooperative game theory.
library.strengths: Precise definitions that separate value creation from value capture and make cooperation as analyzable as competition.
library.limitations: Abstract; real willingness-to-pay and opportunity-cost figures are hard to measure, and the bound on capture depends on modelling assumptions.
library.generalizability: Transfers well to procurement, hiring and partnership decisions in any sector, including the competition for players, coaches and analysts.
library.relevance: Gives you a rigorous way to ask “what do we add that others cannot?” before negotiating price, salary or partnership terms.

library.title: A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population
authors: et al. (Safe Surgery Saves Lives Study Group)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, first author, journal, volume, issue, pages, year (Epub 14 January 2009) and DOI matched on PubMed (PMID 19144931); sample sizes and headline rates matched in press summaries; a repository copy appeared on dash.harvard.edu. The full author list was not displayed in results, so only the first author and study group are recorded.

library.summary: A before-and-after study of a 19-item surgical safety checklist introduced in eight hospitals in eight cities with WHO collaboration. Comparing 3,733 patients before introduction with 3,955 after, the death rate fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%. The results helped make the checklist a global policy model.
arguments: A short, structured checklist used at defined points in an operation was followed by large reductions in deaths and complications.
Improvements appeared across hospitals in very different settings.
A simple process tool can change team behavior at critical moments.
library.design: Prospective before-and-after comparison in eight hospitals; no randomization and no concurrent control group.
library.strengths: Diverse international sites, large absolute changes and a simple, transferable intervention.
library.limitations: A before–after design cannot separate the checklist from secular trends, observation effects and the motivation of volunteer sites. Team training and attention that accompanied implementation are bundled with the tool.
library.contested: Ontario’s mandated, province-wide adoption found no significant reduction in mortality or complications (R-urbach-2014-introduction). The difference is usually discussed in terms of implementation, site selection and baseline risk.
library.generalizability: The tool travels easily; the effect appears to depend on how it is implemented. For organizations and sport, the transferable lesson concerns implementation conditions more than checklist content.
library.relevance: The classic evidence for checklists as decision hygiene and — read with the Ontario study — a lesson in why the same process tool can work in one setting and not another.

library.title: Comparing meta-analyses and preregistered multiple-laboratory replication projects
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Nature Human Behaviour (vol. 4), year and DOI matched on research.hhs.se and econpapers.repec.org; page range not confirmed (removed). Published online Dec 2019; an author correction exists (4(6), 2020).

library.summary: Compares meta-analyses with large preregistered multi-lab replications of the same psychological effects. Meta-analytic effect sizes were substantially larger, on average roughly three times the replication estimates, and bias-correction methods did not fully close the gap.
arguments: Meta-analyses of a biased literature inherit its bias.
Bias-adjustment methods help only partly.
Large preregistered replications are a better benchmark than meta-analyses of published studies.
library.design: Paired comparison of meta-analytic and multi-lab replication estimates for the same effects.
library.strengths: A direct test of meta-analysis against a strong benchmark.
library.limitations: Limited number of effect pairs; psychology only.
library.generalizability: Warns against treating any summary of published studies as the truth, in any field.
library.relevance: Why the top of the evidence pyramid can still be wrong.

library.title: Restatement of the Law Second, Contracts
library.publication: American Law Institute (reporters: Robert Braucher, to 1971; E. Allan Farnsworth, from 1971)
library.license: © The American Law Institute. Linked, not reproduced. Available in law libraries and legal research services.

verified.evidence: Title, publisher (American Law Institute), 1981 edition and reporters (Robert Braucher until 1971; E. Allan Farnsworth from 1971) matched on ali.org; the 1981 imprint is corroborated by Berkeley Law and Villanova Law library catalog records.

library.summary: The American Law Institute's synthesis of the U.S. common law of contracts, stated as black-letter rules with comments and illustrations. It covers formation, consideration and its substitutes, interpretation, conditions, performance and breach, and remedies. Courts frequently cite and adopt its sections, but it is a secondary authority that binds no court unless adopted.
arguments: Contract formation rests on mutual assent (offer and acceptance) and bargained-for consideration.
Some promises are enforceable without consideration because of reasonable reliance.
Interpretation seeks the parties' meaning in context, with tie-breaking principles for ambiguity.
Remedies protect the expectation, reliance or restitution interest, subject to limits such as foreseeability and mitigation.
library.design: Secondary legal authority: rules, comments and illustrations drafted by reporters and approved by the Institute, synthesizing U.S. case law.
library.strengths: The most widely cited single summary of mainstream U.S. contract doctrine; carefully organized and drafted.

Practice design should not rest on a single scheduling principle.

Estimates are pulled toward starting values, even arbitrary ones (anchoring).

Psychological safety is associated with learning behavior.
Learning behavior mediates part of the link to team performance.

Sign errors are possible when power is very low.
Design analysis should use realistic external effect-size assumptions.

library.summary: Argues that randomized trials are valuable but widely misunderstood. Randomization balances confounders only in expectation, estimates average effects that may hide heterogeneity, and says little by itself about whether a result will hold elsewhere.
arguments: A single trial does not guarantee balance in the sample actually drawn.
Average treatment effects can conceal people who are harmed.
Using a result elsewhere requires understanding why it worked.

library.title: How Much Does Industry Matter, Really?

library.summary: McGahan and Porter decompose the variance in business-unit profitability into year, industry, corporate-parent and business-specific effects. They report that industry effects account for roughly 19% of the variance and business-specific effects for roughly 32%, with smaller corporate-parent (about 4%) and year (about 2%) effects. Industry effects were smaller in manufacturing and larger in service sectors such as lodging and entertainment, wholesale and retail trade, and transportation.
arguments: Both industry and business-specific effects explain meaningful shares of profitability differences.
Business-specific effects are larger on average than industry effects.
The importance of industry varies by sector: lower in manufacturing, higher in several service sectors.
Corporate-parent and industry effects covary negatively across sectors.
library.design: Variance-components decomposition of business-unit profitability across U.S. industries.
library.strengths: Large-sample evidence on a question that strategy frameworks often answer by assertion; reports sector differences rather than a single number.
library.limitations: Descriptive, not causal; the business-specific share is partly a residual that includes luck and measurement differences; results depend on industry definitions, period and method.
library.contested: Other variance-decomposition studies report different splits between industry and firm effects depending on sample and method; resource-based scholars (R-barney-1991-firm) read the larger firm share as support for firm-level explanations, while positioning scholars stress the industry share.
library.generalizability: Concerns U.S. commercial business units; transfer to sports leagues or public organizations is by analogy only.
library.relevance: Shows how to weigh “where we compete” against “how well we compete” with evidence, and how to read a variance share without over-interpreting it.

library.summary: Compares the share of supported first hypotheses in a sample of standard psychology papers with a sample of Registered Reports, in which journals accept the study before results are known. Positive results were far rarer among Registered Reports.
arguments: About 96% of standard reports supported their first hypothesis, against about 44% of Registered Reports.
The gap is consistent with publication bias and flexible analysis in the standard literature.
Registered Reports are a practical structural remedy.
library.design: Comparison of two samples of published articles coded for hypothesis support.
library.strengths: Simple, transparent comparison with an informative contrast group.
library.limitations: Registered Reports may test different, riskier hypotheses; the comparison is not randomized.
library.generalizability: Supports pre-commitment devices for internal studies: decide what counts as success before the data arrive.
library.relevance: Shows what the literature looks like when results cannot shape publication.

library.title: Social Structure and Organizations

Citing sources locate the liability-of-newness argument at pp. 148–150. The URL is a library catalog record for the Handbook.

library.summary: Stinchcombe examines how a society’s social structure shapes the organizations founded in it. His best-known argument, the liability of newness, holds that a higher proportion of new organizations fail than old ones because they must invent and teach new roles, bear the costs of building routines, depend on cooperation among strangers and win clients away from established relationships.
arguments: New organizations must create roles and teach them to people who have not performed them.
Inventing roles and routines is costly in time, conflict and inefficiency.
New organizations depend on trust among strangers, which is thin.
They lack stable ties to the people they serve, who can stay with established providers.
library.design: Theoretical essay drawing on historical and sociological evidence.
library.strengths: Specifies mechanisms rather than only a correlation between age and failure, and launched decades of empirical research on organizational founding and mortality.
library.limitations: The mechanisms are argued rather than measured, and the claim concerns whole organizations rather than units inside them.
library.contested: Later work on organizational mortality found that failure risk does not always decline from founding; some populations show low early risk followed by a peak (the liability of adolescence; R-bruderl-1990-organizational).
library.generalizability: Transfers by analogy to new departments and functions inside organizations, where “death” takes the form of merger, starvation or neglect. That transfer is an inference, not a tested result.
library.relevance: The foundational account of why a newly created function is fragile for structural reasons — essential background for designing the capstone department’s first year.

library.title: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance: A Historical Review, a Meta-Analysis, and a Preliminary Feedback Intervention Theory
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: A historical review and meta-analysis of feedback interventions. Feedback improved performance on average, but a large share of interventions reduced performance. The authors propose feedback intervention theory: feedback works by directing attention, and it helps less, or harms, when it draws attention away from the task toward the self.
arguments: Feedback interventions have a positive average effect but highly variable results.
A substantial share of feedback interventions lowered performance.
Feedback that directs attention to the self (praise or criticism of the person) tends to weaken effects; feedback about the task and how to improve it tends to help.
library.design: Meta-analysis of feedback-intervention studies with a control condition, plus a theoretical synthesis.
library.strengths: Seminal; the variability finding has shaped feedback research for three decades.
library.limitations: Many included studies were laboratory tasks; workplace coaching conversations are richer than the interventions coded.
library.generalizability: The attention mechanism is plausible across settings; precise effect sizes should not be transferred to managerial conversations.
library.relevance: The strongest single correction to the belief that more feedback is always better.

library.title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, first author, journal, volume 25(5), pages 1106–1115 and DOI matched on psychologicalscience.org and escholarship.org (which hosts an open copy). library.summary: Reports the Good Judgment Project’s results in a government-sponsored (IARPA) geopolitical forecasting tournament. Training in probabilistic reasoning, working in teams, and tracking (placing top performers together) each improved accuracy, measured with Brier scores; combining them with statistical aggregation produced the best forecasts in both years reported.
arguments: Forecasting accuracy is measurable with proper scoring rules such as the Brier score, which reward calibration and discrimination.
Brief training in probabilistic reasoning improved accuracy.
Teams outperformed individuals, and top performers grouped together improved further.
Statistical aggregation of many forecasts added further accuracy.
library.design: Randomized assignment of volunteer forecasters to training and teaming conditions within a multi-year tournament.
library.strengths: Large, real questions with real resolution, randomized conditions, proper scoring.
library.limitations: Volunteer forecasters on geopolitical questions with months-long horizons; transfer to organizational decisions is plausible but not directly tested.
library.generalizability: Moderate to high for any repeated forecasting (injuries, development timelines, budgets), especially where outcomes resolve and can be scored.
library.relevance: The best evidence that judgment can be trained and measured, and the model for the forecasting fields in your decision journal.

library.title: Multitask Principal–Agent Analyses: Incentive Contracts, Asset Ownership, and Job Design

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: A foundational model of incentives when an agent divides effort among several tasks that differ in how well they can be measured. Strong incentives on the measurable task pull effort away from the hard-to-measure ones, so the optimal contract may use weak incentives, fixed pay, or a redesign of the job itself. The paper explains why many real jobs pay salaries rather than piece rates.
arguments: When tasks compete for the agent’s attention, incentive strength on one task must account for effort diverted from others.
If important tasks cannot be measured, low-powered incentives (salary) can be optimal.
Job design — grouping tasks by measurability — and ownership of assets are incentive instruments too.

library.limitations: A model, not an empirical test; assumes agents respond rationally to the contract and ignores intrinsic motivation and norms.
library.generalizability: High: the multitask logic applies to any role mixing measured output with unmeasured quality, cooperation or development.
library.relevance: The single most useful model for anyone who designs metrics for coaches, analysts or managers whose most important work is hard to count.

library.title: Curbing Optimism Bias and Strategic Misrepresentation in Planning: Reference Class Forecasting in Practice
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Describes reference-class forecasting — basing a project’s cost or demand forecast on the actual outcomes of a class of comparable past projects — and reports its first use in planning practice, for cost estimates of large UK transport investments (including the Edinburgh Tram and London’s Crossrail). Inaccurate forecasts are attributed to optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation, which the method is designed to sidestep.
arguments: Forecast errors in planning are large and systematic, not random, and stem from optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation.
Reference-class forecasting takes the outside view: identify a class of similar past projects, establish the distribution of outcomes, and position the new project within it.
The method can be institutionalized, but adoption faces political and organizational barriers.
library.design: Method description plus a practice case (UK transport cost forecasting); builds on the author’s earlier quantitative studies of cost overruns.
library.strengths: Concrete, implementable method grounded in Kahneman and Tversky’s outside view; documented use by a government.
library.limitations: Practice account rather than a controlled test of forecast accuracy; the choice of reference class is a judgment; the “strategic misrepresentation” explanation is disputed by other researchers.
library.contested: Love and Ahiaga-Dagbui (R-love-2018-debunking) dispute the deception-based explanation of cost underestimation and the methods behind it; Flyvbjerg has published a rebuttal.
library.generalizability: Most transferable where an organization has many comparable past projects (IT systems, facilities, hires); weaker for genuinely novel initiatives with no meaningful reference class.
library.relevance: Gives you a disciplined way to challenge a vendor’s or a colleague’s base case — and your own.

library.summary: In a series of forecasting experiments, people who saw an algorithm make errors became less willing to use it than a human forecaster, even when the algorithm outperformed the human.

People can choose a worse human forecast over a better model.
Adoption depends on perceived error, not only on accuracy.

library.strengths: Pre-specified comparisons with real performance incentives.

library.summary: Participants were considerably more willing to use an imperfect forecasting algorithm when they could adjust its output, even within narrow limits, and their resulting forecasts were better than unaided judgment.

Restricted adjustment keeps most of the model’s accuracy.
Designing for user agency is an adoption lever.

Treating national culture as uniform and causal ignores variation within countries and the influence of institutions, organizations and situations.

library.title: The Preregistration Revolution
library.publication: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(11), 2600–2606
library.summary: The authors distinguish prediction (testing a hypothesis specified in advance) from postdiction (explaining data already seen) and argue that preregistration makes the distinction visible, improving the credibility of confirmatory claims.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of studies relating amount of deliberate practice to performance across five domains. Practice explained about 26% of performance variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions. The authors conclude that deliberate practice is important but not as important as had been argued.

The share of performance differences it explains is modest and varies sharply by domain.
Other factors must account for most individual differences in performance, which calls for a multifactorial account of expertise.

library.relevance: The central counterweight to the belief that more hours reliably produce experts; essential for any talent or development investment.

library.relevance: A model of how a responsible field revisits its own foundations — and a reminder to check whether a famous finding has been replicated.

library.summary: Weiner defines organizational readiness for change as a shared psychological state with two parts: change commitment (members’ shared resolve to implement the change) and change efficacy (their shared belief in their collective capability to do so). library.design: Theoretical article synthesizing motivation and social-cognitive theory; proposes testable relationships.

library.generalizability: Developed with health-care organizations in mind but stated generally; plausible for any organization introducing new practices.
library.relevance: Gives you two separate things to diagnose before rollout—do people want this, and do they believe they can do it?—each with different remedies.

library.title: The Loser’s Curse: Decision Making and Market Efficiency in the National Football League Draft
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. A copy is listed in the University of Pennsylvania ScholarlyCommons repository (seen in search results, not opened). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, July 2013 date and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org and repository.upenn.edu; the method and main finding matched those records and a 2026 critique’s summary.

library.summary: Compares the market price of NFL draft picks — what teams give up in draft-day trades — with the surplus value the drafted players actually deliver (performance value minus compensation). Early picks are significantly overvalued: the very top picks yield less surplus on average than later first-round picks, a pattern the authors attribute to overconfidence and related judgment errors rather than efficient markets.
arguments: Draft-pick trade prices imply that early picks are worth far more than later ones.
Measured surplus value (performance value net of pay) does not decline nearly as steeply, so top picks are overpriced.
Persistent mispricing in a high-stakes, repeated market is consistent with behavioral explanations such as overconfidence rather than with efficient markets.
library.design: Archival analysis of draft-day trades, player performance and compensation data.
library.strengths: Large, repeated, high-stakes market; clear economic benchmark (surplus value).
library.limitations: Performance value must be estimated; conclusions depend on assuming teams should maximize expected surplus.
library.contested: Brill and Wyner (R-brill-2026-losers) argue the overvaluation conclusion depends on the assumed objective; if a team prioritizes landing an elite player, high picks may be rational.
library.generalizability: Transfers to any market where organizations bid for scarce talent with noisy evaluations (hiring, acquisitions, drafts); the precise pricing pattern is sport-specific.
library.relevance: Shows how to value talent as surplus over cost — the right unit for budget decisions in player development and beyond.

library.title: Effects of Devil’s Advocacy and Dialectical Inquiry on Decision Making: A Meta-Analysis
library.publication: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 47(1), 161–176
library.summary: A meta-analysis of studies comparing structured dissent methods with expert-recommendation approaches, finding that devil’s advocacy and dialectical inquiry were associated with better decisions than an uncritical expert approach.
arguments: Structured critique improves decision quality relative to accepting an expert recommendation.
Different dissent techniques have broadly similar benefits.
Critique must be institutionalized to matter.
library.design: Meta-analysis of experimental studies, mostly laboratory.
library.strengths: Quantitative synthesis across studies.
library.limitations: Older literature dominated by lab tasks; small number of studies.
library.generalizability: Moderate: supports building a red-team step into your written defense.
library.relevance: Justifies writing the strongest case against your own plan before the president does.

library.title: Intrinsic Motivation and Extrinsic Incentives Jointly Predict Performance: A 40-Year Meta-Analysis
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 24491020); abstract findings (k = 183, N = 212,468; ρ = .21–.45; salience moderation) matched in indexed abstracts.

library.summary: A meta-analysis across school, work and physical domains asking whether intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives compete or work together in predicting performance. Intrinsic motivation was a medium-to-strong predictor of performance and stayed predictive when incentives were present. How tightly incentives were tied to performance mattered: intrinsic motivation was less important to performance when incentives were directly tied to it, and more important when incentives were indirect.
arguments: Intrinsic motivation predicts performance (ρ = .21–.45 across 183 samples, N = 212,468).
Incentives and intrinsic motivation are not simply opposed; both predict performance.
Incentive salience moderates the relation: directly performance-contingent incentives reduce the predictive importance of intrinsic motivation.
The authors report that intrinsic motivation relates more to the quality of performance and incentives more to its quantity.
library.design: Meta-analysis of 183 independent samples (N = 212,468) from school, work and physical domains spanning about forty years.
library.strengths: Broad, field-heavy synthesis that measures performance, not only free-choice play; tests moderators relevant to managers.
library.limitations: Much of the evidence is correlational, so intrinsic motivation and performance may share causes; heterogeneity across domains is large. The quality-versus-quantity pattern is reported by the authors but should be checked in the full text before relying on specific variance figures.
library.contested: Partly reconciles the Deci–Cameron debate rather than settling it; see R-deci-1999-meta.
library.generalizability: Good for organizational settings, which make up a large part of the sample; sport-specific evidence is thinner.
library.relevance: Replaces the slogan “money kills motivation” with a design question: which part of the work should carry a direct incentive, and which part depends on people caring?

library.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Fines Wells Fargo $100 Million for Widespread Illegal Practice of Secretly Opening Unauthorized Accounts
library.publication: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, press release (September 8, 2016)
library.license: U.S. federal government publication. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Headline and the official consumerfinance.gov newsroom URL matched in search results, with the CFPB enforcement action page (wells-fargo-bank-2016); September 8, 2016 date matched in contemporaneous coverage.

library.summary: The federal regulator’s announcement of its enforcement action against Wells Fargo Bank. The bureau stated that bank employees, working under sales targets and incentive-compensation programs, had opened deposit and credit-card accounts without customers’ knowledge or consent, and it imposed a $100 million penalty alongside a consent order requiring remediation.
arguments: Regulators linked unauthorized account openings to sales goals and incentive compensation.
The consent order required refunds to customers and changes to sales practices.
The case became a reference example of metric gaming at scale inside a large organization.
library.strengths: Primary regulatory source; establishes what a public authority found and ordered.
library.limitations: A press release summarizes a consent order; it does not establish the internal decision processes in detail, and the bank’s own account and later investigations add context not covered here.
library.generalizability: High as an illustration of how volume targets plus weak monitoring produce gaming; it is one organization and should not be over-generalized.
library.relevance: A concrete, documented example of what happens when an organization rewards counted outputs it cannot verify.

library.title: A Critical Assessment of Charismatic—Transformational Leadership Research: Back to the Drawing Board?
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. An author copy appears on a University of Colorado faculty page.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 7 issue 1, pages 1–60 and DOI matched on scholars.duke.edu and econbiz.de; abstract content matched in the same results; an author PDF is listed on leeds-faculty.colorado.edu.

library.summary: A critical review concluding that charismatic–transformational leadership research rests on unclear definitions, underspecified causal models, constructs confounded with their effects, and measurement tools that do not reproduce the theorized structure. The authors recommend abandoning the umbrella construct and studying more precisely defined leader behaviors.
arguments: The construct lacks a clear conceptual definition.
Causal models linking it to outcomes are underspecified.
Measures are confounded with effects: items partly describe outcomes rather than behaviors.
Dominant questionnaires do not show the dimensional structure the theory claims.
library.strengths: Systematic, methodologically focused critique by established leadership scholars in a top review outlet.
library.limitations: A critique, not new data; some scholars defend the construct’s usefulness, and practice has not followed the recommendation.
library.contested: Contrasts with the positive meta-analytic validities in R-judge-2004-transformational; the disagreement is about what those correlations mean.
library.generalizability: The measurement lessons apply to any rating-based evaluation of leaders, including staff and coach evaluations in sport.
library.relevance: Teaches you to ask what a leadership score actually measures before you use it to hire, develop or judge people.

library.title: Timid Choices and Bold Forecasts: A Cognitive Perspective on Risk Taking
library.summary: Managers evaluate projects one at a time from the inside view and therefore produce optimistic forecasts, while also being too risk-averse in isolated choices. Taking the outside view, a reference class of similar projects, corrects the forecasts.
arguments: Inside-view forecasts neglect the distribution of outcomes for similar projects.
Isolated decisions encourage excessive caution; aggregated decisions reduce it.
Reference-class (outside-view) forecasting improves planning.
library.design: Conceptual synthesis of behavioral decision research applied to organizations.
library.strengths: Actionable remedy (the outside view) grounded in a large body of judgment research.
library.limitations: Synthesis rather than a new test; size of correction varies by domain.
library.generalizability: High for budgets and timelines of new departments and technology projects.
library.relevance: Your first-year timeline and benefits estimates will be inside-view forecasts unless you build a reference class.

library.title: Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to Disagree
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, both authors, journal, volume 64(6), pages 515–526 and DOI 10.1037/a0016755 matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 19739881) and bibbase.org.

library.summary: A joint paper by the leading figure of the heuristics-and-biases program and the leading figure of naturalistic decision making. They set out where they agree: intuitive judgment can be trusted only when the environment is regular enough to be predictable and the person has had an adequate opportunity to learn its regularities through practice and feedback.
arguments: Skilled intuition is recognition: patterns stored through long experience in a valid environment.
Two conditions are necessary for genuine intuitive expertise: a high-validity environment and an adequate opportunity to learn it (practice with timely, clear feedback).
Subjective confidence is not a reliable indicator of the accuracy of an intuitive judgment.
Where these conditions fail, experts can be fluent, confident and wrong; where they hold, intuition can outperform deliberate analysis.
library.design: Integrative theoretical review written by two researchers from opposing traditions.
library.strengths: Rare adversarial collaboration; gives executives a usable test for when to trust expert intuition.
library.limitations: Conceptual rather than empirical; ‘validity of the environment’ is easier to name than to measure in practice.
library.contested: Klein has written that the authors disagreed often and the subtitle understates that; the shared criteria themselves are widely accepted.
library.generalizability: High. The criteria apply to any field in which people make repeated judgments — medicine, finance, scouting, hiring.
library.relevance: The single most useful test for deciding when to defer to an experienced evaluator’s intuition and when to demand structure.

library.title: Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, three authors, publisher (Little, Brown Spark) and May 2021 publication matched on hachettebookgroup.com and multiple library catalogs.

library.summary: Argues that unwanted variability in judgments that should be identical — noise — is as damaging as bias and far less noticed. The authors describe noise audits, distinguish types of noise, and propose ‘decision hygiene’: procedures that reduce error without needing to know its direction.
arguments: Error has two components, bias and noise; noise can be measured without knowing the right answer.
System noise divides into level noise (some judges are harsher), pattern noise (judges react differently to particular cases) and occasion noise (the same judge varies over time).
Decision hygiene — independent judgments, aggregation, structuring complex judgments into separate assessments, sequencing information, relative scales and the outside view — reduces noise.
Simple rules and models are often less noisy than human judges, though they can embed bias.
library.design: Book-length synthesis of research and organizational case material.
library.strengths: Brings a neglected problem to executives with practical procedures.
library.limitations: Popular book; some reviewers argue it understates the value of variability (innovation, diversity of view) and the costs of standardization.
library.contested: Whether reducing judgment variability is always desirable is debated; the existence of large noise in professional judgment is well documented.
library.generalizability: High for repeated professional judgments: evaluations, grading, underwriting, triage, scouting reports.
library.relevance: The source of the noise audit and decision-hygiene practices you will apply to evaluation systems.

library.title: Comment on “Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science”
library.license: © AAAS. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Science 351(6277) 1037, year and DOI matched on pubpeer.com and a Science PDF copy (errorstatistics.com).

library.summary: A technical comment arguing that the Open Science Collaboration’s design could not support its pessimistic conclusion, because of sampling error, differences between original and replication studies, and low power of single replications.
arguments: Even perfect replications will fail some of the time because of sampling error.
Several replications departed from the original populations or procedures.
The data are consistent with a more optimistic reading.
library.design: Reanalysis and critique of a published replication project.
library.strengths: Forces precision about what a single failed replication does and does not show.
library.limitations: Itself disputed by the OSC authors and others; does not provide new replication data.
library.contested: Answered in the same issue by the original authors; most methodologists accept that the replication rate was low even if its exact value is uncertain (R-osc-2015-estimating).
library.generalizability: A reminder that replication failures also have to be interpreted with power and fidelity in mind.
library.relevance: Shows that the replication debate is itself an evidence debate, not a morality play.

library.title: The Manager as Negotiator: Bargaining for Cooperation and Competitive Gain
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, publisher (Free Press) and year (c1986) matched in the CiNii catalogue (ci.nii.ac.jp) and on the publisher’s site (simonandschuster.co.uk, Free Press is a Simon & Schuster imprint); Chapter 2, “The Negotiator’s Dilemma: Creating and Claiming Value”, pp. 29–45, matched in University at Buffalo course reading guides (acsu.buffalo.edu).

library.summary: Treats managers as negotiators inside and outside their organizations and builds “negotiation analysis” from case work, decision analysis, game theory and psychology. Its best-known idea is the negotiator’s dilemma: the moves that create value (sharing information, joint problem solving) leave you exposed to the moves that claim it (withholding information, committing to favorable terms), and the two activities cannot be separated.
arguments: Creating value and claiming value are inextricably linked; advice that addresses only one of them is incomplete.
Sharing information about priorities makes joint gains possible but can be exploited by a counterpart who claims aggressively.
Managers negotiate constantly with colleagues and constituencies, not only with outside parties.
library.design: Analytic book built on extensive case analysis plus decision analysis, game theory and psychology.
library.strengths: Holds the cooperative and competitive sides of bargaining in one frame; written for managers; widely adopted in graduate teaching.
library.limitations: Conceptual rather than empirical; the dilemma is a framework, not a measured effect.
library.generalizability: High: the creating–claiming tension appears in vendor deals, internal budget talks, employment negotiations and partnerships.
library.relevance: Required reading (Chapter 2). It names the tension you will feel in the Negotiation Chamber: every question you answer about your priorities helps the deal and helps the other side.

library.title: Evaluating Effect Size in Psychological Research: Sense and Nonsense
library.publication: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 2(2), 156–168
library.license: Open access (license not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, AMPPS 2(2) 156–168, year and DOI matched on psychologicalscience.org; a 2020 corrigendum (10.1177/2515245920979282) also exists.

library.summary: Argues that conventional labels for effect sizes (small, medium, large) are uninformative and that effects should be judged against benchmarks and consequences. Small effects can matter when they accumulate over many occasions or people; very large effects in small studies are probably overestimates.
arguments: Report and interpret effect sizes in context, with confidence intervals.
Small effects can be consequential in the long run or at scale.
Implausibly large effects from small samples should be distrusted.
library.strengths: Practical, balanced guidance.
library.limitations: Offers judgment criteria rather than a rule; benchmark choice remains subjective.
library.generalizability: Directly applicable to judging internal metrics and vendor claims.
library.relevance: Teaches how to ask “is this big enough to matter?”.

library.title: Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, AER 84(4) 772–793, year matched on econpapers.repec.org; NBER w4509 page seen on nber.org. No journal DOI confirmed.

library.summary: Compares fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage in 1992, with neighboring eastern Pennsylvania, which did not, before and after the increase. Finds no reduction in employment in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania.
arguments: A neighboring comparison region can stand in for the counterfactual trend.
The difference-in-differences estimate showed no employment loss.
The result challenged the textbook competitive prediction.
library.design: Difference-in-differences using telephone surveys of fast-food restaurants before and after the policy change.
library.strengths: Transparent design; a natural experiment on a contested policy.
library.limitations: Survey measurement error; a single state pair; short horizon.
library.contested: Neumark and Wascher (2000) found employment declines using payroll records; Card and Krueger replied with other data (R-neumark-2000-minimum). The wider minimum-wage literature remains debated.
library.generalizability: A canonical example of how a comparison group can be both persuasive and attackable.
library.relevance: The case study for difference-in-differences and for how expert disagreement works.

library.title: Flawed Self-Assessment: Implications for Health, Education, and the Workplace
library.publication: Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 5(3), 69–106
library.summary: A review showing that people’s self-assessments of skill and knowledge correlate only modestly with objective performance, with consequences in health, education and work, and suggesting remedies such as external feedback.
arguments: Self-assessments are only modestly accurate.
People often lack the information needed to judge their own competence.
Structured external feedback improves self-knowledge.
library.design: Narrative review of research on self-assessment.
library.strengths: Broad, policy-oriented synthesis.
library.limitations: Some patterns attributed to self-insight may partly reflect statistical artifacts.
library.generalizability: High for a self-assessed capstone rubric.
library.relevance: The reason your capstone self-assessment must be anchored to evidence and outside readers.

library.title: The Mythical Number Two
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, both authors, journal, volume 22(4), pages 280–293 and DOI 10.1016/j.tics.2018.02.001 matched on the Yale ACME lab publications page and library catalog records (katalog.lib.cas.cz).

library.summary: A critique of the idea that mental processes divide into two types. The authors argue that the attributes said to define each type — such as unintentional, uncontrollable, efficient and unconscious versus their opposites — do not reliably travel together, and that the two-type framing has slowed scientific progress.
arguments: The features attributed to ‘Type 1’ and ‘Type 2’ processes are frequently misaligned in actual mental processes.
If the features do not cluster, the two-type taxonomy lacks empirical support and can be internally incoherent.
Researchers should study the specific features of processes rather than sorting processes into two bins.
library.design: Critical theoretical review.
library.strengths: Forces precision; shows how a popular metaphor can outrun its evidence.
library.limitations: Critics replied in the same journal that showing misaligned features does not refute versions of the theory that never claimed alignment.
library.contested: Opposes Evans & Stanovich (2013, R-evans-2013-dual-process); the debate is live.
library.generalizability: Applies to how leaders use psychological frameworks: a vivid metaphor is not a mechanism.
library.relevance: A model of intellectual humility about a framework that has become management common sense.

library.title: Dynamic Capabilities and Strategic Management
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 18, issue 7, pages 509–533 (August 1997) matched on RePEc/IDEAS and EconPapers; the DOI appeared in full in a reference list and garbled on RePEc (an angle-bracket rendering problem). The definition of dynamic capabilities (p. 516) was confirmed from search-result excerpts.

library.summary: Teece, Pisano and Shuen propose the dynamic capabilities framework: a firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments. They argue that competitive advantage rests on the firm’s organizational and managerial processes, shaped by its asset positions and by the paths available to it.
arguments: In fast-changing markets, the ability to reconfigure competences matters more than any fixed resource.
Advantage depends on processes, positions and paths.
Capabilities are path-dependent: what a firm can do next depends on what it has learned.
Many valuable capabilities cannot be bought; they must be built.
library.design: Conceptual framework contrasting dynamic capabilities with other approaches to strategy.
library.strengths: Extends the resource-based view to changing environments and explains why organizational learning and reconfiguration matter.
library.limitations: Concepts are broad and hard to measure; there is a risk of identifying dynamic capabilities by the successful adaptation they are meant to explain.
library.contested: Shares the tautology concern raised against the resource-based view (R-priem-2001-is) when capabilities are inferred from outcomes.
library.generalizability: Useful for any organization facing technological change, including healthcare systems and sports organizations adopting new measurement technology.
library.relevance: Shifts attention from owning the best tools to being able to rebuild routines as tools and markets change.

library.title: Informal Networks: The Company Behind the Chart
library.license: © Harvard Business School Publishing. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, the July–August 1993 issue of Harvard Business Review and pages 104–111 matched in several search results (bookshare.org, a university executive-education reading list, a Sage reprint page in an edited volume); the hbr.org page did not appear in results, so the Sage reprint page is linked.

library.summary: Krackhardt and Hanson argue that much of an organization’s real work runs through informal networks that the formal chart does not show, and that managers can map them with simple questionnaires. They distinguish advice networks (who depends on whom for technical help), trust networks (who shares sensitive information) and communication networks (who talks about work regularly), and describe recurring problem patterns such as a single person bridging otherwise separate groups.
arguments: The formal chart shows authority; informal networks show how work, advice and trust actually flow.
Advice, trust and communication networks differ and answer different managerial questions.
Network maps can be drawn from short surveys and cross-checked against managers’ assumptions.
Structural patterns — isolated groups, gaps, over-reliance on one connector — signal predictable problems.
library.design: Practitioner article drawing on the authors’ network consulting and research; illustrative cases.
library.strengths: Translates social network analysis into a usable managerial diagnostic; clear distinction among types of ties.
library.limitations: Case illustrations rather than systematic evidence; network surveys raise confidentiality and ethical concerns that the article treats briefly.
library.generalizability: Applies to any organization with interdependent work; the network types are general.
library.relevance: The practical bridge from network theory to the Influence Map you will build this week.

library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, AER 90(5) 1362–1396, year and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org (aea:aecrev).

library.summary: Re-estimates the New Jersey minimum-wage effect using payroll records collected from restaurants rather than telephone survey responses, and finds employment declines in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania.
arguments: Measurement of the outcome can reverse a conclusion.
Payroll data show a negative employment effect.
Survey data used in the original contained substantial noise.
library.design: Difference-in-differences with an alternative payroll dataset.
library.strengths: Directly tests the sensitivity of a famous result to measurement.
library.limitations: Data collection and sample construction were themselves criticized.
library.contested: Card and Krueger’s reply in the same issue used other administrative data and found small or no effects (R-card-1994-minimum).

library.relevance: The other side of the Lesson 3 debate.

library.title: Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, first author, journal, volume, issue, pages, publication date (13 March 2014) and DOI matched on PubMed (PMID 24620866); design, sample size (about 200,000 procedures) and mortality rates matched in the abstract as reported by medical news summaries. Co-authors were not displayed in results and are not recorded.

library.summary: A population-based study of roughly 200,000 surgical procedures at virtually all hospitals providing surgery in Ontario, comparing three-month periods before and after each hospital adopted a surgical safety checklist under a provincial requirement. Operative mortality was 0.71% before and 0.65% after, a non-significant difference, and complications did not fall significantly.
arguments: Mandated adoption of surgical safety checklists across a province was not associated with significant reductions in operative mortality or complications.
Results from enthusiastic early-adopter settings may not reproduce under policy-driven rollout.
Safety gains may depend on how teams use a tool more than on the tool itself.
library.design: Population-based before-and-after comparison of three-month periods around each hospital’s adoption under a provincial policy.
library.strengths: Very large, population-wide sample that reduces volunteer-site selection and measures the effect of policy as actually implemented.
library.limitations: Short comparison windows and a low baseline mortality rate limit the ability to detect small changes; outcome data alone cannot show how thoroughly teams used the checklist.
library.contested: Contrasts with the large improvements in the WHO study (R-haynes-2009-surgical); interpretations emphasize mandated versus engaged adoption, differences in baseline risk and the limits of before–after designs on both sides.
library.generalizability: Highly relevant to any organization that scales a process tool by mandate after a successful pilot, including sport organizations rolling out protocols across affiliates.
library.relevance: The counterweight to the checklist success story: a direct lesson in external validity and implementation for anyone who will turn a pilot into an organization-wide policy.

library.title: Principles of Management
library.license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike license, as stated on openstax.org pages (version not shown in the search results). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors (David S. Bright, Anastasia H. Cortes), publisher (OpenStax) and publication date (March 20, 2019) matched on openstax.org details, preface and chapter pages; license wording (CC BY-NC-SA) matched on openstax.org chapter pages.

library.summary: An openly licensed introductory management textbook with chapters written by subject specialists. It is a survey text suited to building vocabulary before graduate readings.
arguments: Management can be organized around planning, organizing, leading and controlling, while recognizing that real managerial work is less tidy than that frame.
Structure, strategy and culture interact; changing one without the others tends to fail.
Decision-making in organizations is bounded by information, time and cognitive limits.

library.relevance: An open alternative to proprietary MBA-core management texts; it backs the foundation-mode prerequisites in the business school weeks.

library.title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
library.license: Open access (license not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: A preregistered randomized trial of a short online growth-mindset intervention in a nationally representative sample of U.S. ninth-grade students. arguments: A brief intervention produced small average improvements in grades among lower-achieving students.
Effects depended on school context.
Preregistration and independent data processing constrained analytic flexibility.

library.relevance: Assignment option (education / learning).

library.title: Is There Such a Thing as “Evidence-Based Management”?
library.summary: Rousseau’s presidential address argues that managers rarely use the best available research and proposes evidence-based management: translating research principles into practice and combining them with local data and judgment.
arguments: Management practice lags research.
Evidence-based practice combines research, local data, professional judgment and stakeholder values.
Organizations need structures that make evidence use routine.
library.design: Conceptual essay (presidential address).
library.strengths: Defines the agenda for evidence-based management.

library.title: The Trouble with Overconfidence
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, both authors, journal, volume 115(2), pages 502–517 and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 18426301); an author copy is hosted on asc.ohio-state.edu.

library.summary: Distinguishes three meanings of overconfidence — overestimation of one’s performance, overplacement relative to others, and overprecision in one’s beliefs — and offers a Bayesian account of when each appears. Overprecision is the most persistent.
arguments: Overestimation, overplacement and overprecision are different phenomena and should not be lumped together.
On hard tasks people tend to overestimate their own performance but believe they are worse than others; on easy tasks the pattern reverses.
Overprecision — intervals that are too narrow — is the most durable form.
library.design: Theory plus a laboratory experiment varying task difficulty.
library.strengths: Resolves apparent contradictions in the literature with a clear model; widely used taxonomy.
library.limitations: Laboratory trivia-style tasks; field magnitudes vary.
library.generalizability: High for overprecision: budgets, timelines and projections routinely carry intervals that are too narrow.
library.relevance: Gives you precise language for the confidence problems you will diagnose in yourself and your staff.

library.title: Why Strategy Execution Unravels—and What to Do About It

library.summary: Drawing on a multi-year survey program of managers in several hundred companies, the authors argue that strategy execution rarely fails for the reasons executives assume. Adherence to the original plan matters less than the organization’s ability to reallocate people and money as conditions change.

Execution depends heavily on distributed middle-manager judgment, not only on top-down control.

library.relevance: Gives you a vocabulary for diagnosing why a well-chosen initiative stalls—especially the gap between vertical alignment and cross-functional coordination that dominates most implementation work.

library.summary: Campbell argues that the more a quantitative indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the process it was meant to monitor. The paper is the source of what is now called Campbell’s law.
arguments: Indicators used for high-stakes decisions invite gaming and distortion.
Multiple indicators and qualitative evidence reduce, but do not remove, the problem.
Evaluation design should anticipate how measured people will respond.

library.strengths: Foundational statement of indicator corruption; pairs with Goodhart’s law.
library.limitations: Conceptual; the size of distortion varies by setting and is not estimated.
library.generalizability: High for any KPI system tied to resources or reputation.
library.relevance: Guards against designing KPIs that your own staff or partner departments will learn to game.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

Verbal rewards (positive feedback) tend to enhance intrinsic motivation, especially for adults.
Whether a reward is felt as controlling or as informational is the moderating mechanism.
The paper rebuts an earlier meta-analysis (Cameron & Pierce, 1994) that reached a more benign conclusion.

library.strengths: Large, systematic synthesis; separates reward types and contingencies rather than asking whether “rewards” in general help or hurt.
library.limitations: Mostly short laboratory sessions with tasks chosen to be interesting; the outcome is minutes of free-choice play, not job performance. Generalization to paid work, where pay is expected and necessary, is indirect.
library.contested: Cameron, Pierce and colleagues disputed the coding and conclusions in a published exchange; the undermining effect’s size and scope in workplaces remains debated. Compare R-cerasoli-2014-intrinsic, which finds intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance.
library.generalizability: Moderate for leaders: the mechanism (controlling vs. informational rewards) transfers well; the effect size from lab play sessions should not be imported into compensation design.
library.relevance: The core evidence behind “rewards can backfire” — and the conditions that claim needs. Essential before designing recognition or bonus systems for people who already care about their craft.

Reciprocity helps enforce contracts and norms that cannot be written down fully.
Cooperation in groups tends to decay without the possibility of punishing free riders and can be sustained with it.
Explicit incentives perceived as hostile or distrustful can reduce reciprocal effort.
library.design: Review of laboratory and some field experiments.
library.strengths: Clear, influential, grounded in incentivized experiments.
library.limitations: Mostly laboratory games with modest stakes; the share of reciprocal types varies by population and setting.
library.contested: Field gift-exchange effects are often smaller or fade over time compared with laboratory results.
library.generalizability: Good for understanding norms, fairness and cooperation in teams; magnitudes from games should not be transferred directly.
library.relevance: Explains why fairness and perceived intent can matter as much as the size of a reward — and why a team can tolerate one free rider but not five.

library.title: Noncompete Agreements in the US Labor Force

library.summary: Uses a nationally representative survey of 11,505 U.S. labor force participants to describe who signs non-competes, when and on what terms. Non-competes appear in low-wage as well as high-wage jobs and in states that do not enforce them; few workers negotiate, and many learn of the clause after accepting an offer.
arguments: Roughly 18 percent of labor force participants were bound by a non-compete; 38 percent had signed one at some point.
Non-competes are more common in high-skill, high-pay jobs but also appear in low-wage jobs and in non-enforcing states.
Only about 10 percent of workers report negotiating over the non-compete; about one-third are presented with it after accepting the offer.
Workers told early about a non-compete fare better than those told late; wages are relatively lower where non-competes are easier to enforce.
library.design: Nationally representative cross-sectional survey of 11,505 labor force participants, with comparisons across state enforceability regimes.
library.strengths: The first large representative evidence on non-compete prevalence and process; published in a leading law-and-economics journal.
library.limitations: Self-reported survey data; associations between enforceability and outcomes are observational and could reflect other state differences. An earlier working-paper version reported different prevalence figures, so cite the published article.
library.contested: Whether non-competes mainly protect investment (training, trade secrets) or mainly suppress mobility and wages remains debated; see the quasi-experimental evidence in R-marx-2009-mobility.
library.generalizability: Describes the U.S. labor force broadly; sector-specific patterns (including sports organizations) are not separately reported.
library.relevance: Grounds the restrictive-covenant lesson in data and shows how often a "standard" clause is imposed rather than negotiated.

Tex., Judge Ada Brown) matched in multiple law-firm reports; the FTC's 3–1 vote on September 5, 2025 to dismiss its appeals and accede to vacatur matched on ftc.gov (the linked press release). Removal of the rule from the Code of Federal Regulations by Federal Register document 2026-02866 (91 FR 6507, published February 12, 2026) appeared on an ftc.gov public-comments page and Federal Register mirrors, not on federalregister.gov itself, so that detail is partially confirmed.
