library.summary: The FTC's 2024 final rule treated most worker non-competes as an unfair method of competition under Section 5 of the FTC Act and, with exceptions, would have barred employers from entering into or enforcing them, while allowing existing non-competes with senior executives to remain in force. A federal district court set the rule aside on August 20, 2024, before its September 4, 2024 effective date; on September 5, 2025 the Commission voted 3–1 to dismiss its appeals and accede to vacatur, and in February 2026 the rule's text was removed from the Code of Federal Regulations. The FTC has said it will pursue non-competes case by case under Section 5; state law continues to govern enforceability.
arguments: The FTC framed non-competes as an unfair method of competition harmful to workers and competition.
The district court held that the FTC lacked statutory authority to issue the rule and that the rule was arbitrary and capricious, and gave its order nationwide effect.
After abandoning the rule, the FTC said it would rely on individual enforcement actions rather than a categorical ban.
library.design: Federal agency final rule and its subsequent litigation history.
library.strengths: Primary source for the federal policy debate; the rulemaking record collected extensive argument and evidence on non-competes.
library.limitations: The rule never took effect; its record reflects the agency's position, and the court that set it aside ruled on authority and process, not on the economic merits. Status details after September 2025 come partly from secondary reports.
library.contested: The economic case against non-competes in the rulemaking is contested by those who argue non-competes protect investment; see R-starr-2021-noncompete and R-marx-2009-mobility for the evidence.
library.generalizability: U.S. federal context only; actual enforceability depends on state law and, outside the U.S., on national law.
library.relevance: A current, concrete example of how legal rules change, get challenged and depend on institutional authority — essential context before relying on anything said about non-competes.

Unstructured interviews are weaker than structured ones.

library.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 48(6), 1467–1478
library.summary: In the hidden-profile paradigm, groups discussed information that all members already shared far more than information held by only one member, and so often missed the best option.

Unique information held by one member is often never surfaced.
Meeting structure, not only member quality, determines what a group knows.

library.relevance: The first step in building your risk register.

library.title: Consequences of Influence Tactics Used with Subordinates, Peers, and the Boss

library.summary: Yukl and Tracey examined how the influence tactics managers use relate to the task commitment of the people they try to influence — subordinates, peers and bosses — and to ratings of the managers’ effectiveness. Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation were the tactics most associated with commitment; pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics were the least effective. Ingratiation and exchange were moderately effective with subordinates and peers but not with superiors.
arguments: Influence tactics differ in how likely they are to produce commitment rather than compliance or resistance.
Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation are most associated with commitment.
Pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics are least associated with commitment.
The direction of influence matters: some tactics work downward or laterally but not upward.
library.design: Field questionnaire study in which targets (subordinates, peers, bosses) described managers’ influence behavior and their own commitment; correlational.
library.strengths: Uses target reports rather than only agents’ self-reports; covers all three directions of influence; built on a validated taxonomy of tactics.
library.limitations: Cross-sectional and correlational; tactic choice is endogenous (people use pressure when they already expect resistance); common-method concerns.
library.generalizability: Reasonable for Western organizational settings; tactic effectiveness may differ across cultures and relationships.
library.relevance: Evidence-based guidance on influencing your peers and your boss, not only your staff.

library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Shows that people solve Bayesian problems far more often when information is presented as natural frequencies (counts of cases) than as probabilities and percentages. The authors argue that whether people ‘can’ reason in a Bayesian way depends on the format of the information.
arguments: Bayesian computation is simpler with natural frequencies than with probabilities.
With frequency formats, statistically naive participants reached Bayesian answers in up to about half of inferences, far more than with probability formats.
Claims about cognitive limits must specify the information format.

library.relevance: The practical fix for base-rate neglect in your own reports: count people, not percentages.

library.summary: A review of the ecological-rationality program. Heuristics are treated not as errors but as strategies that ignore part of the information, and the central question becomes in which environments a given heuristic does well. Under uncertainty, simple rules can match or beat complex models.

A heuristic is ecologically rational to the degree that it is adapted to the structure of an environment.
Less information and computation can produce more accurate predictions when uncertainty is high and samples are small (a less-is-more effect, explained by the bias–variance trade-off).

library.generalizability: High for decisions with small samples and unstable environments — common in talent evaluation and strategy.
library.relevance: Balances the bias literature: some simple rules are good management, not lazy thinking.

library.summary: Mintzberg synthesizes research on structure into a typology. Organizations have five basic parts, coordinate through five mechanisms, and tend to cluster into five configurations—simple structure, machine bureaucracy, professional bureaucracy, divisionalized form and adhocracy—each dominated by one mechanism and one part of the organization.
arguments: Five coordinating mechanisms: direct supervision, standardization of work processes, of outputs and of skills, and mutual adjustment.
Structural elements cluster into internally consistent configurations rather than varying independently.
Each configuration is pulled by a different part of the organization and suits different conditions.
library.design: Conceptual synthesis of prior empirical and theoretical research on organization design.
library.strengths: Memorable, comprehensive and still widely used in teaching; forces a diagnosis of which coordinating mechanism is actually doing the work.
library.limitations: Configurations are ideal types; most real organizations are hybrids. The synthesis predates digital coordination tools, platform organizations and remote work.
library.generalizability: Useful across sectors as a diagnostic vocabulary; weaker as a prescription, because hybrids are the norm.
library.relevance: Helps you see why a department of trained professionals resists process scripts, and when standardization is the right answer.

library.title: Of Strategies, Deliberate and Emergent
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 6, issue 3 and pages 257–272 matched on RePEc/IDEAS and EconPapers. The DOI was seen on the publisher’s download stamp of a copy in search results, not on the Wiley landing page.

library.summary: Mintzberg and Waters distinguish intended strategies (what leaders plan) from realized strategies (the patterns that actually appear in an organization’s actions). Deliberate and emergent strategies are two ends of a continuum along which real strategies lie, and the authors describe intermediate types such as planned, entrepreneurial, ideological, umbrella, process, unconnected, consensus and imposed strategies.
arguments: Strategy can be a pattern in a stream of actions, not only a plan.
Intended strategies may be realized (deliberate) or unrealized; emergent strategies are realized patterns that were never intended.
Purely deliberate and purely emergent strategies are rare; most lie between them.
Emergent strategy allows organizational learning; deliberate strategy provides direction and control.
library.design: Conceptual paper proposing a continuum and a typology of strategies.
library.strengths: Changes how you read an organization: look at what it does and funds, not only at what it says. Widely used and conceptually durable.
library.limitations: A typology rather than a tested theory; classifying a strategy as emergent or deliberate is often done after the fact.
library.contested: Stands in a long-running debate with design and positioning views of strategy (e.g. R-porter-1996-what) about how much strategy should be planned; the debate concerns emphasis, not replication.
library.generalizability: Applies to any organization; especially useful where front-line staff make many decisions that add up to a strategy, as in hospitals, consulting firms and player development.
library.relevance: Supports the week’s central practical point: an organization’s real strategy is visible in its resource allocation.

library.title: Cultural differences in ultimatum game experiments: Evidence from a meta-analysis
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on cambridge.org, econpapers.repec.org and the Tinbergen Institute site (tinbergen.nl). A free working-paper version (EconWPA, January 2004, ewp-exp/0401003) appeared in search results. Findings below come from the abstract.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of 37 papers reporting 75 ultimatum-game results. Proposers offered on average about 40 percent of the pie. Responder behavior, not proposer behavior, varied across regions; rejection rates were lower for larger pies and larger offered shares, and responders were less willing to accept under the strategy method. With one exception, regional differences could not be explained by standard cultural classifications (Hofstede, Inglehart).
arguments: People routinely offer far more than the “rational” minimum in the ultimatum game, and responders reject offers they see as unfair.
Variation across regions shows up mainly in what responders accept.
Popular national-culture scores explain little of that variation, a caution against stereotyping by country.
library.design: Meta-analysis of 75 results from 37 ultimatum-game papers, regressing offers and rejections on study features and regional/cultural indicators.
library.strengths: Pools many experiments; tests cultural explanations explicitly rather than assuming them.
library.limitations: Stylized one-shot game with mostly student samples; regional coding is coarse; small stakes in many studies.
library.contested: Whether ultimatum-game behavior reflects stable fairness preferences or context-specific norms is debated; this meta-analysis cautions against simple national-culture explanations.
library.generalizability: Moderate: the core lesson (offers perceived as unfair get rejected even at a cost) travels well; specific percentages do not transfer to complex deals.
library.relevance: Shows why fairness is a constraint you must design for in any deal, and why “they will accept anything above their alternative” is poor executive reasoning.

library.title: The Art and Science of Negotiation
library.publication: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, year (1982), publisher (Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA), x + 373 pages and ISBN 0674048121 matched in the CiNii catalogue (ci.nii.ac.jp) and the Weber State University library catalogue; the book’s structure (two-party single-issue bargaining, two-party multi-issue bargaining, many-party negotiations; Panama Canal and Camp David cases) matched in catalogue and bookseller descriptions. A 1985 paperback exists.

library.summary: A decision analyst’s treatment of negotiation that moves from two parties bargaining over one issue, to two parties with many issues, to negotiations among many parties. It combines analytic models with cases such as the Panama Canal and Camp David negotiations, and is widely described as a bridge between popular negotiation advice and formal game theory.
arguments: Negotiation can be analyzed systematically: each party’s alternatives and reservation values define whether a zone of agreement exists.
Multi-issue bargaining differs in kind from single-issue haggling because parties can trade across issues they value differently.
Negotiations with many parties introduce coalitions and dynamics that two-party models do not capture.
library.design: Analytic monograph combining formal models with historical cases.
library.strengths: Rigor; separates what a single negotiator can calculate from what depends on the other side; a foundation for later analytic approaches to negotiation.
library.limitations: Written before most of the behavioral research on negotiator bias; some formal material is demanding; historical cases are illustrations, not tests.
library.generalizability: The analytic structure (alternatives, reservation values, multi-issue trades, coalitions) transfers to any deal; the behavioral assumptions should be checked against later research.
library.relevance: The analytic backbone for lessons 1 and 2: it teaches you to treat a negotiation as a structured decision rather than a contest of personalities.

library.title: Leading Teams: Setting the Stage for Great Performances
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (Harvard Business School Press) and 2002 date matched on library catalog records (bemis.marmot.org; openlibrary.telkomuniversity.ac.id) and bookseller listings with ISBN 9781578513338. The publisher’s own page was not seen.

library.summary: Hackman argues that a leader’s main contribution to team performance is not personal style but the design of conditions that let a team manage itself. He identifies five conditions: a real team, a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive organizational context and expert coaching. The book draws on decades of research on work teams and is written for practitioners.
arguments: Team effectiveness depends more on conditions the leader designs than on the leader’s interpersonal style.
Five conditions: a real team, compelling direction, enabling structure, supportive organizational context and expert coaching.
The conditions are guiding principles to be applied to each situation, not a fixed formula.
library.design: Book-length synthesis of the author’s and others’ research on work teams, written for practitioners.
library.strengths: Grounded in long-term field research; actionable diagnostic framework; shifts attention from charisma to design.
library.limitations: Practitioner-oriented book rather than a peer-reviewed test; the conditions are not presented as separately estimated causal effects; some recommendations (such as stable membership) conflict with project-based organizations.
library.generalizability: Broad across work teams in business, health care, government and sport; how much each condition matters varies by setting.
library.relevance: A practical checklist for designing the cross-disciplinary groups that surround players, projects or patients.

library.title: Organizational Behavior
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 per the openstax.org details page (some chapter pages in search results showed a plain Creative Commons Attribution notice; the details page is treated as authoritative). OpenStax also states the book may not be used to train large language models without permission. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors (J. Stewart Black, David S. Bright), publisher (OpenStax) and publication date (June 5, 2019) matched on openstax.org; license (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) matched on the openstax.org details page, with conflicting notices on some chapter pages.

library.summary: An openly licensed organizational behavior textbook covering individual differences, perception, motivation, groups and teams, communication, power and politics, leadership, organizational structure, culture and change. Each chapter includes key terms and critical-thinking cases.
arguments: Behavior in organizations is shaped by individual, group and organizational-level factors at once.
Motivation, power and culture are levers managers can study systematically rather than treat as intuition.
Organizational change requires attention to resistance and to the informal system, not only formal structure.
library.strengths: Free, complete OB survey from established authors; maps closely onto MBA leadership and organizational behavior cores.
library.limitations: Survey level; does not consistently report effect sizes or replication status, so popular ideas sit next to well-replicated findings.
library.generalizability: Broad; supports Weeks 2, 5, 6 and 8 as an open reference, with APERTURE adding evidence-strength labels.
library.relevance: An open counterpart to the organizational behavior and leadership core courses that every MBA reference program requires.

library.title: Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results from the Women’s Health Initiative randomized controlled trial
authors: Writing Group for the Women’s Health Initiative Investigators
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, JAMA 288(3) 321–333, year and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 12117397).

library.summary: Reports the principal results of a large randomized trial of combined hormone therapy. The trial was stopped early because overall risks, including increased coronary heart disease and breast cancer, exceeded benefits — contrary to the cardiovascular protection suggested by earlier observational studies.
arguments: Randomized evidence contradicted a widely accepted observational finding.
The earlier observational association was plausibly driven by healthier women choosing therapy.
library.design: Multicenter randomized, placebo-controlled trial in postmenopausal women.
library.strengths: Large, randomized, clinically decisive.
library.limitations: Later analyses debated whether timing of initiation explains differences from observational data.
library.contested: Subsequent work on the timing hypothesis argues effects differ by age at initiation; the confounding lesson stands.
library.generalizability: A canonical warning about healthy-user selection in any observational comparison.
library.relevance: The cleanest real example of confounding reversing a conclusion.

library.title: An Economic Evaluation of the Moneyball Hypothesis
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 20, issue 3, pages 173–186 and DOI matched on EconPapers (RePEc) and EconBiz; findings (data 1999–2004; on-base percentage undervalued before the book; undervaluation diminished after publication) matched in multiple summaries. The American Economic Association distributes JEP articles free online; one search summary described the article as paywalled, so access should be checked when the link is first opened.

library.summary: Hakes and Sauer test Michael Lewis’s claim that baseball’s labor market mispriced certain skills. Using standard econometric methods on player productivity and compensation data from 1999 to 2004, they find that a hitter’s on-base percentage was undervalued relative to its contribution to winning before the book appeared, and that the undervaluation diminished after its publication.
arguments: Market inefficiencies in a professional labor market can be measured with standard econometric tools.
On-base skill was undervalued relative to its contribution to winning before the book was published.
The mispricing narrowed after the idea became public, consistent with arbitrage eroding the edge.
library.design: Regression analysis of team winning and player salaries using major-league data, 1999–2004.
library.strengths: Clear, testable question; transparent methods; one of the few empirical tests of a famous business story; a later honors thesis reported replicating the main regressions.
library.limitations: Observational, short post-publication window, and sensitive to model specification; publication of the book is one of several possible channels for the correction.
library.contested: The paper prompted public debate, including the argument that the featured club’s success owed more to pitching than to on-base skill. A 2020 University of Vermont honors thesis reported reproducing the regressions and cross-validating them with an agent-based model (not in the library).
library.generalizability: The mechanism — information-based edges eroding once visible — generalizes well to finance, retail and talent markets; the specific estimates apply to that period of the baseball labor market only.
library.relevance: Directly relevant evidence on how quickly an analytical edge in a sports labor market can be competed away, and why advantage must be renewed.

library.title: The Romance of Leadership
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, year, volume 30 issue 1, pages 78–102 and DOI 10.2307/2392813 matched on scilit.com; volume and pages matched in later citations (Durham repository memorial piece, Collinson et al. 2007). An erratum is indexed at ASQ 30(2), p. 294 (JSTOR record via katalog.lib.cas.cz).

library.summary: Meindl and colleagues argue that people hold a romanticized view of leadership: they explain organizational outcomes by pointing to leaders, and they do so more strongly when outcomes are extreme. The paper reports several studies, consistent with that attributional bias. It reframes part of “leadership” as something observers construct after the fact.
arguments: Observers over-attribute organizational performance to leaders relative to other causes.
The tendency strengthens when outcomes are unusually good or unusually bad.
Leadership is partly a perception held by followers and observers, not only a property of the leader.
library.design: A set of empirical studies (a secondary description counts five); design details were not confirmed in search results.
library.strengths: Seminal, widely cited, and opens a falsifiable alternative explanation for why leaders receive credit and blame.
library.limitations: Older studies; shows that attributions are inflated, not that leaders have no effect.
library.contested: Not a replication controversy; the debate is about how large real leader effects are relative to attributions. Read alongside R-vanknippenberg-2013-critical, which argues that outcome-contaminated perceptions also distort leadership measures.
library.generalizability: High for any field where outcomes are noisy and visible (sports, markets, hospitals, politics). Treat as a strong caution, not a precise estimate.
library.relevance: Every evaluation of a manager, coach or executive in a high-variance environment is exposed to this bias, including your own reputation.

library.title: Selling Issues to Top Management
library.license: © Academy of Management. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 18, issue 3 (July 1993), pages 397–428 and DOI 10.5465/AMR.1993.9309035145 matched on bibbase.org and searchworks; JSTOR identifier 10.2307/258903 also reported.

library.summary: Dutton and Ashford argue that middle managers shape what top management pays attention to by “selling” issues — calling attention to trends, events and problems and framing them. They develop a framework drawing on three perspectives: issue selling as upward influence, as claiming behavior (asserting that an issue deserves attention), and as impression management, since sellers risk their image. The framework explains when managers will try to sell an issue and how the way they package it and the process they use affects success.
arguments: Top management’s agenda is shaped from below by the issues middle managers choose to raise.
Whether managers try to sell an issue depends on perceived chances of success and on image risk.
Success depends on how an issue is packaged (framing, bundling) and on the selling process (timing, channels, involvement of others).
Issue selling is a political act and an impression-management act at once.
library.design: Theoretical framework with propositions; later tested in field studies by the authors and colleagues.
library.strengths: Puts middle managers at the center of strategic change; generated a substantial empirical literature.
library.limitations: Propositions rather than tests; draws on U.S. corporate settings.
library.generalizability: Applies to anyone who needs senior attention for an issue they do not own — in firms, agencies, hospitals or sports organizations.
library.relevance: The core theory of managing upward when you want leaders to care about your issue.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 17, issue 1, pages 99–120, publisher (SAGE) and DOI matched on BibBase, Scilit and CiNii; abstract content (value, rareness, imitability, substitutability) confirmed in the same records.

library.title: Firm Resources and Sustained Competitive Advantage
library.summary: The foundational statement of the resource-based view: sustained advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable and non-substitutable. Socially complex and path-dependent resources are hardest to copy.
arguments: Advantage that rivals can buy or copy does not last.
Socially complex capabilities, such as trust between groups, are hard to imitate.
Strategy should build on resources that pass the value, rarity, imitability and substitutability tests.
library.design: Theoretical article.
library.strengths: Clear test for whether an investment can create lasting advantage.
library.limitations: Hard to measure resources ex ante; critics call parts of the logic tautological.
library.generalizability: High: data and software are increasingly buyable; relationships with coaches are not.
library.relevance: Helps you decide what your department should build itself versus buy or borrow.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal (Interfaces, INFORMS), volume 4, issue 3, pages 28–36, May 1974 and DOI matched on RePEc (econpapers.repec.org, ideas.repec.org) and scilit.com.

library.title: Organization Design: An Information Processing View
library.summary: Galbraith treats organizational design as a problem of information processing: the more uncertain the task, the more information must flow during execution. Organizations either reduce the need for information (slack, self-contained units) or increase capacity to process it (vertical information systems, lateral relations such as liaison roles and integrators).
arguments: Task uncertainty drives the information-processing load a structure must carry.
Rules, hierarchy and goals handle routine coordination; exceptions overload them.
Design options either reduce information needs or increase processing capacity, and each has costs.
library.design: Conceptual framework built from organizational case experience.
library.strengths: Gives a concrete menu of coordination mechanisms and the logic for choosing among them.
library.limitations: Pre-dates modern information technology and networked organizations; not a tested predictive model.
library.generalizability: High for coordination-heavy units such as a department that links scouting, analytics, coaching and the front office.
library.relevance: A strategic coordination department is, by definition, a lateral information-processing mechanism; this explains when it is worth its cost.

library.title: The External Control of Organizations: A Resource Dependence Perspective
library.publication: Original edition 1978; reissued as a Stanford Business Classic by Stanford University Press, 2003 (with a new preface by Pfeffer)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors and the 2003 Stanford University Press reissue (Stanford Business Classics, new preface by Pfeffer) matched on gsb.stanford.edu and sup.org; a 1978 original date appeared in a listing but the original publisher was not confirmed in search results, so it is not named here.

library.summary: Pfeffer and Salancik argue that organizations are best understood through their dependence on external actors who control resources they need. Because dependence creates the possibility of external control, much of what organizations do — co-opting outsiders onto boards, forming alliances, merging, diversifying suppliers — can be read as attempts to manage dependence. The same logic, building on power-dependence theory in sociology, explains power inside organizations: units that supply what others critically need, and cannot easily get elsewhere, gain influence.
arguments: An organization’s dependence on another actor grows with the importance of the resource, the other actor’s discretion over it, and the scarcity of alternatives.
Dependence creates the possibility of external control; organizations respond by managing or restructuring their dependencies.
Common responses include co-optation, alliances, mergers and diversification of resource sources.
Power is relational and situational: it shifts when critical contingencies shift.
library.design: Theoretical book synthesizing prior empirical work; tested extensively by later studies.
library.strengths: One of the foundational theories of organizations; turns power from a personality trait into a structural relation that can be mapped and changed.
library.limitations: Explains why actors gain influence better than how they use it; later reviews note that the theory was often invoked as a metaphor rather than tested directly.
library.contested: Broadly accepted as a perspective; individual predictions (for example about mergers or board co-optation) have mixed support. Institutional theory (R-dimaggio-1983-iron) offers a competing explanation of the same organizational behavior.
library.generalizability: High for any organization that depends on outside resources — public agencies, hospitals, firms and sports organizations alike.
library.relevance: The clearest way to answer “who actually has leverage here, and why?” before you try to change anything.

library.title: Managing with Power: Politics and Influence in Organizations
library.publication: Boston: Harvard Business School Press (hardcover 1992; paperback 1994)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (Harvard Business School Press) and 1992 hardcover date matched in the publisher-derived copyright page on an O’Reilly listing and in library catalogs (NYPL, folio.caval.edu.au); Google Books listing found.

library.summary: A book for managers arguing that getting things done in organizations requires understanding and using power, and that discomfort with power leads capable people to fail at implementation. Pfeffer synthesizes research on the sources of power, including structural position and control of resources, together with extended organizational examples, and discusses the strategies and tactics through which power is used.
arguments: Implementation problems are largely problems of influence: mobilizing support and overcoming resistance.
Power comes substantially from structural position, control of resources and information, and alliances, not only from personal attributes.
Timing, framing and the management of interpersonal relations are tools for using power.
Managers who avoid power out of discomfort tend to lose to those who do not.
library.design: Practitioner synthesis by an organizational scholar; illustrative cases and narrative review, not a new empirical test.
library.strengths: Grounded in the author’s own academic research tradition; unsentimental about how organizations work; useful catalog of sources and tactics.
library.limitations: Case-based illustration is vulnerable to selection (vivid successes are chosen); prescriptive claims are not tested as such; limited treatment of the costs of political behavior for trust and for others.
library.contested: The normative stance — that managers should actively build and use power — is contested on ethical and practical grounds; see the influence ethics discussion and R-yukl-1992-consequences on which tactics build commitment.
library.generalizability: Written about large U.S. organizations; the structural insights transfer widely, the tactical advice depends on culture and context.
library.relevance: A deliberately uncomfortable counterweight to the belief that good analysis will be adopted on its merits.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, OBHDP 151 90–103, year and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org and escholarship.org.

library.title: Algorithm Appreciation: People Prefer Algorithmic to Human Judgment
library.publication: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 151, 90–103
library.summary: Across several experiments, lay participants weighted advice more when it was described as coming from an algorithm than from a person; experienced professionals in one study discounted algorithmic advice, to their cost.
arguments: Algorithm aversion is not universal; appreciation is common among lay people.
Expertise can reduce willingness to use algorithmic advice.
Whether people trust models depends on context and on who is judging.
library.design: Series of advice-taking experiments with lay and professional samples.
library.strengths: Challenges a popular generalization with multiple studies.
library.limitations: Advice-taking tasks are simpler than operational use; professional sample was small and specific.
library.contested: Read with R-dietvorst-2015-algorithm: the two lines of work differ on whether errors have been observed and on who the users are.
library.generalizability: Moderate: the expert-discounting finding is the more relevant one for veteran coaches.
library.relevance: Prevents you from assuming coaches will either reject or embrace models by default.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Psychological Bulletin 125(2) 255–275 and year matched on journal indexes (acnpsearch, scienceopen.com); the DOI did not appear in two searches and was removed. URL is the DOI link from the original record and is unconfirmed.

library.title: Accounting for the Effects of Accountability
library.summary: A review showing that accountability improves judgment only under specific conditions: when people expect to justify themselves before they decide, to an audience whose views are unknown, who cares about accuracy and process. Otherwise it produces conformity or defensive bolstering.
arguments: Pre-decisional accountability to an unknown audience promotes careful, self-critical thinking.
Accountability to a known audience promotes telling it what it wants.
Post-decisional accountability promotes defensive justification.
library.design: Narrative review of experimental research.
library.strengths: Specifies conditions rather than treating accountability as uniformly good.
library.limitations: Mostly laboratory evidence.
library.generalizability: Moderate to high for how you prepare and how you run reviews of your staff.
library.relevance: Explains why writing your defense before you know the president’s view makes the plan better.

library.title: A meta-analysis on gender differences in negotiation outcomes and their moderators
library.license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, all six authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on the University of Münster research portal (cris-portal.uni-muenster.de); scope (51 studies, 10,888 participants, several countries) and the moderator findings matched in the APA press release (apa.org, December 2014). Published online November 2014, in the 2015 volume.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of 51 studies (10,888 participants, several countries) comparing the economic outcomes women and men obtain in negotiations. The difference favoring men depended heavily on context: women did better when negotiating on behalf of another person, when they had information about the bargaining range, and when they had negotiation experience. The pattern points to situational rather than fixed-trait explanations, and the authors highlight ways the difference can be lessened or reversed.
arguments: Gender differences in negotiated economic outcomes are context-dependent rather than fixed.
Advocating for someone else, experience, and information about the bargaining range were associated with smaller differences, and in some conditions with women doing better.
Reducing ambiguity about what is negotiable and what the range is can shrink gaps.
library.design: Meta-analysis of 51 studies reporting final economic negotiation outcomes by gender, with moderator analyses; extends an earlier meta-analysis by Stuhlmacher and colleagues.
library.strengths: Large pooled sample across countries; moderator analyses directly useful for organizational design.
library.limitations: Mostly laboratory and classroom negotiations; moderator effects are correlational across studies; gender is measured as a binary category; economic outcomes only (not relationships or subjective value).
library.contested: Popular claims that women “don’t negotiate” or are uniformly worse negotiators are not supported by this evidence, which shows strong situational moderation; the size of field gaps in real compensation negotiations remains debated.
library.generalizability: Moderate: the moderators (advocacy role, information, experience) are plausible levers in organizations, but effect sizes from lab studies should not be transferred to field settings without caution.
library.relevance: Teaches you to read a meta-analysis on a sensitive topic carefully, and points to design choices you control: publishing ranges, clarifying what is negotiable, and how you structure compensation conversations for your staff.

library.title: Contextual Interference Effects on the Acquisition, Retention, and Transfer of a Motor Skill
library.publication: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 5(2), 179–187
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on the swov.nl library record and a scan of the original article; design and findings matched in later reviews indexed on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov. The DOI was not shown in results and is omitted.

library.summary: The experiment that launched contextual-interference research. Participants learned three movement patterns (knocking down barriers in set sequences) either in blocks or in a random order. Blocked practice produced better performance during acquisition, but random practice produced better retention, especially when retention was tested in a random order, and better transfer, especially to the most complex transfer task.
arguments: Practicing several skills in a random order makes practice harder and in-session performance worse.
The same random schedule produced better retention and transfer than blocked practice.
The best acquisition schedule and the best learning schedule can be opposites.
library.design: Laboratory experiment: blocked versus random practice of three barrier knock-down movement patterns; retention after 10 minutes or 10 days under blocked and random test orders; transfer tasks of differing complexity.
library.strengths: Elegant design separating acquisition, retention and transfer; launched a large literature.
library.limitations: Simple laboratory movements, university participants, short training; whether the effect holds for complex sport skills in real practice is a separate question.
library.contested: The laboratory effect is well reproduced; applied-setting effects are smaller and contested (R-czyz-2024-effect, R-ammar-2023-myth).
library.generalizability: Strong as a demonstration of the learning–performance distinction in motor skills; modest and uncertain as a prescription for sport practice.
library.relevance: The classic you will see cited to justify random practice; knowing exactly what it did and did not test protects you from over-reading it.

library.title: Little’s Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Fifty years after his 1961 proof that the long-run average number of items in a queuing system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system (L = λW), Little reviews how the result has been extended and used, with emphasis on practice in operations management and computing, and proves versions of the law for finite observation periods.
arguments: L = λW holds under very general conditions for long-run averages, without assumptions about arrival or service distributions.
In practice it links work-in-process, throughput and cycle time: knowing two gives the third.
Finite-period versions matter for managers, who observe real systems over limited windows.
library.design: Review and mathematical exposition, with proofs of finite-period versions.
library.strengths: Authoritative account by the law’s originator; bridges theory and practical use.
library.limitations: Mathematical; the law describes averages and says nothing by itself about variability or causes.
library.generalizability: Applies to any flow of work—patients, cases, tickets, contracts, player evaluations—when measured consistently over a stable period.
library.relevance: The single most useful equation for reasoning about backlogs and lead times in any operation you run.

library.title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
library.publication: Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on scholars.duke.edu (Duke Scholars record) and fds.duke.edu; the utility ratings matched in the eurekalert.org press release and a texasldcenter.org summary.

library.summary: A long monograph that reviews ten techniques students use to learn and gives each an overall utility rating. Practice testing and distributed practice are rated high; interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation are rated moderate; summarization, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic, imagery for text and rereading are rated low. The striking pattern is that the most popular techniques, rereading and highlighting, are among the weakest.
arguments: Practice testing (retrieving information rather than reviewing it) and distributed practice (spacing study over time) have the broadest support of the ten techniques.
Interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation and self-explanation are promising but rest on a narrower evidence base, so they receive a moderate rating.
Rereading and highlighting feel productive but show low utility for durable learning.
library.design: Narrative review of experimental and applied research on ten learning techniques, each given an overall utility rating (high, moderate or low).
library.strengths: Broad, carefully reasoned synthesis by leading cognitive and educational psychologists; explicit about the limits of each technique’s evidence; widely used as a reference in education.
library.limitations: Ratings are expert judgments rather than pooled effect sizes. The review concerns academic learning (text, facts, concepts, problem solving), not motor skills or workplace performance.
library.contested: The high ratings for testing and spacing are among the most robust conclusions in applied cognitive psychology. Interleaving’s moderate rating reflects a thinner evidence base at the time; how far these principles transfer to motor skills is a separate question (see R-czyz-2024-effect, R-ammar-2023-myth).
library.generalizability: High confidence for learning facts, concepts and procedures that must be recalled later, including professional knowledge (rules, protocols, playbooks). Use caution when extending the ratings to motor skills without motor-learning evidence.
library.relevance: Gives you a defensible evidence ranking for the learning methods your staff and players already use, and a vocabulary for retiring the weakest ones.

library.title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
library.license: Open access under the journal’s Creative Commons license (license version not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, PLoS Medicine 2(8) e124, year and DOI matched on doaj.org and econpapers.repec.org.

library.summary: An essay with a simple model: the probability that a statistically significant finding is true depends on the prior odds that tested hypotheses are true, statistical power, and bias. Under realistic values in many fields, most claimed findings would be false.
arguments: Small studies, small effects, many tested relationships and flexible designs lower the chance a finding is true.
Financial interest and “hot” fields with many competing teams make it worse.
Significance alone says little; the prior and the power matter.
library.design: Analytic model of positive predictive value with illustrative scenarios.
library.strengths: Makes the base-rate logic of research explicit.
library.limitations: The title’s claim depends on assumed inputs; critics argue empirical false-discovery rates in some fields are lower.
library.contested: Some statisticians estimated lower false-discovery rates in medical literatures; the logical argument about priors and power is widely accepted.
library.generalizability: Directly applies to a portfolio of internal experiments: if most ideas tested are long shots, most “wins” are noise.
library.relevance: Connects Week 1 base rates to the reliability of research and analytics.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, HBR volume 73(2), March–April 1995 and pages 59–67 matched on psnet.ahrq.gov and sebokwiki.org (reprint 95204). The hbr.org URL follows HBR’s article path but could not be checked; the date in that path may differ from the print issue.

library.title: Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail
library.summary: Kotter’s eight-step model of organizational change (urgency, guiding coalition, vision, communication, empowerment, short-term wins, consolidation, anchoring in culture), drawn from his consulting observations.
arguments: Change efforts fail through predictable errors such as low urgency and declaring victory too soon.
Sequence matters.
Short-term wins sustain support.
library.design: Practitioner synthesis of observed change efforts; not a controlled study.
library.strengths: Memorable, widely used vocabulary.
library.limitations: A practitioner heuristic with limited direct empirical testing; linear sequence fits messy change poorly.
library.contested: Treat as heuristic; see the broader empirical review in R-oreg-2011-change.
library.generalizability: Useful as a checklist; weak as evidence.
library.relevance: You will be expected to know it, and to know its limits.

library.title: The Theory and Practice of Corporate Finance: Evidence from the Field
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on ideas.repec.org, econpapers.repec.org and scholars.duke.edu; the 392-CFO sample and the main findings matched the abstract shown there.

library.summary: A survey of 392 chief financial officers about how their firms set the cost of capital, choose investments and decide on financing. Large firms relied heavily on present-value techniques and the capital asset pricing model; smaller firms were relatively more likely to use the payback criterion; and a surprising number of firms evaluated new projects with a company-wide rather than a project-specific risk adjustment.
arguments: Present-value methods dominate capital budgeting in large firms, while payback remains common, especially in smaller firms.
Many firms apply a single firm-wide discount rate rather than one matched to each project’s risk.
Financing decisions are shaped by practical concerns such as financial flexibility, credit ratings and dilution more than by several textbook theories.
library.design: Survey of 392 CFOs on cost of capital, capital budgeting and capital structure.
library.strengths: Large practitioner sample; links textbook theory to reported practice; widely cited benchmark.
library.limitations: Self-reported methods, not observed decisions; respondents may report what they believe they should do; data are now more than two decades old.
library.generalizability: Describes for-profit corporate practice; departments inside sports clubs, hospitals or agencies often use simpler rules, which makes the gap between theory and practice even more relevant.
library.relevance: Shows how real executives use NPV, IRR and payback — and the common error of using one discount rate for every project — so you can anticipate how a finance office will read your proposal.

library.title: The Bases of Social Power
library.publication: In D. Cartwright (Ed.), Studies in Social Power (pp. 150–167). Ann Arbor: Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, editor, volume title, 1959 date, Ann Arbor publication and pages 150–167 matched on the Institute for Social Research site (cdn.isr.umich.edu), which hosts a digitized copy of the chapter and of the full volume; bibbase.org lists the same pages. Sources disagree on whether the publisher is styled the University of Michigan Press; the ISR copy was followed.

library.summary: French and Raven proposed that the power one person holds over another rests on a small number of distinct bases: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert power. Each base is defined from the perspective of the person being influenced: power exists because the target believes the agent can reward, punish, rightfully direct, serve as a model of identification, or knows more. The chapter is a theoretical typology, not an empirical study.
arguments: Power is a relation between an agent and a target, located in the target’s perceptions, not a possession of the agent alone.
Five bases are distinguished: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert.
Different bases have different side effects; coercion, for example, requires surveillance and tends to reduce attraction to the agent.
The range of a base differs: expert power, for instance, is limited to the domain in which the agent is seen as knowledgeable.
library.design: Conceptual typology drawing on the authors’ field theory tradition; no new data.
library.strengths: Simple, memorable and still the most widely used vocabulary for the sources of interpersonal power; defined from the target’s perspective, which keeps attention on perception.
library.limitations: The bases overlap (a boss’s legitimate power usually carries reward and coercive power with it); the typology is about interpersonal power and says little about structural sources such as control of resources or network position; later research measuring the bases has relied heavily on self-report questionnaires.
library.contested: Not contested as a vocabulary; its usefulness as a measurement framework is debated. Raven later added informational power as a further base. Structural accounts of power (R-pfeffer-1978-external) treat the bases as consequences of dependence rather than as primary.
library.generalizability: Transfers well as a diagnostic vocabulary for any organization, including sports organizations. It does not predict which base will work in a given setting.
library.relevance: Gives you the language to separate the authority your title grants from the power that colleagues actually attribute to you.

library.title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Educational Psychology Review 31(2) 261–292, year and DOI matched on cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl and deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de.

library.summary: A twenty-year update of cognitive load theory by its principal authors. Learning complex material is constrained by a limited working memory and enabled by a vast long-term memory that stores organized knowledge (schemas). Instruction should manage the load imposed by the material and avoid load created by poor presentation. The review discusses effects such as the benefit of worked examples for novices and the expertise reversal effect, in which methods that help novices become redundant or harmful for more expert learners.
arguments: Working memory is severely limited for new information; long-term knowledge effectively expands it for familiar material.
Instruction should reduce extraneous load (load created by presentation) so that capacity is available for the task itself.
The best instructional method depends on the learner’s expertise: guidance that helps novices can hinder experts.
library.design: Theoretical review summarizing a research program of experiments on instructional design.
library.strengths: Coherent theory linked to many controlled experiments; explicit about how instructional effects depend on expertise.
library.limitations: Written by the theory’s founders; cognitive load is difficult to measure directly and is often assessed by self-rated mental effort; most research concerns academic and technical material rather than motor skills.
library.generalizability: Useful for designing how coaches explain, demonstrate and sequence information, and for onboarding in any knowledge-heavy role. Application to motor skills is by analogy and should be tested.
library.relevance: Explains why the coach who says ten things after every repetition usually helps less than the coach who says one.

library.title: Outcome Bias in Decision Evaluation
library.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(4), 569–579
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on a scanned copy hosted by the University of Florida, the Wikipedia outcome-bias entry and a PubMed Central replication article; a search on the DOI returned this article.

library.summary: In five studies, undergraduates evaluated decisions made under uncertainty — medical decisions and monetary gambles — after being told how they turned out. Decisions with favorable outcomes were rated as better reasoned and their makers as more competent, although the information available at the time was the same. Participants who said outcomes should not matter were still influenced by them.
arguments: People judge the quality of a decision partly by its outcome, even when the outcome could not have been known.
Outcome information also changes judgments of the decision-maker’s competence.
Knowing that outcomes should not matter does not prevent the bias.
library.design: Five experiments in which undergraduate participants rated hypothetical decisions whose outcomes were varied.
library.strengths: Clean manipulation of outcome with the decision held constant; a simple, influential paradigm.
library.limitations: Student participants and written vignettes; the size of the effect in organizations with real stakes and richer information is not established by these studies.
library.contested: Not contested in direction. A later pre-registered replication of Experiment 1 (“Outcomes Affect Evaluations of Decision Quality: Replication and Extensions of Baron and Hershey’s (1988) Outcome Bias Experiment 1”, indexed in PubMed Central) reproduced the effect.
library.generalizability: Strong reason to expect the bias in organizational reviews, where outcomes are known before decisions are evaluated; do not assume the vignette magnitudes.
library.relevance: The research basis for judging process separately from results — the core of every after-action review and personal decision journal.

library.title: Dual-Process Theories of Higher Cognition: Advancing the Debate
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, both authors, journal, volume 8(3), pages 223–241 and DOI 10.1177/1745691612460685 matched on researchportal.plymouth.ac.uk and library catalog records.

library.summary: A defense and refinement of dual-process theory in response to its critics. The authors distinguish Type 1 processing, which is autonomous, from Type 2 processing, which engages working memory and supports hypothetical thinking, and separate these defining features from features that are only typical correlates.
arguments: Type 2 processing is defined by its reliance on working memory and its role in hypothetical thinking (cognitive decoupling); Type 1 processing is defined by autonomy.
Many popular contrasts (fast/slow, unconscious/conscious, biased/normative) are typical correlates, not defining features, and treating them as defining invites valid criticism.
The authors respond to five lines of criticism, accepting that some have force against particular theories while arguing that the core distinction is well supported.
library.design: Theoretical review responding to published criticisms.
library.strengths: The clearest statement of what dual-process theory does and does not claim, by two of its principal theorists.
library.limitations: Written by advocates; much supporting evidence comes from laboratory reasoning tasks.
library.contested: Directly opposed by Melnikoff & Bargh (2018, R-melnikoff-2018-mythical), who argue the two-type framework is not supported.
library.generalizability: Moderate. The framework is a useful description of effortful versus automatic thinking; claims about two separate ‘systems’ should not be applied literally to organizations.
library.relevance: Prevents the most common executive misuse of ‘System 1 / System 2’: treating intuition as always biased and deliberation as always correct.

library.title: Organizational Mortality: The Liabilities of Newness and Adolescence
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on the University of Mannheim repository (madoc.bib.uni-mannheim.de) and citing reference lists; the DOI matched in a citing review and corresponds to the JSTOR stable identifier 2393316. The abstract and data were not available in results; the description below relies on how citing work characterizes the paper.

library.summary: Brüderl and Schüssler contrast two accounts of how organizational failure risk changes with age: the liability of newness, in which risk is highest at founding and declines, and a liability of adolescence, in which risk is low at first — a “honeymoon” sustained by initial resources and commitments — then rises before it declines.
arguments: Failure risk may rise during an organization’s early period before falling, rather than falling from founding.
An initial endowment of resources and commitments can protect a new organization for a time.
The two accounts differ mainly in what they predict for the period shortly after founding.
library.design: Empirical analysis of organizational failure rates by age; sample details were not confirmed in search results and are not described here.
library.strengths: Clarifies that “new organizations are risky” can describe different curve shapes, which changes when risk peaks.
library.limitations: Concerns whole organizations rather than internal units; this record’s description relies on citing sources rather than the full text.
library.contested: Part of a long debate over the shape of age dependence in organizational mortality (newness versus adolescence and other patterns); see R-stinchcombe-1965-social.
library.generalizability: For internal units, it suggests that a sponsor’s initial budget and goodwill act as an endowment, and that the dangerous period may arrive when that endowment runs out. This is an analogy, not a tested result.
library.relevance: Shifts the question for a new department from “how do we survive launch?” to “what must be true before the honeymoon ends?” — a timing insight for any first-year plan.

library.title: False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Psychological Science 22(11) 1359–1366, year and DOI matched on scopus/x-mol records and papers.ssrn.com (preprint).

library.summary: Using simulations and two deliberately absurd experiments, the authors show that common, individually defensible analytic choices can push the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%. They propose disclosure requirements for authors and reviewers.
arguments: Choosing among dependent variables, adding observations after peeking, adding covariates and dropping conditions each inflate false positives.
Combined, these researcher degrees of freedom can produce a false-positive rate above 60% in their simulation.
Simple disclosure rules would make this flexibility visible.
library.design: Monte Carlo simulation plus two small demonstration experiments.
library.strengths: Clear mechanism, memorable demonstration, practical remedies.
library.limitations: Simulated rates depend on assumed combinations of choices; it does not estimate how often researchers actually do this.
library.generalizability: Applies to any dashboard or analysis where the analyst can choose metrics, windows, segments and stopping rules after seeing the data.
library.relevance: The cleanest explanation of why an honest analyst can still produce false findings.

library.title: Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? A Truth in the Law of Small Numbers
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Econometrica 86(6) 2019–2047 (Nov 2018) and DOI matched on econometricsociety.org and econpapers.repec.org.

library.summary: Shows that a standard way of measuring streak shooting is biased: in finite sequences, the proportion of successes following a run of successes is expected to be below the true rate. Correcting this bias reverses the classic conclusion that the hot hand in basketball is a fallacy.
arguments: Selecting outcomes that follow streaks within finite sequences creates a downward bias.
Reanalysis of the original controlled shooting data shows evidence of streak shooting.
A celebrated “bias” finding rested partly on a statistical artifact.
library.design: Mathematical proof plus reanalysis of controlled shooting data.
library.strengths: Rigorous; overturns a famous result through measurement logic.
library.limitations: Size and practical importance of the hot hand in games remains debated.
library.contested: The original hot-hand-fallacy research (Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985) concluded the opposite; debate continues about effect size in game conditions.
library.generalizability: Directly relevant to sports performance analysis and to any streak-based judgment.
library.relevance: Assignment option (sports performance).

library.title: The Credibility Revolution in Empirical Economics: How Better Research Design Is Taking the Con out of Econometrics
library.license: Free to read from the American Economic Association (terms not re-confirmed). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, JEP 24(2) 3–30, year and DOI matched on nber.org (w15794) and eprints.lse.ac.uk.

library.summary: Argues that empirical economics became more credible because researchers focused on research design — randomized trials and natural experiments — rather than on elaborate models. Reviews how designs such as instrumental variables, regression discontinuity and differences-in-differences answer causal questions.
arguments: Design-based studies make the source of identifying variation explicit.
Randomized and quasi-experimental evidence has changed conclusions in labor, education and health economics.
Structural modeling and macroeconomics have been slower to adopt design-based standards.
library.strengths: Readable overview by two leading practitioners; free to read.
library.limitations: An advocate’s account; critics argue design-based studies answer narrow questions with limited external validity.
library.contested: Deaton and Cartwright, among others, argue the credibility gained comes at a cost in generalizability (R-deaton-2018-understanding).
library.generalizability: The design logic transfers to any organization evaluating its own programs.
library.relevance: The intellectual backbone of Lesson 3.

library.title: Mastering ’Metrics: The Path from Cause to Effect
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, publisher (Princeton University Press), year and ISBN 9780691152844 matched on econpapers.repec.org (pup:pbooks) and booksellers; press.princeton.edu page not seen in results.

library.summary: An introductory text built around five tools: randomized trials, regression, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity and differences-in-differences, each taught through real studies. Written for readers without heavy mathematics.
arguments: Every causal question is a comparison with a counterfactual.
Good designs make treated and comparison groups comparable in ways regression alone cannot guarantee.
Each design rests on a specific, checkable assumption.
library.strengths: Clear intuition, real examples, honest about assumptions.
library.limitations: Introductory; little on DAGs, heterogeneity or machine-learning approaches.
library.generalizability: The five tools are the standard toolkit for program evaluation in any organization.
library.relevance: The best single book for an executive who wants to read causal claims competently.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Academy of Management Journal 55(2) 381–398, year and DOI matched on dash.harvard.edu and econbiz.de.

library.title: Change Agents, Networks, and Institutions: A Contingency Theory of Organizational Change
library.summary: A study of change initiatives in a national health system finding that change agents’ network positions mattered differently depending on how much a change departed from institutional norms; ties to potential resisters helped with some changes and not others.
arguments: Network position shapes a change agent’s success.
The useful network structure depends on how divergent the change is.
Ties to fence-sitters and resisters can be an asset.
library.design: Field study of change initiatives led by clinical managers, with network and outcome data.
library.strengths: Real organizational changes; network measures.
library.limitations: One institutional setting; findings are contingent by design.
library.generalizability: Moderate for a professional sports organization with strong occupational norms.
library.relevance: Helps you choose whose support to seek first among coaches and department heads.

library.title: Principles of Finance
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 per the openstax.org preface and book pages (some chapter pages in search results showed a plain Creative Commons Attribution notice). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, senior contributing authors (Julie Dahlquist, Rainford Knight), publisher (OpenStax) and publish date (March 24, 2022) matched on openstax.org details, preface and index pages; license (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) matched on the preface, with conflicting notices on some chapter pages.

library.summary: An openly licensed introductory finance textbook covering financial statements, the time value of money, valuation, risk and return, capital budgeting, cost of capital and financial planning. It is written for readers without prior finance training.
arguments: Value depends on the timing and risk of cash flows, which is why discounting and net present value sit at the center of investment decisions.
Financial statements are tools for analysis, not just compliance documents.
Capital budgeting choices should be compared against the opportunity cost of capital.
library.strengths: Free, current (2022) and structured for self-study; covers the corporate-finance and accounting foundations found in every MBA reference core.
library.limitations: Introductory; less depth than an MBA corporate-finance course on capital structure and valuation under uncertainty.
library.generalizability: High: finance tools are domain-general and apply directly to budgeting and capital allocation in sports organizations.
library.relevance: The open backbone for Week 10 and for the budget model in the Week 14 capstone.

library.title: The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched in the KU Leuven Lirias repository record (lirias.kuleuven.be), scilit.net and the reference list of a 2016 reply by Macnamara and colleagues; the abstract’s ten-year claim matched in a summary of the paper.

library.summary: The founding statement of deliberate-practice theory. The authors argue that expert performance results from a long period of deliberate practice — effortful activity designed to improve specific aspects of performance — and that many characteristics once attributed to innate talent are the product of intense practice extended over at least ten years. They support the framework with studies in which music students of different skill levels gave retrospective estimates of their accumulated practice.
arguments: Deliberate practice is distinct from play, work and mere repetition: it targets specific weaknesses, is effortful, and relies on feedback and, often, a teacher’s design.
Groups at higher skill levels reported more accumulated deliberate practice.
Expert performance reflects acquired adaptations more than fixed innate capacity.
library.design: Theoretical framework supported by cross-sectional studies of music students grouped by skill level, using retrospective estimates of accumulated practice.
library.strengths: Precise definition of a kind of practice; shifted research attention from innate talent to the structure of training; generated decades of research.
library.limitations: Cross-sectional comparisons of groups already differing in skill; retrospective self-reports of practice over many years; small samples; cannot separate the effect of practice from the possibility that more able or motivated people practice more.
library.contested: Meta-analyses find practice explains a modest share of performance differences (R-macnamara-2014-deliberate, R-macnamara-2016-relationship), and a replication of the violin study found a smaller effect (R-macnamara-2019-role). Ericsson and colleagues reply that those analyses used a broader definition than deliberate practice (R-ericsson-2019-deliberate).
library.generalizability: The definition of high-quality practice is useful in sport, music, medicine and professional work. The strong claim that accumulated deliberate practice largely explains individual differences is not well supported outside the original framework.
library.relevance: You will hear its ideas (and its popular distortions) in every conversation about talent and reps; you need the original to separate the two.

library.title: Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice on the Acquisition of Expert Performance
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Authors, journal, volume, article number, date and DOI matched on frontiersin.org, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC6824411) and doaj.org; the reanalysis figures matched in the abstract text shown in results. Only the main title was confirmed; any subtitle is omitted.

library.summary: Ericsson’s reply to the meta-analytic critiques. The authors argue that the meta-analyses counted structured practice in general rather than deliberate practice as originally defined (individualized training designed by a teacher to improve specific aspects of performance). Reanalyzing only studies that match the original definition, they report that practice explained considerably more variance — figures of 29% and, after correcting for measurement attenuation, 61%. They recommend measuring the quality of practice, not only its duration.
arguments: Definitions matter: averaging across loosely defined practice underestimates the effect of deliberate practice.
Studies that match the original definition show larger relationships with performance.
Future research should measure concentration, analysis and problem solving during practice, not just hours.
library.design: Critical review and reanalysis of a subset of studies selected by the original definition of deliberate practice.
library.strengths: Clarifies the theory’s definition; makes a fair point that hours are a crude proxy for practice quality.
library.limitations: Written by the theory’s originator; the reanalysis rests on a small, selected set of studies; corrections for attenuation can inflate estimates when reliability is uncertain.
library.contested: Responds to R-macnamara-2014-deliberate and R-macnamara-2016-relationship; the replication R-macnamara-2019-role bears on the same question.
library.generalizability: The emphasis on practice quality is directly useful to coaches; the larger variance estimates should be held loosely until independent tests confirm them.
library.relevance: Lets you see the strongest version of the other side of the debate, which is what an executive must do before deciding.

library.title: A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ties
library.license: © AAAS. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, five authors, journal, volume 377, issue 6612, pages 1304–1310 and DOI 10.1126/science.abl4476 matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab publication page; an author copy is posted on ide.mit.edu.

library.summary: Using multiple large-scale randomized experiments on LinkedIn’s “People You May Know” recommendation feature, which varied the kinds of connections offered to more than 20 million members, the authors provide a causal test of Granovetter’s weak-ties hypothesis for job mobility. They find an inverted-U relationship: moderately weak ties were most associated with job transmission, while the weakest and strongest ties were less helpful, and weak ties mattered more in more digital industries.
arguments: Experimental variation in network formation allows a causal estimate of the value of weak ties, which earlier observational work could not provide.
The relationship between tie strength and job mobility is nonlinear (inverted U), not “the weaker the better”.
The value of weak versus strong ties differs across industries.
library.design: Randomized experiments embedded in a platform’s connection-recommendation algorithm, analysed for downstream job transitions.
library.strengths: Very large scale; randomization addresses the selection problem that weakens most network studies; directly tests a classic theory.
library.limitations: One platform and one outcome (job mobility); tie strength is measured by structural proxies on an online network; raised public discussion about experimentation on platform users.
library.contested: Supports and refines R-granovetter-1973-strength rather than contradicting it.
library.generalizability: Strong for information-driven labor markets; inferences to influence inside a single organization are by analogy.
library.relevance: A model of how a famous idea can be tested causally — and of how the tested version turns out more nuanced than the slogan.

library.title: The Oregon Experiment — Effects of Medicaid on Clinical Outcomes
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, NEJM 368(18) 1713–1722, year and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 23635051) and dspace.mit.edu.

library.summary: Uses Oregon’s 2008 lottery for Medicaid slots to estimate the effects of coverage two years later. Coverage increased use of care, reduced depression and financial strain, but produced no statistically significant improvement in measured blood pressure, cholesterol or glycated hemoglobin.
arguments: A lottery created a randomized comparison for a major policy.
Some outcomes improved; measured physical-health markers did not significantly change.
Whether the null physical-health findings reflect no effect or insufficient power is debated.
library.design: Randomized lottery with instrumental-variable estimates of the effect of coverage.
library.strengths: Randomization of a real policy; pre-specified analysis.
library.limitations: Two-year horizon; low prevalence of the targeted conditions limited power; one state.
library.contested: Commentators disagreed about whether the physical-health results show no effect or an underpowered test.
library.generalizability: Excellent for practicing the difference between “no evidence of effect” and “evidence of no effect”.
library.relevance: Assignment option (healthcare / policy).

library.title: Fostering Implementation of Health Services Research Findings into Practice: A Consolidated Framework for Advancing Implementation Science
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, all six authors, journal, article 50, 7 August 2009 publication and DOI matched on implementationscience.biomedcentral.com, pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (19664226) and deepblue.lib.umich.edu.

library.summary: The authors consolidate constructs from published implementation theories into the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), organized in five domains: characteristics of the intervention, the outer setting, the inner setting, characteristics of the individuals involved, and the process of implementation. CFIR is a common vocabulary for diagnosing why an effective practice takes hold in one setting and not another, and for structuring evaluations across studies.
arguments: Effective interventions frequently fail to produce results when moved into new settings; context explains much of the difference.
