Constructs from many theories can be merged into one structured menu covering five domains.
Interventions have core components and an adaptable periphery that can be tailored locally.
The framework is meant to guide formative evaluation and to accumulate knowledge across studies.
library.design: Review and synthesis of published implementation theories, with constructs selected for conceptual or empirical support and measurability.
library.strengths: Open access; widely adopted; gives a systematic checklist of contextual factors.
library.limitations: A determinant framework, not a predictive model; many constructs; developed in health services. The authors published an updated version in 2022.
library.generalizability: Designed for health care but used across education, social services and other sectors; works as a diagnostic structure for any multi-site rollout.
library.relevance: Gives you a disciplined way to separate what must stay constant in a rollout from what each site should adapt.

library.title: Superiority of External Attentional Focus for Motor Performance and Learning: Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author surnames, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on digitalscholarship.unlv.edu and pure.psu.edu; study counts and effect sizes matched in the abstract text shown in results. The first author’s full name matched; other given names are as commonly listed.

library.summary: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses comparing an external focus of attention (on the movement’s effect, such as the target or the implement) with an internal focus (on body movements). Pooling 73 studies for performance and 40 for learning, the authors report advantages for an external focus: Hedges’ g of about 0.26 for performance, 0.58 for retention and 0.58 for transfer, with no significant moderation by age, health status or skill level.
arguments: Directing attention to the intended movement effect rather than to body parts improves performance and learning on average.
The benefit appeared across ages, health conditions and skill levels in the included studies.
Electromyography studies suggested more efficient muscular activity under an external focus, and a more distant external focus did better than a near one.
library.design: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses: 73 studies (1,824 participants) for performance and 40 studies (1,274 participants) for retention and transfer; subsets of 12 electromyography studies and 9 studies of distance of focus.
library.strengths: Large, systematic synthesis of a well-known coaching principle.
library.limitations: Many small studies; authors include the principle’s leading proponent; a later reanalysis argues that publication bias explains most of the effect.
library.contested: Reanalysis with bias-correction methods finds effects near zero (R-mckay-2024-reporting).
library.generalizability: Plausible and cheap to apply in coaching language; the size of the benefit in real sport settings is uncertain.
library.relevance: The best case for one of the most widely taught coaching principles — read it with its critique.

library.title: Social perception in negotiation
library.publication: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 47(1), 98–123
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 47, issue 1, pages 98–123 and year matched on ideas.repec.org and on kellogg.northwestern.edu faculty research listings. The DOI was not shown in search results, so it is omitted. Findings below are taken from abstract-level descriptions and citing work.

library.summary: A study of how negotiators perceive the other side’s interests. It reports that most negotiators enter a negotiation expecting the other party’s interests to be completely opposed to their own, and argues that such misperceptions of the other side’s interests are a primary cause of agreements that leave joint value unclaimed. It is the standard citation for the “fixed-pie” perception.
arguments: Negotiators commonly assume the pie is fixed: whatever one side gains, the other loses.
Misjudging the other side’s priorities leads to inefficient agreements, not just tougher bargaining.
Accurate perception of the counterpart’s interests is a learnable source of joint gains.
library.design: Laboratory negotiation simulation with measures of negotiators’ judgments of the other party’s interests (details beyond the abstract not confirmed here).
library.strengths: Identifies a perceptual mechanism behind inefficient deals; foundational for later integrative-bargaining research.
library.limitations: Lab simulation with structured point tables; real negotiations often have genuinely opposed interests, so the fixed-pie assumption is sometimes correct.
library.contested: Later work notes that a fixed-pie perception is not always inaccurate; the error is assuming it without checking. The mechanism is well accepted; its magnitude in the field is less studied.
library.generalizability: High as a caution for multi-issue deals (contracts, partnerships, budgets); limited for genuinely single-issue, one-shot haggling.
library.relevance: Explains why intelligent people split the difference on every issue and leave value behind, the mistake the Negotiation Chamber is designed to expose.

library.title: Rules Versus Standards: An Economic Analysis
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. A free copy is posted in the Duke Law Scholarship Repository and in Harvard's DASH repository.

verified.evidence: Title, author, Duke Law Journal volume 42, issue 3, pages 557–629, year 1992 and DOI 10.2307/1372840 matched on scholarship.law.duke.edu, hls.harvard.edu and dash.harvard.edu.

library.summary: An economic analysis of whether laws should take the form of rules, whose content is fixed before people act, or standards, whose content is supplied afterward by an adjudicator. Kaplow argues that rules cost more to promulgate and standards cost more to apply and to advise on, so the frequency of the regulated conduct is central to the choice. He separates the rule–standard question from the question of how detailed a law should be.
arguments: Rules are costlier to create; standards are costlier for individuals to interpret and for adjudicators to apply.
When conduct is frequent and similar, the up-front cost of a rule is spread across many cases, favoring rules.
People can learn rules cheaply before acting, so behavior tends to track rules more closely than standards.
The choice between rules and standards is distinct from the choice of how complex or detailed a law should be.
library.design: Formal economic analysis of legal form; no empirical data.
library.strengths: Clear, general framework that applies to statutes, contracts and internal policies; widely cited as the standard economic treatment.
library.limitations: A theoretical model; real legal systems mix rules and standards, and the costs it identifies are rarely measured. Long and technical in places.
library.generalizability: Transfers directly to organizational policy design (codes of conduct, approval thresholds, travel and compensation policies) and to contract drafting.
library.relevance: Gives the learner a principled way to decide when to write precise rules and when to rely on judgment, in contracts and in management systems.

library.title: The Mirroring Hypothesis: Theory, Evidence, and Exceptions
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 25, issue 5, pages 709–738 (2016) and DOI matched on the Harvard DASH repository record and RePEc (econpapers.repec.org, ideas.repec.org). An open author copy is listed on dash.harvard.edu; an earlier 2010 HBS working paper reviewed fewer studies.

library.summary: Colfer and Baldwin restate Conway’s observation as the mirroring hypothesis—organizational ties in a project or firm will correspond to the technical dependencies in the work—and review 142 empirical studies. Mirroring is common but not universal in industries and firms, and studies of open collaborative projects, mostly in software, generally did not support it. They explain the exceptions by coordination that travels through shared tools, standards and transparent work rather than organizational ties.
arguments: Organizations tend to produce work whose structure mirrors their communication ties, and vice versa.
Across 142 studies, mirroring is common but not universal in industries and firms.
Open collaborative projects are the main exception: shared code, documentation and tools let distributed contributors coordinate without organizational ties.
library.design: Literature review classifying 142 empirical studies (industry, firm and open-collaborative-project studies).
library.strengths: Systematic look at a popular heuristic; explicitly catalogues exceptions rather than only confirming cases; open author copy.
library.limitations: Studies vary widely in method and quality; much of the evidence is descriptive and cannot establish the direction of causation between organization and product structure.
library.contested: The review itself documents the contest: supportive industry and firm studies versus non-supportive open-collaboration studies.
library.generalizability: Most evidence comes from technology and product development; transfer to service organizations and sports departments is plausible as a heuristic but untested here.
library.relevance: Turns “Conway’s law” from a slogan into a hypothesis with known exceptions—useful when you design teams around the products, reports or processes you want.

library.title: Psychological Safety: A Meta-Analytic Review and Extension
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.method: web-search (by the Week 5 writer in this build; cross-checked against that record)
verified.evidence: Not searched by this writer (search budget exhausted). The identical record in sources/w05.json reports title, five authors, journal, volume 70 issue 1, pages 113–165 and DOI matched on econbiz.de, zendy.io and university repositories; every field here matches that record.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of the psychological safety literature — the shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as asking questions or admitting errors. Psychological safety was associated with information sharing, learning behavior, engagement and performance, and was itself associated with supportive leadership and work design. Most of the underlying studies are correlational.
arguments: Psychological safety correlates positively with learning behavior, engagement and task performance.
Supportive leadership, peer support and work design characteristics are associated with higher psychological safety.
The construct operates at individual, team and organizational levels.
library.design: Meta-analysis of primarily cross-sectional field studies.
library.strengths: Aggregates a large field literature; examines antecedents and outcomes together.
library.limitations: Primary studies are mostly cross-sectional and often single-source, so causal direction and common-method bias are real concerns.
library.contested: Causal claims (“building psychological safety raises performance”) rest on thinner experimental and longitudinal evidence than popular accounts suggest.
library.generalizability: Relevant to any team that depends on speaking up about errors; sport-specific evidence is limited.
library.relevance: Separates the evidence on psychological safety from the slogan, so you can use the idea without overselling it.

library.title: Do 70 Per Cent of All Organizational Change Initiatives Really Fail?
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 11(4), pages 451–464 and December 2011 publication matched on research.brighton.ac.uk (University of Brighton repository). The DOI was given in the search query and is consistent with the journal’s DOI pattern but was not shown on an authoritative page in the results.

library.summary: Hughes traces the widely repeated claim that about 70 per cent of organizational change initiatives fail to the published sources usually cited for it and concludes that there is no valid and reliable empirical evidence supporting the figure. Some of the sources concerned narrower programs such as business-process reengineering, and others offered the figure without a documented method.
arguments: The 70 per cent figure circulates as a narrative, not as a measured base rate.
The five sources examined do not provide valid and reliable evidence for a general failure rate of organizational change.
“Failure” is rarely defined, making any single rate across all change initiatives hard to measure.
Repeating the figure may itself shape how change is managed and justified.
library.design: Critical review tracing the evidence behind five frequently cited sources of the 70 per cent claim.
library.strengths: Goes back to primary sources; a model of how to audit a popular statistic.
library.limitations: Shows the absence of evidence for 70 per cent, not that change usually succeeds; does not produce an alternative base rate.
library.contested: Challenges claims associated with practitioner literature (see R-kotter-1995-leading); the author revisited the topic in later work.
library.generalizability: The methodological lesson—ask where a number comes from and what its denominator is—applies to every field, including sport.
library.relevance: Trains the reflex of checking the provenance of a statistic before using it to justify urgency or budget.

library.title: The Strength of Weak Ties
library.license: © The University of Chicago. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 78, issue 6, pages 1360–1380 and DOI 10.1086/225469 matched in a BibSonomy record and Wikipedia’s reference list; JSTOR stable URL also reported. Copies circulate on university course pages; library access recommended.

library.summary: Granovetter argues that weak ties — acquaintances rather than close friends — are disproportionately important for moving information and opportunity across social groups, because strong ties tend to connect people who already know each other and share the same information. He links this micro-level property of ties to macro outcomes such as diffusion, mobility and community organization, and supports it with evidence from a study of how professional, technical and managerial workers found jobs.
arguments: Strongly tied people tend to share contacts, so their information is redundant; bridges between groups are almost always weak ties.
Weak ties therefore carry novel information and opportunities across social boundaries.
In the job-search data, people who found jobs through contacts had more often seen those contacts only occasionally or rarely than often.
Communities with few weak ties may struggle to organize collectively.
library.design: Theoretical argument illustrated with data from the author’s survey of people who had recently changed jobs; descriptive, not causal.
library.strengths: Elegant mechanism linking network structure to outcomes; one of the most cited papers in social science; generated decades of testable predictions.
library.limitations: Original evidence is descriptive and limited to one labor market; tie strength was measured crudely by frequency of contact; cannot separate the effect of ties from the characteristics of people who have them.
library.contested: Core claim has been refined rather than overturned: a large randomized test (R-rajkumar-2022-causal) found that moderately weak ties, not the weakest, were most helpful for job mobility.
library.generalizability: Strong for information flow in labor markets and organizations; the importance of weak versus strong ties varies by industry and by what is being transmitted (information versus trust or support).
library.relevance: Explains why the colleague you rarely talk to in another department may be your best source of new information and your best route for spreading a change.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, The Information Society 20(5) 325–344, year and DOI matched on tisj.sitehost.iu.edu (journal abstract page) and alexandria.unisg.ch.

library.title: The Concept of Information Overload: A Review of Literature from Organization Science, Accounting, Marketing, MIS, and Related Disciplines
library.summary: A cross-disciplinary literature review of information overload: its definitions, causes, symptoms and countermeasures. It describes a recurring finding that decision performance rises with information up to a point and then declines.
arguments: Beyond a point, more information lowers decision quality.
Causes include the information itself, the task, the person, the organization and technology.
Countermeasures include filtering, structuring, better formats and changed processes.
library.design: Narrative literature review across several management disciplines.
library.strengths: Broad synthesis with a usable framework of causes and remedies.
library.limitations: Review of heterogeneous studies; the inverted-U pattern is a summary, not a precise estimate.
library.generalizability: High for report and meeting design.
library.relevance: Explains why a 22-page report can be worse than a two-page brief.

library.title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect
library.publication: Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546–573 (registered replication report; many co-authors)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, lead authors, Perspectives on Psychological Science 11(4) 546–573, year and DOI matched on cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl and mro.massey.ac.nz.

library.summary: A registered replication report in which more than twenty laboratories ran the same preregistered protocol testing whether an initial act of self-control impairs performance on a later self-control task. The pooled effect was close to zero, in contrast to the sizable effects summarized in earlier meta-analyses of the ego-depletion literature.
arguments: A preregistered, multi-site test found an ego-depletion effect near zero.
Earlier meta-analytic estimates were likely inflated by publication bias and flexible analysis.
The result does not prove self-control never fatigues; it shows the standard laboratory paradigm did not reproduce the effect.
library.design: Preregistered multi-laboratory replication using a common randomized protocol.
library.strengths: Preregistration, many labs and large pooled sample remove most of the flexibility that inflated earlier estimates.
library.limitations: Tested one paradigm chosen in consultation with proponents; defenders argued the manipulation was too weak.
library.contested: Proponents dispute the protocol choice; later multisite tests have also found small or null effects. The popular “willpower is a muscle that runs out” claim should be treated as unsupported.
library.generalizability: Cautions against designing schedules or policies on the assumption that self-control is a depletable resource.
library.relevance: A model case of a once-famous finding that did not survive a rigorous test — a template for how to read the next one.

library.title: Mobility, Skills, and the Michigan Non-Compete Experiment
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. An author/working-paper version is hosted by the Fung Institute at UC Berkeley.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Management Science volume 55, issue 6 (June 2009), pages 875–889 and DOI 10.1287/mnsc.1080.0985 matched on pubsonline.informs.org and econpapers.repec.org; design and headline estimates matched the Berkeley-hosted paper.

library.summary: Treats Michigan's 1985 reversal of its policy of not enforcing non-competes as a natural experiment. Comparing inventors in Michigan with inventors in states that continued not to enforce, the authors estimate that mobility fell after the reversal, with larger effects for inventors with firm-specific skills and for specialists.
arguments: Enforcing non-competes reduced inventor mobility in Michigan by about 8.1 percent relative to comparison states.
The effect was larger for inventors with more firm-specific skills (about 15.4 percent at one standard deviation above the mean).
The effect was larger for specialists in narrow technical fields (about 16.2 percent at one standard deviation above the mean).
library.design: Difference-in-differences around Michigan's 1985 policy reversal, comparing inventors in Michigan with inventors in states that continued not to enforce non-competes.
library.strengths: A credible natural-experiment design that addresses the selection problems of cross-sectional comparisons.
library.limitations: One state, one period and one occupational group (inventors); measures mobility, not wages or welfare; relies on the comparison states being a valid counterfactual.
library.contested: Consistent with harm-to-mobility arguments; defenders of non-competes argue that reduced mobility can protect training and information investments. See R-starr-2021-noncompete.
library.generalizability: Strongest for technical knowledge workers; transfer to other occupations, including coaching and analytics roles, is plausible but untested here.
library.relevance: Shows how to read causal evidence on a legal rule — and what it cannot tell an executive.

library.title: Reporting Bias, Not External Focus: A Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review of the External Focus of Attention Literature
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Author surnames, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on experts.mcmaster.ca; findings matched in the abstract shown on x-mol.com. Title wording differs between listings (preprint and published versions), and given names were not confirmed and are omitted.

library.summary: A reanalysis of the external-focus literature using robust Bayesian meta-analysis, which models several forms of publication bias. The authors found moderate to strong evidence of publication bias in every analysis. After correction, estimated effects were near zero — about g = 0.01 for performance, 0.15 for retention and 0.09 for transfer — and Bayes factors favored the null. They conclude that an external-focus advantage has not been established.
arguments: The external-focus literature shows strong signs that small studies with positive results were more likely to be published.
Once bias is modeled, the evidence favors little or no average benefit.
A widely taught coaching principle can rest on a literature that looks stronger than it is.
library.design: Robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of external- versus internal-focus studies, modeling multiple publication-bias scenarios.
library.strengths: Uses modern bias-correction methods; transparent about assumptions; addresses the exact literature coaches rely on.
library.limitations: Bias-correction methods rest on their own assumptions and can understate true effects; absence of evidence for an average benefit is not proof that no learner benefits.
library.contested: Directly contradicts the conclusion of R-chua-2021-superiority.
library.generalizability: A general lesson for sport science: small-sample literatures can produce confident principles that shrink under scrutiny.
library.relevance: Shows you how to hold a coaching principle at the right level of confidence when the evidence base is contested.

library.title: Specific and General Knowledge, and Organizational Structure
library.publication: In L. Werin & H. Wijkander (Eds.), Contract Economics (pp. 251–274). Blackwell. Author version on SSRN (abstract 6658).
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, editors (Werin and Wijkander), volume (Contract Economics, Blackwell, 1992) and pages 251–274 matched on econbiz.de and scilit.com; the SSRN version (abstract 6658, DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6658) matched on scilit.com and the author’s own listing. Search results note later reprints (Journal of Applied Corporate Finance, 1995).

library.summary: Jensen and Meckling argue that organizational structure is shaped by the cost of moving knowledge. Specific knowledge is costly to transfer and general knowledge is cheap, so organizations must either move knowledge to decision-makers or move decision rights to those who hold the knowledge. Moving rights down reduces the costs of poor information but raises agency costs, so decision rights must be designed together with systems for measuring and rewarding performance.
arguments: Specific knowledge (costly to transmit) and general knowledge (cheap to transmit) call for different locations of decision rights.
As decision rights move lower, costs from poor information fall and agency costs rise; the right level minimizes their sum.
Organizational structure combines the assignment of decision rights with performance-measurement and reward systems, which must be designed together.
library.strengths: A parsimonious, general mechanism that explains many design choices; open author version; widely used in organizational economics teaching.
library.limitations: Theory rather than evidence; assumes formal rights are the rights that matter and largely sets aside informal power, identity and fairness.
library.generalizability: Broad: applies to firms, hospitals, agencies and sports organizations deciding who decides. Empirical effect sizes depend on setting and are not supplied by the paper.
library.relevance: The core logic for allocating decisions across coaches, analysts, medical staff and executives—and for pairing every delegation with measurement and accountability.

library.title: The First 90 Days: Proven Strategies for Getting Up to Speed Faster and Smarter
library.publication: Harvard Business Review Press, Boston (updated and expanded edition; first published 2003)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, subtitle, author, publisher (Harvard Business Review Press), publication date (14 May 2013), ISBN 9781422188613 and description as the updated, expanded tenth-anniversary edition matched on retailer and public-library catalog listings; chapter topics (prepare yourself, accelerate your learning, match strategy to situation, negotiate success) matched in a library record; IMD’s page for the book appeared in results.

library.summary: A practitioner guide to leadership transitions. Watkins organizes the first months in a new role around tasks such as preparing yourself, accelerating your learning, matching strategy to the situation, negotiating success with your boss and securing early wins, and offers a typology of situations — start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment and sustaining success — that changes what a leader should do first.
arguments: Transitions fail when leaders misdiagnose the situation they have inherited or misread their boss’s expectations.
What to do first depends on whether the unit is a start-up, a turnaround, in accelerated growth, in need of realignment or sustaining success.
Early wins build credibility and momentum if they serve the longer-term agenda.
library.design: Practitioner synthesis based on the author’s teaching, consulting and work with leaders in transition; not a controlled study.
library.strengths: Concrete, well-organized sequencing; the situational typology guards against one-size-fits-all advice.
library.limitations: Prescriptions have not been tested against comparison groups; success stories dominate; “ninety days” is a planning convention rather than an empirically derived window.
library.contested: No replication literature exists for its prescriptions; treat them as practitioner heuristics.
library.generalizability: Used across industries and the public sector; transfers to new roles in sport organizations as a sequencing aid rather than as evidence.
library.relevance: The most widely used practitioner playbook for a leader’s first months, read here beside the research on new organizations so you can see where the two agree and where the book outruns the evidence.

library.title: What Is Strategy?
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, year, journal, volume 74, issue 6 and pages 61–78 matched in a university course listing and a library bibliography; an article index summarized the same central argument. The hbr.org address is HBR’s archive address for the November 1996 issue; it was not returned in search results and the link was not opened.

library.summary: Porter argues that operational effectiveness — performing similar activities better than rivals — is necessary but not sufficient for superior performance, because its techniques diffuse and competitors converge. Strategy is the creation of a unique and valuable position, rooted in a system of activities, which requires trade-offs and fit among those activities. Choosing what not to do is, in his account, the essence of strategy.
arguments: Operational effectiveness is not strategy: best practices spread, producing competitive convergence.
Positions can rest on the variety of products served, the needs of a customer group, or differences in access to customers.
A position is sustainable only with trade-offs; rivals that copy without accepting them end up straddling.
Fit among activities makes a strategy hard to imitate because rivals must copy a system, not a practice.
library.design: Conceptual essay illustrated with company examples; no systematic data or statistical test.
library.strengths: Exceptionally clear conceptual distinctions (operational effectiveness vs. positioning, trade-offs, fit) that remain the reference point for strategy teaching; the argument is precise enough to be used as a test of real plans.
library.limitations: Evidence is illustrative and drawn from successful firms, so survivorship and hindsight bias are possible; it says little about how positions should change when technology moves the productivity frontier quickly.
library.contested: Mintzberg and Waters’ emergent view (R-mintzberg-1985-strategies) challenges the emphasis on deliberate design; critics of static positioning argue that fast-moving markets erode positions quickly. These are disagreements about emphasis and setting rather than failed replications.
library.generalizability: The logic transfers well to any organization competing for customers, talent or funding, including public agencies and sports organizations; the specific examples are commercial.
library.relevance: Gives you the sharpest available test of whether a departmental or organizational plan is a strategy or a list of improvements, and why “what we will stop doing” belongs in every plan.

library.title: The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, January 2008 issue, volume 86, issue 1 matched on the HBR Store (product R0801E) and a library catalogue; pages given as 78–93 in one citation and 79–93 in another catalogue. Confirmed as an update of Porter’s 1979 HBR article.

library.summary: Porter restates and extends his 1979 framework: industry profitability is shaped by the threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of suppliers and buyers, the threat of substitutes and the intensity of rivalry. The strongest forces determine how much of the value an industry creates its firms can keep. He distinguishes these forces from factors such as growth, technology, government and complements, which matter through the forces, and describes common errors in applying the framework.
arguments: Five forces shape the long-run average profitability of an industry.
The strongest force or forces matter most and differ by industry.
Growth, technology, government and complementary products are factors, not forces.
Good strategy positions a firm where the forces are weakest, exploits changes in them, or reshapes them.
library.design: Conceptual article grounded in industrial-organization economics, with industry illustrations.
library.strengths: A durable, widely taught structure for analyzing why industries differ in profitability; the 2008 version addresses common misapplications.
library.limitations: Largely static; treats buyers and suppliers mainly as bargaining threats; handles platforms, ecosystems and cooperation only indirectly.
library.contested: Variance-decomposition studies disagree on how much industry explains relative to firm-specific factors (R-mcgahan-1997-much; R-barney-1991-firm offers the firm-level counterpoint).
library.generalizability: Works best for commercial industries with identifiable products and rivals; applying it to sports leagues, public services or platforms requires care in defining the industry.
library.relevance: Teaches you to ask who captures the value an activity creates, which matters for any organization buying talent, technology or services.

library.title: Business Law I Essentials
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (OpenStax). Attribution, non-commercial use and share-alike required. Linked, not reproduced. OpenStax's 2e pages add a notice that the book may not be used to train large language models without permission.

verified.evidence: Title, publisher (OpenStax, Rice University), 2019 first-edition publication date (details page: September 27, 2019) and the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license matched on openstax.org (preface, details page and web PDF). Mirande Valbrune and Renee De Assis are listed first among the contributors; Suzanne Cardell, Tess C. Taylor and Natalie Sappleton are also listed. A second edition (2e) is listed on openstax.org with a June 24, 2026 publication date. Individual chapter titles were not confirmed in search results, so readings refer to topics rather than chapter numbers.

library.summary: A free, openly licensed introductory business law textbook covering the U.S. legal system, contracts, torts, agency, employment, intellectual property, business organizations and related topics at an undergraduate level. It is designed for readers without legal training and includes examples and review questions.
arguments: Business law sits within a layered system of constitutional, statutory, regulatory and judge-made law.
Contracts require mutual assent, consideration, capacity and legality, with remedies for breach.
Agency and employment relationships create duties and liabilities for organizations.
Intellectual property law gives organizations distinct tools — copyright, patent, trademark and trade secret.
library.strengths: Free, accessible and openly licensed; good foundation for readers new to law.
library.limitations: Introductory and general; does not track recent state-law changes (for example on non-competes) and is not a substitute for current, jurisdiction-specific advice. The license is non-commercial, not CC BY.
library.generalizability: U.S.-centric general principles; useful as vocabulary for any U.S. organization.
library.relevance: The week's open foundation text: the learner can fill gaps in legal vocabulary without paywalls.

library.title: Negotiation and Conflict Management (15.667, Spring 2001)
library.publication: MIT OpenCourseWare, MIT Sloan School of Management (graduate course materials)
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (MIT OpenCourseWare terms of use); third-party readings and items marked as excluded are not covered. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Course number, title, term (Spring 2001), instructor (Prof. Mary Rowe), graduate level and Sloan School affiliation matched on ocw.mit.edu (course home, lecture notes, readings and assignments pages). Sitewide CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license matched on ocw.mit.edu/pages/privacy-and-terms-of-use/.

library.summary: An archived MIT Sloan graduate course that teaches negotiation theory in employment settings, with eleven topic sessions built around role-play simulations. It treats conflict from both the first-party (negotiator) and third-party (mediator, arbitrator) perspectives and includes difficult workplace situations. The posted materials include lecture notes, simulations, self-assessments and assignment instructions.
arguments: Negotiation skill is built through repeated simulation, self-assessment and analysis of others’ negotiations, not through reading alone.
Conflict management in organizations includes third-party options such as mediation and arbitration, not only direct bargaining.
Workplace conflicts such as whistle-blowing and discrimination complaints require procedures and due process, not just bargaining tactics.
library.strengths: Real graduate course materials from a business school, openly licensed; emphasizes practice, self-assessment and workplace conflict systems, which most negotiation primers omit.
library.limitations: Materials date from 2001; several assigned books (for example Getting to Yes) and course-pack readings are copyrighted and not included on OCW. It is a course archive, not an evidence review.
library.generalizability: High for organizational settings: the employment-relations focus transfers directly to staff, vendor and internal resource negotiations, including in sports organizations.
library.relevance: The owner named this course as a starting example. It supplies open simulations and a conflict-systems view that complement Week 7 (negotiation) and the dispute-resolution material in Week 11.

library.title: Team Project (15.328, Fall 2003)
library.publication: MIT OpenCourseWare, MIT Sloan School of Management (graduate course materials)
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (MIT OpenCourseWare sitewide terms of use); items marked as excluded are not covered. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Course number, title, term (Fall 2003) and graduate level matched on an ocw.mit.edu page title (course-pedagogy page). Instructors and the course description were not shown in the search results, so the record names only MIT OpenCourseWare as author. Sitewide license matched on ocw.mit.edu/pages/privacy-and-terms-of-use/.

library.summary: An archived MIT Sloan graduate course on structured team projects, published on MIT OpenCourseWare with a page on its pedagogy. APERTURE lists it as an open example of how a business school structures team-based applied work; its specific contents were not confirmed in search results.
arguments: Business schools treat team project work as a designed learning experience with its own pedagogy, not an add-on.
Applied team projects are a common way to integrate core-course concepts.
library.strengths: Open, from an MBA program in the reference set; shows how project-based integration is organized.
library.limitations: Only title, number, term and level were confirmed; materials are from 2003 and their content and completeness were not verified.
library.generalizability: Moderate: useful as a model for structuring the incremental Week 14 capstone rather than as subject content.
library.relevance: Supports the design of APERTURE’s incremental capstone (Weeks 8–14) as integrated, project-based work.

library.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (OpenStax, Rice University). Linked, not reproduced; APERTURE summarizes in its own words.

verified.evidence: Title, the three authors and the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license matched on openstax.org (book preface); 2019 publication and Rice University as copyright holder matched on catalog and bookseller records (bookshare.org, abebooks.com, open.umn.edu). The chapter title “Introduction to Financial Statements” (Chapter 2) matched on the openstax.org preface listing.

library.summary: A free, peer-reviewed introductory financial-accounting textbook. It builds the income statement, statement of owner’s equity, balance sheet and statement of cash flows from the accounting equation and the accrual concept, with worked transactions throughout. For a non-specialist executive it is the clearest open route into how the statements are built and why they connect.
arguments: Financial statements are built from a small set of principles and assumptions — accrual (revenue when earned, expenses matched to the period), going concern and the accounting equation (assets = liabilities + equity).
Each statement answers a different question: performance over a period, position at a moment, and the sources and uses of cash.
The statements are linked: net income flows into equity, and the cash flow statement reconciles accrual profit to the change in cash.
library.strengths: Open license, worked examples, end-of-chapter exercises; written for learners without prior accounting training.
library.limitations: Introductory and U.S.-GAAP oriented; it teaches mechanics more than the judgment involved in reading statements critically, and it does not cover analysis of intangible-heavy organizations in depth.
library.generalizability: The mechanics apply to any organization that keeps accrual accounts (companies, hospitals, clubs). Government and some partnerships budget on a cash or obligation basis, so translation is needed there.
library.relevance: Gives you enough command of the statements to interrogate a CFO’s summary, read a department’s cost reports and translate a proposal into its effect on profit, cash and the balance sheet.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author (NIST), date (January 16, 2020) and DOI 10.6028/NIST.CSWP.01162020 matched on nist.gov, nvlpubs.nist.gov and csrc.nist.gov.

library.title: NIST Privacy Framework: A Tool for Improving Privacy Through Enterprise Risk Management, Version 1.0
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
library.publication: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
library.summary: A voluntary U.S. framework that helps organizations manage privacy risk through core functions (Identify, Govern, Control, Communicate, Protect) and profiles that match practices to risk.
arguments: Privacy risk arises from data processing, not only from security breaches.
Governance and inventory of data come before controls.
Organizations should tailor practices to their own risk profile.
library.design: Government framework developed with public consultation.
library.strengths: Free, structured and sector-neutral.
library.limitations: Voluntary; does not state what any particular law requires.
library.generalizability: High as a structure for a data governance plan.
library.relevance: A neutral scaffold for your data-governance section that is not legal advice.

library.title: Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems that Never Happened: Creating and Sustaining Process Improvement
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 43(4), pages 64–88 and DOI 10.2307/41166101 matched on cmr.berkeley.edu and journals.sagepub.com; an author-hosted copy is linked from John Sterman’s MIT faculty page (web.mit.edu/jsterman).

library.summary: Using field studies of improvement programs and system-dynamics models, the authors explain why organizations that adopt proven improvement methods so often fail to sustain them. Under pressure to hit targets, people “work harder” instead of “working smarter”; the time diverted from improvement lets capability erode, which raises pressure further—a self-reinforcing capability trap. Managers then tend to blame people rather than the system.
arguments: Improvement competes with production for the same scarce time; short-run pressure systematically favors production.
Working harder produces immediate gains while capability decays slowly and invisibly, so the trap is hard to see from inside.
Managers tend to attribute performance shortfalls to worker effort rather than to the system, reinforcing pressure and control.
Escaping the trap requires deliberately protecting improvement time and accepting a temporary dip in output.
library.design: Comparative field studies of process-improvement initiatives combined with formal system-dynamics modelling.
library.strengths: Mechanism-rich explanation that links individual attribution, incentives and system structure; widely used in operations and healthcare improvement teaching; award-winning article.
library.limitations: Case-based evidence from a limited number of organizations; the models illustrate plausible dynamics rather than estimate effect sizes.
library.generalizability: The mechanism is generic to any setting where improvement work competes with daily output—hospitals, software teams, coaching staffs. Confidence in the mechanism is moderate to high; in any specific magnitude, low.
library.relevance: Explains why departments that are “too busy to improve” stay busy, and why blaming staff for implementation shortfalls is usually the wrong diagnosis.

library.title: Measuring and Explaining Management Practices Across Firms and Countries
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 122, issue 4, pages 1351–1408 (November 2007) and DOI matched on RePEc (econpapers.repec.org) and econbiz.de; an earlier open version is NBER Working Paper 12216 (nber.org). Survey method details matched on the NBER Reporter and LSE Centre for Economic Performance pages.

library.summary: Bloom and Van Reenen develop a double-blind interview method to score management practices in monitoring, targets and people management, and apply it to 732 medium-sized manufacturing firms in the United States, France, Germany and the United Kingdom. Management quality varies widely within every country, with a long tail of badly managed firms, and higher scores are associated with productivity, profitability, Tobin’s Q and survival. Poor practices are more common where product-market competition is weak and where family firms pass control to the eldest son.
arguments: Management practices can be measured systematically with structured, double-blind interviews.
Practice scores vary widely within and across countries and are strongly associated with firm performance.
Weak competition and primogeniture in family succession are associated with worse practices.
library.design: Double-blind telephone interviews with plant managers in 732 medium-sized manufacturing firms in four countries, scored on a 1–5 grid across monitoring, targets and people management and matched to firm performance data.
library.strengths: Large sample, careful measurement designed to limit bias from both respondents and interviewers, transparent instrument, open working-paper version.
library.limitations: Cross-sectional associations cannot establish causation; the sample is manufacturing; the scoring grid embodies a view of what good practice is.
library.contested: Whether practices are universally good (“management as a technology”) or contingent on context remains debated; compare contingency theory (R-lawrence-1967-differentiation). The causal question was later tested experimentally (R-bloom-2013-does).
library.generalizability: Strong for medium-sized manufacturing in rich countries; plausible but less certain for professional services, health care and sports organizations.
library.relevance: Shows that “soft” management practices can be measured and matter for performance—and models the measurement discipline you should demand of any claim about management.

library.title: Does Management Matter? Evidence from India
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 128, issue 1, pages 1–51 and DOI matched on RePEc (econpapers.repec.org), LSE Research Online and the UK government research-outputs page. An open earlier version is NBER Working Paper 16658 (nber.org), which reports a smaller first-year productivity figure (11%) than the published article (17%).

library.summary: A randomized field experiment in large Indian textile firms gave free, intensive management consulting to randomly chosen plants, while control plants received only the initial diagnostic. The published article reports that adopting the practices raised productivity by 17 percent in the first year through better quality, efficiency and lower inventory, and that within three years treated firms opened more production plants. The authors attribute earlier non-adoption mainly to informational barriers.
arguments: Management practices causally affect productivity in this setting.
Firms had not adopted profitable practices mainly because of informational barriers—owners did not know them or doubted their value.
Limited managerial time constrained growth, which helps explain why badly managed firms were not driven out by competition.
library.design: Randomized field experiment: plants chosen at random received about five months of consulting on a defined set of operational practices; control plants received only the one-month diagnostic. Published descriptions report 28 plants across 17 firms.
library.strengths: Randomization addresses the main confound in the survey evidence; detailed measurement of operational outcomes; open working-paper version.
library.limitations: Small number of firms; one industry and country with low baseline practices; the treatment bundles many practices and expert attention, so the active ingredient is unclear; working-paper and published estimates differ.
library.contested: No failed replication is known to this course; durability was tested in a follow-up (R-bloom-2020-do), which found partial decay.
library.generalizability: Strong internal validity; external validity to knowledge work, services and sports organizations is uncertain and likely smaller where baseline practices are already structured.
library.relevance: The cleanest causal evidence that management practices matter, and a model of how to test an organizational intervention rather than assume it works.

library.title: Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, QJE 130(1) 165–218 and year matched on econpapers.repec.org and nber.org (w18871); DOI 10.1093/qje/qju032 matched in a separate search (academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn).

library.summary: A randomized experiment at a Chinese travel agency’s call center in which volunteers were randomly assigned to work from home or in the office. Home workers’ performance rose and attrition fell; when offered a choice afterwards, many workers switched.
arguments: Working from home raised measured performance in this setting.
Attrition fell among home workers.
Self-selection after the experiment changed who worked from home.
library.design: Randomized field experiment among volunteer call-center employees, followed by a period of free choice.
library.strengths: Randomization inside a real firm with objective performance data.
library.limitations: One firm, one occupation, volunteers only, a measurable and solitary task.
library.generalizability: Strong internal validity; transfer to collaborative or creative work is uncertain.
library.relevance: Assignment option (organizational behavior).

library.title: Do Management Interventions Last? Evidence from India
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 12, issue 2, pages 198–219 and DOI matched on RePEc (econpapers.repec.org). Open working-paper versions matched on nber.org (Working Paper 24249), the Stanford King Center page and the World Bank Open Knowledge Repository (Policy Research Working Paper 8339).

library.summary: The authors revisit the Indian textile firms from the 2013 management experiment about nine years later. Roughly half of the practices adopted in the experimental plants had been dropped, yet a large and significant gap with control plants remained. Practices spread within firms to non-experimental plants but rarely across firms, and managerial turnover and lack of directors’ time were among the most cited reasons for dropping practices.
arguments: Management interventions can have lasting effects even as many adopted practices decay.
Practices diffused within firms but rarely across firms.
Practice decay was linked to people: managerial turnover and limited director time.
library.design: Long-run follow-up of the plants in the randomized management experiment, comparing treatment and control plants roughly nine years after the experiment.
library.strengths: Rare long-run evidence on an organizational intervention with an experimental baseline.
library.limitations: Same small sample and single industry as the original experiment; attrition and changes in firms over nine years complicate comparison.
library.generalizability: Suggestive for any organization where practices depend on a few people; magnitudes specific to the setting.
library.relevance: Evidence that practices live in people and routines—directly relevant when key staff turn over in a department you lead.

library.title: Learning Versus Performance: An Integrative Review
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 25910388); scope of the review matched in the PubMed abstract.

library.summary: An integrative review of research showing that performance during training and long-term learning are different things. Drawing on animal learning, motor learning and verbal learning, the authors show that learning can occur without visible performance gains, that performance gains can fail to produce learning, and that some manipulations move the two in opposite directions. They also review how learners and instructors misread current performance as evidence of learning.
arguments: Learning (a relatively permanent change that supports retention and transfer) must be inferred from delayed or changed-context tests, not from performance during practice.
Conditions that slow acquisition — spacing, variation, interleaving, reduced guidance — can enhance long-term retention and transfer.
Learners and instructors are prone to treating fluent, error-free practice as proof of learning.
library.design: Narrative integrative review spanning animal learning, motor-skill learning, verbal learning and metacognition.
library.strengths: Unifies findings from several traditions under one distinction; written by a leading researcher on desirable difficulties; covers both motor and verbal learning.
library.limitations: Narrative rather than meta-analytic; much of the underlying evidence comes from laboratory tasks with short retention intervals. The review predates recent bias-corrected meta-analyses of some motor-learning effects.
library.contested: The distinction itself is well established. The size and applied reliability of specific desirable difficulties in motor learning are debated (see R-czyz-2024-effect, R-ammar-2023-myth, R-mckay-2024-reporting).
library.generalizability: The distinction applies to any training program, in sport, medicine, aviation or business. Effect sizes for particular techniques should not be assumed to carry over from the laboratory.
library.relevance: The single most useful idea for anyone who evaluates practice: what you see in the session is performance, and learning is what remains later.

library.title: Does Social Psychology Persist over Half a Century? A Direct Replication of Cialdini et al.’s (1975) Classic Door-in-the-Face Technique
library.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 120(2)
library.license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, journal, volume 120, issue 2 and DOI 10.1037/pspa0000261 matched on fis.leuphana.de, research.tilburguniversity.edu, zendy.io and the FORRT FLoRA replication atlas; first authors confirmed on kups.ub.uni-koeln.de. The full author list and page numbers were not confirmed, so only confirmed authors are listed. Some listings give 2020 (online-first).

library.summary: The authors directly replicated Cialdini and colleagues’ 1975 door-in-the-face study, in which a large initial request that is refused increases compliance with a smaller follow-up request. Running the study on a German university campus with 410 people approached by confederates, they found compliance rates similar to the original’s, and results consistent with the reciprocal-concessions explanation. The authors caution that this is one replication of one finding.
arguments: A classic compliance technique replicated in a different country, decades later.
The results support reciprocity norms (reciprocal concessions) as the mechanism.
Older social psychology findings have rarely been the target of direct replication.
library.design: Direct replication with confederates approaching people on a university campus; 410 participants.
library.strengths: Direct, preregistered-style replication of a field finding in a new culture; tests the theoretical mechanism, not only the effect.
library.limitations: One replication of one technique; student-campus setting with one-off requests by strangers, unlike repeated relationships at work.
library.contested: A positive data point in a mixed replication picture for the influence literature reviewed in R-cialdini-2004-social.
library.generalizability: Supports the existence of reciprocity-based concession effects; their size between colleagues who will deal with each other again is unknown.
library.relevance: Shows what a well-replicated influence finding looks like, so you can weigh the rest of the persuasion literature accordingly.

library.title: The Path of the Law
library.license: Public domain (published 1897; JSTOR lists the issue as public domain). Free full text is also available from Project Gutenberg.

verified.evidence: Title, author, Harvard Law Review volume 10, issue 8, pages 457–478 and year 1897 matched on jstor.org (stable 1322028) and scilit.net (DOI 10.2307/1322028). Public-domain full text listed on gutenberg.org. Search results also note it was first delivered as an address at Boston University School of Law in January 1897 and printed in the Boston Law School Magazine shortly before the Harvard Law Review.

library.summary: An address on what lawyers actually study when they study law. Holmes argues that, for practical purposes, law is a set of predictions about what courts will do, and that viewing law through the eyes of a "bad man" who cares only about consequences helps separate legal rules from moral judgments. He criticizes the idea that legal development follows from logic alone and urges attention to history, policy and economics.
arguments: Law, for the practitioner, is a prediction of how courts will apply public force.
The "bad man" perspective separates what the law requires from what morality requires.
Legal reasoning dressed as logic often conceals judgments about social advantage that should be made explicit.
Lawyers should study the reasons and consequences of rules, not only their history.
library.strengths: Short, influential and freely available; gives non-lawyers a practical frame (law as forecast) that maps directly onto risk-based decision-making.
library.limitations: A nineteenth-century jurisprudential essay, not empirical work. The prediction theory has been criticized by later legal philosophers for neglecting why officials and citizens treat rules as obligations; some passages reflect the views and language of its time.
library.contested: The prediction theory is debated within jurisprudence; this course uses it as a working tool, not as a settled account of what law is.
library.generalizability: The frame transfers well to any organization that must estimate legal risk; it is a lens for thinking, not a method that produces numbers.
library.relevance: Teaches the executive habit of asking counsel for forecasts with conditions and confidence rather than verdicts.

library.title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, group author, Science 349(6251) aac4716, year and DOI matched on discovery.dundee.ac.uk and research-portal.uu.nl.

library.summary: A large collaboration repeated 100 studies published in three prominent psychology journals, using high-powered designs and materials from the original authors where possible. Far fewer replications than originals produced statistically significant results, and replication effect sizes were on average about half the original estimates. Social psychology studies replicated less often than cognitive psychology studies.
arguments: Most original studies reported significant results; roughly a third or so of replications did.
Replication effects were, on average, about half the size of the originals.
Original effects that were larger and more strongly significant were more likely to replicate.
Replication rates differed by subfield, with social psychology lower than cognitive psychology.
library.design: Coordinated replication of 100 published studies by many independent teams.
library.strengths: Systematic sampling from journals rather than hand-picked targets; open materials.
library.limitations: One replication per study; some replications differed from originals in population or procedure; what counts as a successful replication is itself debated.
library.contested: Critics argued that differences in samples and procedures depress replication rates; the authors and later many-lab projects responded. The broad conclusion — many published effects are smaller or less reliable than reported — has held.
library.generalizability: Directly relevant to how much weight to give any single classic study cited in management or coaching.
library.relevance: Calibrates your trust in the famous studies that leadership books lean on.

library.title: Introduction to Psychology (PSYC 110, Spring 2007)
library.publication: Open Yale Courses, Yale University (recorded lecture course)
library.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (Open Yale Courses terms of use); third-party content is excluded unless a lecture’s Credits section says otherwise. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Course number, title, instructor (Paul Bloom) and recording term (Spring 2007) matched on oyc.yale.edu course and lecture pages; license (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, third-party exclusion) matched on oyc.yale.edu/terms and the course page.

library.summary: A full recorded Yale undergraduate survey of psychology, with lectures on foundations (including Freud), cognition, development, emotion, social behavior and the psychology of the good life. It is a broad, accessible map of the discipline taught by a prominent researcher. Lecture videos and transcripts are openly available.
arguments: Human behavior is best understood by combining evolutionary, cognitive, developmental and social explanations rather than any single lens.
Emotion and reason are intertwined; emotions are not simply errors in an otherwise rational system.
Some historically influential theories (for example, Freud’s) are presented for their influence, not as current scientific consensus.
library.strengths: Complete, openly licensed lecture series with transcripts; strong on the conceptual map of the field.
library.limitations: Recorded in 2007, before the replication crisis reshaped parts of social psychology; some findings presented then (for example in priming research) need to be checked against later replications. Introductory level.
library.contested: Parts of the social-psychology canon covered in introductory courses of this period have since failed large replication attempts; APERTURE flags these in the relevant weeks.
library.generalizability: Moderate: it builds vocabulary and theory, but organizational transfer requires the applied and replication-aware material in Weeks 1–3.
library.relevance: The owner named this course as a starting example. It is the open foundation for the behavioral-science school (Weeks 1–3) for a learner without formal psychology training.

library.title: The Iron Cage Revisited: Institutional Isomorphism and Collective Rationality in Organizational Fields
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 48, issue 2, pages 147–160 and DOI 10.2307/2095101 matched in a BibSonomy record, a ScienceGate record and Walter W. Powell’s Wikipedia bibliography.

library.summary: DiMaggio and Powell ask why organizations in the same field become so similar. They argue that once a field is established, organizations converge not mainly because similarity is efficient but through institutional isomorphism: coercive pressure from those they depend on and from the state, mimetic copying of organizations seen as successful when uncertainty is high, and normative pressure from professions and their training. Similarity confers legitimacy.
arguments: Organizational fields become homogeneous over time through institutional isomorphism.
Coercive isomorphism stems from dependence and political influence; mimetic isomorphism from uncertainty; normative isomorphism from professionalization.
Practices may be adopted for legitimacy whether or not they improve efficiency.
The paper offers testable hypotheses about which organizations and fields will change fastest.
library.design: Theoretical article with formal hypotheses; tested by a large later literature on the diffusion of practices.
library.strengths: Foundational to neo-institutional theory; explains why “everyone is doing it” is a powerful force independent of results.
library.limitations: Tends to overpredict sameness and underplay agency; isomorphic mechanisms are hard to separate empirically from rational learning.
library.contested: Debate continues on how to distinguish legitimacy-driven adoption from efficiency-driven adoption; resource dependence (R-pfeffer-1978-external) offers a competing explanation of conformity.
library.generalizability: High for public agencies, hospitals, universities, professional services and sports leagues, where professions and peer comparison are strong.
library.relevance: Helps you ask whether a proposed change is being adopted because it works or because peers have it — and how to use legitimacy honestly.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages (1–47), June 1967 date and DOI matched on scienceopen.com and scilit.net records. Search results also distinguish it from the authors’ separate 1967 book, Organization and Environment.

library.title: Differentiation and Integration in Complex Organizations
library.summary: A comparative field study of firms showing that effective organizations in uncertain environments combine strong differentiation between specialized units with strong integration across them, often through dedicated integrating roles or departments.
arguments: Specialized units develop different goals, time horizons and styles.
The more different the units, the harder and more valuable integration becomes.
Integrators are effective when they are seen as competent and balanced, not as agents of one unit.
library.design: Comparative field study of firms in several industries.
library.strengths: Empirical grounding for the idea of an integrating department.
library.limitations: Small number of firms from one era; cross-sectional associations.
library.generalizability: Moderate to high: coaches, analysts and scouts are classically differentiated groups.
library.relevance: Your department is an integrator; its legitimacy depends on being seen as balanced rather than as analytics’ outpost.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Journal of Applied Psychology 107(11) 2040–2068, year and DOI matched on ink.library.smu.edu.sg and siop.org (online Dec 2021).

library.title: Revisiting Meta-Analytic Estimates of Validity in Personnel Selection: Addressing Systematic Overcorrection for Restriction of Range
library.summary: The authors argue that earlier meta-analyses overcorrected for range restriction, inflating validity estimates for several selection methods. Their revised estimates place structured interviews at or near the top and lower the estimate for general cognitive ability tests.
arguments: Range-restriction corrections were often applied where they were not justified.
Revised validities are lower overall.
Structured, job-specific methods rank highly.
library.design: Re-analysis of meta-analytic evidence with revised corrections.
library.strengths: Transparent re-examination of a foundational literature.
library.limitations: Still debated; estimates depend on correction assumptions.
library.contested: Revises R-schmidt-1998-validity; the debate over corrections continues.
library.generalizability: Moderate: selection research comes mostly from large-sample jobs, not elite specialist roles.
library.relevance: Your first hires shape the department; structured, work-sample-based hiring is the defensible default.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Harvard Business Review January 2006 matched on store.hbr.org (product R0601D) and bain.com; volume/issue not confirmed (removed). The hbr.org article URL itself was not seen in results.

library.title: Who Has the D? How Clear Decision Roles Enhance Organizational Performance
library.summary: Consultants describe the RAPID approach to decision roles (Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide) and argue that bottlenecks usually come from unclear decision rights rather than from poor analysis.
arguments: Each important decision should have one clear owner of the final call.
Confusing Input with veto rights slows decisions.
Decision roles should be designed around the few decisions that create the most value.
library.design: Practitioner framework illustrated with client examples; no controlled evidence.
library.strengths: Simple, widely used vocabulary for decision rights.
library.limitations: A consulting heuristic; evidence is anecdotal and the firm has a commercial interest in the method.
library.generalizability: Useful as a design checklist anywhere; not evidence that clarity alone improves results.
library.relevance: Gives you a language to separate what Advance recommends from what the manager decides.

library.title: Debunking Fake News in a Post-Truth Era: The Plausible Untruths of Cost Underestimation in Transport Infrastructure Projects
library.publication: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice, 113, 357–368
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. An accepted manuscript is listed as open access in Curtin University’s espace repository (handle 20.500.11937/68682), seen in search results but not opened. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, pages and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org and espace.curtin.edu.au; the critique of Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl (2002) and the existence of a Flyvbjerg rebuttal matched trade-press coverage (transportxtra.com).

library.summary: A critique of the influential claim that cost underestimation in transport projects is best explained by optimism or deliberate deception. The authors argue that the “error or lie” framing is a false dichotomy, question the methodology and conclusions of the earlier work, and call for evidence-based approaches to setting capital cost estimates. Flyvbjerg replied that this view would keep planners getting costs wrong.
arguments: Framing cost underestimation as either honest error or deliberate lie is a false dichotomy given how large infrastructure assets are actually procured.
The methodology, analysis and conclusions of Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl (2002) are questioned and described as unfounded.
Policy-makers should rely on evidence-based research when setting capital cost estimates at the front end of major transport projects.
library.design: Critical methodological review and argument; no new controlled study.
library.strengths: Forces precision about causal explanations of forecast error; represents a live scholarly dispute.
library.limitations: Polemical in tone; offers critique more than an alternative validated forecasting method; only the abstract and secondary summaries were seen for this record.
library.contested: Directly contests the explanation advanced by Flyvbjerg and colleagues (see R-flyvbjerg-2008-curbing); the dispute remains unresolved.
library.generalizability: Reminds any organization that a single behavioral explanation of forecast error should be tested against alternatives, and that behavioral and technical causes can co-exist.
library.relevance: Models the kind of skepticism you should apply even to a celebrated explanation: ask what else could produce the pattern before accepting a claim about bias or deception.

library.title: TVA and the Grass Roots: A Study in the Sociology of Formal Organization
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (University of California Press, Berkeley) and 1949 date matched in a 1949 American Political Science Review book-review record (econpapers.repec.org) and Wikipedia’s entry on Selznick; later editions (1980; 2010 reissue) reported. The publisher’s own page did not appear in results, so the review record is linked. Details of the argument were confirmed only at a general level (co-optation of local elites).

library.summary: Selznick’s study of the Tennessee Valley Authority examines how a federal agency committed to “grass-roots” democratic administration worked through established local institutions and elites. He develops the concept of co-optation — absorbing outside elements into an organization’s leadership or policy-making to avert threats to its stability — and shows how informal co-optation can shift an organization’s actual commitments away from its stated goals.
arguments: Co-optation is a mechanism for gaining support or neutralizing threat by bringing outsiders into the organization’s decision structure.
Formal co-optation shares the appearance of power; informal co-optation shares its substance with powerful local interests.
Co-opted interests can redirect an organization’s programs, so the price of support can be drift from the original mission.
Formal organizations develop informal structures and commitments that constrain leaders.
library.design: Historical-institutional case study of a single federal agency.
library.strengths: Rich case analysis; founding text for the “old” institutionalism and for the study of co-optation; directly relevant to public administration.
library.limitations: Single case; interpretive analysis; the agency’s history is specific to its era.
library.generalizability: The mechanism of co-optation generalizes well to any organization that buys support by sharing control; the specific findings are historical.
library.relevance: Every coalition strategy that gives a resister a seat at the table has the trade-off Selznick documented.

library.title: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 2(2), pages 175–220 matched on a pages.ucsd.edu copy of the article’s first page and cir.nii.ac.jp; DOI prefix 10.1037 (APA) consistent with the APA copyright line.

library.summary: The standard review of confirmation bias: the seeking or interpreting of evidence in ways that are partial to existing beliefs, expectations or hypotheses. It catalogs many forms of the bias across laboratory tasks and real domains such as medicine, law, science and policy.
arguments: People tend to consider only the favored hypothesis, look for evidence that would be expected if it were true, and treat ambiguous evidence as support.
Confirmation bias appears in hypothesis testing tasks (for example the 2-4-6 rule-discovery task) and in professional settings.
The bias need not be deliberate; it operates even when people sincerely try to be objective.
library.design: Narrative review of experimental and historical evidence.
library.strengths: Comprehensive and readable; distinguishes many mechanisms that share a name.
library.limitations: Narrative rather than quantitative synthesis; some cited studies are older laboratory tasks.
library.generalizability: High. Any evaluation process that begins with a hypothesis — hiring, scouting, diagnosis, investment — is exposed.
library.relevance: Names the mechanism behind ‘we saw what we expected to see’ in evaluations and reviews.

library.title: The Effectiveness of Workplace Coaching: A Meta-Analysis of Learning and Performance Outcomes from Coaching
library.publication: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology, 89(2), 249–277
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology 89(2) 249–277, year and DOI matched on research.aston.ac.uk and centaur.reading.ac.uk.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of workplace coaching studies reporting positive average effects on learning and performance outcomes, and examining moderators of those effects.
arguments: Workplace coaching shows positive average effects on learning and performance outcomes.
Effects vary by outcome type and coaching arrangement.
The primary literature is small relative to the size of the coaching industry.
library.design: Meta-analysis of workplace coaching studies.
library.strengths: Focuses on organizational coaching rather than therapy or education.
library.limitations: Small number of primary studies; many rely on self-reported outcomes; coached people are rarely randomly selected.
library.generalizability: Moderate for managerial coaching; transfer to athletic coaching of skills is not established by this work.
library.relevance: Calibrates how much you should expect from coaching programs you buy or run.

library.title: Investigating Variation in Replicability: A “Many Labs” Replication Project
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, first author, journal, volume 45(3), pages 142–152 and DOI matched on research.tilburguniversity.edu, pure.psu.edu and a core.ac.uk copy; the very long author list differs slightly across records, so only the first authors are listed here and the order should be checked against the journal.

library.summary: Thirty-six samples in several countries ran the same 13 classic and contemporary effects. Ten replicated consistently, one received weak support and two priming effects did not replicate; variation across samples and settings was small relative to variation across effects.
arguments: Replicability depended mostly on the effect, not on the lab, country or online versus in-person setting.
Several judgment effects central to this week, including anchoring, replicated strongly.
Two flag and currency priming effects did not replicate.
library.design: Coordinated multi-site replication: 13 effects, 36 samples, 6,344 participants.
