library.strengths: Large, pre-specified, multi-site design with open data and materials (OSF).
library.limitations: Tests the selected effects only; short online or lab versions of each paradigm.
library.generalizability: Tells you which classic judgment effects are robust in the laboratory; it does not show their size in organizations.
library.relevance: Lets you separate robust judgment findings from fragile ones before you build a practice on them.

library.title: Is the Resource-Based “View” a Useful Perspective for Strategic Management Research?
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 26, issue 1 and pages 22–40 matched on EconBiz, Scilit-linked records and reference lists on journals.aom.org. Search results gave conflicting DOIs, so the DOI is omitted and the EconBiz catalogue record is used as the link.

library.summary: Priem and Butler argue that the resource-based view, as then formulated, is not yet a theoretical structure. They contend that it risks tautology when valuable resources are defined by the advantage they are meant to explain, that it assumed stable product markets, and that it did not explain how resource value is determined. They outline challenges for improving it, including formalization and integration with demand-side considerations.
arguments: The elemental RBV is at risk of being true by definition rather than testable.
Resource value is determined outside the firm, in product markets, which the RBV had not addressed.
The RBV had assumed stable product markets and paid little attention to time.
The framework needs formalization and integration with models of demand.
library.design: Critical conceptual review of the resource-based literature.
library.strengths: Forces precision about what counts as a valuable resource; its demand-side point remains influential.
library.limitations: A critique of theory construction rather than an empirical test; supporters dispute how much of the critique applies to Barney’s 1991 framework.
library.contested: Barney replied in the same issue (Academy of Management Review 26(1), 41–56) that the direct criticisms of his 1991 article were unfounded, while acknowledging the requirements the critique highlighted; Priem and Butler’s further comments in the same issue (pp. 57–66) reaffirmed the tautology charge for the elemental business-level RBV. See R-barney-1991-firm.
library.generalizability: The lesson — define value from customers and costs, before the fact — applies to any organization judging its own strengths.
library.relevance: Protects you from the most common misuse of strategy frameworks: labelling whatever a winner has as the cause of its winning.

library.title: A Behavioral Theory of the Firm
library.publication: Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall (Prentice-Hall Behavioral Sciences in Business Series); second edition Blackwell, 1992
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, publisher (Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J.), 1963 date and series matched in library catalog records (catalog.lib.msu.edu, tuklas.up.edu.ph) and a 1964 review in the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science (cambridge.org); 1992 second edition reported.

library.summary: Cyert and March replace the profit-maximizing firm of economic theory with a firm that is a coalition of participants whose goals conflict and are negotiated. Goals emerge from bargaining, are stated as aspiration levels, are attended to sequentially, and are held together by side payments and organizational slack; firms search for solutions when performance falls below aspirations and settle for satisfactory rather than optimal outcomes.
arguments: The firm is a coalition of individuals and groups, not a single decision maker with one goal.
Organizational goals are the outcome of bargaining among coalition members and are revised by experience.
Conflict is never fully resolved; it is managed by attending to goals one at a time and by slack resources.
Firms satisfice and search locally, prompted by problems.
library.design: Theoretical book with case studies and computer models of firm decision making.
library.strengths: Founding text of the behavioral theory of organizations; makes politics a normal feature of organizational decision making rather than a pathology.
library.limitations: Abstract about the mechanics of coalition formation; empirical support comes mainly from later research rather than the book itself.
library.generalizability: High: the coalition view fits public agencies, professional service firms and sports organizations as well as industrial firms.
library.relevance: Any change you propose alters a negotiated settlement among coalition members; this book explains why that settlement exists.

library.title: Self-Determination Theory and the Facilitation of Intrinsic Motivation, Social Development, and Well-Being
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, American Psychologist 55(1) 68–78, year and DOI matched on scilit.com and bibbase.org.

library.summary: The standard short statement of self-determination theory. It proposes three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — and a continuum of motivation from amotivation through externally controlled forms to internalized and intrinsic forms. Social environments that support the three needs are argued to foster internalization, persistence and well-being.
arguments: Motivation varies in kind (autonomous vs. controlled), not only in amount.
Autonomy, competence and relatedness are proposed as universal psychological needs.
Extrinsic motivation can be internalized (identified, integrated regulation) when the context supports the three needs.
library.design: Theoretical review summarizing a research program.
library.strengths: Clear, influential framework with a large empirical literature behind it.
library.limitations: Written by the theory’s founders; summarizes supportive evidence. The universality of the needs and the measurement of the regulation continuum are debated.
library.generalizability: Widely applied to work, education, health and sport; the distinctions are useful for leaders even where effect sizes vary.
library.relevance: Gives you the vocabulary — autonomy, competence, relatedness, internalization — for diagnosing why the same incentive energizes one group and alienates another.

library.title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (Crown Business, New York), year 2011 and ISBN 9780307886231 matched in library catalogue records and the Penguin Random House listing. The kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action) and the hallmarks of bad strategy were confirmed from multiple secondary summaries, not from the book text.

library.summary: Rumelt distinguishes good strategy from the goals, slogans and wish lists that often pass for it. A good strategy has a kernel: a diagnosis that names the critical challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that carry the policy out. He catalogues the hallmarks of bad strategy, including fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy and poorly chosen strategic objectives.
arguments: The kernel of a strategy is diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action.
Goals and aspirations are not strategies; a strategy explains how a specific obstacle will be overcome.
Bad strategy is common and recognizable: fluff, failure to face the challenge, goals mistaken for strategy, and jumbled or unattainable objectives.
Good strategy concentrates resources and action where they will have the greatest effect.
library.design: Book-length argument drawing on the author’s consulting and teaching experience and on business and historical examples; no systematic empirical test.
library.strengths: Highly practical; the kernel can be applied at any level, from a whole company to a single department, and makes weak plans easy to spot.
library.limitations: A practitioner framework built from experience and selected examples; there is no evidence that plans containing a kernel outperform others, and examples are chosen by the author.
library.generalizability: Applies broadly to business, government, military and sports organizations; best used as a diagnostic checklist rather than as a predictive model.
library.relevance: Provides the template for this week’s strategy memo and a language for challenging plans that confuse ambition with strategy.

library.title: An Evolutionary Theory of Economic Change
library.publication: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, publisher (Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge, Mass.) and year matched on the CiNii academic library record (ci.nii.ac.jp) and a Journal of Economic History book review on cambridge.org listing xi + 437 pages. The publisher’s own page was not seen; the link is a library catalog record.

library.summary: Nelson and Winter build an evolutionary theory of the firm in which organizational routines—regular, predictable patterns of activity—play the role that skills play for individuals and genes play in biology. Routines store an organization’s operational knowledge, much of it tacit; they settle internal conflicts as a working truce; and markets select among firms partly on the basis of their routines. The result explains why capabilities persist, why they are hard to copy and why firms change slowly.
arguments: Routines are the main form in which organizations store operational knowledge, much of it tacit.
Routines function as a truce that settles conflicts over who does what.
Firms change through search and selection among routines, so capabilities are persistent and hard to imitate.
library.strengths: Foundational; supplies the mechanism behind organizational memory, inertia and capabilities; influential across economics, strategy and organization theory.
library.limitations: Long, technical in places and partly devoted to formal economic modeling; “routine” can become a label for anything that persists; mechanisms are illustrated more than measured.
library.generalizability: High as a conceptual lens for any organization; it does not predict which routines will matter in a particular department.
library.relevance: Explains why reorganizations and staff turnover can destroy capability that appears in no document—and why new practices count only once they become routine.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Harvard Business Review and 1995 (July issue) matched on business.columbia.edu and ritamcgrath.com; volume/pages conflict between sources (44–52 vs 44–54) and were removed. The hbr.org URL was not seen in results.

library.title: Discovery-Driven Planning
library.summary: For new ventures, the authors propose planning backward from required results, listing assumptions explicitly and organizing milestones around testing the riskiest assumptions before committing more resources.
arguments: New ventures run on assumptions, not facts.
Milestones should be checkpoints where assumptions are tested.
Commitment should grow as assumptions are confirmed.
library.design: Practitioner method with illustrative examples.
library.strengths: Directly usable for staged roadmaps.
library.limitations: Practitioner heuristic; little controlled evidence.
library.generalizability: High for a new department with an unproven value case.
library.relevance: The model for a roadmap with decision gates rather than a calendar of tasks.

library.title: Social Influence: Compliance and Conformity
library.license: © Annual Reviews. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 55, pages 591–621 and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 14744228) and citedrive.com.

library.summary: A review of compliance and conformity research published mainly between 1997 and 2002. Cialdini and Goldstein organize the literature around the goals that make people susceptible to influence — the desire to be accurate, to affiliate with others, and to maintain a positive self-concept — and argue that influence often operates subtly and outside awareness. The review covers the classic compliance principles, including reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity.
arguments: Compliance and conformity serve three broad goals: accuracy, affiliation and a positive self-concept.
Classic compliance principles can be understood as shortcuts toward those goals.
Influence often works through subtle, indirect processes outside awareness.
Norms — descriptive (what people do) and injunctive (what people approve) — are powerful influences on behavior.
library.design: Narrative review of the social influence literature.
library.strengths: Authoritative synthesis by the field’s best-known researcher; theoretical organization rather than a list of tricks.
library.limitations: Narrative, not meta-analytic; published before the replication crisis reshaped social psychology, so effect sizes of individual studies were not re-examined.
library.contested: Several individual findings in the influence literature have shown smaller or inconsistent effects in later replications; others, such as the door-in-the-face technique, replicated well (R-genschow-2021-does).
library.generalizability: The principles are general; the size of any technique’s effect in an organizational, repeated-relationship setting is uncertain.
library.relevance: Teaches the mechanisms behind persuasion so you can recognize them — when you use them and when they are used on you.

library.title: Culture and Conformity: A Meta-Analysis of Studies Using Asch’s (1952b, 1956) Line Judgment Task
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Psychological Bulletin 119(1) 111–137, year and DOI matched on bibliographic indexes (data.zhenzhi.com, synapsesocial.com) and a scan of the article.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of studies that used Asch’s line-judgment task, in which a participant faces a unanimous group giving a clearly wrong answer. Conformity was a robust phenomenon, but its size varied: it was larger with larger majorities and in more collectivist cultures, and in U.S. studies it declined over the decades after Asch’s original work.
arguments: Conformity to a unanimous majority is a replicated phenomenon.
Its magnitude depends on group size, the participant’s relationship to the group and culture.
Conformity levels in U.S. samples declined over time, suggesting historical context matters.
library.design: Meta-analysis of Asch-paradigm studies conducted in many countries.
library.strengths: Quantifies a classic finding across time and cultures rather than relying on one iconic study.
library.limitations: Laboratory task with unambiguous stimuli and strangers; conformity in real organizations involves ambiguity, status and consequences.
library.generalizability: The direction (people shift toward unanimous groups) generalizes well; the specific rates do not.
library.relevance: Shows what a robust classic finding looks like when examined carefully: real, but variable and context-dependent.

library.title: An Integrative Model of Organizational Trust
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, year, volume 20 issue 3 and pages 709–734 matched on bibbase.org and verdi.cs.ucl.ac.uk. Two DOIs appear in results: 10.2307/258792 (JSTOR, bibbase) and 10.5465/amr.1995.9508080335 (linked by explore.psychsafety.com); the AOM DOI is used here but was not resolved directly.

library.summary: Defines trust as willingness to be vulnerable to another party and separates it from trustworthiness. Perceived trustworthiness rests on ability, benevolence and integrity, moderated by the trustor’s propensity to trust; trust leads to risk-taking in the relationship, whose outcomes update the perceptions.
arguments: Trust is a willingness to accept vulnerability, distinct from its antecedents.
Trustworthiness has three factors: ability, benevolence and integrity.
Trust propensity differs between people and matters most when information is scarce.
Trust produces risk-taking, and outcomes feed back into perceived trustworthiness.
library.strengths: Clear definitions that later empirical work has used widely; distinguishes causes of trust from trust itself.
library.limitations: A conceptual model; its components were tested later by other researchers rather than in this paper.
library.generalizability: High as a diagnostic frame across industries; the relative weight of each factor likely varies by context and relationship stage.
library.relevance: Lets you diagnose which part of trust is broken — competence, care or consistency — instead of treating trust as a mood.

library.title: Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In
library.publication: Houghton Mifflin, Boston (1st ed.); 2nd ed. 1991 and 3rd ed. 2011 with Bruce Patton (Penguin)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors (Roger Fisher, William Ury), 1981 first edition with Houghton Mifflin, later editions (1991, 2011) adding Bruce Patton, the four principles of principled negotiation and the origin of the term BATNA matched on en.wikipedia.org and an EBSCO Research Starters entry (ebsco.com). No publisher page was found in search results, so the URL is a reference page rather than the publisher’s.

library.summary: The founding practitioner text of “principled negotiation”, written by members of the Harvard Negotiation Project. It argues for separating the people from the problem, focusing on interests rather than positions, inventing options for mutual gain and insisting on objective criteria. It introduced the term BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) as the standard against which any proposed agreement should be measured.
arguments: Positions are what parties say they want; interests are why they want it. Agreements built on interests are easier to find and more durable.
Your BATNA, not a fixed “bottom line”, is the proper benchmark for judging a proposed deal; developing it starts with listing what you could do if no agreement is reached.
Objective criteria (market data, precedent, professional standards) let parties settle distributive questions without a contest of wills.
library.design: Prescriptive book drawing on the authors’ practice and teaching; not an empirical study.
library.strengths: Clear, durable vocabulary (interests, options, criteria, BATNA) that most later research and teaching adopted; usable immediately.
library.limitations: Practitioner prescription, not tested evidence. Critics argue it underplays the distributive side of bargaining and the role of power; its examples are illustrative rather than systematic.
library.contested: Its advice to focus on interests and joint gains is broadly consistent with later laboratory work on integrative bargaining (e.g. R-thompson-1990-social), but the book itself presents no data, and its treatment of value claiming is thinner than analytic treatments such as R-lax-1986-manager and R-raiffa-1982-art.
library.generalizability: High as a preparation vocabulary across industries and in sport; the claims about what works best should be treated as heuristics to test.
library.relevance: Gives you the core vocabulary for this week (interests, BATNA, objective criteria) and the language most counterparts, agents and lawyers will use with you.

library.title: The Opposable Mind: How Successful Leaders Win Through Integrative Thinking
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, year and publisher (Harvard Business School Press, ISBN 9781422118924) matched on publishersweekly.com, a Wikipedia entry and library listings. The companion article “How Successful Leaders Think” (Harvard Business Review, June 2007, vol. 85, no. 6, starting p. 60) matched in secondary listings; no official HBR page for it appeared in results, so it is not given its own record.

library.summary: Martin, then dean of the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management, argues that many effective leaders share a habit of mind he calls integrative thinking: holding two opposing models in tension and constructing a new model that keeps elements of each and is superior to both, rather than accepting a trade-off. He develops the idea from work with business leaders and argues that it can be learned and practiced.
arguments: Effective leaders resist forced choices between opposing models and search for a creative resolution.
Integrative thinkers treat more factors as salient, accept nonlinear and multidirectional causal relationships, and keep the whole problem in view while working on its parts.
An integrative resolution is better than either opposing model, not a compromise between them.
The capacity can be developed through practice and teaching.
library.design: Practitioner argument drawn from the author’s interviews and teaching with business leaders; no controlled comparison.
library.strengths: A clear, memorable prompt for looking past binary choices, and a useful distinction between integration and compromise.
library.limitations: Built on successful leaders’ accounts of their own thinking, so it is exposed to survivorship and to retrospective storytelling. There is no controlled evidence that training integrative thinking improves decisions.
library.contested: Not tested experimentally as a causal claim; treat it as a practitioner heuristic rather than a research finding.
library.generalizability: Usable as a deliberation prompt in any setting where opposing models compete, including sport organizations. Claims about its effectiveness do not generalize because they have not been tested.
library.relevance: Gives you a vocabulary for refusing false trade-offs when behavioral, financial, legal and strategic considerations collide — while practicing the course’s habit of labelling practitioner ideas as such.

library.title: The ASA’s Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 70, issue 2, pages 129–133 and DOI matched in search results (EPA HERO reference record; tandfonline.com / informahealthcare.com DOI page). Free availability is believed but was not separately confirmed.

library.summary: The American Statistical Association’s first formal statement on a matter of statistical practice. It sets out six principles about what p-values can and cannot tell you and explains why the board felt a statement was needed.
arguments: A p-value measures how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model, not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not rest only on whether a p-value passes a threshold.
Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency; a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect.
By itself a p-value is not a good measure of evidence regarding a model or hypothesis.
library.strengths: Consensus statement from a professional body after deliberation among statisticians with differing views; short and readable.
library.limitations: Deliberately says what not to do more than what to do; the accompanying commentaries show statisticians still disagree about replacements (Bayesian methods, estimation, lower thresholds).
library.contested: The principles are broadly accepted; what should replace threshold-based testing remains debated.
library.generalizability: Fully general: applies to any analytics report, vendor study or internal A/B test that reports p-values.
library.relevance: Gives you precise language for challenging analysts and vendors who treat “significant” as “true and important”.

library.title: Structural Holes and Good Ideas
library.license: © The University of Chicago. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 110, issue 2, pages 349–399 and DOI 10.1086/421787 matched in search results (doi listing, Stanford SNAP course reading copy, scilit.com).

library.summary: Burt argues that people whose networks span structural holes — gaps between groups that are not otherwise connected — are more likely to have good ideas, because they see combinations of perspectives that people inside one group do not. Using data on supply-chain managers in a large American electronics company, he reports that managers whose networks spanned holes were more likely to voice ideas, less likely to have them dismissed and more likely to have them judged valuable, and also received more favorable evaluations, compensation and promotion.
arguments: Opinion and behavior are more homogeneous within groups than between them, so brokers across groups see alternatives earlier.
Brokerage across structural holes is associated with ideas that senior managers rate as valuable.
Brokerage is also associated with compensation, positive performance evaluations and promotion.
The value of a good idea depends on being able to move it across groups, not only on generating it.
library.design: Network survey of managers in one company linked to ideas they proposed (rated by senior managers) and to career outcomes; cross-sectional association.
library.strengths: Direct measurement of network structure; outcome measures independent of the respondent (ideas rated by others, compensation records); clear mechanism.
library.limitations: Single firm; observational design cannot rule out that able or ambitious people build brokerage networks (reverse causation); brokerage may carry costs, such as distrust, that the design does not capture.
library.contested: The benefits of brokerage versus closure (dense, trusting networks) remain debated, and appear to depend on culture and task; see R-granovetter-1973-strength for the related weak-ties argument.
library.generalizability: Plausible in knowledge work where combining perspectives matters; less certain in settings that reward loyalty and closure.
library.relevance: Bridging groups — for example across departments, languages or countries — is a structural asset, and also a responsibility.

library.title: Ethical and unethical bargaining tactics: An empirical study
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Surveyed MBA students at two business schools (320 and 736 respondents) on how appropriate they considered 18 bargaining tactics. Factor analysis found five clusters of tactics that were similar across the two samples. Tough but not outright dishonest tactics, such as inflating an opening demand, were widely accepted; outright lies and bribery were widely rejected. Acceptability differed by sample, gender, age and work experience, and nationality.
arguments: Negotiators distinguish “traditional competitive bargaining” (e.g. inflated opening demands) from misrepresentation, bluffing about facts and bribery.
There is broad agreement at the extremes and real disagreement in the middle of the spectrum.
Judgments of acceptability vary with personal characteristics and context, so your counterpart’s ethics may not match yours.
library.design: Cross-sectional survey of two MBA samples rating the appropriateness of 18 tactics; factor analysis and group comparisons.
library.strengths: Large samples; replicated factor structure across two schools; gives a shared vocabulary for tactic types.
library.limitations: Self-reported judgments of hypothetical tactics by MBA students; acceptability is not the same as behavior; data from the 1990s.
library.generalizability: Moderate: useful as a map of where norms agree and disagree; actual behavior under pressure may differ from stated judgments.
library.relevance: Helps you write a personal policy for the grey zone of bargaining and predict where counterparts will draw their own lines.

library.title: The Loser’s Curse and the Critical Role of the Utility Function

Evaluations of decision quality should make the assumed objective explicit.

library.strengths: Highlights a hidden assumption in a famous finding; statistically careful.

library.relevance: Reminds you that “efficient” spending depends on the organization’s objective — wins, championships, profit or development — which must be stated before any budget is judged.

library.title: Do Team and Individual Debriefs Enhance Performance? A Meta-Analysis
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year (online June 2012) and DOI matched on PubMed (PMID 23516804) and journals.sagepub.com; the main result (46 samples, N = 2,136, about 25%, d = .67) and moderators matched the abstract; a full-text copy appeared on cebma.org (Center for Evidence-Based Management).

library.summary: A meta-analysis of 46 samples (N = 2,136) of team and individual debriefs drawn from published and unpublished research. On average, debriefs improved performance over control conditions by approximately 25% (d = 0.67). Effects were stronger when debriefs were aligned with objectives, and facilitation and structure appeared to contribute.
arguments: Debriefs improve individual and team performance on average by a practically meaningful amount.
Alignment between the debrief and specific objectives strengthens the effect.
Facilitation and structure may increase benefits.
A debrief must meet a defined set of essential elements; loosely run reviews are not what the estimate describes.
library.design: Meta-analysis of published and unpublished studies of interventions that met the authors’ definition of a debrief.
library.strengths: Pools many studies across team and individual settings; tests moderators; includes unpublished work.
library.limitations: Included studies vary in setting and design; moderator findings rest on fewer studies; an average effect does not tell any single organization what to expect.
library.generalizability: Supports structured reviews in organizations and sport, with the caveat that implementation quality varies and field settings with long feedback delays are less directly represented.
library.relevance: The strongest single summary of whether after-action reviews and debriefs work, and of the design features that matter.

library.title: Opportunity Cost Neglect
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, all five authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, December 2009 issue and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org, ideas.repec.org and profiles.wustl.edu; main findings matched the abstract and Yale School of Management news summaries.

library.summary: A set of experiments showing that people often fail to consider what else they could do with their money. Simple cues that remind decision-makers of the alternative uses of funds reduced purchase rates and shifted choices toward cheaper options, sensitivity varied with people’s chronic spending attitudes, and the authors argue that effort alone typically does not overcome the neglect.
arguments: Opportunity costs are frequently neglected unless they are made explicit.
Making the alternative use of resources salient changes choices, even under conditions that promote careful thought.
Individual differences in spending attitudes moderate the effect.
library.design: Several consumer-choice experiments manipulating whether the option of not buying was framed as keeping money for other purchases.
library.strengths: Clean manipulations of a single framing cue; directly relevant to how alternatives are presented.
library.limitations: Consumer purchases with modest stakes; organizational budget decisions involve committees, other people’s money and longer horizons, so the effect size will not transfer directly.
library.generalizability: The mechanism — alternatives that are not presented are not weighed — plausibly applies to organizational budgets, where proposals are often evaluated one at a time; treat magnitude as unknown.
library.relevance: Supports a practical rule for your budget process: every proposal must name the next-best use of the same money and staff time.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Journal of Applied Behavioral Science 47(4) 461–524, year and DOI matched on journals.sagepub.com and cris.huji.ac.il.

library.title: Change Recipients’ Reactions to Organizational Change: A 60-Year Review of Quantitative Studies
library.summary: A review of quantitative studies on how employees react to organizational change, organizing antecedents (recipient characteristics, internal context, change process, perceived benefit) and consequences.
arguments: Reactions depend heavily on the change process, especially participation, communication and trust in management.
Perceived personal impact shapes reactions.
Resistance is multidimensional (affective, cognitive, behavioral).
library.design: Systematic narrative review of quantitative studies.
library.strengths: Broad coverage across decades.
library.limitations: Many included studies are cross-sectional self-reports.
library.generalizability: High for coaching-staff reactions to a new department.
library.relevance: Gives an evidence base for change management beyond step models.

library.title: The Effect of Contextual Interference on Transfer in Motor Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, article number, publication date (14 August 2024) and DOI matched on frontiersin.org and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC11349744); effect sizes matched in the abstract text shown in results.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of 34 studies on whether high contextual interference (random practice) improves transfer of motor skills. Overall, random practice was favored with a medium effect (SMD = 0.55). In laboratory studies the effect was medium and statistically significant (SMD = 0.75); in applied settings it was small and not statistically significant (SMD = 0.34); in young participants it was negligible (SMD = 0.12). A companion paper by the same group reports a retention benefit.
arguments: Random practice tends to improve transfer of motor skills on average.
The effect is clearer in laboratory tasks than in applied sport and physical-education settings.
Age and setting moderate the effect, so a single prescription for all learners is not justified.
library.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of experiments comparing high and low contextual interference with a transfer test; subgroup analyses by setting and age.
library.strengths: Recent, focused on transfer (the outcome coaches care about), and reports the laboratory–applied gap explicitly.
library.limitations: Applied studies are fewer and noisier, so the applied estimate is imprecise; the authors favor the contextual-interference hypothesis, while other recent meta-analyses read the evidence more skeptically.
library.contested: Read alongside R-ammar-2023-myth, which finds little support for applied benefits; the two groups have exchanged published critiques.
library.generalizability: The most relevant single estimate for sport: expect a smaller and less certain benefit in real practice than in laboratory demonstrations.
library.relevance: Shows exactly where a famous laboratory effect becomes uncertain — at the point where you would apply it.

library.title: Unfreezing Change as Three Steps: Rethinking Kurt Lewin’s Legacy for Change Management
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 69(1), pages 33–60 and DOI matched on the Victoria University of Wellington repository (openaccess.wgtn.ac.nz, which hosts an accepted manuscript) and iro.uiowa.edu; the Paper of the Year 2016 award is reported on wgtn.ac.nz.

library.summary: The authors compare what Kurt Lewin actually wrote about change with how the “unfreeze–change–refreeze” model is presented in later textbooks and argue that Lewin never developed such a model: it took its familiar form after his death in 1947. They suggest that treating the three-step model as the field’s foundation has narrowed how change is taught and studied.
arguments: The three-step model attributed to Lewin is largely a later reconstruction.
Lewin’s broader work—field theory, group dynamics and action research—is richer and less linear than the model bearing his name.
Foundational myths shape what a field treats as settled; re-examining them opens space for new approaches.
library.design: Historical and textual analysis comparing Lewin’s writings with later accounts.
library.strengths: Primary-source scholarship; highly cited and widely read in its journal.
library.limitations: A historiographical argument: it changes how we read the model’s pedigree, not whether a staged view of change is useful.
library.contested: Some scholars defend the practical value of a staged view regardless of its attribution.
library.generalizability: Applies to how any leader uses inherited frameworks: know where a model comes from before treating it as evidence.
library.relevance: Shows that even the most-taught change model rests on a shaky citation trail—useful discipline for an evidence-minded executive.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, Academy of Management Journal 18(4) 769–783 and year matched in reference lists (talkingaboutorganizations.com, typeset.io); the DOI could not be confirmed in two searches and was removed. URL is the AOM DOI link from the original record and is unconfirmed.

library.title: On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B
library.summary: A classic essay showing how organizations routinely reward behavior different from the behavior they say they want, using examples from government, medicine, universities and business. The reward system, not the stated goal, predicts what people do.
arguments: Stated goals and actual reward criteria often diverge, and people follow the rewards.
Measurable proxies crowd out hard-to-measure goals.
Fixing behavior usually requires changing what is counted and rewarded, not exhorting people.
library.design: Conceptual essay built on case illustrations; no original data analysis.
library.strengths: Durable, clear mechanism that travels across sectors.
library.limitations: Illustrative examples rather than systematic evidence; does not quantify how often misalignment occurs.
library.generalizability: High as a diagnostic lens for any department scorecard, including sports operations.
library.relevance: Your performance indicators will become the department’s real job description; this paper explains why.

library.title: Decoding the DNA of the Toyota Production System
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, both authors (Harvard Business School), the September–October 1999 issue and the four-year study of Toyota plants matched on copies indexed at uottawa.ca and labqualityconfab.com and on Steven Spear’s Wikipedia entry. Volume and page numbers were not confirmed, so they are omitted; the hbr.org URL follows HBR’s pattern and was not opened.

library.summary: Based on a multi-year study of Toyota and its suppliers, the authors argue that Toyota’s performance comes not from visible tools such as kanban cards or andon cords but from tacit rules: work is highly specified, connections between people are direct and unambiguous, pathways are simple, and improvements are made by the scientific method at the lowest possible level. The rigid specification of work is what makes flexibility and learning possible.
arguments: Specified work turns every activity into a testable hypothesis, so deviations become visible immediately.
Direct customer–supplier connections and simple pathways make problems traceable to their source.
Improvement is experimentation, done by the people doing the work, under the guidance of a teacher.
Organizations that copy the tools without the underlying rules rarely reproduce the results.
library.design: Multi-year field study of Toyota and supplier plants, reported in a practitioner journal.
library.strengths: Deep field observation; moves the discussion from tools to mechanisms; widely used in healthcare and service operations.
library.limitations: Focused on one exemplary company; rules are inferred by the authors; not a comparative test of performance effects.
library.generalizability: The rules apply most directly to repetitive work but have been adapted widely; transfer depends on management capability, not on tool adoption.
library.relevance: Shows how standardization and learning can reinforce each other—central to any operations or development system you design.

library.title: Non-Contractual Relations in Business: A Preliminary Study
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, American Sociological Review volume 28, issue 1 (February 1963), pages 55–67 and JSTOR stable 2090458 matched in search results (JSTOR-derived PDF hosted at edisciplinas.usp.br; University of Wisconsin Law repository record; a Springer reprint in Stewart Macaulay: Selected Works). A journal DOI was not confirmed, so none is given.

library.summary: An exploratory interview study of how businesspeople actually manage exchange relationships. Macaulay reports that they often plan transactions incompletely and seldom use legal sanctions to adjust relationships or settle disputes, relying instead on reputation, continuing relationships and shared norms. The paper became a foundation of the "relational contract" and law-and-society traditions.
arguments: Businesspeople frequently leave exchanges only partly planned.
Legal sanctions are seldom used to adjust relationships or resolve disputes.
Non-legal sanctions — reputation, repeat dealing, personal relationships — do much of the enforcement work.
Formal contract planning has costs as well as benefits and is used selectively.
library.design: Exploratory interview study; the article reports interviews with 68 businesspeople.
library.strengths: Rich, grounded observation that challenged a purely doctrinal view of contracts; still a standard reading in contracts and economic sociology.
library.limitations: Interviews rather than measured outcomes; a particular time, region and industry mix; described by its author as preliminary.
library.contested: Later commentators accept the core observation but argue it needs specification: formal contracts may matter little in healthy ongoing relationships and much more at their end or in one-off deals. Contrast the doctrinal view summarized in R-ali-1981-restatement.
library.generalizability: Likely to generalize to repeat-dealing relationships in many industries, including sports; weaker for one-off, high-stakes or adversarial transactions.
library.relevance: Connects the learner's sociology background to contract practice: contracts work alongside relationships and reputation, and matter most when those fail.

library.title: Smith v. Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d 858
library.license: Judicial opinion (public record). Linked via Justia, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Case name, citation 488 A.2d 858, court (Supreme Court of Delaware) and 1985 decision matched on law.justia.com and opencasebook.org; the holding (directors who approved a merger without informing themselves were grossly negligent, breached the duty of care and lost business-judgment-rule protection) matched in several case summaries. Some summaries give a January 29, 1985 decision date.

library.summary: The Delaware Supreme Court held that the directors of a public company breached their duty of care by approving a cash-out merger without first informing themselves of reasonably available information, and that their decision was therefore not protected by the business judgment rule. The court reversed the lower court's judgment for the directors and sent the case back for a determination of damages.
arguments: The business judgment rule presumes an informed decision; it does not protect directors who failed to inform themselves.
The duty to make an informed decision is a duty of care, breached by gross negligence in the process.
A favorable price does not by itself cure an uninformed decision process.
library.design: Appellate judicial decision reviewing a board's approval of a merger.
library.strengths: Canonical case on the duty of care; widely taught; illustrates process-based review clearly.
library.limitations: One state's law (Delaware) and one fact pattern; later legal developments changed how often directors face personal liability for care claims; summaries simplify a long opinion.
library.contested: The decision has long been debated: some see it as a needed demand for diligence, others as encouraging defensive documentation.
library.generalizability: Delaware law governs many U.S. corporations, so the principles are influential; nonprofits, public bodies and non-U.S. entities follow different rules.
library.relevance: Teaches that leaders are judged on the quality of their decision process — a principle that applies inside any organization.

library.title: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
library.license: Official U.S. government publication (United States Reports). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Case name, citation 449 U.S. 383 (1981), decision date January 13, 1981 and majority opinion by Justice Rehnquist matched on govinfo.gov, law.cornell.edu and americanbar.org; holdings (rejection of the "control group" test; work-product doctrine applies to IRS summonses) matched in the official syllabus.

library.summary: The Supreme Court held that the attorney-client privilege can protect communications between a corporation's counsel and employees below senior management, made to gather information needed to give the corporation legal advice. The case arose from an internal investigation into questionable foreign payments, in which counsel used questionnaires and interviews; the IRS sought those materials. The Court also held that the work-product doctrine applies to IRS summonses.
arguments: A narrow "control group" test would discourage the flow of information counsel needs and is rejected.
Communications from employees to corporate counsel, made at the direction of superiors to secure legal advice, can be privileged.
The privilege protects communications, not the underlying facts.
Work-product protection applies to materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, including in tax-summons proceedings.
library.design: U.S. Supreme Court decision.
library.strengths: The foundational federal case on corporate privilege; short and readable.
library.limitations: Applies to federal law; state privilege rules and other countries' rules can differ, and later cases refine how privilege applies to in-house counsel and mixed business-legal communications.
library.generalizability: Applies to U.S. organizations of all kinds in federal matters; the practical habits it implies transfer widely.
library.relevance: Explains why organizational lawyers say "I represent the company" and why forwarding legal advice can waive protection.

library.title: Transnational Transfer of Strategic Organizational Practices: A Contextual Perspective
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 24(2), pages 308–324 matched across several indexes (scinapse.io, proquest.com, academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn); DOI 10.2307/259084 matched on the last.

library.summary: Kostova defines the success of transferring a practice across borders within a multinational as its institutionalization at the receiving unit and proposes a model in which factors at three levels—country (the institutional distance between home and host settings), organization, and individual relationships—shape whether the practice takes hold.
arguments: Transfer success means institutionalization: the practice is both implemented and given meaning and value by the recipients.
The greater the difference between the regulatory, cognitive and normative environments of the two countries, the harder the transfer.
Organizational culture and relationships between units (trust, identification, dependence) also shape transfer.
library.design: Theoretical model with propositions; later tested empirically by the author and colleagues.
library.strengths: Gives precise vocabulary for why a practice can be followed on paper but not believed in.
library.limitations: Propositions rather than tests in this article; measurement of institutional distance is difficult.
library.generalizability: Directly relevant to multi-country organizations, including sports organizations with international academies.
library.relevance: Explains why a development system can be “implemented” at a foreign site while staff privately ignore it—and what to work on instead.

library.title: Predictors and Consequences of Intellectual Humility
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, all six authors, journal, volume 1(9), pages 524–536 and DOI matched on pubmed.gov (PMID 35789951) and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC9244574, open copy).

library.summary: Reviews research on intellectual humility, whose common core across definitions is a metacognitive ability to recognize the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge. It covers what predicts it, its benefits and drawbacks for decisions, relationships, science and society, and the limits of the evidence.
arguments: Intellectual humility is best understood as metacognitive: recognizing that one’s beliefs may be wrong.
It varies with situations and can be encouraged, not only a fixed trait.
It is associated with more careful evaluation of evidence, but much of the evidence is correlational and drawn from Western samples.
library.design: Narrative review.
library.strengths: Recent, careful about definitions, explicit about the weakness of the evidence.
library.limitations: Mostly correlational and self-report evidence; generalizability beyond WEIRD societies is weakly supported.
library.generalizability: Moderate: plausible in leadership settings, but causal effects of humility on organizational outcomes are not established.
library.relevance: Grounds the week’s theme in evidence and keeps it from becoming a slogan.

library.title: Transformational and Transactional Leadership: A Meta-Analytic Test of Their Relative Validity
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 89, pages 755–768 and DOI matched in abstract copies (academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn, core.ac.uk listings); abstract figures .44 (transformational), .39 (contingent reward), −.37 (laissez-faire) and “626 correlations from 87 sources” matched in the same results.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of the full-range model of leadership. Transformational leadership showed the highest overall validity, but contingent reward, a transactional behavior, was close behind and stronger on several criteria; laissez-faire leadership was negatively related to the criteria.
arguments: Overall validity of .44 for transformational leadership across 626 correlations from 87 sources.
Contingent reward (.39) is nearly as strongly related to outcomes and stronger for some criteria.
Laissez-faire leadership relates negatively (−.37) to the criteria.
library.design: Meta-analysis of 626 correlations from 87 sources relating leadership dimensions to criteria such as follower satisfaction, motivation and leader effectiveness.
library.strengths: Large evidence base; directly compares transformational and transactional behaviors.
library.limitations: Inherits the designs of the primary studies, many of which rate leadership and outcomes from the same source; correlations are not causal estimates.
library.contested: R-vanknippenberg-2013-critical argues that the measures behind these correlations are confounded with the outcomes they predict, so the size of the validities may overstate leader effects.
library.generalizability: Moderate. Associations appear across many settings, but subjective criteria dominate; transfer to objective team performance is less certain.
library.relevance: Gives you the strongest pro-transformational numbers in the field, so you can weigh them against the critique rather than against a slogan.

library.title: The Artful Dodger: Answering the Wrong Question the Right Way
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on a PubMed-indexed listing (PMID 21517203), the American Psychological Association press release (EurekAlert) and Harvard Magazine; an author-hosted PDF appeared on toddrogers.scholars.harvard.edu. One result gave a DOI, but a second search could not confirm it, so no DOI is recorded.

library.summary: In four studies using recorded debate answers, listeners often failed to notice when a speaker answered a similar but different question, and rated that speaker as trustworthy and likable as one who answered directly. Clearly different answers were penalized, and so were halting answers to the right question. Displaying the question while the speaker answered made dodges far easier to detect.
arguments: Answers to a similar question frequently go undetected as dodges.
Fluent delivery is rewarded even when the content dodges; a smooth dodger can be preferred to a stammering answerer.
Keeping the original question salient sharply increases detection — in the press summary, from 39% to 88% of listeners.
library.design: Four experiments in which participants evaluated debate answers that addressed the question asked, a similar question or a clearly different question.
library.strengths: Controlled manipulations separate the content of an answer from its delivery.
library.limitations: Participants had no relationship with the speaker and no stake in the decision; the setting is political debate; how often dodges succeed in boardrooms is unknown.
library.generalizability: The mechanism plausibly transfers to executive settings; the magnitudes do not. Boards that read pre-reads, know the speaker and repeat their questions may catch dodges more often.
library.relevance: Shows why direct answers to hard questions are a matter of integrity and governance, not style — and how a skilled questioner keeps a dodge from working.

library.title: Artful paltering: The risks and rewards of using truthful statements to mislead others
library.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 112(3), 456–473
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 112, issue 3, pages 456–473 and date (March 2017; online December 2016) matched on hks.harvard.edu and in the APA press release (apa.org, December 2016). The DOI did not appear in search results, so it is omitted. Findings come from the abstract and press release.

library.summary: Defines paltering as the active use of truthful statements to create a misleading impression, distinct from lying by commission (false statements) and lying by omission (passively not sharing). Across pilot studies and six experiments (over 1,750 participants), paltering in negotiation helped palterers claim value but also raised the likelihood of impasse and harmed their reputations when detected. Targets judged paltering about as unethical as lying; palterers and observers judged it more favorably.
arguments: Paltering is common and many people prefer it to outright lying.
It can claim value in the short run but increases impasse risk and reputational damage.
Targets treat paltering as the ethical equivalent of a false statement, a perception gap palterers underestimate.
library.design: Two pilot studies and six experiments, including negotiation tasks, with more than 1,750 participants in total.
library.strengths: Names and measures a tactic that ethics codes often miss; multiple studies; includes the target’s perspective.
library.limitations: Laboratory and online samples with modest stakes; detection is engineered by the design; legal consequences are not studied.
library.contested: No independent replication of the negotiation studies was confirmed in our search; treat this as a multi-study paper from one research team, consistent with but not yet established by other work.
library.generalizability: Moderate to high: repeated-game settings (staff, agents, vendors, partner organizations) make the reputational costs larger than in one-shot lab tasks.
library.relevance: Draws the line most executives blur: technically true but misleading statements. Essential for an executive whose reputation is a long-term negotiating asset.

library.title: When and Why Incentives (Don’t) Work to Modify Behavior
library.license: Free to read from the American Economic Association. Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year and DOI matched on econpapers.repec.org and econbiz.de. Open access is from the AEA’s public JEP archive (not separately re-checked this session).

library.summary: A readable review of field and laboratory evidence on when monetary incentives change behavior in the intended direction. The authors argue that incentives have a direct price effect but also change how people interpret a task and what their behavior signals to others and to themselves, so incentives can raise effort in the short run while weakening intrinsic or social motives. They examine education, contributions to public goods, and lifestyle change such as smoking and exercise.
arguments: Incentives have a standard price effect and a psychological effect; the second can work against the first.
Paying for a behavior can change its meaning (from a social obligation to a market exchange), as in the authors’ discussion of fines for late pickup at day-care centers.
Short-run gains under incentives may not persist after incentives are removed, and can crowd out later voluntary engagement.
Design lessons: size, framing, timing and what the incentive signals all matter.
library.design: Narrative review of field experiments and laboratory studies in economics and psychology.
library.strengths: Written for non-specialists; draws on field experiments; balanced about when incentives do work.
library.limitations: A narrative review, not a meta-analysis; selection of studies reflects the authors’ program of research.
library.contested: Crowding-out is well documented in some settings and absent in others; see R-cerasoli-2014-intrinsic for a quantitative synthesis.
library.generalizability: High for public policy, education and health; reasonable for workplaces, where pay is already expected.
library.relevance: The best single entry point into the economics of incentives with behavioral caveats — the vocabulary this week’s exercise and assignment use.

library.title: Examining the Impact of Culture’s Consequences: A Three-Decade, Multilevel, Meta-Analytic Review of Hofstede’s Cultural Value Dimensions
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 95(3), pages 405–439 and DOI 10.1037/a0018938 matched in search results; a post-print is held in the University of Calgary repository (prism.ucalgary.ca), which notes it is not the copy of record.

library.summary: A meta-analysis of 598 studies covering more than 200,000 individuals tests how well Hofstede’s original four cultural value dimensions predict organizational outcomes. Relationships are modest on average (an overall absolute weighted correlation of about .18 at the individual level), stronger for emotions and attitudes than for behaviors and job performance, and stronger in culturally “tighter” countries.
arguments: Cultural values have real but modest predictive power for work outcomes.
They predict job performance, absenteeism and turnover less well than personality and demographics do, but predict commitment and citizenship behavior better.
Effects are strongest for emotions, then attitudes, then behaviors, and weakest for performance.
Context matters: effects are larger in tighter societies with stronger norms.
library.design: Multilevel meta-analysis of 598 studies (more than 200,000 individuals).
library.strengths: Very large evidence base; tests the dimensions against outcomes rather than assuming them; compares with other predictors.
library.limitations: Depends on the quality of primary studies, most of which are correlational; aggregate effects say little about any one person or workplace.
library.contested: Hofstede’s framework itself is criticized on conceptual and methodological grounds (see R-mcsweeney-2002-hofstedes).
library.generalizability: Supports using cultural dimensions as weak priors about groups, not as predictions about individuals or as the main design input for a rollout.
library.relevance: Lets you use cultural frameworks with calibrated confidence instead of either dismissing or over-applying them.

library.title: Negotiation behavior when cultures collide: The United States and Japan
library.license: © American Psychological Association. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 86, issue 3, pages 371–385 and year matched in the ACNP union catalogue index (acnpsearch, University of Bologna) and a bibliographic database; the DOI was listed by one index and follows the journal’s DOI pattern. Findings below come from the abstract.

library.summary: Japanese and U.S. managers negotiated an integrative task with partners from their own culture and from the other culture; transcripts were coded and analyzed. U.S. negotiators shared information directly and avoided influence tactics within and across cultures; Japanese negotiators shared information indirectly and used influence with each other but adapted their behavior in intercultural negotiations. Culturally typical behaviors partly explained why intercultural pairs reached lower joint gains than intracultural pairs.
arguments: Cultures differ in how negotiators exchange information (direct questions and answers versus indirect inference from offers).
Intercultural pairs reached lower joint gains than same-culture pairs, partly because their information-exchange routines did not mesh.
Negotiators can and do adapt their behavior when they cross cultures; adaptation is part of the skill.
library.design: Simulation with Japanese and U.S. managers in intra- and intercultural dyads; coded transcripts analyzed with logistic and linear regression.
library.strengths: Managers rather than students; behavioral coding of what negotiators actually said; links behavior to joint gains.
library.limitations: Two countries only; one simulation; culture measured by nationality, which hides large within-country variation.
library.contested: National culture as an explanatory variable is debated: individual and regional variation is large, and meta-analytic evidence in other bargaining paradigms finds weak links to cultural indices (R-oosterbeek-2004-cultural).
library.generalizability: The mechanism (mismatched information-exchange routines lower joint gains) plausibly transfers to other cross-cultural pairs; the specific U.S.–Japan profiles do not.
library.relevance: Gives you an evidence-based way to think about cross-border negotiations, including those in Latin America, without relying on national stereotypes.

library.title: The Case for Motivated Reasoning
library.license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 108(3), pages 480–498 and DOI matched on pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMID 2270237) and a fbaum.unc.edu course copy.

library.summary: Argues that motivation affects reasoning through the cognitive processes people use to search for and evaluate evidence. Accuracy goals lead to more careful processing; directional goals lead people to reach the conclusions they prefer — but only as far as they can construct a seemingly reasonable justification.
arguments: Two kinds of goals shape reasoning: accuracy goals and directional goals.
Directional goals bias which memories, rules and beliefs are accessed and how evidence is weighed.
People are constrained by an ‘illusion of objectivity’: they reach desired conclusions only when they can justify them to a dispassionate observer.
library.design: Theoretical review of experimental studies.
library.strengths: Explains why intelligent, honest people reach self-serving conclusions; widely confirmed in later work.
library.limitations: Older evidence base, largely laboratory studies with students.
library.generalizability: High. Wherever a person has a stake in a conclusion — their own draft pick, hire or project — directional goals apply.
library.relevance: Explains why the person who championed a decision is the worst-placed to review it alone.
