c-legal-risk-management.name: Legal risk management and working with counsel

glossary.definition: A family of theories distinguishing autonomous (Type 1) processing from processing that requires working memory and supports hypothetical thinking (Type 2). Whether there are two distinct types is debated.

Holding a representation of a possibility separate from what you currently believe so that you can reason about it hypothetically; a defining function of Type 2 processing in Evans and Stanovich’s account.
A setting in which observable cues are reliably related to outcomes, so that the regularities can in principle be learned.
Fast, recognition-based judgment that is accurate because it was learned in a high-validity environment with ample practice and timely, clear feedback.
Monitoring and regulating your own thinking: knowing where a judgment came from, how reliable it is likely to be, and when to slow down or seek a check.
A mental shortcut or strategy that ignores part of the available information; efficient and often adequate, but predictably wrong in some environments.
The tendency of numerical estimates to stay close to an initial value, even an arbitrary one, because adjustment from it is insufficient.
How common an outcome or category is in the relevant population before considering the specifics of a case; the starting point for any probability judgment.
Presenting probabilistic information as counts of cases from one reference population (for example, 9 of 98 positives), which makes Bayesian reasoning far easier.
Seeking or interpreting evidence in ways that are partial to existing beliefs, expectations or hypotheses.
Reasoning steered by a directional goal toward a preferred conclusion, constrained by the need to construct a seemingly reasonable justification.
The degree to which a decision strategy is adapted to the structure of the environment in which it is used.
Excessive certainty in the accuracy of one’s beliefs, visible as ranges and forecasts that are too narrow; the most persistent form of overconfidence.
The match between stated confidence and actual frequency: a calibrated forecaster’s 70% predictions come true about 70% of the time.
The mean squared difference between stated probabilities and outcomes (1 or 0); a proper scoring rule in which lower is better and 0.25 is what constant 50% forecasts earn.
Forecasting by first asking how often outcomes of this kind occur in a reference class of similar cases, before adjusting for the specifics of the case.
Unwanted variability in judgments that should be identical; divided into level, pattern and occasion noise.
A study in which several judges evaluate the same cases independently, so that the variability of their judgments can be measured.
Procedures that reduce judgment error without knowing its direction: independent judgments, structured assessments, sequenced information, relative scales, the outside view and aggregation.
Recognizing the limits of one’s beliefs and knowledge and that one might be wrong; shown in proportional updating.
The tendency of observers to explain others’ behavior by their dispositions while underweighting the situational pressures acting on them; also called correspondence bias.
Changing one’s judgments or behavior to match those of a group. In Asch-type tasks it is robust but varies with majority size, culture and era.
Repeating a study’s procedure as closely as possible with new participants to test whether the original result is reliable.
A replication whose protocol and analysis are fixed and reviewed in advance, often run across many laboratories, so that results are published regardless of outcome.
The claim that self-control draws on a limited resource used up by earlier acts of self-control; a large preregistered multi-lab test found an effect near zero.
A theory of motivation distinguishing autonomous from controlled motivation and proposing that support for autonomy, competence and relatedness fosters the former.
Doing an activity because it is interesting or satisfying in itself, rather than for a separable outcome such as pay or approval.
The process by which an externally prompted behavior comes to be valued and self-endorsed (identified or integrated regulation), making it autonomous though not intrinsically enjoyable.
When an external incentive weakens an existing intrinsic or social motive, for example by turning a moral obligation into a purchasable service; the reverse is crowding in.
The difficulty that arises when a principal delegates work to an agent whose actions cannot be fully observed and whose interests differ, creating hidden action and hidden information.

When an agent divides effort among tasks that differ in measurability, strong incentives on the measured tasks divert effort from the unmeasured ones; weaker incentives or job redesign may be optimal.
The heuristic that a measure loses its value as an indicator once it becomes a target, because people find cheaper ways to move the measure than the goal. Related to Campbell’s law.
How incentive pay changes with the measure — linear, threshold, capped, relative or deferred — which determines where marginal incentives are strongest and which gaming strategies pay.
Responding to kind actions with kindness and to unkind actions with retaliation, even at personal cost; it helps enforce incomplete contracts and norms.
Contributing to shared efforts when others do and withdrawing when others free ride, which makes group cooperation fragile without sanctions.
A shared expectation about what people do and ought to do, enforced informally through approval and disapproval.
The benchmark — prior outcome, peer outcome or expectation — against which an outcome is judged as a gain, a loss, fair or unfair.
A shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as asking questions or admitting errors; associated with learning and performance, mostly in correlational studies.
A relatively permanent change in capability that supports retention and transfer; it must be inferred from delayed or changed-context tests.
What a learner does during or immediately after practice; an observable but potentially misleading index of learning.
A condition that slows or complicates acquisition but improves long-term retention or transfer, provided the learner can eventually succeed.
Practicing by recalling information or a procedure from memory rather than reviewing it; the basis of the testing effect.
Distributing a fixed amount of practice across separated sessions rather than massing it into one.
Mixing different kinds of problems or tasks within a session so that the learner must choose the approach, not only execute it.
A test of a practiced skill or knowledge after a delay, usually without feedback, used to infer learning.
Effortful, individualized practice designed, often by a teacher, to improve a specific aspect of performance, with immediate feedback and repetition with refinement.
The share of the differences in an outcome across a sample that can be predicted from a variable; for one predictor, the square of the correlation.
Reduced variation in a variable within a selected sample, which weakens its observed relationship with outcomes even if it matters.
The effect in which practicing several tasks in a mixed or random order depresses practice performance but can improve retention and transfer relative to blocked practice.

glossary.term: Knowledge of results and of performance
glossary.definition: Augmented feedback about the outcome of a movement (results) or about the movement pattern itself (performance).
The proposal that frequent augmented feedback aids practice performance but can impair retention by creating dependence on the feedback.
Where a performer directs attention: internally to body movements or externally to the movement’s effect; the claimed external-focus advantage is contested.
An ecological-dynamics coaching method that manipulates individual, task and environmental constraints so that effective movement solutions emerge.
The demand that a task and its presentation place on limited working memory; instruction should reduce load created by poor presentation.
The finding that instructional methods that help novices, such as detailed guidance, can become redundant or harmful for more expert learners.
Use of learning in a similar task or context (near) versus a substantially different domain (far); far transfer is rare.
The claim that instruction matched to a learner’s preferred modality improves learning; it lacks the crossover evidence needed to support it.
The tendency of cases selected for extreme values on a noisy measure to be closer to the average when measured again, with or without any intervention.
The consistency of a measure: the share of its variation that reflects stable differences rather than noise. Low reliability attenuates observed effects.
The degree to which a measure captures the construct it claims to measure, and supports the inferences drawn from it.
A range produced by a procedure that captures the true value in a stated share of repeated samples (for example 95%); read as the effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data.
The probability of data at least as extreme as those observed if a specified model, usually of no effect, were true. Not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
The probability that a study detects a true effect of a given size at its significance threshold; it rises with sample size, effect size and measurement precision.

glossary.term: Type M and type S errors
glossary.definition: A type M error is an exaggerated estimate of an effect’s magnitude; a type S error is an estimate with the wrong sign. Both are common among significant results from low-powered studies.
The many analytic choices (outcomes, samples, covariates, stopping rules) that, when made after seeing the data, inflate false positives.
The selective publication or presentation of results depending on their significance or direction, which distorts the visible body of evidence.
A time-stamped plan specifying hypotheses, outcomes and analyses before data are collected or seen.
A publication format in which a journal reviews and accepts a study’s question and design before results exist, so publication does not depend on the outcome.
The outcome that would have occurred for the same units without the treatment; every causal effect compares an observed outcome with a counterfactual.
A variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, creating an association that is not the treatment’s effect.
A variable caused by both the treatment and the outcome (or their causes); selecting on or adjusting for it creates a spurious association.
A design that compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group, assuming their trends would otherwise have been parallel.
A design that compares units just above and just below a cutoff that determines treatment.
A factor that changes the likelihood of treatment but affects the outcome only through the treatment, such as a lottery for program slots.
Whether a result obtained in one population, setting and time holds in others.
The principle that an indicator used as a target or for high-stakes decisions tends to be gamed and to lose its value as a measure.
A statistical synthesis that pools estimates from several studies, weighted by precision, and examines how much they vary (heterogeneity).
The tendency of observers to explain organizational outcomes by pointing to leaders, strongest after extreme outcomes.
An observer’s inference that a person is or is not an effective leader, often drawn from outcomes and impressions rather than observed behavior.
A family of leader behaviors — articulating a vision, modeling values, stimulating and supporting followers — claimed to raise performance beyond expectations; its measurement is disputed.
A transactional leader behavior: agreeing on goals with people and recognizing or rewarding them when the goals are met.
The absence of leadership: avoiding decisions, being unavailable and not responding to problems; consistently associated with worse outcomes.
A perspective holding that leaders form relationships of different quality with different followers, and that relationship quality relates to outcomes.
A willingness to be vulnerable to another party based on the expectation that they will act in a way important to you, without your being able to monitor or control them.
The perceived characteristics that lead someone to trust another: ability, benevolence and integrity.
A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, such as admitting errors or raising concerns.
The theory that feedback works by directing attention, and that it helps less or harms when it draws attention from the task toward the self.
A practitioner technique of asking for suggestions about future behavior instead of evaluating past behavior; plausible but thinly researched.
The explicit degree of decision authority given to a person for a type of decision, from being told what to do to full ownership.
A practitioner writing convention, from U.S. military usage, that places the conclusion or request in the opening sentences.
A practitioner structure, associated with Barbara Minto’s consulting writing, that places a governing idea first, supported by grouped arguments and then evidence.
Working out an audience’s decision rights, prior beliefs, accountability and vocabulary before deciding what to say and in what order.
A popular term for the impression that a person has the judgment and composure of a senior leader; mostly described in practitioner writing rather than validated research.
The capacity to affect what others do, including when they would prefer otherwise; relational and situational rather than a fixed possession.
Power accepted as legitimate because of a position or rule; the right to direct, recognized by those who are directed.
French and Raven’s typology of the reasons a target complies: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert power, with informational power added later by Raven.
The principle that A’s power over B equals B’s dependence on A, which grows with the importance of what A controls, A’s discretion over it, and B’s lack of alternatives.

Pfeffer and Salancik’s theory that organizations are shaped by dependence on actors who control critical resources, and act to manage that dependence through co-optation, alliances, mergers and diversification.
A relationship of low frequency or intimacy, such as an acquaintance; per Granovetter, the kind of tie that usually bridges groups and carries new information.
A gap between two groups that are not otherwise connected and hold different information; spanning it gives a broker earlier, more diverse information.
A person whose ties connect otherwise disconnected people or groups; gains information and control benefits and may face distrust or overload.
A dense network in which most members are connected to one another; it supports trust and norm enforcement but tends to circulate redundant information.
The informal network showing whom people rely on for technical help and information; distinct from the trust network.
The informal network showing with whom people share sensitive information and whom they back in a crisis; decisive for whether a change is believed.
The subset of organizational members whose agreement actually determines major decisions; not necessarily the top of the formal chart.
In the behavioral theory of the firm, the inducements — budget, status, autonomy, policy commitments — that keep coalition members committed to the organization.
Resources beyond what is strictly needed for current operations, which allow an organization to satisfy several coalition members at once and to absorb conflict.
The process by which organizations in a field become similar through coercive, mimetic and normative pressures rather than only through efficiency.
The perception that an organization or practice is appropriate and proper within a system of norms and beliefs; it helps secure resources and support.
Absorbing outside or opposing elements into an organization’s leadership or decision structure to avert threats; Selznick showed it can shift the organization’s actual commitments.
Efforts by people below the top to direct senior leaders’ attention to particular issues and shape how they are understood, through packaging and process.
A behavior used to change another person’s attitudes or actions, such as rational persuasion, consultation, exchange, legitimating or pressure.
Commitment is inward agreement and effort to make a request succeed; compliance is doing what is asked without belief, often minimally.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you will take if this negotiation fails. It is the benchmark for judging any proposed deal.
The worst terms you would accept in this negotiation; the point at which you are indifferent between agreeing and taking your BATNA.
The ambitious but defensible outcome you are trying to achieve; it governs how much of the zone of agreement you try to claim.
The range of outcomes that both parties prefer to their alternatives; it exists only when their reservation values overlap.
A situation in which one party knows something relevant, such as its own reservation value, that the other does not. Distributive bargaining largely consists of managing it.
Bargaining over a fixed amount of value, where one side’s gain is the other’s loss; also called value claiming.
Bargaining that finds agreements better for both parties than other available agreements, usually by exploiting differences in priorities, forecasts or capabilities; also called value creation.
Trading concessions across issues, so that each side gives ground on what matters less to it in return for what matters more.
The set of agreements that cannot be improved for one party without making the other worse off. Agreements inside it leave value unclaimed.
An agreement whose terms depend on a future, observable outcome, such as an earnout or performance fee, used when parties disagree about the future.
The tension, named by Lax and Sebenius, that the moves that create value, such as revealing priorities, also expose a negotiator to the moves that claim it.
A practitioner technique: presenting several complete packages of equal value to you at once and learning about the other side’s priorities from which one it prefers.
The assumption that the other side’s interests are directly opposed to yours on every issue, which leads negotiators to miss trades and compatible issues.
A number, often the first offer, that pulls subsequent judgments and the final settlement toward itself.
An experiment in which one player proposes a split of money and the other accepts it or rejects it, in which case both get nothing; used to study fairness.
The conflict that arises when someone acting on another’s behalf has different incentives or information from the person they represent.
Approval of a negotiated agreement by people who were not at the table, such as a board, legislature or membership; it bounds what negotiators can agree.
Using truthful statements to create a misleading impression; distinct from lying by commission and from passively omitting information.
The degree to which an organization’s subunits develop different goals, time horizons, interpersonal styles and formality as each adapts to its own part of the environment.
The quality of collaboration among differentiated subunits that an organization needs to achieve unity of effort, and the mechanisms that produce it.
The view that no single structure is best; effective structure depends on fit with the organization’s task, technology and environment.
The gap between the information a task requires and the information the organization already has; in the information-processing view, it drives how much information must be processed during the work.
Deliberate spare capacity—longer lead times, buffers, less demanding targets—that reduces the need for coordination at the cost of idle resources.
Coordinating devices that let units decide together without escalating: direct contact, liaison roles, task forces, teams, integrating roles and matrix structures.

A unit given every skill and resource a product, customer or region needs, so that fewer decisions require coordination with other units; it trades duplicated specialists for a lighter information load.
A position whose job is to coordinate differentiated units—such as a bed-management coordinator or a technical director—often with authority to resolve conflicts between them without escalation.
One of Mintzberg’s five ways of aligning work: direct supervision, standardization of work processes, outputs or skills, and mutual adjustment.
The number of people who report directly to one manager; wider spans mean fewer managers and layers but less supervision and coaching per person.
The formal authority to initiate, approve, carry out or veto a decision, and the allocation of that authority across roles.
Knowledge that is costly to transmit—tacit, local or perishable—so that decisions using it are best made by the people who hold it; contrasted with cheaply transmitted general knowledge.
The cost that arises when a principal delegates to an agent with different interests: monitoring and incentive spending, the agent’s reassurance costs, and value lost to remaining divergence.
A practitioner heuristic that assigns, for each task or decision, who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. Not an empirically validated instrument.
A practitioner heuristic from management consulting that assigns decision roles: Recommend, Agree (a formal veto), Perform, Input and Decide. Not an empirically validated instrument.
The observation that organizations design systems mirroring their own communication structures; studied as the mirroring hypothesis and found common but not universal.
The research program, begun by Bloom and Van Reenen, that scores firms’ monitoring, targets and people-management practices from double-blind interviews.
A regular, predictable pattern of interdependent action through which an organization does its work; it stores tacit knowledge and settles who does what.
In Hackman’s terms, a group with clear boundaries, genuinely interdependent work and reasonably stable membership—the first condition for team effectiveness.
Performing similar activities better than rivals — faster, cheaper, with fewer errors. Necessary for superior performance but, in Porter’s account, not sufficient, because the practices diffuse.
Performing different activities from rivals, or similar activities in different ways, to deliver a distinctive mix of value to a chosen set of customers.
A strategic choice in which more of one thing means less of another, so that activities suited to one position are unsuited to another. Trade-offs make positions hard to copy.
Trying to occupy two incompatible positions at once, which carries the costs of both and the advantages of neither.
The degree to which an organization’s activities are consistent with its strategy and reinforce one another. Fit protects a position because rivals must copy a system, not a single practice.
Rumelt’s core of a good strategy: a diagnosis of the critical challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that carry the policy out.
The value of the best alternative given up by making a choice. Every allocation of money, people or attention has one.
Porter’s framework for industry profitability: threat of entry, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes and rivalry among competitors.
The most a customer would pay for a product rather than go without it. The top of the value line; value created is willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost.
The total value created with a particular player minus the total value created without it. Brandenburger and Stuart show that a firm cannot capture more than its added value.
The theory that sustained competitive advantage comes from resources and capabilities that differ across firms and cannot easily be traded or copied.
Barney’s criteria for a resource that can sustain advantage: valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable and non-substitutable.
Uncertainty, even inside the firm, about which resources produce an advantage, which leaves rivals unsure what to copy.
A firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences in response to rapidly changing environments (Teece, Pisano and Shuen).
A strategic investment treated as the right but not the obligation to act later — to expand, stage, wait or abandon — which gives flexibility value under uncertainty.
A practitioner method that tests a strategy against a few plausible, internally consistent futures rather than a single forecast, to find no-regret moves, options and risks.
A pattern in an organization’s actions that was realized without having been intended (Mintzberg and Waters); contrasted with deliberate strategy.
Executive slang for spreading resources thinly and evenly across all initiatives to avoid conflict, which usually contradicts any stated strategy.
Recording revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred to produce that revenue, regardless of when cash changes hands.
The statement of performance over a period: revenues minus expenses, on an accrual basis, equal net income.
The statement of position at a moment: assets equal liabilities plus owners’ equity.
The statement that explains the change in cash over a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities, and reconciles accrual profit to cash.
Current assets minus current liabilities; increases in receivables and inventory absorb cash, increases in payables release it.
Commonly, cash from operations minus capital expenditure: the cash available to lenders and owners after maintaining and growing the asset base.
The sum of all of a project’s cash flows, each discounted to today at the opportunity cost of capital, including the initial outlay; positive NPV means the project beats its alternative.
The discount rate at which a project’s NPV equals zero; useful as a summary but unreliable for ranking mutually exclusive projects or non-conventional cash flows.
The time until cumulative cash inflows recover the initial outlay; discounted payback uses discounted cash flows. It ignores cash after the cutoff.
The blended required return of a firm’s lenders (after tax) and owners, weighted by their shares of financing; the right discount rate only for projects of average risk.
The present value of a project’s future cash flows divided by its initial cost; ranking by it is exact under capital rationing only when projects are divisible.
Price minus variable cost per unit: what each additional unit contributes to fixed costs and profit. Fixed costs divided by it give break-even volume.
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered under any option; irrelevant to the decision except through any salvage or reuse value.
The value of the best alternative forgone by a choice, including alternative uses of scarce staff time; real even though no invoice records it.
Allocating a fixed budget among positive-NPV projects that cannot all be funded, by maximizing total NPV across feasible combinations.

Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time to see which drive value; scenario analysis changes several together in coherent stories, often weighted by probability to give an expected value.
The right, but not the obligation, to take a future action on a real investment — to wait, stage, expand or abandon — whose value rises with uncertainty and irreversibility.
Forecasting a project’s cost, timing or results from the actual outcomes of a class of comparable past projects (the outside view), then adjusting only for documented differences.
The additional revenue from employing one more unit of an input: its marginal product (such as wins) times the marginal revenue of that output.
The value of a person’s performance to the organization minus what the organization pays them; the return on talent and development investments.
A teaching and writing structure — Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion — for organizing legal analysis. A heuristic for disciplined thinking, not a theory of how judges decide.
Identifying the legal and commercial questions that a set of facts or a document raises, before attempting to answer them.
A rule fixes the content of a command before people act (“within 30 days”); a standard leaves the content to be supplied afterward by a decision-maker (“within a reasonable time”).
The practice of following earlier decisions of higher courts in the same jurisdiction on materially similar questions; decisions from other jurisdictions are persuasive only.

Which party must persuade the decision-maker, and to what standard: preponderance of the evidence in most civil cases, beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal cases, and clear and convincing evidence for some civil claims.
What each party gives in a bargained-for exchange — a promise or performance sought in return for the other side’s — required for most contracts to be enforceable.
A doctrine under which a promise may be enforced without consideration when the promisor should have expected reliance, the promisee did rely, and injustice can be avoided only by enforcement.
The interpretive principle that genuinely ambiguous contract language is construed against the party that drafted it, usually as a tie-breaker of last resort.
An event that must occur before a party’s duty to perform arises. If it does not occur, the duty never becomes due and there is no breach.
A representation is a statement of fact made to induce a contract; a warranty is a promise that a stated fact is true, backed by a remedy. Commercial contracts often combine them.
A promise by one party to cover specified losses or claims suffered by the other, often including the cost of defending claims brought by third parties.
Money that puts the injured party where it would have been had the contract been performed, limited by foreseeability, reasonable certainty and the duty to mitigate.
The U.S. default under which either party may end employment at any time for any lawful reason, subject to statutory, public-policy, contractual and collective-bargaining limits.

A clause restricting a worker from working for, or starting, a competing business for a period and area after leaving; enforceability depends mainly on state law. Non-solicitation clauses, by contrast, bar soliciting clients or employees.
A clause transferring to an employer or client ownership of inventions and work product; its wording determines whether personal or pre-existing work is captured.

Authority a third party reasonably believes an agent has because of the principal’s own conduct, such as a title or a history of honored deals; it can bind the principal even if internal limits were exceeded.
The duties of care and loyalty owed by those who act for others — directors, officers, agents — to decide on an informed basis and to put the principal’s interests ahead of their own.
A presumption that directors made an informed decision in good faith and without conflicts. If it holds, courts do not second-guess the merits of the decision.
Protection from disclosure for confidential communications between a client and its lawyer made to obtain or give legal advice. It covers communications, not facts, and can be waived by sharing.
Protection for materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, such as a lawyer’s notes and analysis, with especially strong protection for the lawyer’s opinions and mental impressions.
The difference between an organization’s stated strategic choices and the pattern of work, resource allocation and attention that actually follows.
A self-reinforcing loop in which pressure to meet targets diverts time from improvement, capability erodes, performance falls further, and leaders blame people rather than the system.
The recurring cadence of reviews—daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly—through which an organization notices deviations and makes decisions.
In Weiner’s definition, a shared psychological state combining change commitment and change efficacy among the members of an organization.
Members’ shared resolve to implement a change; strongest when they value it, weaker when they comply from obligation or lack of choice.
Members’ shared belief that they can carry out a change, based on their appraisal of task demands, resources and circumstances.
For a stable system over the long run, average work-in-process equals throughput multiplied by average time in the system (L = λW).
The number of items started but not yet finished in a system, such as open cases, contracts or patients.
The step in a process with the least capacity relative to demand; it sets the pace of the whole system.
The share of available time a resource is busy; with variability, waiting time rises steeply as utilization approaches 100 per cent.
A precise specification of how a task is done and what result it should produce, used as a hypothesis so that deviations become visible and can be investigated.
A measure of a behavior or condition believed to drive a later outcome, observable quickly enough to act on; its causal link should be tested.
A measure of the outcome an organization ultimately cares about, which arrives late and reflects many causes.
The degree of difference between two countries’ regulatory, cognitive and normative environments, which makes transferring organizational practices harder.
A practice carried out formally—forms filed, meetings held—while the people involved do not value it, so it produces little of its intended effect.
The distinction between the elements of an intervention believed to produce its benefit, which should be kept, and elements that can be tailored to each setting.

The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research: a structured set of constructs in five domains—intervention, outer setting, inner setting, individuals and process—for diagnosing implementation.
The error of inferring individual characteristics or relationships from group-level averages, such as assuming a person holds their country’s average values.

Roger Martin’s practitioner term for holding two opposing models in mind and constructing a new option that keeps the core of each and is better than either, instead of choosing one or splitting the difference.
APERTURE’s written procedure for testing a decision through behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law and ethics, with each lens answered independently before discussion.
A limit that actually restricts the choice you would otherwise make; relaxing it would improve the outcome, whereas relaxing a non-binding constraint changes nothing.
Procedures that reduce judgment error without needing to diagnose which bias is operating, such as independent estimates before discussion, structured criteria and an outside view.
Stinchcombe’s argument that new organizations fail at higher rates than old ones because roles must be learned, routines built, trust formed among strangers and ties established with those served.
A pattern in which failure risk is low at first, rises as an organization’s initial endowment of resources and goodwill runs out, and then declines.
The probability that something fails in a short period, given that it has survived until the start of that period; its shape over time shows when risk peaks.
The generalized belief among relevant people that a unit’s actions are appropriate and worth relying on; it can rest on authority, conformity to standards, results or relationships.
A modest, finished result that people outside a new unit value for its own sake — distinct from a publicity win, whose value lies mainly in its announcement.
Michael Watkins’s practitioner typology of leadership situations: start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment and sustaining success.
In Stephen Toulmin’s scheme of argument, the reasoning that connects the evidence (grounds) to a claim; the step skeptical questions most often target.
Gary Klein’s practitioner method in which a team imagines that a plan has already failed and each member independently writes the reasons before the plan is finalized.
The strongest version of an opposing position — one its most thoughtful advocate would endorse; the opposite of a straw man.
An answer to a different question from the one asked; Rogers and Norton (2011) found that fluent answers to similar questions often go unnoticed by listeners.
Rating the quality of a decision by how it turned out rather than by what was known and reasonable at the time it was made.

A structured discussion after an event that compares what was supposed to happen with what happened, explains the difference and assigns actions to sustain or change; formalized in U.S. Army practice.
A short list of questions a leader is trying to answer better over a defined period, each paired with the evidence that would show improvement.

manifest.method: Metadata verified through web-search results on the date shown per record. The build environment could not open pages, so every link is flagged link-untested until checked in a browser.
